contexts.text: A 30‑year‑old man presented with pain in his lower limbs and a non‑itchy erythematous rash over both lower limbs. He had low‑grade intermittent fever for three months. On examination he was pale and malnourished (BMI 18.4 kg/m2) and had palpable purpura over both thighs and buttocks. Abdominal examination revealed palpable hepatomegaly with massive splenomegaly. Laboratory testing showed pancytopenia (hemoglobin 6.8 g/dL, total leukocyte count 2800/mm3, platelet count 45 000/muL) and polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia (4.9 g/dL); liver and renal function tests were within reference ranges. Contrast‑enhanced CT of chest and abdomen confirmed hepatosplenomegaly and was otherwise unremarkable. The treating team considered hematologic malignancy and a connective‑tissue disorder with vasculitis. Other infectious etiologies entertained included HIV, scrub typhus/rickettsial infection, and visceral leishmaniasis (given the patient lived in an endemic area). Initial testing showed: anti‑nuclear antibodies, complement levels (C3 = 94 mg/dL and C4 = 20 mg/dL), and rheumatoid factor were negative; urine examination was normal and serum cryoglobulins were not raised. Viral markers (HIV, hepatitis B surface antigen, and anti‑hepatitis C) were negative. Serology for rickettsia and scrub typhus were also negative.

A 24-year-old man from a small rural village near the Pacific coast of Esmeraldas province, Ecuador, reports that at age 16 papules first appeared on his left knee and right cheek and gradually increased in size and number over years. For about 2 years he received various medications without a confirmed diagnosis; he was at one point treated clinically for leprosy with multidrug therapy (dapsone, rifampicin, clofazimine) for 1 month. On examination there are numerous cutaneous lesions: pea- to rice-grain–sized reddish papules on both ear lobes and auricles with palpable induration; miliary to pea-sized papules on the face; papules and nodules on the left shoulder; many miliary to hen-egg–sized papules, nodules, erythema, infiltrated erythema, and brownish freckles on the upper extremities, some with scaly or crusted surfaces; rice-grain to thumb-sized papules grouped on brownish freckle lesions of the lower back; satellite miliary papules around plaque-like lesions; thumb- to palm-sized erythema on the thigh; and various papules, nodules, infiltrated erythemas, and brownish freckles on the lower extremities. No loss of sensation was recognized anywhere on the body and there was no hypertrophy of peripheral nerves. The rK39 kit test gave a strong positive reaction. Stained slit-skin smears from lesions demonstrated numerous intracellular amastigotes identified as Leishmania on microscopy, and Ziehl–Neelsen stains showed no acid-fast bacilli.

A 38-year-old man presented with low-grade fever, weight loss, and anorexia for 6 weeks. On general examination he had mild pallor, splenomegaly, and mild hepatomegaly, with discrete enlarged lymph nodes at the right epitrochlear area and right cervical region. Routine biochemical tests were within normal limits except for mild elevation of liver enzymes (serum glutamic pyruvic transaminase 60 IU/L, serum glutamic oxaloacetic transaminase 53 IU/L) and lactic dehydrogenase 370 IU/L. Hemoglobin was 10.2 g/dL and erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 68 mm/h. Serologic screening was reactive for HIV‑1. Fine‑needle aspiration cytology of the lymph nodes was planned.

A 65-year-old woman was admitted in March after collapsing in the street. She had been unwell for 14 months with night sweats and progressive loss of energy but denied fever. On examination she was afebrile and had hepatic enlargement and lymphadenopathy; liver function tests were within reference limits. Initial blood tests showed hemoglobin 8.1 g/dL, leukocyte count 4.62 × 10^9/L, and platelet count 143 × 10^9/L. Serologic tests for HIV, hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and Strongyloides spp. were negative. Her CD4 count was 790 cells/μL, rheumatoid factor was weakly positive, and immunoglobulin levels were within reference ranges. She was born in Guyana and had recent travel to Guyana in 2012 and 2013, to Grenada in 2012, to Ghana in 2005, and to France in 2003. Because a hematologic malignancy was suspected, a bone marrow aspiration was performed; Leishmania amastigotes were visible. Leishmania serology was negative by an rK39 rapid test and weakly positive by direct agglutination (1:3,200; cutoff 1:1,600).

A 65-year-old man presented with diffuse abdominal pain for one year, 14 kg weight loss and fever for 4 months. The fever occurred once or twice daily with profuse sweating and shivers. He had no prior illnesses recorded and was a long‑time smoker. He was born in Paraiba, lived in Sao Paulo since age 9, and reported no recent travel outside the city; he denied contact with unpasteurized milk, domestic animals, rodents or farm animals. On examination he had swollen lymph nodes in several body regions; the largest measured 3 cm in the left inguinal region. Laboratory tests showed elevated C-reactive protein (99.9 mg/L), normocytic normochromic anemia (hemoglobin 11.1 g/dL; hematocrit 32.4%), sodium 130 mEq/L, leucocytes 5300/mm3 (neutrophils 3260/mm3; lymphocytes 910/mm3), gamma-glutamyl transferase 570 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 574 U/L, and beta-2 microglobulin 3.3 mcg/mL; all other routine blood tests, blood cultures, electrolytes, and kidney and liver functions were reported as normal. (L.) major-like antigen. Positron emission tomography showed increased glycolytic metabolism in several lymph nodes (some forming conglomerates) above and below the diaphragm, with increased glycolytic metabolism in the spleen, liver and bones, findings described as suggestive of a lymphoproliferative disorder. Bone marrow aspiration identified the presence of Leishmania spp. on direct microscopy.

A 13‑year‑old boy, born in São Paulo, who had traveled at age 12 to the state of Minas Gerais, presented with fever on alternate days, pallor, increased abdominal volume and unquantified weight loss. He had no prior history of recurrent infections. On admission he had anemia and thrombocytopenia. Bone marrow aspirate showed amastigotes of Leishmania. He was treated with liposomal amphotericin B (LAB) at a dose of 35 mg/kg and was discharged. Four months later he returned with fever and thrombocytopenia; a bone marrow aspirate again showed amastigotes of Leishmania and parasites were detected in bone marrow culture. He was treated with meglumine antimoniate and intravenous human immunoglobulin with clinical and laboratory improvement and was discharged in good health. Three weeks later he presented with seven days of fever, weakness, pallor and increased abdominal volume. On exam the spleen was palpable 23 cm below the left costal margin and the liver 5 cm from the right costal margin. Leishmania ELISA immunoassay and the rK‑39 antigen test were negative. Bone marrow biopsy showed a lymphocytic and histiocytic inflammatory reaction with a granulomatous pattern; no amastigotes were observed in the aspirate. He was re‑treated empirically for visceral leishmaniasis with liposomal amphotericin B. Notably, the patient had silvery hair and eyebrows, described as a phenotype suggestive of Griscelli Syndrome.

A 37-year-old man from Maranhão, Brazil, employed as a sugarcane cutter, and the son of a consanguineous marriage, presented with 5 months of daily fevers up to 39°C, progressive asthenia, about 10 kg weight loss, and increasing abdominal volume. He had a remote history: at age 21 he was diagnosed with rheumatoid arthritis and received NSAIDs and prednisone, with maintenance corticosteroid therapy (10 mg/day) for 7 years. He and his family reported no history of recurrent infections. On examination he had pallor of skin and mucous membranes, splenomegaly extending 21 cm below the left costal margin, and hepatomegaly 4 cm below the right costal margin. Laboratory testing demonstrated pancytopenia and hypoalbuminemia. Bone marrow aspirate showed relative hypocellularity of the granulocytes without visualization of amastigotes. Bone marrow biopsy showed a proportional increase in granulocytes. A liver biopsy was performed; immunohistochemistry was negative for Leishmania.

A 15-year-old female from the Macanao municipality on Margarita Island, Venezuela presented with a 6-month history of intermittent fever predominantly occurring at night, malaise, 6 kg weight loss, arthralgias, loss of appetite, dizziness, and amenorrhea. She lives in a rural area close to a landfill in a house built with cement ground, brick walls, and a metal roof without running water. She has one dog (unknown Leishmania infection status) and various turtles as pets. She has no history of traveling outside Venezuela. On examination she was pale, with increased respiratory and heart rate, and a fever of 39 C. Weight was 49 kg, height 1.57 m, and abdominal circumference 76 cm. She had cervical, axillary, and inguinal adenopathy. Cardiac and lung exams were normal. Abdominal exam revealed right upper-quadrant tenderness and hepatosplenomegaly (liver palpable 9.5 cm from the midclavicular line; spleen Hackett grade V). Laboratory values on admission demonstrated pancytopenia. Abdominal ultrasound and computed tomography confirmed hepatosplenomegaly. The initial clinical suspicion was a lymphoproliferative or myeloproliferative disorder. From an infectious disease perspective, the possibility of visceral leishmaniasis, a systemic mycosis, or tuberculosis were entertained. A bone marrow biopsy was performed to rule out a hematologic malignancy and to assess for infectious causes.

A 60-year-old woman from Uttar Pradesh, India presented with a six‑week history of high‑grade continuous fever with chills and rigors, anorexia, malaise, joint pains, and severe lethargy. She reported "crops of round, raised lesions" that began on the left upper limb, progressed to the right upper limb and then involved the whole face, upper back, chest, and upper abdomen; the lesions were "closely associated with the febrile episodes." Some lesions enlarged, became nodular, developed sunken centers that drained pus‑like material, and were painful and red. One week before admission she developed jaundice with mild to moderate upper‑quadrant abdominal pain. She also noted nonpainful bilateral leg swelling (pitting) and painful red eyes with nodular lesions on the eyelids and in the conjunctiva, associated with decreased vision. She had no prior comorbidities, was a teetotaler, and denied taking over‑the‑counter or steroid/complementary medications or other potentially immunosuppressive drugs. Pallor and icterus were present; there was bilateral pitting, non‑tender symmetrical pedal edema. Skin exam showed "multiple crops of nodular, noduloulcerative, and papular lesions, dispersed throughout the body surface, mostly segregated to the face and upper back," some with pus drainage from central sunken areas. Eye exam demonstrated nodular lesions over the eyes and conjunctiva with conjunctival suffusion. Fundoscopy showed uveitis and small retinal hemorrhages. Serum IgG 22.6 g/L.

Five months before admission she developed intermittent nocturnal fevers up to 39 °C that did not respond to antipyretics, with poor appetite, postprandial fullness, nausea and vomiting. Over the following months she noted progressive jaundice (yellow sclera and skin), dark urine, weight loss of ~10 kg, increasing abdominal girth and soft bilateral lower‑extremity edema to the knees. On admission her general state was poor with malnutrition; examination showed pallor 3–4/4, mild dehydration, jaundice 2/4, cyanosis, fever and tachycardia. Abdominal exam showed moderate ascites, hepatomegaly 7 cm below the right costal margin and splenomegaly palpable 2 cm below the umbilicus. Laboratory testing revealed severe pancytopenia, prolonged prothrombin time, marked elevation of aminotransferases, hypoalbuminemia and hypergammaglobulinemia with severe cholestatic jaundice. Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated free peritoneal fluid, hepatomegaly ≈20 cm, splenomegaly ≈25 cm and gallstones. The initial diagnostic hypotheses included disseminated tuberculosis and visceral leishmaniasis; other considered diagnoses were dengue, yellow fever, prolonged septicemic salmonellosis, brucellosis, malaria, Chagas disease and lymphoproliferative malignancies. Investigations ordered included thick and thin blood smears, blood cultures, stool tests, bone marrow biopsy and aspiration and serologies for dengue, yellow fever, brucellosis and Chagas disease. HIV testing was performed and was negative.

Additional labs: hypoalbuminemia 13 g/L, hypertriglyceridemia 4.57 g/L, hyperferritinemia 626 µg/L, LDH 337 IU/L, prothrombin time 56%, fibrinogen 1 g/L. Direct Coombs test was positive. A 15‑year‑old boy presented to the emergency fever clinic with fever and cough for more than 10 days. He developed fever after a cold, with temperatures initially 37–38°C, later peaking at 41°C. Symptoms included cough, fatigue, chills, and pharyngeal discomfort. Initial local-hospital testing showed WBC 3.3 × 10^9/L, Hb 85 g/L, and PLT 87 × 10^9/L. Bone marrow puncture at that time "indicated that hematopoietic tissue hyperplasia was active and the proportion of three-line blood cells was roughly normal. Lymphocytes accounted for 9.5%, and atypical lymphocytes were found occasionally." Adenovirus IgM was weakly positive; ferritin was >2,000 ng/mL; procalcitonin was 4.14 ng/mL. Abdominal ultrasound and CT indicated hepatomegaly and splenomegaly. He was referred for further care after lack of improvement with initial treatment. On arrival his vital signs were: T 37.1°C, pulse 110/min, RR 19/min, BP 110/72 mmHg. Admission labs showed WBC 4.68 × 10^9/L, Hb 100 g/L, RBC 3.65 × 10^12/L; ALT 204 IU/L; AST 176 IU/L; GGT 153 IU/L; LDH 889 IU/L; ferritin >2,000 ng/mL; PCT 2.11 ng/mL; CRP 53.5 mg/L; IL‑6 31.58 pg/mL. Chest CT was unremarkable. Abdominal ultrasound showed intercostal spleen thickness ≈6.6 cm, consistent with splenomegaly. Do not exclude the possibility of parasitic diseases? Hemophilic cell syndrome? Lymphoma? Autoimmune disease?" An mNGS test on blood was performed on the second day after admission because the cause of fever remained unclear.

He had developed fever after a cold >10 days before admission, with temperatures fluctuating between 37 and 38°C initially, later peaking to 41°C; associated symptoms included cough, fatigue, chills, and pharyngeal discomfort. A 22‑month‑old girl presented with 8 days of fever to 40°C and mild cough. Past history: failure to thrive; normal neurologic development. She was the first child of a non‑consanguineous couple; no family history of albinism; normal hair and skin. On exam she was stunted, pale, had non‑tender hepatomegaly 5–6 cm and splenomegaly palpable 4 cm below the left costal margin. Petechial rash developed on the chest and legs as she worsened. Initial laboratory results: WBC 5100/mm3 (ANC 1200/mm3), Hb 9.1 g/dl, platelets 47,000/mm3; mild transaminase elevation; hypoalbuminemia. Ferritin 1,134 ng/ml; soluble IL‑2 receptor (sCD25) 3,183 U/ml. Blood cultures were negative. Serum immunoglobulins and lymphocyte subsets were reported as normal. Leishmania testing was discordant: immunochromatography and indirect immunofluorescence were negative, serum ELISA was slightly positive, and leishmanial antigen in urine was negative. Bone‑marrow aspiration revealed hemophagocytosis. Over the next day she clinically worsened with progressive splenomegaly and cytopenias (WBC 4,800/mm3 with ANC 800/mm3, Hb 6.8 g/dl, platelets 27,000/mm3), triglycerides 686 mg/dl, ferritin 3,849 ng/ml, and sCD25 3,596 U/ml. Clotting tests were normal and perforin expression by flow cytometry was reported as normal.

contexts.text: A 30-year-old woman from an area endemic for tegumentary leishmaniasis presented with a single skin complaint. She reported a small papular lesion on her right leg that had developed over 7–10 days. At age 10 she had had an ulcer on the left thigh that healed spontaneously and left a well-defined atrophic scar. On examination there was a depressed papular lesion on the right leg measuring 8 × 7 mm; there was a 30 × 20 mm atrophic scar on the left thigh and no lymphadenopathy. Because early lesions of the locally prevalent Leishmania species may be papular and nonulcerated, a Leishmania skin test (LST) was performed on the left forearm. After 48 hours the intradermal reaction was strongly positive, with an induration measuring 38 × 32 mm. Eight days after the skin test the original papular lesion on the right leg had resolved, and a new round cutaneous ulcer with raised borders measuring 26 × 24 mm was present at the site of the LST. A culture of aspirated material from the forearm lesion was negative for Leishmania.

A 52-year-old woman presented with a single lesion on the tip of her nose that had existed for 14 months. It began as a papule and was slowly increasing in size, enlarging to a plaque. A smear of the lesion performed about 1 year earlier was positive, "showing leishmania bodies." All five members of her family had a history of proven leishmaniasis. Her past medical history was notable for renal failure diagnosed 11 years earlier; she "received a renal transplant 4 years after the diagnosis of renal failure." She also had hypertension and hyperlipidemia and was taking oral mycophenolate mofetil (2 g daily) and cyclosporine (100 mg daily). Skin examination showed skin type IV, "No actinic keratosis was present," and a 3x3 cm indurated ulcer with elevated borders was present on the tip of her nose. The therapeutic plan was intralesional glucantime injections (approximately 1 ml of 1.5 g vial per week). "After completing a therapeutic course of 20 sessions receiving intralesional glucantime injections, she was considered as glucantime therapy resistant."

A 59-year-old Caucasian woman with a medical history of diabetes, hypertension, congestive heart failure, chronic renal disease, and paraparesis secondary to HTLV-1 infection presented in June 2012 with a skin lesion on her face. She initially noted a papule in the left malar region that later ulcerated and increased in size. Fifteen days after the facial lesion appeared, she developed another lesion on the right knee.

A 24-year-old man from a small rural village near the Pacific coast of Esmeraldas province, Ecuador, reports that at age 16 papules first appeared on his left knee and right cheek and gradually increased in size and number over years. For about 2 years he received various medications without a confirmed diagnosis; he was at one point treated clinically for leprosy with multidrug therapy (dapsone, rifampicin, clofazimine) for 1 month. On examination there are numerous cutaneous lesions: pea- to rice-grain–sized reddish papules on both ear lobes and auricles with palpable induration; miliary to pea-sized papules on the face; papules and nodules on the left shoulder; many miliary to hen-egg–sized papules, nodules, erythema, infiltrated erythema, and brownish freckles on the upper extremities, some with scaly or crusted surfaces; rice-grain to thumb-sized papules grouped on brownish freckle lesions of the lower back; satellite miliary papules around plaque-like lesions; thumb- to palm-sized erythema on the thigh; and various papules, nodules, infiltrated erythemas, and brownish freckles on the lower extremities. No loss of sensation was recognized anywhere on the body and there was no hypertrophy of peripheral nerves. The rK39 kit test gave a strong positive reaction. Stained slit-skin smears from lesions demonstrated numerous intracellular amastigotes identified as Leishmania on microscopy, and Ziehl–Neelsen stains showed no acid-fast bacilli.

A 43-year-old man from Cumanda (Chimborazo province, Ecuador), a subtropical mountainous community at ~500 m above sea level, presented with multiple chronic skin lesions. History of present illness: The lesion began as an insect-bite–like papular lesion on the forearm. Lesions then appeared on the right ear and the nose. About 2 years later, lesions developed on a wide range of the lower extremities and subsequently became multiple and confluent on the abdomen, thorax, body side, and thigh. A superficial involvement of mucosae of the nose and upper lip was observed. Treatment history: At the time of examination the patient had already received injections of nine ampoules of trivalent antimonials (Repodral, 20 mg/kg/day) at a rural health center; after finishing several courses he received pentavalent antimonials (Glucantime, 10 mg/kg/day) for about 5 months. Early investigations performed from active lesions included smear specimens, skin biopsies, syringe aspirates for culture, and material on FTA cards. Montenegro skin test showed a 17-mm induration, and an rK39 kit test revealed a strongly positive band. The smear specimen was positive for Leishmania amastigotes in scanty numbers. Promastigotes grown in vitro showed a tendency to decrease gradually and then disappear, an effect attributed by the investigators to prior antimonial treatment.

A 15-year-old female from the Macanao municipality on Margarita Island, Venezuela presented with a 6-month history of intermittent fever predominantly occurring at night, malaise, 6 kg weight loss, arthralgias, loss of appetite, dizziness, and amenorrhea. She lives in a rural area close to a landfill in a house built with cement ground, brick walls, and a metal roof without running water. She has one dog (unknown Leishmania infection status) and various turtles as pets. She has no history of traveling outside Venezuela. On examination she was pale, with increased respiratory and heart rate, and a fever of 39 C. Weight was 49 kg, height 1.57 m, and abdominal circumference 76 cm. She had cervical, axillary, and inguinal adenopathy. Cardiac and lung exams were normal. Abdominal exam revealed right upper-quadrant tenderness and hepatosplenomegaly (liver palpable 9.5 cm from the midclavicular line; spleen Hackett grade V). Laboratory values on admission demonstrated pancytopenia. Abdominal ultrasound and computed tomography confirmed hepatosplenomegaly. The initial clinical suspicion was a lymphoproliferative or myeloproliferative disorder. From an infectious disease perspective, the possibility of visceral leishmaniasis, a systemic mycosis, or tuberculosis were entertained. A bone marrow biopsy was performed to rule out a hematologic malignancy and to assess for infectious causes.

A 39-year-old woman with known HIV infection for 1 year was admitted with a 6-month history of skin lesions that were initially present on her face and later extended to the chest, abdomen, and extremities. On examination she had papules and nodules of varying size across these areas. Laboratory data showed leukopenia with a WBC of 1700 cells/mm3 and a CD4 cell count of 280 cells/mm3.

A 78-year-old man from a rural area in western Iran was referred for multiple ulcerative, exudative lesions involving the mid-face (upper lip and anterior nasal fossa), above the eyebrows, dorsal aspects of both hands, and posterior aspects of both heels. Lesions began three years earlier as papules on the dorsal hands and progressively enlarged to involve the face and heels and became ulcerative; involvement of the right hand progressed to destruction of tendons and soft tissue of the fifth finger, resulting in amputation of that finger. He had no history of comorbid conditions, no regular medications reported, and denied systemic symptoms — there was no weight loss, fever, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly or other signs of systemic involvement on examination or routine laboratory survey. Multiple prior empirical treatments for different presumed diagnoses, including pyoderma gangrenosum, sarcoidosis, and leishmaniasis, had been tried without improvement. An initial skin biopsy showed a necrotizing and palisading granulomatous tissue pattern that suggested an infectious etiology, but initial smears of lesion material for fungal elements, mycobacteria and Leishmania were negative. A tuberculin skin test produced a 27 mm induration, and anti-tuberculosis therapy (isoniazid, rifampin, ethambutol, and pyrazinamide) was started.

A 52-year-old male farm worker from Ceara state, northeast Brazil, presented with a 4-month history of skin lesions. Lesions appeared first on the face and legs, than spread across much of his body, including the genitalia, soles of feet, and scalp. He reported daily fevers for the first 2 weeks of illness. On examination the patient had 178 lesions of different sizes and aspects; ulcerated, crusted, papular, nodular, and pustular. Many had apparent bacterial superinfections. The remainder of the physical examination was normal. A complete blood count and liver and kidney function tests were within normal limits. Serological tests for syphilis and human immunodeficiency virus were negative.

A 13‑year‑old boy, born in São Paulo, who had traveled at age 12 to the state of Minas Gerais, presented with fever on alternate days, pallor, increased abdominal volume and unquantified weight loss. He had no prior history of recurrent infections. On admission he had anemia and thrombocytopenia. Bone marrow aspirate showed amastigotes of Leishmania. He was treated with liposomal amphotericin B (LAB) at a dose of 35 mg/kg and was discharged. Four months later he returned with fever and thrombocytopenia; a bone marrow aspirate again showed amastigotes of Leishmania and parasites were detected in bone marrow culture. He was treated with meglumine antimoniate and intravenous human immunoglobulin with clinical and laboratory improvement and was discharged in good health. Three weeks later he presented with seven days of fever, weakness, pallor and increased abdominal volume. On exam the spleen was palpable 23 cm below the left costal margin and the liver 5 cm from the right costal margin. Leishmania ELISA immunoassay and the rK‑39 antigen test were negative. Bone marrow biopsy showed a lymphocytic and histiocytic inflammatory reaction with a granulomatous pattern; no amastigotes were observed in the aspirate. He was re‑treated empirically for visceral leishmaniasis with liposomal amphotericin B. Notably, the patient had silvery hair and eyebrows, described as a phenotype suggestive of Griscelli Syndrome.

contexts.text: A 74-year-old woman from Tunis presented with several weeks of fever (oral temperature 38–39°C), sweats, chills, fatigue, diarrhea, intermittent vague abdominal pain, and occasional dry cough. Her only medical history was well-controlled hypertension. Examination showed a palpable spleen just below the left costal margin. On the right arm near the axilla there was "a single well-defined, ulcer surrounded by erythematous edging, with serous oozing" about 3 × 3 cm; the patient reported the lesion was painless, nonhealing, and present for 2–3 years. A Leishmania rk39 immunochromatography test was positive. Bone marrow aspiration parasitology revealed Leishmania amastigote forms, and serum immunofluorescence for Leishmania antibodies was positive (titer 1:400). Blood qPCR detected Leishmania DNA (400 parasites/mL). Direct microscopy of skin smears from the arm lesion showed no amastigotes, but Leishmania DNA amplification was obtained from dermal DNA extract by qPCR. ITS1 sequencing showed the Leishmania strains from the blood and the arm lesion corresponded to L. infantum and were 100% identical. Systemic response was rapid: fever resolved, general condition improved, splenomegaly regressed, blood counts normalized, and blood qPCR became negative after 28 days. However, "the skin lesion did not improve although Leishmania qPCR on dermal sample became negative." A skin biopsy was initially refused. One year later the lesion remained essentially unchanged.

A 38‑year‑old man from Yayu district, western Ethiopia, presented to the outpatient clinic with multiple skin lesions on his face and hands and mutilation of the nose; his upper lip was injured and swollen. Eight years earlier he had a small papule on the right cheek that progressed to an open ulcer, then to ulcers on the left cheek and forehead; those active lesions lasted about six months and healed spontaneously, leaving permanent hypopigmented scars. He had no fever, hepatosplenomegaly or lymphedema and reported no history of HIV, chronic disease, alcohol abuse, or immunomodulatory drug use. Parasitological testing of lesion smears at that time showed many macrophages filled with amastigote stages of Leishmania, graded as +6. A nonreactive rK39 rapid diagnostic test and absence of related systemic signs made visceral leishmaniasis unlikely. Based on the clinical manifestations and smear result he was diagnosed with mucocutaneous leishmaniasis and treated with intramuscular sodium stibogluconate (20 mg/kg/day for 30 days) with clinical cure. Two years later he returned with a different cutaneous eruption that had appeared over the previous three months and had been preceded by intense itching. On exam he had multiple, nonpitting, closed papules on his face, nose, hands and legs. A skin smear again showed intramacrophage amastigotes with a parasite load graded +6, and culture grew promastigotes.

A 35-year-old man from Russia presented to dermatology with two ulcerative skin lesions described as semi-dry with active borders: one in the lower left pre-atrial region and the other on the dorsal region of the left forearm. He reported travel to multiple countries between May and June 2019, including Middle Eastern countries (Israel, Turkey), the Balkan region (Armenia, Georgia), and Russia. In August 2019 he noted red, indurated papules and sought care in late August in San Cristobal de las Casas, Chiapas, Mexico. Cryotherapy with liquid nitrogen was applied initially with temporary reduction, followed by renewed flare-up of the lesion edges. At the Tropical Medicine Center he was clinically diagnosed as having localized cutaneous leishmaniasis (LCL). For confirmation, Giemsa-stained smears of the lesion and ELISA tests for L. braziliensis, L. infantum/chagasi, L. major and L. mexicana were performed. The Giemsa-stained smears showed abundant amastigotes within macrophages. The ELISA of the patient's serum revealed some degree of cross reactivity between four Leishmania species, with higher antibody levels recorded for L. major and L. mexicana antigens.

A 24-year-old Cuban immigrant presented with worsening nonhealing lower-extremity ulcers despite oral antibiotic therapy and wound care. The lesions gradually grew with subsequent ulceration over the course of 1 to 2 months. He recently arrived in the United States seeking asylum and first noticed the lesions while traveling in the jungle between Panama and Colombia (Darien Gap region). On examination, there was an ulcerative lesion measuring 4 cm on the dorsum of the right foot and a second 3.5 cm ulcer on the lower anterior shin. There was no evidence of mucosal or visceral involvement on initial physical exam. Photographs show ulcerative lesions on the right foot and left shin. As part of the clinical workup to rule out malaria, a rapid malaria antigen test for Plasmodium falciparum was obtained and reported positive.

A 45-year-old Iranian man presented to dermatology in March 2008 with two large tumoral skin lesions. History of present illness and past history:
- Several years of chronic renal failure secondary to non–insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus (NIDDM). - In April 2006, after travel to an endemic area (Natanz in Isfahan province, Iran), he developed small papular lesions (reported as 2 x 5 millimeter) on the left wrist and the right shin. Those small lesions were left untreated. - Due to chronic renal failure, he underwent renal transplantation in August 2007. - After transplantation he was started on immunosuppression with prednisolone 50 mg/day and cyclosporine 7.5 mg/kg daily (reported as equivalent to 600 mg for an 80 kg patient). - Several weeks after transplantation and initiation of immunosuppressive therapy, the previously small papular lesions enlarged markedly into cauliflower-like, tumoral lesions. Physical examination:
- Two exophytic, cauliflower-like tumoral lesions: one on the left wrist measuring approximately 3 x 4 x 5 cm and one on the right shin measuring approximately 4 x 5 x 6 cm. No vital signs, routine laboratory values, or tissue diagnostic results are provided here.

A 60‑year‑old Austrian man presented in September 2016 with a three‑week history of fever of unknown origin, fatigue, and unintentional weight loss of 6 kg. Initial physical examination was inconspicuous. His medical history was notable for adequately treated diabetes mellitus type 2 and hypothyroidism. Travel history included a two‑week trip to the south of Crete in September 2015 and a two‑week trip the south of Spain in May 2016. Laboratory tests showed markedly elevated C‑reactive protein (CRP 94.2–188.9 mg/L), slight hypochromic normocytic anemia without signs of hemolysis (hemoglobin 12.5 g/dL), mild thrombocytopenia (127,000/µL), and a discreetly elevated gamma‑glutamyltransferase (GGT). The soluble interleukin‑2 receptor (IL‑2R) was elevated to 5156.1 pg/mL. Chest x‑ray, urine analysis, abdominal sonography, transthoracic and transesophageal echocardiography revealed no focus of infection but did show splenomegaly (7.2 × 16.4 cm). Empiric antibiotic therapy (initially ampicillin/sulbactam, later piperacillin/tazobactam plus vancomycin) did not lead to improvement. Over the next three weeks the patient’s discrete bicytopenia progressed to severe pancytopenia requiring blood transfusions. Lactate dehydrogenase rose to 1107 U/L, liver enzymes including GGT, alkaline phosphatase and AST increased, and fever persisted up to 40°C. Positron emission tomography–computed tomography showed tracer enhancement in the central and peripheral bone marrow.

A 47-year-old man, a traveling companion of another migrant, presented with multiple chronic skin lesions after migration through Central America. He had a total of 10 lesions on bilateral upper and lower extremities and the flank; all lesions were larger than 1 cm and the largest measured 5 cm. The patients likely acquired their illness in the Darien Gap region of Panama during their migratory path to the United States. Tissue samples were sent to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention for diagnostic confirmation. As part of the clinical workup to rule out malaria, a rapid malaria antigen test for P. falciparum (BinaxNOW) was obtained and reported positive in both patients.

A 60-year-old woman from Uttar Pradesh, India presented with a six‑week history of high‑grade continuous fever with chills and rigors, anorexia, malaise, joint pains, and severe lethargy. She reported "crops of round, raised lesions" that began on the left upper limb, progressed to the right upper limb and then involved the whole face, upper back, chest, and upper abdomen; the lesions were "closely associated with the febrile episodes." Some lesions enlarged, became nodular, developed sunken centers that drained pus‑like material, and were painful and red. One week before admission she developed jaundice with mild to moderate upper‑quadrant abdominal pain. She also noted nonpainful bilateral leg swelling (pitting) and painful red eyes with nodular lesions on the eyelids and in the conjunctiva, associated with decreased vision. She had no prior comorbidities, was a teetotaler, and denied taking over‑the‑counter or steroid/complementary medications or other potentially immunosuppressive drugs. On examination her temperature was 100.8°F, blood pressure 128/88 mm Hg, heart rate 100/min. Pallor and icterus were present; there was bilateral pitting, non‑tender symmetrical pedal edema. Skin exam showed "multiple crops of nodular, noduloulcerative, and papular lesions, dispersed throughout the body surface, mostly segregated to the face and upper back," some with pus drainage from central sunken areas. Fundoscopy showed uveitis and small retinal hemorrhages. Serum IgG 22.6 g/L.

A 40‑year‑old woman from Balao Chico (Guayas province, Ecuador) presented in August 1979 with a progressive widespread skin eruption. The illness began with a lesion on the lumbar region; papular lesions developed and became pustulous vesicles at the right lumbar region and then disseminated over the body, with 308 generalized lesions counted. She reported marked right lumbar pain; some body‑surface lesions were thought clinically to resemble herpes zoster. She was admitted to a private hospital for 16 days and then transferred to a national hospital in Guayaquil, where she was admitted under a suspected diagnosis of smallpox without a precise diagnosis. Examination of the ulcers showed most lesions to be crusty; when crusts were lifted they were excavated with purulent fluid from severe secondary infections. Ulcer sizes ranged from 0.5 to 20 mm in diameter; some lesions had thick, adherent crusts that bled when separated, others were small crusty ulcers with excavations, and confluent erythematous papular plaques were present on the lumbar–dorsal region. Laboratory tests on ulcer material did not demonstrate Paracoccidioides braziliensis or Staphylococcus aureus. Routine laboratory examinations revealed positivity for beta‑hemolytic streptococcus (antibiotic‑sensitive), and stool examination was positive for Trichuris trichiura, Ascaris lumbricoides, and Ancylostoma duodenale. Several smear samples from diverse regions of the body surface were taken at random.

A 59‑year‑old man, mixed ethnicity, unemployed, previously healthy, reported that an erythematous‑crusty lesion appeared in the region of the mental protuberance and over two months evolved to involve other parts of the body, including the frontal and occipital regions, nasal septum, ears, hands, and lower limbs. Oral examination showed scattered ulcers on the face, lower labial mucosa, and on the left lip commissure, a pseudomembrane on the marginal gingiva, and an exophytic nodule in the left labial mucosa. The patient had a positive Montenegro intradermal test and was admitted to the University Hospital in December 2018. After admission, clinicians noted enlarged lymph nodes of hard consistency in the left inguinal region and an extensive irregular melanocytic lesion in the left plantar region presenting an area of hyperkeratosis with a grey‑bluish center; the plantar lesion was biopsied for further evaluation. A PCR analysis had been performed in an external laboratory.

A 78-year-old man from a rural area in western Iran was referred for multiple ulcerative, exudative lesions involving the mid-face (upper lip and anterior nasal fossa), above the eyebrows, dorsal aspects of both hands, and posterior aspects of both heels. He had no history of comorbid conditions, no regular medications reported, and denied systemic symptoms — there was no weight loss, fever, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly or other signs of systemic involvement on examination or routine laboratory survey. Multiple prior empirical treatments for different presumed diagnoses, including pyoderma gangrenosum, sarcoidosis, and leishmaniasis, had been tried without improvement. An initial skin biopsy showed a necrotizing and palisading granulomatous tissue pattern that suggested an infectious etiology, but initial smears of lesion material for fungal elements, mycobacteria and Leishmania were negative. A tuberculin skin test produced a 27 mm induration, and anti-tuberculosis therapy (isoniazid, rifampin, ethambutol, and pyrazinamide) was started.

A 9-year-old boy presented with multiple papular lesions on the left cheek that had been present for three months and had gradually enlarged. His medical history was notable for an episode of cutaneous leishmaniasis located on the nose two years earlier, which had completely regressed after treatment with intralesional meglumine antimonate. Dermatologic examination showed multiple, coalescing, rough, slightly elevated, yellowish-brown papular lesions 3–6 mm in diameter on the left cheek. He also had a large atrophic scar on the nose. Nothing of interest was noted in his family history or his laboratory tests.

A 27-year-old man from central Iran noted a small pimple on his right upper eyelid 4 months before presentation. The eyelid lesion enlarged slowly. On examination it was a well-defined, firm, nontender, subcutaneous, skin-colored nodule measuring about 1 cm × 1 cm, with slightly erythematous, raised borders; it was crusty and painless. CBC, ESR, CRP, and blood chemistries were within normal limits. A sample culture of the lesion grew Staphylococcus aureus. The lesion was treated sequentially with cephalexin, cloxacillin, amoxicillin–clavulanate, and steroids for 10 days, but these treatments failed to heal the lesion. Because cutaneous leishmaniasis occurs in the patient's area of residence and because of the lack of response to treatment, cutaneous leishmaniasis or basal cell carcinoma was proposed as the differential diagnosis.

A 75-year-old man was referred with lesions on the hands, legs, face, and the upper lid of the right eye. He is a farmer from Aran va Bidgol city, Isfahan province (central Iran). He reported that sandflies had bitten him when he went to the farm for irrigation on nights during the sandfly season. He described the appearance of 25 multiple nodular, ulcerative, and crusted lesions on his body. On examination the lesions varied in size from a few millimeters to several centimeters; there were eight lesions on the face, including one on the upper right eyelid. He had no particular medical history, no fever, the lesions were painless, and his general condition was good.

A 61-year-old immunocompetent Italian man, born and residing in Abruzzo, presented because of the persistence of multiple ulcerative nodules on the skin of his right cheek; the largest nodule measured 2 cm in maximum diameter and was partially covered by scaly scabs. A complete blood picture was normal. The patient reported no travel history and had received several topical treatments (antibiotics, antimycotics, steroids), which had failed. After cleaning off the excess blood, cytology smears were performed by sampling cells from the ulcer with a sterile lancet and by smearing the sample directly onto glass slides.

A 24-year-old Cuban immigrant presented with worsening nonhealing lower-extremity ulcers despite oral antibiotic therapy and wound care. The lesions gradually grew with subsequent ulceration over the course of 1 to 2 months. He recently arrived in the United States seeking asylum and first noticed the lesions while traveling in the jungle between Panama and Colombia (Darien Gap region). On examination, there was an ulcerative lesion measuring 4 cm on the dorsum of the right foot and a second 3.5 cm ulcer on the lower anterior shin. There was no evidence of mucosal or visceral involvement on initial physical exam. Photographs show ulcerative lesions on the right foot and left shin. As part of the clinical workup to rule out malaria, a rapid malaria antigen test for Plasmodium falciparum was obtained and reported positive.

A 52-year-old male farm worker from Ceara state, northeast Brazil, presented with a 4-month history of skin lesions. Lesions appeared first on the face and legs, than spread across much of his body, including the genitalia, soles of feet, and scalp. He reported daily fevers for the first 2 weeks of illness. On examination the patient had 178 lesions of different sizes and aspects; ulcerated, crusted, papular, nodular, and pustular. Many had apparent bacterial superinfections. The remainder of the physical examination was normal. A complete blood count and liver and kidney function tests were within normal limits. Serological tests for syphilis and human immunodeficiency virus were negative.

A 36-year-old man presented with painless nodules on his left foot for a two-month duration. He had received a three-week course of systemic (ampicillin-cloxacillin) antibiotics without improvement. His medical and family history were unremarkable. Dermatologic examination showed a large ulcerative plaque on the dorsal aspect of the left foot surrounded by two satellite purple papules. There were also multiple grouped dusky erythematous nontender ulcerative nodules behind the lateral malleolus of the left leg. Histopathological examination of the margin of the ulcerative plaque showed ulceration of the epidermis and a diffuse dense mononuclear cellular infiltration of lymphocytes, histiocytes, and numerous plasma cells throughout the dermis with early granuloma formation. These changes involved the panniculus, causing septal and lobular panniculitis.

The ulcers were first observed by the parents at age one month and progressively increased in size; there was no history of fever. He was the third child of healthy unrelated Bedouin Saudi Arabian parents (mother 35 years, father 40 years). There was no history of perinatal or postnatal complication. The child was delivered in a tent in the desert where his parents live.

On physical examination there was severe disfigurement of the face with three crusty ulcers surrounded by a notable erythematous reaction: the largest on the right cheek measured 2 × 2 cm; a second on the right lower eyelid measured 1 × 1.5 cm; a third on the forehead measured 0.5 × 0.5 cm. Examination revealed no lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly. The ulcers were surrounded by extensive edema that often kept the eyes closed, obscuring some facial features. Noted findings that suggested an underlying chromosomal syndrome included hypotonia, flat occiput, short neck, low-set ears, short broad hands, clinodactyly of the fifth finger, bilateral simian creases of the hands, and a gap between the first and second toes, which prompted a request for karyotyping.

contexts.text: A 1-year-old boy was admitted with continuous fever for 3 months. On evaluation he had hepatosplenomegaly and anemia, and laboratory testing showed hypertriglyceridemia and increased ferritin; he experienced hemodynamic instability requiring blood transfusion. An immunochromatographic rapid test with rK39 antigen was positive for Leishmania, and the myelogram demonstrated Leishmania spp with hemophagocytosis. Treatment with meglumine antimoniate (glucantime) was started. As fever persisted, on day 8 nonresponse to glucantime was considered and therapy was changed to liposomal amphotericin. Due to fever and neutropenia, cefepime was also started.

A 7‑month‑old male infant presented with fever for 10 days. On examination he had hepatosplenomegaly, pallor, and anasarca. Laboratory evaluation showed bicytopenia and increased ferritin. An immunochromatographic rapid test with rK39 antigen was positive for Leishmania spp., and amastigotes were detected on myelogram.

A 13‑year‑old boy, born in São Paulo, who had traveled at age 12 to the state of Minas Gerais, presented with fever on alternate days, pallor, increased abdominal volume and unquantified weight loss. He had no prior history of recurrent infections. On admission he had anemia and thrombocytopenia. Bone marrow aspirate showed amastigotes of Leishmania. He was treated with liposomal amphotericin B (LAB) at a dose of 35 mg/kg and was discharged. Four months later he returned with fever and thrombocytopenia; a bone marrow aspirate again showed amastigotes of Leishmania and parasites were detected in bone marrow culture. He was treated with meglumine antimoniate and intravenous human immunoglobulin with clinical and laboratory improvement and was discharged in good health. Three weeks later he presented with seven days of fever, weakness, pallor and increased abdominal volume. On exam the spleen was palpable 23 cm below the left costal margin and the liver 5 cm from the right costal margin. Leishmania ELISA immunoassay and the rK‑39 antigen test were negative. Bone marrow biopsy showed a lymphocytic and histiocytic inflammatory reaction with a granulomatous pattern; no amastigotes were observed in the aspirate. He was re‑treated empirically for visceral leishmaniasis with liposomal amphotericin B. Notably, the patient had silvery hair and eyebrows, described as a phenotype suggestive of Griscelli Syndrome.

A 30‑year‑old man presented with pain in his lower limbs and a non‑itchy erythematous rash over both lower limbs. He had low‑grade intermittent fever for three months. On examination he was pale and malnourished (BMI 18.4 kg/m2) and had palpable purpura over both thighs and buttocks. Abdominal examination revealed palpable hepatomegaly with massive splenomegaly. Laboratory testing showed pancytopenia (hemoglobin 6.8 g/dL, total leukocyte count 2800/mm3, platelet count 45 000/muL) and polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia (4.9 g/dL); liver and renal function tests were within reference ranges. Contrast‑enhanced CT of chest and abdomen confirmed hepatosplenomegaly and was otherwise unremarkable. The treating team considered hematologic malignancy and a connective‑tissue disorder with vasculitis. Other infectious etiologies entertained included HIV, scrub typhus/rickettsial infection, and visceral leishmaniasis (given the patient lived in an endemic area). Initial testing showed: anti‑nuclear antibodies, complement levels (C3 = 94 mg/dL and C4 = 20 mg/dL), and rheumatoid factor were negative; urine examination was normal and serum cryoglobulins were not raised. Viral markers (HIV, hepatitis B surface antigen, and anti‑hepatitis C) were negative. Serology for rickettsia and scrub typhus were also negative.

A 65-year-old woman was admitted in March after collapsing in the street. She had been unwell for 14 months with night sweats and progressive loss of energy but denied fever. On examination she was afebrile and had hepatic enlargement and lymphadenopathy; liver function tests were within reference limits. Initial blood tests showed hemoglobin 8.1 g/dL, leukocyte count 4.62 × 10^9/L, and platelet count 143 × 10^9/L. Serologic tests for HIV, hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and Strongyloides spp. were negative. Her CD4 count was 790 cells/μL, rheumatoid factor was weakly positive, and immunoglobulin levels were within reference ranges. She was born in Guyana and had recent travel to Guyana in 2012 and 2013, to Grenada in 2012, to Ghana in 2005, and to France in 2003. Because a hematologic malignancy was suspected, a bone marrow aspiration was performed; Leishmania amastigotes were visible. Leishmania serology was negative by an rK39 rapid test and weakly positive by direct agglutination (1:3,200; cutoff 1:1,600).

A 74-year-old man from Yangquan City, Shanxi Province, presented with more than six months of generalized fatigue and pancytopenia. He had a history of COVID-19 infection in January 2023 and reported persistent weakness thereafter. He lost approximately 10 kg over six months. Prior intermittent evaluations included bone marrow aspirations that reportedly showed no special abnormalities. On admission he was afebrile; examination showed pallor and scattered hyperpigmented skin lesions from scratching. Liver was palpable 5 cm below the right costal margin; spleen was palpable 8 cm below the left costal margin. Abdominal ultrasound and CT reported hepatomegaly, cirrhotic-appearing liver, splenomegaly and ascites (spleen longitudinal diameter up to ~19–21 cm on serial imaging). Laboratory testing demonstrated persistent pancytopenia. Initial infectious-serology testing showed a positive HCV antibody; repeat hepatitis C antigen and antibody testing later returned negative. Tumor markers were negative. Hematology testing included a positive direct antiglobulin test; CD55 and CD59 testing were normal. Immunology testing showed elevated IgG and positive anti-cardiolipin antibody IgG and IgM. Multiple blood transfusions had little effect on the anemia. Repeat peripheral smear and bone marrow evaluation demonstrated some toxic granules in mature granulocytes but otherwise no diagnostic abnormalities and no parasites were seen.

A 42‑year‑old man presented with 1 year of progressive weakness and significant weight loss and intermittent low‑grade fevers. He had been treated for pulmonary tuberculosis 2 years earlier and was recently restarted on antitubercular therapy for the past month without improvement. On examination he was thin, pale, afebrile, and had abdominal distension. Left submandibular and left axillary lymph nodes were palpable, each about 1.5 cm. Mild hepatosplenomegaly was noted. Ultrasound of the abdomen showed multiple enlarged conglomerate mesenteric lymph nodes, the largest 22 × 18 mm. Clinical chemistry showed reversal of the albumin:globulin ratio with total protein 9.5 g/dL, albumin 2.0 g/dL, globulin 7.5 g/dL. Other liver and renal tests were within normal limits. Complete blood count showed pancytopenia: hemoglobin 6 g/dL, total leukocyte count 1,800/µL (polymorphs 47%, lymphocytes 51%), platelets 48,000/µL; ESR 50 mm/h. Peripheral smear demonstrated rouleaux formation. Fine needle aspiration cytology of left submandibular and axillary lymph nodes yielded thick aspirate; smears showed few epithelioid cell granulomas interspersed with discrete aggregates of histiocytes in a background of reactive lymphoid cells and many plasma cells.

A 15-year-old male student presented to the emergency fever clinic with "fever accompanied with cough for more than 10 days." He had developed fever after a cold >10 days before admission, with temperatures fluctuating between 37 and 38°C initially, later peaking to 41°C; associated symptoms included cough, fatigue, chills, and pharyngeal discomfort. A local hospital workup showed WBC 3.3 x 10^9/L, Hb 85 g/L, and PLT 87 x 10^9/L. Bone marrow puncture there showed "hematopoietic tissue hyperplasia was active and the proportion of three-line blood cells was roughly normal," with occasional atypical lymphocytes. Adenovirus IgM was weakly positive, ferritin was >2,000 ng/ml, and procalcitonin 4.14 ng/ml. Abdominal ultrasound and CT at the local hospital indicated hepatomegaly and splenomegaly. After transfer, his vital signs were: T 37.1°C, pulse 110/min, respirations 19/min, BP 110/72 mmHg. Admission tests included WBC 4.68 x 10^9/L, Hb 100 g/L, RBC 3.65 x 10^12/L; ALT 204 IU/L, AST 176 IU/L, GGT 153 IU/L, LDH 889 IU/L; ferritin >2,000 ng/ml; PCT 2.11 ng/ml; CRP 53.5 mg/L; IL-6 31.58 pg/ml. Abdominal ultrasound showed intercostal spleen thickness ~6.6 cm, compatible with splenomegaly. Empiric antibiotics (cefoperazone–sulbactam, then ceftriaxone) and dexamethasone were given without clear improvement. Lymphoma? Autoimmune disease?" Because the cause remained unclear, an mNGS test was performed on the second day after admission to the emergency department.

A 15‑year‑old boy presented to the emergency fever clinic with fever and cough for more than 10 days. He developed fever after a cold, with temperatures initially 37–38°C, later peaking at 41°C. Symptoms included cough, fatigue, chills, and pharyngeal discomfort. Initial local-hospital testing showed WBC 3.3 × 10^9/L, Hb 85 g/L, and PLT 87 × 10^9/L. Bone marrow puncture at that time "indicated that hematopoietic tissue hyperplasia was active and the proportion of three-line blood cells was roughly normal. Lymphocytes accounted for 9.5%, and atypical lymphocytes were found occasionally." Adenovirus IgM was weakly positive; ferritin was >2,000 ng/mL; procalcitonin was 4.14 ng/mL. Abdominal ultrasound and CT indicated hepatomegaly and splenomegaly. He was referred for further care after lack of improvement with initial treatment. On arrival his vital signs were: T 37.1°C, pulse 110/min, RR 19/min, BP 110/72 mmHg. Admission labs showed WBC 4.68 × 10^9/L, Hb 100 g/L, RBC 3.65 × 10^12/L; ALT 204 IU/L; AST 176 IU/L; GGT 153 IU/L; LDH 889 IU/L; ferritin >2,000 ng/mL; PCT 2.11 ng/mL; CRP 53.5 mg/L; IL‑6 31.58 pg/mL. TORCH/EBV panel: CMV, HSV, rubella virus, and EBV IgG positive. Direct Coombs' test was positive (++). Chest CT was unremarkable. Abdominal ultrasound showed intercostal spleen thickness ≈6.6 cm, consistent with splenomegaly. Lymphoma? Autoimmune disease?" An mNGS test on blood was performed on the second day after admission because the cause of fever remained unclear.

A male born June 26, 1986, was seen at a tropical diseases referral center. Between 2009 and 2011 he was hospitalized seven times with a consistent diagnosis of kala-azar. He received multiple recommended treatments during these hospitalizations, including pentavalent antimony (glucantime, 20 mg of Sb + 5 kg/d for 30 d in the first hospitalization), liposomal amphotericin B (for 14 d at 3 mg/kg/d in three subsequent hospitalizations), and pentamidine in the last hospitalization before surgery (4 mg/kg/d every other day, total 15 doses), with only transient symptomatic improvement followed by recurrence. He had a negative HIV serological test. During two hospitalizations he presented with anemia and was transfused twice with packed red blood cells. After all possibilities of medical treatment were exhausted and the patient maintained a pancytopenia profile on blood counts attributed to hypersplenism, splenectomy was recommended. In January 2012 he was hospitalized for the planned surgical procedure. His clinical examination revealed mucocutaneous pallor (2+/4+), fever (38.5 C), dehydration (2+/4+), a distended abdomen with mild pain on deep palpation, and splenomegaly 8 cm below the left costal margin. Laboratory testing showed anemia, leukopenia, hypergammaglobulinemia, and elevated ESR and CRP.

contexts.text: A 17-month-old boy was initially admitted in March 2022 for insidious onset of fever, ecchymosis of skin, anhelation, and pancytopenia. On admission, blood routine examination results were: white blood cell (WBC) 2.5 x 109/L, hemoglobin (Hb) 60 g/L, platelet (PLT) 45 x 109/L, and immature granulocytes found in peripheral blood smears. Bone marrow studies established a diagnosis of B‑cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (B‑ALL), and the patient received induction chemotherapy with achievement of complete remission. During consolidation therapy, the child was hospitalized again in October 2022 for a repeated fever of 13 days and coagulopathy after the second cycle of consolidation chemotherapy. Color Doppler ultrasonic examination showed swollen liver and spleen. The treating team considered chemotherapy-related bone marrow suppression, infection, and coagulation dysfunction, and started empiric antimicrobial therapy with vancomycin, imipenem, and voriconazole; fresh frozen plasma, fibrinogen, and prothrombin complex were given to improve coagulation. Seven days after therapy the patient remained febrile (38.4–39.4 C) and continued to have hepatosplenomegaly; CRP and PCT levels were 125.5 mg/L and 3.99 mg/L, respectively. No microorganisms were detected by blood culture. Metagenomic next‑generation sequencing (mNGS) was then performed on peripheral blood.

A 44‑year‑old man from Shanxi Province with a 5‑year history of antisynthetase antibody syndrome on cyclosporine A was admitted in January 2020 with fever to 38.6°C. He reported exertional breathlessness (after walking ~100 m) and increasing weakness; broad‑spectrum antimicrobials produced no improvement. By March 2020 he had persistent fever. Laboratory results then showed WBC 1.3 × 10^9/L, hemoglobin 96 g/L, platelets 113 × 10^9/L, fibrinogen 1.36 g/L, serum ferritin >1500 μg/L, NK‑cell activity 14.96%, and soluble CD25 12,947 pg/mL; ALT, AST, CK and CK‑MB were normal. The clinical picture met criteria for hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH), and treatment was started with methylprednisolone (10 mg/kg per day) and etoposide (100 mg/m^2). After 2 weeks the patient became afebrile and WBC rose to 10.8 × 10^9/L, hemoglobin was 95 g/L and platelets 55 × 10^9/L. In June 2020, during prednisone taper, he redeveloped high fever to 39.5°C, was unable to stand independently, and subsequently had pancytopenia with recurrence of high ferritin, low NK‑cell activity, markedly elevated sCD25, splenomegaly, and hemophagocytosis on bone marrow examination.

His medical history included chronic hepatitis B, legionellosis, chronic Q fever and cytomegalovirus infection. The most recent transplant had required treatment for acute rejection with anti‑thymoglobulin, plasma exchanges, rituximab and maintenance immunosuppression consisting of mycophenolate mofetil 1 g/day, tacrolimus 4.5 mg/day and prednisone 10 mg/day. Leishmania PCR in blood had been positive in 2004; initial treatment with liposomal amphotericin B (L‑AmB) produced clinical cure. However, relapse occurred in August 2009 following plasma exchanges and corticosteroid boluses for graft rejection, with fever, anemia (Hb 9.1 g/dL), leukopenia (leukocytes 1,600/mm3) and quantitative PCR showing 431 Leishmania/ml of blood. L‑AmB (induction total dose 40 mg/kg) reduced parasitemia to 6.9 Leishmania/ml. L‑AmB was reintroduced and maintenance infusions were adjusted (including weekly and twice‑weekly dosing) with parasitemia fluctuating (from 88 to 0.6 Leishmania/ml). A fourth recurrence in April–June 2011 again featured fever, leukopenia (leukocytes 1,200/mm3, CD4 186/mm3), anemia (Hb 9.1 g/dL) and parasitemia 40 Leishmania/ml. The patient later underwent transplant nephrectomy and returned to chronic dialysis. In February 2012 he had fever, splenomegaly, anemia (Hb 8.6 g/dL) and thrombocytopenia (platelets 50,000/mm3) with quantitative PCR showing 12,870 Leishmania/ml in blood and 60,440 Leishmania/ml in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid.

A 60‑year‑old Austrian man presented in September 2016 with a three‑week history of fever of unknown origin, fatigue, and unintentional weight loss of 6 kg. Initial physical examination was inconspicuous. His medical history was notable for adequately treated diabetes mellitus type 2 and hypothyroidism. Travel history included a two‑week trip to the south of Crete in September 2015 and a two‑week trip the south of Spain in May 2016. Laboratory tests showed markedly elevated C‑reactive protein (CRP 94.2–188.9 mg/L), slight hypochromic normocytic anemia without signs of hemolysis (hemoglobin 12.5 g/dL), mild thrombocytopenia (127,000/µL), and a discreetly elevated gamma‑glutamyltransferase (GGT). The soluble interleukin‑2 receptor (IL‑2R) was elevated to 5156.1 pg/mL. Chest x‑ray, urine analysis, abdominal sonography, transthoracic and transesophageal echocardiography revealed no focus of infection but did show splenomegaly (7.2 × 16.4 cm). Empiric antibiotic therapy (initially ampicillin/sulbactam, later piperacillin/tazobactam plus vancomycin) did not lead to improvement. Over the next three weeks the patient’s discrete bicytopenia progressed to severe pancytopenia requiring blood transfusions. Lactate dehydrogenase rose to 1107 U/L, liver enzymes including GGT, alkaline phosphatase and AST increased, and fever persisted up to 40°C. Positron emission tomography–computed tomography showed tracer enhancement in the central and peripheral bone marrow.

A 42‑year‑old man presented with 1 year of progressive weakness and significant weight loss and intermittent low‑grade fevers. He had been treated for pulmonary tuberculosis 2 years earlier and was recently restarted on antitubercular therapy for the past month without improvement. On examination he was thin, pale, afebrile, and had abdominal distension. Left submandibular and left axillary lymph nodes were palpable, each about 1.5 cm. Mild hepatosplenomegaly was noted. Ultrasound of the abdomen showed multiple enlarged conglomerate mesenteric lymph nodes, the largest 22 × 18 mm. Clinical chemistry showed reversal of the albumin:globulin ratio with total protein 9.5 g/dL, albumin 2.0 g/dL, globulin 7.5 g/dL. Other liver and renal tests were within normal limits. Complete blood count showed pancytopenia: hemoglobin 6 g/dL, total leukocyte count 1,800/µL (polymorphs 47%, lymphocytes 51%), platelets 48,000/µL; ESR 50 mm/h. Peripheral smear demonstrated rouleaux formation. Fine needle aspiration cytology of left submandibular and axillary lymph nodes yielded thick aspirate; smears showed few epithelioid cell granulomas interspersed with discrete aggregates of histiocytes in a background of reactive lymphoid cells and many plasma cells.

He had intermittent fever, nausea and vomiting for 5 months; prior local evaluation found pancytopenia and splenomegaly. Bone marrow imaging earlier showed dysplasia of megakaryocytes with visible plasma cells and markedly reduced proliferation. Five days before admission he developed fever to 39.5°C with chills, chest tightness and shortness of breath but without cough or sputum production. Piperacillin‑tazobactam was given without symptom relief. Bone marrow aspiration detected Leishmania amastigotes. Bone marrow hyperplasia was extremely reduced without an increase in immature cells or lymphocytes. Blood mNGS performed at the referring hospital detected 40904 Leishmania infantum, 17878 Leishmania donovani, and 13978 Leishmania chagasi sequence readings, and "combined with clinical symptoms, the diagnosis of 'visceral leishmaniasis' was made." On transfer, renal lab values were abnormal (serum glucose 16.31 mmol/L, urea 39.74 mmol/L, creatinine 286.2 mmol/L, uric acid 591 mmol/L), and because of renal dysfunction and concern about amphotericin B toxicity, sodium antimony gluconate was started. Chest X‑ray demonstrated bilateral pulmonary edema. After ventilatory support and diuretics the pulmonary edema improved on chest X‑ray and respiratory symptoms were relieved. On July 6, 2022, blood smear and bone marrow cytology revealed no Leishmania bodies. Nevertheless, pancytopenia and respiratory failure did not fully resolve and cardiotoxic damage appeared.

A 60-year-old European man with longstanding HIV infection (diagnosed 1985) presented with chronic systemic symptoms and progressive cytopenias. In April 1996 he developed drenching sweats and hepatosplenomegaly. In March 1997 a bone marrow specimen demonstrated intracellular organisms consistent with the causal agent, and infection was thought likely acquired during travel to Spain in 1992. Initial antimonial therapy produced clinical improvement and apparent clearance from bone marrow, but disease relapsed in July 1997 and remained a chronic relapsing problem over the next 15 years despite multiple courses and combinations of systemic therapies, including antimonials (sodium stibogluconate), paromomycin, liposomal amphotericin B (various dosing regimens), and, from 2005, intermittent courses of oral miltefosine. Organisms were visualized repeatedly in bone marrow (multiple dates between 2004–2011) and in biopsies from skin, lymph nodes and sigmoid colon. The patient developed progressive symptomatic splenomegaly with increasing transfusion requirements and pancytopenia. A Leishmania isolate cultured from a bone marrow aspirate in October 2007 was tested in January 2008 with reported in vitro resistance to antimonials but susceptibility to other agents. In view of the worsening clinical picture and increasing amastigote density in marrow despite available treatment, alternative therapeutic approaches were discussed with the patient and external experts.

A 55‑year‑old man presented with recurrent high fevers and acute febrile symptoms. On admission he had a body temperature of 39.6 C. One month before admission he had developed a fever of unknown origin, with a highest temperature of 41 C accompanied by shivering. Before transfer he received piperacillin/tazobactam without improvement. He reported a past history of pancreatitis and prior septicemia and denied relevant family history. On admission (January 25, 2021) laboratory testing showed reduced WBC, RBC, hemoglobin, and platelets. Abdominal color ultrasound demonstrated hepatosplenomegaly. Serum amylase and lipase were elevated. A positive result was noted for Epstein‑Barr virus (EBV); no other blood or respiratory pathogens were detected. Over the next 14 days the cytopenias persisted. On February 7, 2021, bone marrow aspiration showed active marrow hyperplasia and hemophagocytosis, but no pathogenic microorganism was identified on the smear.

A 57-year-old man underwent orthotopic liver transplantation in March 2019 for alcoholic-related liver disease and portal hypertension after 2 years of abstinence. He was born in Wales; his only travel outside the UK was a transient visit to Calais 15 years before transplantation. Postoperative care included a 2-day intensive-care admission. Immunosuppression was commenced with prednisolone, tacrolimus and mycophenolate (MMF); cotrimoxazole prophylaxis was given. Both donor and recipient were CMV IgG negative. One month after transplantation he had biopsy-proven moderate acute cellular rejection treated with 3 days of pulsed steroids. His graft function improved, with normalisation of alanine aminotransferase coinciding with the development of pancytopenia 4 months after transplantation. MMF dose was reduced from 1 g twice daily to 500 mg twice daily, but neutropenia worsened and pancytopenia persisted. He developed systemic symptoms of fever and rigours and was admitted to his local hospital with neutropenic sepsis and an acute kidney injury. He was transferred to the liver transplant centre for further investigation. He was treated empirically with meropenem, vancomycin and fluconazole. A bone marrow biopsy was performed in view of his pancytopenia.

A 55-year-old man with chronic severe hepatitis B (HBV‑DNA positive) was admitted for intermittent fever of 1 month (maximum 40°C). He had worked on a farm in Xinjiang Province one month earlier. On examination he had hepatosplenomegaly below the costal margin. Initial laboratory tests showed marked hepatic abnormalities (ALT 490 U/L, AST 558 U/L), low total protein and albumin (TP 51.54 g/L, ALB 26.83 g/L), TBIL 23.23 μmol/L, DBIL 14.37 μmol/L, and HBV‑DNA 3.19 × 10^4 IU/mL. Routine blood counts were abnormal (WBC 3.12 × 10^9/L, platelets 100 × 10^9/L). After 2 weeks the patient remained febrile with worsening labs (WBC 0.95 × 10^9/L, platelets 56 × 10^9/L, ALT 524 U/L, AST 640 U/L). Abdominal enhanced CT showed an enlarged spleen with multiple low‑density nodules that demonstrated sustained/delayed enhancement; angioma/hemangioma was suspected. 18F‑FDG PET/CT demonstrated a significant diffuse increase in FDG uptake in the enlarged spleen (SUVmax 6.6) and slightly diffuse bone‑marrow uptake. Bone‑marrow aspiration and biopsy were performed twice (2 months apart) and both showed phagocytosis of reticulum cells. Based on the clinical and imaging findings, splenic lymphoma was considered highly likely. The patient received chemotherapy for hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) and was discharged in remission, but was readmitted 2 months later with recurrent fever and pancytopenia; splenectomy was then undertaken to establish a diagnosis and reduce disease burden.

retrieval_query_text: A 50-year-old Caucasian man with no significant past medical history underwent allogeneic stem-cell transplantation for high‑risk B‑cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia in first complete remission. The graft was peripheral‑blood stem cells from an unrelated Portuguese donor matched at 9/10 (HLA‑A disparity). Myeloablative conditioning included busulfan, cyclophosphamide, and antilymphocytic serum. Graft‑versus‑host disease prophylaxis consisted of tacrolimus and methotrexate. There were no major complications during the neutropenic period. Two months after transplant he received corticosteroid therapy for upper‑digestive graft‑versus‑host disease. In the following months he developed mild, fluctuating cytopenias, most prominent as thrombocytopenia (platelet counts between 60 and 80 × 10^9/L). The only significant complaint was intermittent tiredness.
