contexts.text: A 52-year-old male farm worker from Ceara state, northeast Brazil, presented with a 4-month history of skin lesions. Lesions appeared first on the face and legs, than spread across much of his body, including the genitalia, soles of feet, and scalp. He reported daily fevers for the first 2 weeks of illness. On examination the patient had 178 lesions of different sizes and aspects; ulcerated, crusted, papular, nodular, and pustular. Many had apparent bacterial superinfections. The remainder of the physical examination was normal. A complete blood count and liver and kidney function tests were within normal limits. Serological tests for syphilis and human immunodeficiency virus were negative.

A 78-year-old man from a rural area in western Iran was referred for multiple ulcerative, exudative lesions involving the mid-face (upper lip and anterior nasal fossa), above the eyebrows, dorsal aspects of both hands, and posterior aspects of both heels. Lesions began three years earlier as papules on the dorsal hands and progressively enlarged to involve the face and heels and became ulcerative; involvement of the right hand progressed to destruction of tendons and soft tissue of the fifth finger, resulting in amputation of that finger. He had no history of comorbid conditions, no regular medications reported, and denied systemic symptoms — there was no weight loss, fever, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly or other signs of systemic involvement on examination or routine laboratory survey. Multiple prior empirical treatments for different presumed diagnoses, including pyoderma gangrenosum, sarcoidosis, and leishmaniasis, had been tried without improvement. An initial skin biopsy showed a necrotizing and palisading granulomatous tissue pattern that suggested an infectious etiology, but initial smears of lesion material for fungal elements, mycobacteria and Leishmania were negative. A tuberculin skin test produced a 27 mm induration, and anti-tuberculosis therapy (isoniazid, rifampin, ethambutol, and pyrazinamide) was started.

A 30-year-old Caucasian man, unemployed, HIV-negative and with no other concomitant infections, presented in 2014 with a papule on the inferior eyelid of the right eye. His past history included, in 2008, an isolated nodulation in the right leg that resolved after treatment. Over time new lesions progressively appeared on the chest, abdomen, back, feet, and in the oral cavity. Ulcerated oral lesions were present on the hard palate and on the left and right jugal mucosa. Disease progression was associated with fever, headache, and weight loss.

A 43-year-old male laborer with known HIV infection for 2 years (on antiretroviral therapy) and on anti-tubercular treatment for 9 months presented with a 7-month history of asymptomatic skin lesions all over his body. Lesions first appeared on the arm and progressively spread to involve the face, legs, and trunk. On examination there were multiple bilateral asymmetrical diffuse papulonodular, non‑itchy skin lesions measuring 2–25 mm on the face, trunk, and extremities. There were no signs of ulceration or scarring. There was no lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly. A photograph showed multiple papulonodular lesions of varying size over the elbow. Laboratory tests showed anemia (hemoglobin 9.1 g/dL); liver and renal function tests and lipid profile were within normal limits. Ultrasonography of the abdomen was normal. CD4 count was 50 cells/µL and HIV viral load was 1750 copies/mL. There was no history of travel to known endemic areas for leishmaniasis.

A 45-year-old Iranian man presented to dermatology in March 2008 with two large tumoral skin lesions. History of present illness and past history:
- Several years of chronic renal failure secondary to non–insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus (NIDDM). - In April 2006, after travel to an endemic area (Natanz in Isfahan province, Iran), he developed small papular lesions (reported as 2 x 5 millimeter) on the left wrist and the right shin. Those small lesions were left untreated. - Due to chronic renal failure, he underwent renal transplantation in August 2007. - After transplantation he was started on immunosuppression with prednisolone 50 mg/day and cyclosporine 7.5 mg/kg daily (reported as equivalent to 600 mg for an 80 kg patient). - Several weeks after transplantation and initiation of immunosuppressive therapy, the previously small papular lesions enlarged markedly into cauliflower-like, tumoral lesions. Physical examination:
- Two exophytic, cauliflower-like tumoral lesions: one on the left wrist measuring approximately 3 x 4 x 5 cm and one on the right shin measuring approximately 4 x 5 x 6 cm. No vital signs, routine laboratory values, or tissue diagnostic results are provided here.

A 38‑year‑old man from Yayu district, western Ethiopia, presented to the outpatient clinic with multiple skin lesions on his face and hands and mutilation of the nose; his upper lip was injured and swollen. Eight years earlier he had a small papule on the right cheek that progressed to an open ulcer, then to ulcers on the left cheek and forehead; those active lesions lasted about six months and healed spontaneously, leaving permanent hypopigmented scars. He had no fever, hepatosplenomegaly or lymphedema and reported no history of HIV, chronic disease, alcohol abuse, or immunomodulatory drug use. Parasitological testing of lesion smears at that time showed many macrophages filled with amastigote stages of Leishmania, graded as +6. A nonreactive rK39 rapid diagnostic test and absence of related systemic signs made visceral leishmaniasis unlikely. Based on the clinical manifestations and smear result he was diagnosed with mucocutaneous leishmaniasis and treated with intramuscular sodium stibogluconate (20 mg/kg/day for 30 days) with clinical cure. Two years later he returned with a different cutaneous eruption that had appeared over the previous three months and had been preceded by intense itching. On exam he had multiple, nonpitting, closed papules on his face, nose, hands and legs. A skin smear again showed intramacrophage amastigotes with a parasite load graded +6, and culture grew promastigotes.

A 32-year-old man from Djelfa, Algeria, with a history of contact eczema presented with a 6-week history of painless, non-healing skin lesions on the dorsal aspect of his right hand. He had applied topical corticosteroids and antiseptics without improvement and had received two courses of antibiotics (pristinamycin, amoxicillin + clavulanic acid) with no significant results. On examination there was a limited erythematous-papular plaque, approximately 8 cm in diameter, on the dorsal right hand formed by confluence of several papules with satellite lesions at the periphery. The initial plaque was associated with several firm, painless subcutaneous nodules 0.5–1.5 cm in diameter that tracked proximally along lymphatic drainage toward the elbow. The patient did not recall an insect bite, no other body sites were involved, and the remainder of the examination was unremarkable. Direct mycological examination and culture on Sabouraud medium at 25 °C and on BHI medium at 37 °C were negative for fungal presence.

A 35-year-old man from Russia presented to dermatology with two ulcerative skin lesions described as semi-dry with active borders: one in the lower left pre-atrial region and the other on the dorsal region of the left forearm. He reported travel to multiple countries between May and June 2019, including Middle Eastern countries (Israel, Turkey), the Balkan region (Armenia, Georgia), and Russia. In August 2019 he noted red, indurated papules and sought care in late August in San Cristobal de las Casas, Chiapas, Mexico. Cryotherapy with liquid nitrogen was applied initially with temporary reduction, followed by renewed flare-up of the lesion edges. At the Tropical Medicine Center he was clinically diagnosed as having localized cutaneous leishmaniasis (LCL). For confirmation, Giemsa-stained smears of the lesion and ELISA tests for L. braziliensis, L. infantum/chagasi, L. major and L. mexicana were performed. The Giemsa-stained smears showed abundant amastigotes within macrophages. The ELISA of the patient's serum revealed some degree of cross reactivity between four Leishmania species, with higher antibody levels recorded for L. major and L. mexicana antigens.

A 30‑year‑old man presented with pain in his lower limbs and a non‑itchy erythematous rash over both lower limbs. He had low‑grade intermittent fever for three months. On examination he was pale and malnourished (BMI 18.4 kg/m2) and had palpable purpura over both thighs and buttocks. Abdominal examination revealed palpable hepatomegaly with massive splenomegaly. Laboratory testing showed pancytopenia (hemoglobin 6.8 g/dL, total leukocyte count 2800/mm3, platelet count 45 000/muL) and polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia (4.9 g/dL); liver and renal function tests were within reference ranges. Contrast‑enhanced CT of chest and abdomen confirmed hepatosplenomegaly and was otherwise unremarkable. The treating team considered hematologic malignancy and a connective‑tissue disorder with vasculitis. Other infectious etiologies entertained included HIV, scrub typhus/rickettsial infection, and visceral leishmaniasis (given the patient lived in an endemic area). Initial testing showed: anti‑nuclear antibodies, complement levels (C3 = 94 mg/dL and C4 = 20 mg/dL), and rheumatoid factor were negative; urine examination was normal and serum cryoglobulins were not raised. Viral markers (HIV, hepatitis B surface antigen, and anti‑hepatitis C) were negative. Serology for rickettsia and scrub typhus were also negative.

A 30-year-old woman from an area endemic for tegumentary leishmaniasis presented with a single skin complaint. She reported a small papular lesion on her right leg that had developed over 7–10 days. At age 10 she had had an ulcer on the left thigh that healed spontaneously and left a well-defined atrophic scar. On examination there was a depressed papular lesion on the right leg measuring 8 × 7 mm; there was a 30 × 20 mm atrophic scar on the left thigh and no lymphadenopathy. Because early lesions of the locally prevalent Leishmania species may be papular and nonulcerated, a Leishmania skin test (LST) was performed on the left forearm. After 48 hours the intradermal reaction was strongly positive, with an induration measuring 38 × 32 mm. Eight days after the skin test the original papular lesion on the right leg had resolved, and a new round cutaneous ulcer with raised borders measuring 26 × 24 mm was present at the site of the LST. A culture of aspirated material from the forearm lesion was negative for Leishmania.

contexts.text: An 8‑year‑old Caucasian boy from Salvador, Bahia, Brazil, presented with a hyperemic, pruritic lesion of the upper lip that had persisted for six months. Initial outpatient therapy consisted of topical acyclovir 5% applied five times daily and oral cefadroxil (50 mg/kg/day) for seven days, without clinical improvement. The lesion subsequently worsened, and a Montenegro intradermal examination was performed.

A 65-year-old man from Brasilia presented with an erythematous plaque on his nose that began one month after fishing in the state of Amazonas, Brazil. HIV serology was negative. The Leishmania skin test (LST) and indirect immunofluorescence results were negative. The patient was treated with NMG (meglumine antimoniate) 20 mg SbV/kg/day for 20 days without improvement; treatment was continued with additional dosing that again did not result in improvement. After a month off therapy he resumed NMG combined with allopurinol (1,200 mg/day); NMG was stopped at one point because of intense myalgia, then resumed to a cumulative dose reported in the chart, yet clinical improvement was not achieved during these courses of therapy.

A 59‑year‑old man, mixed ethnicity, unemployed, previously healthy, reported that an erythematous‑crusty lesion appeared in the region of the mental protuberance and over two months evolved to involve other parts of the body, including the frontal and occipital regions, nasal septum, ears, hands, and lower limbs. Oral examination showed scattered ulcers on the face, lower labial mucosa, and on the left lip commissure, a pseudomembrane on the marginal gingiva, and an exophytic nodule in the left labial mucosa. The patient had a positive Montenegro intradermal test and was admitted to the University Hospital in December 2018. After admission, clinicians noted enlarged lymph nodes of hard consistency in the left inguinal region and an extensive irregular melanocytic lesion in the left plantar region presenting an area of hyperkeratosis with a grey‑bluish center; the plantar lesion was biopsied for further evaluation. A PCR analysis had been performed in an external laboratory.

A 45-year-old man from Apucarana, Paraná, presented with one atypical lesion on the right side of his back of approximately one month’s duration. He had applied topical antibiotics before seeking care without improvement. On examination the lesion was a rounded plaque with an erythematous-violaceous center, desquamative ulcerated edges, and an extensive surrounding area of lichenification, measuring 20 cm, located on the right scapular/back region. Based on the clinical appearance, the initial differential diagnosis included chronic simple lichen, psoriasis, squamous cell carcinoma, chromomycosis, cutaneous tuberculosis, syphilis, paracoccidioidomycosis, and sarcoidosis.

A 55-year-old man from the Manaus region with no comorbidities had been treated for cutaneous leishmaniasis. He had completed treatment with a pentavalent antimonial drug 40 days earlier and had received a second outpatient 30-day cycle; ten days after the end of that treatment his leishmaniasis lesion was healed. He then developed grouped microvesicles on an erythematous-infiltrated base that began in the neck and ascended toward the right scalp margin. The vesicles involved the right pinna, external auditory canal, and right ear lobe and were associated with severe torticollis-like pain along the nerve distribution. HIV serology was negative.

A 29-year-old man from Cutris de San Carlos (Alajuela province), in northern Costa Rica, presented with a single skin lesion on the right side of the neck. The lesion was a 5-cm, 3-month–old, deep ulcer with pruritic and sanguine-purulent tissue. A visibly swollen lymph node was present below the right ear, just above the ulcer. No other symptoms were reported. At the Area de Salud de Santa Rosa de Pocosol the diagnosis was confirmed locally through light microscopy of a direct smear, and the stained slide, along with culture media seeded with lesion aspirate, were sent to the national reference laboratory (Inciensa) for confirmation and species characterization.

A 13‑year‑old boy, born in São Paulo, who had traveled at age 12 to the state of Minas Gerais, presented with fever on alternate days, pallor, increased abdominal volume and unquantified weight loss. He had no prior history of recurrent infections. On admission he had anemia and thrombocytopenia. Bone marrow aspirate showed amastigotes of Leishmania. He was treated with liposomal amphotericin B (LAB) at a dose of 35 mg/kg and was discharged. Four months later he returned with fever and thrombocytopenia; a bone marrow aspirate again showed amastigotes of Leishmania and parasites were detected in bone marrow culture. He was treated with meglumine antimoniate and intravenous human immunoglobulin with clinical and laboratory improvement and was discharged in good health. Three weeks later he presented with seven days of fever, weakness, pallor and increased abdominal volume. On exam the spleen was palpable 23 cm below the left costal margin and the liver 5 cm from the right costal margin. Leishmania ELISA immunoassay and the rK‑39 antigen test were negative. Bone marrow biopsy showed a lymphocytic and histiocytic inflammatory reaction with a granulomatous pattern; no amastigotes were observed in the aspirate. He was re‑treated empirically for visceral leishmaniasis with liposomal amphotericin B. Notably, the patient had silvery hair and eyebrows, described as a phenotype suggestive of Griscelli Syndrome.

A 40‑year‑old woman from Balao Chico (Guayas province, Ecuador) presented in August 1979 with a progressive widespread skin eruption. The illness began with a lesion on the lumbar region; papular lesions developed and became pustulous vesicles at the right lumbar region and then disseminated over the body, with 308 generalized lesions counted. She reported marked right lumbar pain; some body‑surface lesions were thought clinically to resemble herpes zoster. The presumptive clinical diagnoses listed were paracoccidioidomycosis, cutaneous leishmaniasis, or staphylococcal infections. Examination of the ulcers showed most lesions to be crusty; when crusts were lifted they were excavated with purulent fluid from severe secondary infections. Ulcer sizes ranged from 0.5 to 20 mm in diameter; some lesions had thick, adherent crusts that bled when separated, others were small crusty ulcers with excavations, and confluent erythematous papular plaques were present on the lumbar–dorsal region. Laboratory tests on ulcer material did not demonstrate Paracoccidioides braziliensis or Staphylococcus aureus. Routine laboratory examinations revealed positivity for beta‑hemolytic streptococcus (antibiotic‑sensitive), and stool examination was positive for Trichuris trichiura, Ascaris lumbricoides, and Ancylostoma duodenale. Several smear samples from diverse regions of the body surface were taken at random.

contexts.text: A 78-year-old man from a rural area in western Iran was referred for multiple ulcerative, exudative lesions involving the mid-face (upper lip and anterior nasal fossa), above the eyebrows, dorsal aspects of both hands, and posterior aspects of both heels. Lesions began three years earlier as papules on the dorsal hands and progressively enlarged to involve the face and heels and became ulcerative; involvement of the right hand progressed to destruction of tendons and soft tissue of the fifth finger, resulting in amputation of that finger. He had no history of comorbid conditions, no regular medications reported, and denied systemic symptoms — there was no weight loss, fever, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly or other signs of systemic involvement on examination or routine laboratory survey. Multiple prior empirical treatments for different presumed diagnoses, including pyoderma gangrenosum, sarcoidosis, and leishmaniasis, had been tried without improvement. An initial skin biopsy showed a necrotizing and palisading granulomatous tissue pattern that suggested an infectious etiology, but initial smears of lesion material for fungal elements, mycobacteria and Leishmania were negative. A tuberculin skin test produced a 27 mm induration, and anti-tuberculosis therapy (isoniazid, rifampin, ethambutol, and pyrazinamide) was started.

A 45-year-old Iranian man presented to dermatology in March 2008 with two large tumoral skin lesions. History of present illness and past history:
- Several years of chronic renal failure secondary to non–insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus (NIDDM). - In April 2006, after travel to an endemic area (Natanz in Isfahan province, Iran), he developed small papular lesions (reported as 2 x 5 millimeter) on the left wrist and the right shin. Those small lesions were left untreated. - Due to chronic renal failure, he underwent renal transplantation in August 2007. - After transplantation he was started on immunosuppression with prednisolone 50 mg/day and cyclosporine 7.5 mg/kg daily (reported as equivalent to 600 mg for an 80 kg patient). - Several weeks after transplantation and initiation of immunosuppressive therapy, the previously small papular lesions enlarged markedly into cauliflower-like, tumoral lesions. Physical examination:
- Two exophytic, cauliflower-like tumoral lesions: one on the left wrist measuring approximately 3 x 4 x 5 cm and one on the right shin measuring approximately 4 x 5 x 6 cm. No vital signs, routine laboratory values, or tissue diagnostic results are provided here.

A 52-year-old male farm worker from Ceara state, northeast Brazil, presented with a 4-month history of skin lesions. Lesions appeared first on the face and legs, than spread across much of his body, including the genitalia, soles of feet, and scalp. He reported daily fevers for the first 2 weeks of illness. On examination the patient had 178 lesions of different sizes and aspects; ulcerated, crusted, papular, nodular, and pustular. Many had apparent bacterial superinfections. The remainder of the physical examination was normal. A complete blood count and liver and kidney function tests were within normal limits. Serological tests for syphilis and human immunodeficiency virus were negative.

Eight years earlier he had a small papule on the right cheek that progressed to an open ulcer, then to ulcers on the left cheek and forehead; those active lesions lasted about six months and healed spontaneously, leaving permanent hypopigmented scars. On one presentation, physical examination showed multiple nodular lesions on his hands, face and nose, swelling of the upper lip, and crusted central ulcers with raised peripheral contours; multiple healed scars were present on both cheeks. He had no fever, hepatosplenomegaly or lymphedema and reported no history of HIV, chronic disease, alcohol abuse, or immunomodulatory drug use. Parasitological testing of lesion smears at that time showed many macrophages filled with amastigote stages of Leishmania, graded as +6. A nonreactive rK39 rapid diagnostic test and absence of related systemic signs made visceral leishmaniasis unlikely. Based on the clinical manifestations and smear result he was diagnosed with mucocutaneous leishmaniasis and treated with intramuscular sodium stibogluconate (20 mg/kg/day for 30 days) with clinical cure. Two years later he returned with a different cutaneous eruption that had appeared over the previous three months and had been preceded by intense itching. On exam he had multiple, nonpitting, closed papules on his face, nose, hands and legs. A skin smear again showed intramacrophage amastigotes with a parasite load graded +6, and culture grew promastigotes.

A 35-year-old man from Russia presented to dermatology with two ulcerative skin lesions described as semi-dry with active borders: one in the lower left pre-atrial region and the other on the dorsal region of the left forearm. He reported travel to multiple countries between May and June 2019, including Middle Eastern countries (Israel, Turkey), the Balkan region (Armenia, Georgia), and Russia. In August 2019 he noted red, indurated papules and sought care in late August in San Cristobal de las Casas, Chiapas, Mexico. Cryotherapy with liquid nitrogen was applied initially with temporary reduction, followed by renewed flare-up of the lesion edges. At the Tropical Medicine Center he was clinically diagnosed as having localized cutaneous leishmaniasis (LCL). For confirmation, Giemsa-stained smears of the lesion and ELISA tests for L. braziliensis, L. infantum/chagasi, L. major and L. mexicana were performed. The Giemsa-stained smears showed abundant amastigotes within macrophages. The ELISA of the patient's serum revealed some degree of cross reactivity between four Leishmania species, with higher antibody levels recorded for L. major and L. mexicana antigens.

A 75-year-old man was referred with lesions on the hands, legs, face, and the upper lid of the right eye. He is a farmer from Aran va Bidgol city, Isfahan province (central Iran). He reported that sandflies had bitten him when he went to the farm for irrigation on nights during the sandfly season. He described the appearance of 25 multiple nodular, ulcerative, and crusted lesions on his body. On examination the lesions varied in size from a few millimeters to several centimeters; there were eight lesions on the face, including one on the upper right eyelid. He had no particular medical history, no fever, the lesions were painless, and his general condition was good.

A 9-year-old boy presented with multiple papular lesions on the left cheek that had been present for three months and had gradually enlarged. His medical history was notable for an episode of cutaneous leishmaniasis located on the nose two years earlier, which had completely regressed after treatment with intralesional meglumine antimonate. Dermatologic examination showed multiple, coalescing, rough, slightly elevated, yellowish-brown papular lesions 3–6 mm in diameter on the left cheek. He also had a large atrophic scar on the nose. Nothing of interest was noted in his family history or his laboratory tests.

A 61-year-old man (weight 65 kg) was referred in January with a 2-month history of a 1 × 3 cm lesion on the left ear. He has diabetes and had not traveled outside Kashan during the previous year. He reported that the ear lesion felt uncomfortable and scabrous but was not painful and he had no systemic complaints. Direct microscopy of scales with 10% potassium hydroxide (KOH) preparation was negative for fungal elements. The lesion was cleaned and specimens were collected from the margin by scraping; two smears were fixed with methanol and stained with 10% Giemsa for 30 minutes. On microscopic examination of the stained smears, amastigote forms of Leishmania spp. were observed.

Her only medical history was well-controlled hypertension. Examination showed a palpable spleen just below the left costal margin. On the right arm near the axilla there was "a single well-defined, ulcer surrounded by erythematous edging, with serous oozing" about 3 × 3 cm; the patient reported the lesion was painless, nonhealing, and present for 2–3 years. The rest of the exam was essentially normal. A Leishmania rk39 immunochromatography test was positive. Bone marrow aspiration parasitology revealed Leishmania amastigote forms, and serum immunofluorescence for Leishmania antibodies was positive (titer 1:400). Blood qPCR detected Leishmania DNA (400 parasites/mL). Direct microscopy of skin smears from the arm lesion showed no amastigotes, but Leishmania DNA amplification was obtained from dermal DNA extract by qPCR. ITS1 sequencing showed the Leishmania strains from the blood and the arm lesion corresponded to L. infantum and were 100% identical. Systemic response was rapid: fever resolved, general condition improved, splenomegaly regressed, blood counts normalized, and blood qPCR became negative after 28 days. However, "the skin lesion did not improve although Leishmania qPCR on dermal sample became negative." A skin biopsy was initially refused. One year later the lesion remained essentially unchanged. A polarized dermoscopy examination showed "ulcerations and short, fine arborizing vessels," described as evocative of a basal cell carcinoma.

A 45-year-old man from Apucarana, Paraná, presented with one atypical lesion on the right side of his back of approximately one month’s duration. He had applied topical antibiotics before seeking care without improvement. On examination the lesion was a rounded plaque with an erythematous-violaceous center, desquamative ulcerated edges, and an extensive surrounding area of lichenification, measuring 20 cm, located on the right scapular/back region. Based on the clinical appearance, the initial differential diagnosis included chronic simple lichen, psoriasis, squamous cell carcinoma, chromomycosis, cutaneous tuberculosis, syphilis, paracoccidioidomycosis, and sarcoidosis.

retrieval_query_text: A 78-year-old man was referred for evaluation of disseminated skin lesions over the left arm and hemithorax. He had a one-month history of multiple skin lesions that began as a small furuncle on the left forelimb and progressed to other parts of the arm and hemithorax. He lived in Esfarayen city in Northeastern Iran, described as one of the new endemic regions of cutaneous leishmaniasis. He reported edema and lymphedema of the arm and hemithorax prior to the lesion dissemination. Physical examination was notable for mild peripheral edema and lymphedema but no systemic symptoms such as fever or hepatosplenomegaly; radiological and routine laboratory tests showed no abnormalities. His medical history included a 10-year history of opium smoking and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease treated with salbutamol and fluticasone/salmeterol inhalers. He was hospitalized with an initial suspicion of diffuse bacterial infection because of the lymphedema, opium smoking, and respiratory disease. On examination he had multiple, disseminated, wet-looking skin lesions that were papular, crusted, and severely ulcerated over the left arm and hemithorax; lesions had spread to the palm and left fingernails. Three days before presentation he had bandaged the lesions with plastic covers, and “all covered parts turned into creamy, wet-looking and severely inflammatory lesions which looked like second-degree burn wounds.”

contexts.text: A 55-year-old man from the Manaus region with no comorbidities had been treated for cutaneous leishmaniasis. He had completed treatment with a pentavalent antimonial drug 40 days earlier and had received a second outpatient 30-day cycle; ten days after the end of that treatment his leishmaniasis lesion was healed. He then developed grouped microvesicles on an erythematous-infiltrated base that began in the neck and ascended toward the right scalp margin. The vesicles involved the right pinna, external auditory canal, and right ear lobe and were associated with severe torticollis-like pain along the nerve distribution. HIV serology was negative.

A 47-year-old man, a traveling companion of another migrant, presented with multiple chronic skin lesions after migration through Central America. He had a total of 10 lesions on bilateral upper and lower extremities and the flank; all lesions were larger than 1 cm and the largest measured 5 cm. The patients likely acquired their illness in the Darien Gap region of Panama during their migratory path to the United States. Tissue samples were sent to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention for diagnostic confirmation. As part of the clinical workup to rule out malaria, a rapid malaria antigen test for P. falciparum (BinaxNOW) was obtained and reported positive in both patients.

A 65-year-old man from Brasilia presented with an erythematous plaque on his nose that began one month after fishing in the state of Amazonas, Brazil. HIV serology was negative. The Leishmania skin test (LST) and indirect immunofluorescence results were negative. The patient was treated with NMG (meglumine antimoniate) 20 mg SbV/kg/day for 20 days without improvement; treatment was continued with additional dosing that again did not result in improvement. After a month off therapy he resumed NMG combined with allopurinol (1,200 mg/day); NMG was stopped at one point because of intense myalgia, then resumed to a cumulative dose reported in the chart, yet clinical improvement was not achieved during these courses of therapy.

A male born June 26, 1986, was seen at a tropical diseases referral center. Between 2009 and 2011 he was hospitalized seven times with a consistent diagnosis of kala-azar. He received multiple recommended treatments during these hospitalizations, including pentavalent antimony (glucantime, 20 mg of Sb + 5 kg/d for 30 d in the first hospitalization), liposomal amphotericin B (for 14 d at 3 mg/kg/d in three subsequent hospitalizations), and pentamidine in the last hospitalization before surgery (4 mg/kg/d every other day, total 15 doses), with only transient symptomatic improvement followed by recurrence. He had a negative HIV serological test. During two hospitalizations he presented with anemia and was transfused twice with packed red blood cells. After all possibilities of medical treatment were exhausted and the patient maintained a pancytopenia profile on blood counts attributed to hypersplenism, splenectomy was recommended. In January 2012 he was hospitalized for the planned surgical procedure. His clinical examination revealed mucocutaneous pallor (2+/4+), fever (38.5 C), dehydration (2+/4+), a distended abdomen with mild pain on deep palpation, and splenomegaly 8 cm below the left costal margin. Laboratory testing showed anemia, leukopenia, hypergammaglobulinemia, and elevated ESR and CRP.

A 37-year-old man from Georgia presented in France in October 2012. He had HIV infection since 2006 that had been treated inconsistently with HAART. Other medical history included adrenal insufficiency, cirrhosis due to chronic hepatitis C virus infection, and treatment-controlled tuberculosis. Visceral leishmaniasis had been diagnosed in 2010 and treated in Georgia with meglumine antimoniate and liposomal amphotericin B (doses and schedules unknown). In November 2012 he had hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathies, infiltrated cutaneous lesions, and anemia. Laboratory testing showed a CD4 lymphocyte count of 133/mm3, plasma HIV viral load <50 copies/mL, and parasitemia of 6 Leishmania/ml. He received a course of liposomal amphotericin B followed by maintenance therapy for 5 months. In May 2013 he developed weight loss with persistent hepatosplenomegaly and anemia. CD4 count was 177/mm3, viral load <40 copies/mL, and parasitemia was 12 Leishmania/ml. Liposomal amphotericin B treatment was intensified, but renal insufficiency and acute thrombocytopenia occurred. In June 2013 the splenomegaly and parasitemia remained unchanged.

A stray male cat, approximately 3 years old, was presented after being fed by a resident at the door of his house in the COAB complex, Marambaia neighbourhood, Belém, Pará state, Brazil. The owner reported an ear lesion present for about 6 months and the appearance of new cutaneous lesions elsewhere. On physical examination the cat had lymphadenopathy and erythematous, edematous, non-painful papular lesions around the edges of both ears, the snout, and the dewclaw of the left hind limb. A complete blood count showed neutrophilia with a regenerative left shift. Serum alkaline phosphatase, creatinine, urea, transaminase glutamic-oxaloacetic (TGO) and glutamate-pyruvate transaminase (GPT) were within reference limits for Felis catus. Serological tests for visceral leishmaniasis using ELISA and indirect immunofluorescence assay (IFA) were nonreactive. Histopathologic examination of skin lesions indicated severe infectious pyogranulomatous dermatitis described as "caused by Leishmania spp. or Toxoplasma gondii." PCR assays to screen for other haemoparasites (Ehrlichia spp., Cytauxzoon felis, Anaplasma spp., Mycoplasma spp.) and for viruses (Feline leukemia virus and feline immunodeficiency virus) were also performed.

A male born June 6, 1960, from Acaua municipality, Piaui State, married, was diagnosed with kala-azar in January 2014 and had a negative serology to HIV. Since then he had recurrent pancytopenia, persistent splenomegaly and a history of five previous hospitalizations at the IDTNP for kala-azar treatment. Prior anti-leishmanial therapies included pentavalent antimony (glucantime, 20 mg of Sb + 5 kg/d for 30 d at the first hospitalization) and liposomal amphotericin B (for 14 d at a dose of 3 mg/kg/d, given during three hospitalizations), without durable clinical resolution. On admission in July 2015 he had a palpable spleen 12 cm below the left costal margin. Abdominal ultrasound showed an enlarged spleen extending to the left iliac fossa. Preoperative complete blood count: hemoglobin 8.7 g/dL, hematocrit 27.9%, leukocytes 1,090/microL, and platelets 155,000/microL.

Clinical Context: In December 2015 a 50-year-old woman presented with a cutaneous lesion on the left hand. She reported that the infection may be related to labor activities and that it was acquired on "Estrada do Indio" (Federal Road 319), a federal highway that connects Porto Velho and Humaita in the Brazilian states of Rondonia and Amazonas. This highway is surrounded by Amazon forest and is described as "an area with frequent reports of TL." She did not report any chronic disease, and investigation for HIV coinfection was negative. Clinical data and biological samples were collected as part of a research project; samples for molecular detection and identification were obtained using sterile cervical brushes placed in direct contact with the edge of the lesion.

A 52-year-old woman presented with a single lesion on the tip of her nose that had existed for 14 months. It began as a papule and was slowly increasing in size, enlarging to a plaque. A smear of the lesion performed about 1 year earlier was positive, "showing leishmania bodies." All five members of her family had a history of proven leishmaniasis. Her past medical history was notable for renal failure diagnosed 11 years earlier; she "received a renal transplant 4 years after the diagnosis of renal failure." She also had hypertension and hyperlipidemia and was taking oral mycophenolate mofetil (2 g daily) and cyclosporine (100 mg daily). Skin examination showed skin type IV, "No actinic keratosis was present," and a 3x3 cm indurated ulcer with elevated borders was present on the tip of her nose. The therapeutic plan was intralesional glucantime injections (approximately 1 ml of 1.5 g vial per week). "After completing a therapeutic course of 20 sessions receiving intralesional glucantime injections, she was considered as glucantime therapy resistant."

A 30-year-old woman from an area endemic for tegumentary leishmaniasis presented with a single skin complaint. She reported a small papular lesion on her right leg that had developed over 7–10 days. At age 10 she had had an ulcer on the left thigh that healed spontaneously and left a well-defined atrophic scar. On examination there was a depressed papular lesion on the right leg measuring 8 × 7 mm; there was a 30 × 20 mm atrophic scar on the left thigh and no lymphadenopathy. Because early lesions of the locally prevalent Leishmania species may be papular and nonulcerated, a Leishmania skin test (LST) was performed on the left forearm. After 48 hours the intradermal reaction was strongly positive, with an induration measuring 38 × 32 mm. Eight days after the skin test the original papular lesion on the right leg had resolved, and a new round cutaneous ulcer with raised borders measuring 26 × 24 mm was present at the site of the LST. A culture of aspirated material from the forearm lesion was negative for Leishmania.

A 59-year-old Caucasian woman with a medical history of diabetes, hypertension, congestive heart failure, chronic renal disease, and paraparesis secondary to HTLV-1 infection presented in June 2012 with a skin lesion on her face. She initially noted a papule in the left malar region that later ulcerated and increased in size. Fifteen days after the facial lesion appeared, she developed another lesion on the right knee.

A 45-year-old man with known HIV infection presented with nodules and plaques on the nasal area, dorsum of the left wrist, the right index finger, and the back; cervical lymphadenopathy was noted. He reported a history of fever 6 months earlier while working in the state of Bihar, and since then had mild intermittent fever and weight loss. Routine blood and urine examinations were reported as not revealing any abnormalities. Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay for HIV was positive, and the CD4 count was 210/muL. On inspection there were infiltrated plaques on the nose, left dorsum of the wrist, and on the index finger of the right hand.

A 32-year-old man from Djelfa, Algeria, with a history of contact eczema presented with a 6-week history of painless, non-healing skin lesions on the dorsal aspect of his right hand. He had applied topical corticosteroids and antiseptics without improvement and had received two courses of antibiotics (pristinamycin, amoxicillin + clavulanic acid) with no significant results. On examination there was a limited erythematous-papular plaque, approximately 8 cm in diameter, on the dorsal right hand formed by confluence of several papules with satellite lesions at the periphery. The initial plaque was associated with several firm, painless subcutaneous nodules 0.5–1.5 cm in diameter that tracked proximally along lymphatic drainage toward the elbow. The patient did not recall an insect bite, no other body sites were involved, and the remainder of the examination was unremarkable. Direct mycological examination and culture on Sabouraud medium at 25 °C and on BHI medium at 37 °C were negative for fungal presence.

A tuberculin skin test produced a 27 mm induration, and anti-tuberculosis therapy (isoniazid, rifampin, ethambutol, and pyrazinamide) was started.

A 30-year-old woman with a history of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) diagnosed during pregnancy in 2010 presented with skin lesions. History of present illness and past medical history:
- She received antiretroviral therapy from 2013 to 2018 (zidovudine 300 mg orally twice daily, lamivudine 150 mg orally twice daily, efavirenz 600 mg orally once daily) but the antiretroviral regimen was discontinued several times. - In October 2020 she developed a single ulcerative lesion on a lower limb. - At that time a diagnosis of tegumentary leishmaniasis (TL) was confirmed by Giemsa‑stained slides from skin scraping. - She began treatment with meglumine antimoniate (20 mg Sb+5/kg IV daily for 20 days) but discontinued treatment soon after starting. - In late 2021 she returned with new lesions on the left lower limb and right upper limb; a biopsy sample was collected for parasite isolation. - She subsequently received liposomal amphotericin B (3 mg/kg) for 20 days, experienced a relapse, started another antimonial regimen which she abandoned after a few days, and in August 2022 had recurrence of the lower‑limb lesion followed by a 10‑day course of liposomal amphotericin B with complete healing. - Geographic context: patient resides in a municipality in the State of Maranhão, Brazil, within an ecotone region where leishmaniasis is endemic.

Clinical data and biological samples were collected as part of a research project; samples for molecular detection and identification were obtained using sterile cervical brushes placed in direct contact with the edge of the lesion.

contexts.text: A male born June 26, 1986, was seen at a tropical diseases referral center. Between 2009 and 2011 he was hospitalized seven times with a consistent diagnosis of kala-azar. He received multiple recommended treatments during these hospitalizations, including pentavalent antimony (glucantime, 20 mg of Sb + 5 kg/d for 30 d in the first hospitalization), liposomal amphotericin B (for 14 d at 3 mg/kg/d in three subsequent hospitalizations), and pentamidine in the last hospitalization before surgery (4 mg/kg/d every other day, total 15 doses), with only transient symptomatic improvement followed by recurrence. He had a negative HIV serological test. During two hospitalizations he presented with anemia and was transfused twice with packed red blood cells. After all possibilities of medical treatment were exhausted and the patient maintained a pancytopenia profile on blood counts attributed to hypersplenism, splenectomy was recommended. In January 2012 he was hospitalized for the planned surgical procedure. His clinical examination revealed mucocutaneous pallor (2+/4+), fever (38.5 C), dehydration (2+/4+), a distended abdomen with mild pain on deep palpation, and splenomegaly 8 cm below the left costal margin. Laboratory testing showed anemia, leukopenia, hypergammaglobulinemia, and elevated ESR and CRP.

A male born June 6, 1960, from Acaua municipality, Piaui State, married, was diagnosed with kala-azar in January 2014 and had a negative serology to HIV. Since then he had recurrent pancytopenia, persistent splenomegaly and a history of five previous hospitalizations at the IDTNP for kala-azar treatment. Prior anti-leishmanial therapies included pentavalent antimony (glucantime, 20 mg of Sb + 5 kg/d for 30 d at the first hospitalization) and liposomal amphotericin B (for 14 d at a dose of 3 mg/kg/d, given during three hospitalizations), without durable clinical resolution. On admission in July 2015 he had a palpable spleen 12 cm below the left costal margin. Abdominal ultrasound showed an enlarged spleen extending to the left iliac fossa. Preoperative complete blood count: hemoglobin 8.7 g/dL, hematocrit 27.9%, leukocytes 1,090/microL, and platelets 155,000/microL.

A 41-year-old Caucasian man was admitted during treatment with intravenous liposomal amphotericin B for laryngeal and facial mucocutaneous leishmaniasis because of marked elevation of creatine kinase (CK) (more than 10× upper limit of normal during admission; pretreatment CK up to ~2× ULN previously) and rising serum creatinine. Past medical history was notable for visceral leishmaniasis at age 13, recurrent otitis and an episode of bronchopneumonia in childhood, long-standing unexplained elevated CK attributed in the past to occupation and boxing, and chronic periorbital/facial swelling first noted in 2013. In January 2019 he developed hoarseness and dysphonia; laryngoscopy and biopsy were positive for Leishmania spp., and earlier periocular skin samples (2015) were retrospectively PCR-positive for Leishmania spp. He reported no travel outside Europe. There was a family history notable for a brother who died at age 20 from an unspecified lymphoproliferative disease and a sister with chronic myalgias. On examination he was in good general condition with bilateral orbital swelling. Peripheral blood count was unremarkable. T-lymphocyte subpopulations were within reference limits except for reduced circulating Tfh cells. There was no history of liver or biliary tract disease or neutropenia. The patient met criteria for common-variable immunodeficiency, but because of the opportunistic, persistent Leishmania infection further genetic studies were pursued.

A 13‑year‑old boy, born in São Paulo, who had traveled at age 12 to the state of Minas Gerais, presented with fever on alternate days, pallor, increased abdominal volume and unquantified weight loss. He had no prior history of recurrent infections. On admission he had anemia and thrombocytopenia. Bone marrow aspirate showed amastigotes of Leishmania. He was treated with liposomal amphotericin B (LAB) at a dose of 35 mg/kg and was discharged. Four months later he returned with fever and thrombocytopenia; a bone marrow aspirate again showed amastigotes of Leishmania and parasites were detected in bone marrow culture. He was treated with meglumine antimoniate and intravenous human immunoglobulin with clinical and laboratory improvement and was discharged in good health. Three weeks later he presented with seven days of fever, weakness, pallor and increased abdominal volume. On exam the spleen was palpable 23 cm below the left costal margin and the liver 5 cm from the right costal margin. Leishmania ELISA immunoassay and the rK‑39 antigen test were negative. Bone marrow biopsy showed a lymphocytic and histiocytic inflammatory reaction with a granulomatous pattern; no amastigotes were observed in the aspirate. He was re‑treated empirically for visceral leishmaniasis with liposomal amphotericin B. Notably, the patient had silvery hair and eyebrows, described as a phenotype suggestive of Griscelli Syndrome.

A 37-year-old man from Georgia presented in France in October 2012. He had HIV infection since 2006 that had been treated inconsistently with HAART. Other medical history included adrenal insufficiency, cirrhosis due to chronic hepatitis C virus infection, and treatment-controlled tuberculosis. Visceral leishmaniasis had been diagnosed in 2010 and treated in Georgia with meglumine antimoniate and liposomal amphotericin B (doses and schedules unknown). In November 2012 he had hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathies, infiltrated cutaneous lesions, and anemia. Laboratory testing showed a CD4 lymphocyte count of 133/mm3, plasma HIV viral load <50 copies/mL, and parasitemia of 6 Leishmania/ml. He received a course of liposomal amphotericin B followed by maintenance therapy for 5 months. In May 2013 he developed weight loss with persistent hepatosplenomegaly and anemia. CD4 count was 177/mm3, viral load <40 copies/mL, and parasitemia was 12 Leishmania/ml. Liposomal amphotericin B treatment was intensified, but renal insufficiency and acute thrombocytopenia occurred. In June 2013 the splenomegaly and parasitemia remained unchanged.

A 30‑year‑old man presented with pain in his lower limbs and a non‑itchy erythematous rash over both lower limbs. He had low‑grade intermittent fever for three months. On examination he was pale and malnourished (BMI 18.4 kg/m2) and had palpable purpura over both thighs and buttocks. Abdominal examination revealed palpable hepatomegaly with massive splenomegaly. Laboratory testing showed pancytopenia (hemoglobin 6.8 g/dL, total leukocyte count 2800/mm3, platelet count 45 000/muL) and polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia (4.9 g/dL); liver and renal function tests were within reference ranges. Contrast‑enhanced CT of chest and abdomen confirmed hepatosplenomegaly and was otherwise unremarkable. The treating team considered hematologic malignancy and a connective‑tissue disorder with vasculitis. Other infectious etiologies entertained included HIV, scrub typhus/rickettsial infection, and visceral leishmaniasis (given the patient lived in an endemic area). Initial testing showed: anti‑nuclear antibodies, complement levels (C3 = 94 mg/dL and C4 = 20 mg/dL), and rheumatoid factor were negative; urine examination was normal and serum cryoglobulins were not raised. Viral markers (HIV, hepatitis B surface antigen, and anti‑hepatitis C) were negative. Serology for rickettsia and scrub typhus were also negative.

A 1-year-old boy was admitted with continuous fever for 3 months. On evaluation he had hepatosplenomegaly and anemia, and laboratory testing showed hypertriglyceridemia and increased ferritin; he experienced hemodynamic instability requiring blood transfusion. An immunochromatographic rapid test with rK39 antigen was positive for Leishmania, and the myelogram demonstrated Leishmania spp with hemophagocytosis. Treatment with meglumine antimoniate (glucantime) was started. As fever persisted, on day 8 nonresponse to glucantime was considered and therapy was changed to liposomal amphotericin. Due to fever and neutropenia, cefepime was also started.

A 39‑year‑old man from Central America, living in Southeast Georgia, presents to the emergency department with abdominal pain and rectal bleeding. Past medical history: HIV/AIDS, alcohol abuse, tobacco dependency, and previously documented leishmaniasis diagnosed by bone marrow biopsy. He denied recent travel. Course and prior presentations: At initial presentation several years earlier he had diffuse moderate abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, chills and dysphagia; on exam he was tachycardic (heart rate 140/min) with mild abdominal tenderness. He was leukopenic and thrombocytopenic and was treated with amphotericin B and initiation of HAART; he was discharged on a 3‑month course of amphotericin B with ongoing HAART. Six months later he returned with acute abdominal pain and nausea; exam then showed a fine nodular skin rash across chest, abdomen and back described as consistent with cutaneous leishmaniasis, and thrombocytopenia persisted. At that time a bone marrow biopsy was performed to evaluate whether his new symptoms were due to HIV or a relapse of leishmaniasis, and he again received intravenous amphotericin B (inpatient 6 weeks) with plans for outpatient infusions. The patient subsequently was lost to follow‑up. Current presentation: Several years later he returned with a flare characterized by rectal bleeding and continued abdominal pain. Gastroenterology was consulted and an esophagogastroduodenoscopy was planned.

A 33‑year‑old Italian man with HIV infection and a history of visceral leishmaniasis (VL) presented initially in May 2002 with fever, weight loss, diarrhea, mucocutaneous lesions suggestive of Kaposi's sarcoma, hepatosplenomegaly, pancytopenia, and polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia. Bone marrow smear at that time showed Leishmania spp. amastigotes and he was treated with meglumine antimoniate for 30 days and started on HAART. He had multiple clinical relapses of VL over the ensuing years, each treated with intravenous liposomal amphotericin B (L‑AMB) given as 4 mg/kg/day for 5 days then weekly for 4 weeks. In February 2008 maintenance secondary prophylaxis with L‑AMB 4 mg/kg once monthly was started. At that time his HIV RNA was stably below 50 copies/mL and CD4+ T‑cell count was 125 cells/µL; his HAART regimen was Abacavir‑Lamivudine‑Lopinavir/ritonavir. Some weeks after starting secondary prophylaxis with L‑AMB, he developed a maculopapular and nodular rash on his trunk and upper limbs that gradually worsened. The rash was described as diffuse maculopapular and nodular on the upper limbs and trunk. Four months later, L‑AMB was stopped and a cutaneous biopsy was performed.

A 68-year-old man from a mountainous area in Hebei Province, China, presented with fever, sweating, and fatigue. He first sought care on February 1 and was hospitalized at a local hospital with temperature 39.0°C, chills, and no respiratory, abdominal, diarrheal, or urinary symptoms. He had lost approximately 10 kg over the prior 6 months. Initial blood tests showed pancytopenia, a rapid erythrocyte sedimentation rate, elevated C-reactive protein and ferritin, hyponatremia, hypokalemia, hypoproteinemia, and elevated serum enzyme levels. Bone marrow aspiration smear at that time showed granulocytopenia with megakaryocyte maturation disorder. Abdominal ultrasound showed splenomegaly; brain CT showed bilateral basal ganglia lacunar infarction; chest CT showed bilateral fibrotic/bronchitic changes. After 11 days of antibiotic and supportive treatment his fever and fatigue persisted with temperatures >39°C, so he presented for further evaluation on February 16. On arrival his SARS-CoV-2 PCR was negative. On examination he was febrile to 38.2°C, poorly nourished, unable to walk (bilateral leg strength grade 3), and had pitting edema of the anterior tibias and dorsal feet. Repeat laboratory testing again showed pancytopenia, increased ESR, CRP and ferritin, and elevated liver enzymes. Empiric antibiotic therapy had not relieved his febrile illness.

contexts.text: A 38‑year‑old man from Yayu district, western Ethiopia, presented to the outpatient clinic with multiple skin lesions on his face and hands and mutilation of the nose; his upper lip was injured and swollen. Eight years earlier he had a small papule on the right cheek that progressed to an open ulcer, then to ulcers on the left cheek and forehead; those active lesions lasted about six months and healed spontaneously, leaving permanent hypopigmented scars. He had no fever, hepatosplenomegaly or lymphedema and reported no history of HIV, chronic disease, alcohol abuse, or immunomodulatory drug use. Parasitological testing of lesion smears at that time showed many macrophages filled with amastigote stages of Leishmania, graded as +6. A nonreactive rK39 rapid diagnostic test and absence of related systemic signs made visceral leishmaniasis unlikely. Based on the clinical manifestations and smear result he was diagnosed with mucocutaneous leishmaniasis and treated with intramuscular sodium stibogluconate (20 mg/kg/day for 30 days) with clinical cure. Two years later he returned with a different cutaneous eruption that had appeared over the previous three months and had been preceded by intense itching. On exam he had multiple, nonpitting, closed papules on his face, nose, hands and legs. A skin smear again showed intramacrophage amastigotes with a parasite load graded +6, and culture grew promastigotes.

A 78-year-old man from a rural area in western Iran was referred for multiple ulcerative, exudative lesions involving the mid-face (upper lip and anterior nasal fossa), above the eyebrows, dorsal aspects of both hands, and posterior aspects of both heels. Lesions began three years earlier as papules on the dorsal hands and progressively enlarged to involve the face and heels and became ulcerative; involvement of the right hand progressed to destruction of tendons and soft tissue of the fifth finger, resulting in amputation of that finger. He had no history of comorbid conditions, no regular medications reported, and denied systemic symptoms — there was no weight loss, fever, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly or other signs of systemic involvement on examination or routine laboratory survey. Multiple prior empirical treatments for different presumed diagnoses, including pyoderma gangrenosum, sarcoidosis, and leishmaniasis, had been tried without improvement. An initial skin biopsy showed a necrotizing and palisading granulomatous tissue pattern that suggested an infectious etiology, but initial smears of lesion material for fungal elements, mycobacteria and Leishmania were negative. A tuberculin skin test produced a 27 mm induration, and anti-tuberculosis therapy (isoniazid, rifampin, ethambutol, and pyrazinamide) was started.

A 40‑year‑old woman from Balao Chico (Guayas province, Ecuador) presented in August 1979 with a progressive widespread skin eruption. The illness began with a lesion on the lumbar region; papular lesions developed and became pustulous vesicles at the right lumbar region and then disseminated over the body, with 308 generalized lesions counted. She reported marked right lumbar pain; some body‑surface lesions were thought clinically to resemble herpes zoster. The presumptive clinical diagnoses listed were paracoccidioidomycosis, cutaneous leishmaniasis, or staphylococcal infections. Examination of the ulcers showed most lesions to be crusty; when crusts were lifted they were excavated with purulent fluid from severe secondary infections. Ulcer sizes ranged from 0.5 to 20 mm in diameter; some lesions had thick, adherent crusts that bled when separated, others were small crusty ulcers with excavations, and confluent erythematous papular plaques were present on the lumbar–dorsal region. Laboratory tests on ulcer material did not demonstrate Paracoccidioides braziliensis or Staphylococcus aureus. Routine laboratory examinations revealed positivity for beta‑hemolytic streptococcus (antibiotic‑sensitive), and stool examination was positive for Trichuris trichiura, Ascaris lumbricoides, and Ancylostoma duodenale. Several smear samples from diverse regions of the body surface were taken at random.

A 60-year-old woman from Uttar Pradesh, India presented with a six‑week history of high‑grade continuous fever with chills and rigors, anorexia, malaise, joint pains, and severe lethargy. She reported "crops of round, raised lesions" that began on the left upper limb, progressed to the right upper limb and then involved the whole face, upper back, chest, and upper abdomen; the lesions were "closely associated with the febrile episodes." Some lesions enlarged, became nodular, developed sunken centers that drained pus‑like material, and were painful and red. One week before admission she developed jaundice with mild to moderate upper‑quadrant abdominal pain. Pallor and icterus were present; there was bilateral pitting, non‑tender symmetrical pedal edema. Skin exam showed "multiple crops of nodular, noduloulcerative, and papular lesions, dispersed throughout the body surface, mostly segregated to the face and upper back," some with pus drainage from central sunken areas. Eye exam demonstrated nodular lesions over the eyes and conjunctiva with conjunctival suffusion. Fundoscopy showed uveitis and small retinal hemorrhages. Chest imaging was within normal limits. Laboratory studies: hemoglobin 10.5 g/dL, total leukocyte count 5600/mm3, platelet count 80,000/mm3, ESR 80 mm/hr with normocytic normochromic anemia. Liver tests: total bilirubin 3.2 mg/dL (direct 1.8), AST 50 IU/L, ALT 60 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 221 IU/L, GGT 150 IU/L, albumin 1.9 g/dL, INR 1.3. Serum IgG 22.6 g/L.

A 24-year-old man from Tancredo Neves, State of Bahia, Brazil, was admitted in January 2012 with diffuse bullous lesions on the body, osteoarthritis of the distal interphalangeal joints and proteinuria of 399 mg/day. He was diagnosed with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and treated with mycophenolate mofetil (MMF), with the dose increased to 1 g per day intravenously. Two years after the SLE diagnosis (2014) he was hospitalized again, presenting with ulcerated, painless skin lesions on the face, upper lip, scalp, neck, and on the upper and lower limbs. Oral examination showed crusty upper lip lesions, poor oral health status, and amelogenesis imperfecta. He developed secondary infection with fever and was started on cephalexin (1 g/day) and maintained on prednisone 5 mg/day intravenously. On the third day of this hospitalization, biopsies were performed on the left nasal mucosa and on lesions of the right lower limb.

A 52-year-old male farm worker from Ceara state, northeast Brazil, presented with a 4-month history of skin lesions. Lesions appeared first on the face and legs, than spread across much of his body, including the genitalia, soles of feet, and scalp. He reported daily fevers for the first 2 weeks of illness. On examination the patient had 178 lesions of different sizes and aspects; ulcerated, crusted, papular, nodular, and pustular. Many had apparent bacterial superinfections. The remainder of the physical examination was normal. A complete blood count and liver and kidney function tests were within normal limits. Serological tests for syphilis and human immunodeficiency virus were negative.

A 43-year-old man from Cumanda (Chimborazo province, Ecuador), a subtropical mountainous community at ~500 m above sea level, presented with multiple chronic skin lesions. History of present illness: The lesion began as an insect-bite–like papular lesion on the forearm. Lesions then appeared on the right ear and the nose. About 2 years later, lesions developed on a wide range of the lower extremities and subsequently became multiple and confluent on the abdomen, thorax, body side, and thigh. A superficial involvement of mucosae of the nose and upper lip was observed. Treatment history: At the time of examination the patient had already received injections of nine ampoules of trivalent antimonials (Repodral, 20 mg/kg/day) at a rural health center; after finishing several courses he received pentavalent antimonials (Glucantime, 10 mg/kg/day) for about 5 months. Early investigations performed from active lesions included smear specimens, skin biopsies, syringe aspirates for culture, and material on FTA cards. Montenegro skin test showed a 17-mm induration, and an rK39 kit test revealed a strongly positive band. The smear specimen was positive for Leishmania amastigotes in scanty numbers. Promastigotes grown in vitro showed a tendency to decrease gradually and then disappear, an effect attributed by the investigators to prior antimonial treatment.

A 39-year-old woman with known HIV infection for 1 year was admitted with a 6-month history of skin lesions that were initially present on her face and later extended to the chest, abdomen, and extremities. On examination she had papules and nodules of varying size across these areas. Laboratory data showed leukopenia with a WBC of 1700 cells/mm3 and a CD4 cell count of 280 cells/mm3.

A 50‑year‑old male agriculturist with known HIV infection (diagnosed 1½ years earlier) on antiretroviral therapy presented with a 6‑month history of asymptomatic skin lesions over his limbs. Physical examination showed multiple, diffuse, non‑ulcerating, papulonodular and non‑itchy skin lesions measuring 2–18 mm; history indicated the lesions first appeared on the feet and then involved the hands. There was no history of travel to endemic areas of leishmaniasis. There was no hepatosplenomegaly and lymphadenopathy. Laboratory investigations showed anemia with hemoglobin 8.3 g/dL; platelet count reported as "2 lacs/muL" and total leukocyte count 5,100/muL. Liver and renal function tests, lipid profile and blood sugar were within normal limits. Chest X‑ray and ultrasound of the abdomen were normal. His CD4 count was 126 cells/muL and HIV viral load was <47 copies/mL.

A 22‑month‑old girl presented with 8 days of fever to 40°C and mild cough. Past history: failure to thrive; normal neurologic development. She was the first child of a non‑consanguineous couple; no family history of albinism; normal hair and skin. On exam she was stunted, pale, had non‑tender hepatomegaly 5–6 cm and splenomegaly palpable 4 cm below the left costal margin. Petechial rash developed on the chest and legs as she worsened. Initial laboratory results: WBC 5100/mm3 (ANC 1200/mm3), Hb 9.1 g/dl, platelets 47,000/mm3; mild transaminase elevation; hypoalbuminemia. Ferritin 1,134 ng/ml; soluble IL‑2 receptor (sCD25) 3,183 U/ml. Blood cultures were negative. Serum immunoglobulins and lymphocyte subsets were reported as normal. Infectious testing: EBV serology positive for IgM and IgG anti‑VCA with negative IgG anti‑EBNA; EBV viral load 637 copies/ml. Leishmania testing was discordant: immunochromatography and indirect immunofluorescence were negative, serum ELISA was slightly positive, and leishmanial antigen in urine was negative. Bone‑marrow aspiration revealed hemophagocytosis. Over the next day she clinically worsened with progressive splenomegaly and cytopenias (WBC 4,800/mm3 with ANC 800/mm3, Hb 6.8 g/dl, platelets 27,000/mm3), triglycerides 686 mg/dl, ferritin 3,849 ng/ml, and sCD25 3,596 U/ml. Clotting tests were normal and perforin expression by flow cytometry was reported as normal.

contexts.text: A 52‑year‑old woman who works in sugarcane fields in a rural area was referred to Oral Medicine for evaluation of a granulomatous lesion on the palate and for hoarseness that she thought followed a flu 3 months earlier. According to the referring surgeon, she had an extensive oral lesion and had undergone laryngoscopy and biopsy; that biopsy produced a histopathological result of “pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia and an active chronic inflammatory process, suggesting a fungus investigation,” prompting the referral. She reported no chronic systemic disease or regular medications. She described a history of crusting and nasal bleeding that began about 4 years earlier. On examination she had nasal obstruction, a nasal (hyponasal) voice, and was a mouth breather. She had smoked for 6 months and used both upper and lower complete dental prostheses continuously. Extrabuccal exam showed a lowering of the right nasal wing and a nasal septum perforation. Intrabuccal exam revealed a granulomatous lesion involving the entire palate and uvula, extending bilaterally to the pharynx with an erythematous appearance and areas of scratchable white plaques.

A 30-year-old Caucasian man, unemployed, HIV-negative and with no other concomitant infections, presented in 2014 with a papule on the inferior eyelid of the right eye. His past history included, in 2008, an isolated nodulation in the right leg that resolved after treatment. Over time new lesions progressively appeared on the chest, abdomen, back, feet, and in the oral cavity. Ulcerated oral lesions were present on the hard palate and on the left and right jugal mucosa. Disease progression was associated with fever, headache, and weight loss.

A 38‑year‑old man from Yayu district, western Ethiopia, presented to the outpatient clinic with multiple skin lesions on his face and hands and mutilation of the nose; his upper lip was injured and swollen. Eight years earlier he had a small papule on the right cheek that progressed to an open ulcer, then to ulcers on the left cheek and forehead; those active lesions lasted about six months and healed spontaneously, leaving permanent hypopigmented scars. He had no fever, hepatosplenomegaly or lymphedema and reported no history of HIV, chronic disease, alcohol abuse, or immunomodulatory drug use. Parasitological testing of lesion smears at that time showed many macrophages filled with amastigote stages of Leishmania, graded as +6. A nonreactive rK39 rapid diagnostic test and absence of related systemic signs made visceral leishmaniasis unlikely. Based on the clinical manifestations and smear result he was diagnosed with mucocutaneous leishmaniasis and treated with intramuscular sodium stibogluconate (20 mg/kg/day for 30 days) with clinical cure. Two years later he returned with a different cutaneous eruption that had appeared over the previous three months and had been preceded by intense itching. On exam he had multiple, nonpitting, closed papules on his face, nose, hands and legs. A skin smear again showed intramacrophage amastigotes with a parasite load graded +6, and culture grew promastigotes.

A 9-year-old boy presented with multiple papular lesions on the left cheek that had been present for three months and had gradually enlarged. His medical history was notable for an episode of cutaneous leishmaniasis located on the nose two years earlier, which had completely regressed after treatment with intralesional meglumine antimonate. Dermatologic examination showed multiple, coalescing, rough, slightly elevated, yellowish-brown papular lesions 3–6 mm in diameter on the left cheek. He also had a large atrophic scar on the nose. Nothing of interest was noted in his family history or his laboratory tests.

A 61-year-old man (weight 65 kg) was referred in January with a 2-month history of a 1 × 3 cm lesion on the left ear. He has diabetes and had not traveled outside Kashan during the previous year. He reported that the ear lesion felt uncomfortable and scabrous but was not painful and he had no systemic complaints. Direct microscopy of scales with 10% potassium hydroxide (KOH) preparation was negative for fungal elements. The lesion was cleaned and specimens were collected from the margin by scraping; two smears were fixed with methanol and stained with 10% Giemsa for 30 minutes. On microscopic examination of the stained smears, amastigote forms of Leishmania spp. were observed.

A 74-year-old woman from Tunis presented with several weeks of fever (oral temperature 38–39°C), sweats, chills, fatigue, diarrhea, intermittent vague abdominal pain, and occasional dry cough. Her only medical history was well-controlled hypertension. Examination showed a palpable spleen just below the left costal margin. The rest of the exam was essentially normal. Renal, liver, and coagulation tests were normal. A Leishmania rk39 immunochromatography test was positive. Bone marrow aspiration parasitology revealed Leishmania amastigote forms, and serum immunofluorescence for Leishmania antibodies was positive (titer 1:400). Blood qPCR detected Leishmania DNA (400 parasites/mL). Direct microscopy of skin smears from the arm lesion showed no amastigotes, but Leishmania DNA amplification was obtained from dermal DNA extract by qPCR. ITS1 sequencing showed the Leishmania strains from the blood and the arm lesion corresponded to L. infantum and were 100% identical. Systemic response was rapid: fever resolved, general condition improved, splenomegaly regressed, blood counts normalized, and blood qPCR became negative after 28 days. However, "the skin lesion did not improve although Leishmania qPCR on dermal sample became negative." A skin biopsy was initially refused. One year later the lesion remained essentially unchanged. A polarized dermoscopy examination showed "ulcerations and short, fine arborizing vessels," described as evocative of a basal cell carcinoma.

A 52-year-old male farm worker from Ceara state, northeast Brazil, presented with a 4-month history of skin lesions. Lesions appeared first on the face and legs, than spread across much of his body, including the genitalia, soles of feet, and scalp. He reported daily fevers for the first 2 weeks of illness. On examination the patient had 178 lesions of different sizes and aspects; ulcerated, crusted, papular, nodular, and pustular. Many had apparent bacterial superinfections. The remainder of the physical examination was normal. A complete blood count and liver and kidney function tests were within normal limits. Serological tests for syphilis and human immunodeficiency virus were negative.

A 41-year-old Caucasian man was admitted during treatment with intravenous liposomal amphotericin B for laryngeal and facial mucocutaneous leishmaniasis because of marked elevation of creatine kinase (CK) (more than 10× upper limit of normal during admission; pretreatment CK up to ~2× ULN previously) and rising serum creatinine. Past medical history was notable for visceral leishmaniasis at age 13, recurrent otitis and an episode of bronchopneumonia in childhood, long-standing unexplained elevated CK attributed in the past to occupation and boxing, and chronic periorbital/facial swelling first noted in 2013. In January 2019 he developed hoarseness and dysphonia; laryngoscopy and biopsy were positive for Leishmania spp., and earlier periocular skin samples (2015) were retrospectively PCR-positive for Leishmania spp. He reported no travel outside Europe. There was a family history notable for a brother who died at age 20 from an unspecified lymphoproliferative disease and a sister with chronic myalgias. On examination he was in good general condition with bilateral orbital swelling. Peripheral blood count was unremarkable. B-cell immunophenotyping disclosed a defect in the memory compartment with markedly low switched-memory B cells. There was no history of liver or biliary tract disease or neutropenia. The patient met criteria for common-variable immunodeficiency, but because of the opportunistic, persistent Leishmania infection further genetic studies were pursued.

A 55-year-old man from the Manaus region with no comorbidities had been treated for cutaneous leishmaniasis. He had completed treatment with a pentavalent antimonial drug 40 days earlier and had received a second outpatient 30-day cycle; ten days after the end of that treatment his leishmaniasis lesion was healed. He then developed grouped microvesicles on an erythematous-infiltrated base that began in the neck and ascended toward the right scalp margin. The vesicles involved the right pinna, external auditory canal, and right ear lobe and were associated with severe torticollis-like pain along the nerve distribution. HIV serology was negative.

A 53-year-old man from Mundo Novo, State of Bahia, Brazil, presented in July with pain, nasal obstruction, odynophagia, and dysphagia. On examination there was a painful, hyperemic, friable lesion in the right nasal cavity and an infiltrative lesion involving the hard palate, soft palate, and uvula. Additional findings included an ulcerated lesion on the left eyebrow and right eye with seropurulent secretion, a small ulcer on the lower eyelid, a lesion on the lobe of the right ear, and a lesion in the malar region. The patient was admitted for diagnosis and management of disseminated skin lesions. A biopsy of the palate lesions showed a non-specific erosive chronic inflammatory process. HIV testing was negative.
