contexts.text: On July 2019, a 29-year-old female with no history of immunodeficiency or underlying diseases presented to an ENT clinic in northern Iran. She had a 3-month history of an itching intranasal lesion on the right side of her nasal canal and recurrent nasal congestion each year. An ENT specialist diagnosed her with an intranasal polyp and recommended polypectomy and rhinoplasty. Three months after surgery, she returned to the specialist with swelling and inflammation in the nasal cavity, suggesting recurrence. To rule out bacterial infections as possible complications of polypectomy, the specialist performed a fine needle aspiration (FNA) from the intranasal lesion. The FNA fluid specimen was stored at ambient temperature for 3 hours before being delivered to the laboratory, where a direct smear was prepared, fixed, and stained using the Gram technique. Microscopic examination revealed spindle-shaped Leishmania promastigote-like structures without any amastigotes of the parasite. In reviewing the history, the patient reported traveling to an endemic area of cutaneous leishmaniasis in Mashhad (eastern Iran) suburb area 3 months prior and noticing a bite in her nasal cavity. A direct smear of the FNA sample stained with Gram stain showed numerous developed and undeveloped promastigote forms of Leishmania parasite on microscopy.

A 59‑year‑old man, mixed ethnicity, unemployed, previously healthy, reported that an erythematous‑crusty lesion appeared in the region of the mental protuberance and over two months evolved to involve other parts of the body, including the frontal and occipital regions, nasal septum, ears, hands, and lower limbs. Oral examination showed scattered ulcers on the face, lower labial mucosa, and on the left lip commissure, a pseudomembrane on the marginal gingiva, and an exophytic nodule in the left labial mucosa. The patient had a positive Montenegro intradermal test and was admitted to the University Hospital in December 2018. After admission, clinicians noted enlarged lymph nodes of hard consistency in the left inguinal region and an extensive irregular melanocytic lesion in the left plantar region presenting an area of hyperkeratosis with a grey‑bluish center; the plantar lesion was biopsied for further evaluation. A PCR analysis had been performed in an external laboratory.

A 54-year-old healthy woman presented to ophthalmology with a few months' history of a symptomatic lesion of the right eye. The lesion was located in the nasal bulbar conjunctiva within the interpalpebral zone. On examination there was an erythematous fibrovascular lesion approximately 5 mm in length. The lesion produced foreign-body sensation and discomfort. The lesion was clinically diagnosed as a pterygium, and surgical removal was performed.

A 35-year-old man from Rio de Janeiro with a history of alcohol and cocaine abuse presented in 2014 with progressively enlarging mucocutaneous lesions that began in 2013 as erythematous, painful papules. On admission he had ulcerated lesions involving the nasal septum and nasal cavity, the palate, and the balanopreputial sulcus. He reported headache, nasal obstruction, asthenia, and weight loss. The initial differential diagnoses listed by the treating team were mucocutaneous infectious and inflammatory conditions, neoplasia, and tuberculosis. Early laboratory and imaging testing reported that viral and fungal serological tests, direct mycological examination, acid-fast bacilli testing (BAAR), chest tomography, and respiratory function tests were all negative.

A 53-year-old man from Mundo Novo, State of Bahia, Brazil, presented in July with pain, nasal obstruction, odynophagia, and dysphagia. On examination there was a painful, hyperemic, friable lesion in the right nasal cavity and an infiltrative lesion involving the hard palate, soft palate, and uvula. Additional findings included an ulcerated lesion on the left eyebrow and right eye with seropurulent secretion, a small ulcer on the lower eyelid, a lesion on the lobe of the right ear, and a lesion in the malar region. The patient was admitted for diagnosis and management of disseminated skin lesions. A biopsy of the palate lesions showed a non-specific erosive chronic inflammatory process. HIV testing was negative.

A 31-year-old woman from Salvador, State of Bahia, presented in 2013 with submandibular lymphadenopathy and multiple ulcerated lesions involving the lower lip frenulum, gingiva, nasal septum and a lesion on her back. She reported a prior cutaneous lesion on her back that had been recurrent over the prior year. On oral examination there was poor oral health and ulcerated lesions of the lower lip frenulum and adjacent gingiva. Excisional biopsies of the oral lesions were performed and reported as unspecific; microbiological analysis for fungi was negative.

A 52-year-old woman presented with a single lesion on the tip of her nose that had existed for 14 months. It began as a papule and was slowly increasing in size, enlarging to a plaque. A smear of the lesion performed about 1 year earlier was positive, "showing leishmania bodies." All five members of her family had a history of proven leishmaniasis. Her past medical history was notable for renal failure diagnosed 11 years earlier; she "received a renal transplant 4 years after the diagnosis of renal failure." She also had hypertension and hyperlipidemia and was taking oral mycophenolate mofetil (2 g daily) and cyclosporine (100 mg daily). Skin examination showed skin type IV, "No actinic keratosis was present," and a 3x3 cm indurated ulcer with elevated borders was present on the tip of her nose. The therapeutic plan was intralesional glucantime injections (approximately 1 ml of 1.5 g vial per week). "After completing a therapeutic course of 20 sessions receiving intralesional glucantime injections, she was considered as glucantime therapy resistant."

An 84‑year‑old woman presented with a large nodular lesion on the forehead of 2.5 months' duration. She had been seen at another hospital where a pre‑diagnosis of lymphoma was recorded; the prior punch biopsy report listed basal cell carcinoma, sarcoidosis, lupus vulgaris and pseudolymphoma among the clinical pre‑diagnoses and the material was sent for pathology consultation. Microscopic examination of the punch biopsy showed a dense nodular and diffuse lymphohistiocytic cell infiltration within the dermis. In the cytoplasm of histiocytes, small, round structures resembling organisms were noted. Immunohistochemical staining showed reactive T lymphocytes labelled with CD3 and CD5, reactive B lymphocytes labelled with CD20, and large clusters of histiocytes labelled with CD68; there was no staining with CD30. The pathology report recommended investigation of the aetiology of granulomatous dermatitis, especially cutaneous leishmaniasis.

A 45-year-old woman presented with painless nodules on the anterior upper chest for a 10-week duration. She was treated with oral amoxicillin–clavulanic acid for two weeks without any response; otherwise she was completely healthy. On examination she had two nontender, nonulcerative, indurated dusky erythematous plaques on her upper anterior chest. Complete workup included chest radiograph, complete blood film, liver function tests, renal function tests, and abdominal sonography; all of these investigations were reported as normal. A 6 mm punch biopsy was taken from one of the nodules.

A 39-year-old woman with known HIV infection for 1 year was admitted with a 6-month history of skin lesions that were initially present on her face and later extended to the chest, abdomen, and extremities. On examination she had papules and nodules of varying size across these areas. Laboratory data showed leukopenia with a WBC of 1700 cells/mm3 and a CD4 cell count of 280 cells/mm3.

contexts.text: A 2-year-old domestic European neutered male cat was referred with a 1-year history of skin disease characterized by multiple nodular skin lesions, ulcerative dermatitis of all four limbs and fever. The owner reported prior empirical treatment for a presumptive pyodermatitis with prednisolone, amoxicillin/clavulanic acid and doxycycline without clinical improvement. At first admission the only abnormalities on physical examination were mild fever (39.5oC) and dermatological lesions on the head and limbs. Approximately 20–25 cutaneous nodules (2–10 mm diameter) were distributed on the outer pinnal surfaces and orbital regions, most notably on the pinnae with some coalescence. Single ulcerative dermatitis spots (20–50 mm diameter) with raised margins affected the antebrachial and hock regions. Differential diagnosis at presentation included pyodermatitis, allergic reaction, autoimmune disease, neoplastic disease or leishmaniosis. A complete blood count and biochemical profile were performed and values were within reference intervals; serum protein electrophoresis showed a slight hypergammaglobulinaemia. Fine-needle aspiration puncture from the ear skin nodules was performed for further analysis.

Eight years earlier he had a small papule on the right cheek that progressed to an open ulcer, then to ulcers on the left cheek and forehead; those active lesions lasted about six months and healed spontaneously, leaving permanent hypopigmented scars. On one presentation, physical examination showed multiple nodular lesions on his hands, face and nose, swelling of the upper lip, and crusted central ulcers with raised peripheral contours; multiple healed scars were present on both cheeks. He had no fever, hepatosplenomegaly or lymphedema and reported no history of HIV, chronic disease, alcohol abuse, or immunomodulatory drug use. Parasitological testing of lesion smears at that time showed many macrophages filled with amastigote stages of Leishmania, graded as +6. A nonreactive rK39 rapid diagnostic test and absence of related systemic signs made visceral leishmaniasis unlikely. Based on the clinical manifestations and smear result he was diagnosed with mucocutaneous leishmaniasis and treated with intramuscular sodium stibogluconate (20 mg/kg/day for 30 days) with clinical cure. Two years later he returned with a different cutaneous eruption that had appeared over the previous three months and had been preceded by intense itching. On exam he had multiple, nonpitting, closed papules on his face, nose, hands and legs. A skin smear again showed intramacrophage amastigotes with a parasite load graded +6, and culture grew promastigotes.

A stray male cat, approximately 3 years old, was presented after being fed by a resident at the door of his house in the COAB complex, Marambaia neighbourhood, Belém, Pará state, Brazil. The owner reported an ear lesion present for about 6 months and the appearance of new cutaneous lesions elsewhere. On physical examination the cat had lymphadenopathy and erythematous, edematous, non-painful papular lesions around the edges of both ears, the snout, and the dewclaw of the left hind limb. A complete blood count showed neutrophilia with a regenerative left shift. Serum alkaline phosphatase, creatinine, urea, transaminase glutamic-oxaloacetic (TGO) and glutamate-pyruvate transaminase (GPT) were within reference limits for Felis catus. Serological tests for visceral leishmaniasis using ELISA and indirect immunofluorescence assay (IFA) were nonreactive. Histopathologic examination of skin lesions indicated severe infectious pyogranulomatous dermatitis described as "caused by Leishmania spp. or Toxoplasma gondii." PCR assays to screen for other haemoparasites (Ehrlichia spp., Cytauxzoon felis, Anaplasma spp., Mycoplasma spp.) and for viruses (Feline leukemia virus and feline immunodeficiency virus) were also performed.

A 7-year-old castrated male domestic short-haired cat, stray with unknown history, from the greater Athens area of Greece was presented for examination because of facial swelling and eye lesions. On examination there was a raised, nonalopecic, semifirm, poorly demarcated, painless swelling of the forehead. Periocular hypotrichosis, edema, and slight hyperpigmentation were present. Edema of the conjunctiva and third eyelid of the right eye was also observed. Clinical examination revealed no other abnormalities. A blood sample for complete blood count and biochemistry profile was obtained, and fine needle aspirates and a trucut biopsy were taken from the forehead swelling for cytological and histopathological examination. The patient had a nonregenerative anemia, hyperglobulinemia, and thrombocytopenia. Urinalysis showed no abnormalities. Further suggested serological tests for vector-borne diseases were not done because of financial restrictions. At presentation the clinicians listed the differential diagnosis as: subcutaneous abscess, atypical bacterial and mycobacterial infection, deep fungal infection, and neoplasia.

A 24-year-old Cuban immigrant presented with worsening nonhealing lower-extremity ulcers despite oral antibiotic therapy and wound care. The lesions gradually grew with subsequent ulceration over the course of 1 to 2 months. He recently arrived in the United States seeking asylum and first noticed the lesions while traveling in the jungle between Panama and Colombia (Darien Gap region). On examination, there was an ulcerative lesion measuring 4 cm on the dorsum of the right foot and a second 3.5 cm ulcer on the lower anterior shin. There was no evidence of mucosal or visceral involvement on initial physical exam. Photographs show ulcerative lesions on the right foot and left shin. As part of the clinical workup to rule out malaria, a rapid malaria antigen test for Plasmodium falciparum was obtained and reported positive.

A 45-year-old man from Apucarana, Paraná, presented with one atypical lesion on the right side of his back of approximately one month’s duration. He had applied topical antibiotics before seeking care without improvement. On examination the lesion was a rounded plaque with an erythematous-violaceous center, desquamative ulcerated edges, and an extensive surrounding area of lichenification, measuring 20 cm, located on the right scapular/back region. Based on the clinical appearance, the initial differential diagnosis included chronic simple lichen, psoriasis, squamous cell carcinoma, chromomycosis, cutaneous tuberculosis, syphilis, paracoccidioidomycosis, and sarcoidosis.

A 59‑year‑old man, mixed ethnicity, unemployed, previously healthy, reported that an erythematous‑crusty lesion appeared in the region of the mental protuberance and over two months evolved to involve other parts of the body, including the frontal and occipital regions, nasal septum, ears, hands, and lower limbs. Oral examination showed scattered ulcers on the face, lower labial mucosa, and on the left lip commissure, a pseudomembrane on the marginal gingiva, and an exophytic nodule in the left labial mucosa. The patient had a positive Montenegro intradermal test and was admitted to the University Hospital in December 2018. After admission, clinicians noted enlarged lymph nodes of hard consistency in the left inguinal region and an extensive irregular melanocytic lesion in the left plantar region presenting an area of hyperkeratosis with a grey‑bluish center; the plantar lesion was biopsied for further evaluation. A PCR analysis had been performed in an external laboratory.

A 78-year-old man from a rural area in western Iran was referred for multiple ulcerative, exudative lesions involving the mid-face (upper lip and anterior nasal fossa), above the eyebrows, dorsal aspects of both hands, and posterior aspects of both heels. Lesions began three years earlier as papules on the dorsal hands and progressively enlarged to involve the face and heels and became ulcerative; involvement of the right hand progressed to destruction of tendons and soft tissue of the fifth finger, resulting in amputation of that finger. He had no history of comorbid conditions, no regular medications reported, and denied systemic symptoms — there was no weight loss, fever, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly or other signs of systemic involvement on examination or routine laboratory survey. Multiple prior empirical treatments for different presumed diagnoses, including pyoderma gangrenosum, sarcoidosis, and leishmaniasis, had been tried without improvement. An initial skin biopsy showed a necrotizing and palisading granulomatous tissue pattern that suggested an infectious etiology, but initial smears of lesion material for fungal elements, mycobacteria and Leishmania were negative. A tuberculin skin test produced a 27 mm induration, and anti-tuberculosis therapy (isoniazid, rifampin, ethambutol, and pyrazinamide) was started.

A 10-year-old neutered male domestic shorthair cat (5.2 kg, BCS 4/9) was evaluated for halitosis and several weeks of occasional discomfort and difficulty eating. The cat was a rescued animal with previous outdoor access and currently lives indoors alone. At adoption, immunologic tests for FIV and FeLV were negative. On clinical examination there was more severe periodontal disease on the right side and a right maxillary local stomatitis with a nodular, ulcerative appearance; on inspection the nodular lesion was slightly painful with spontaneous bleeding. Bilateral mandibular lymph node enlargement was present; no other abnormalities were noted. Under anesthesia a detailed oral exam and full-mouth radiographs demonstrated periodontal pocketing (7 mm) at the site of the nodular ulcero-hemorrhagic lesion (third right maxillary premolar), advanced periodontitis of multiple teeth on the right maxilla, tooth resorption in six teeth including the affected premolar, and radiographic vertical bone loss adjacent to the lesion. Treatment at that time included extraction of teeth with resorption and advanced attachment loss, routine closure of gingival flaps, and incisional biopsies of the maxillary lesion for histopathologic assessment. Two weeks after surgery the cat's appetite and weight had improved, but a nodular ulcero-hemorrhagic lesion with persistent swelling and inflammation of the right maxilla remained.

A 27-year-old man from central Iran noted a small pimple on his right upper eyelid 4 months before presentation. The eyelid lesion enlarged slowly. On examination it was a well-defined, firm, nontender, subcutaneous, skin-colored nodule measuring about 1 cm × 1 cm, with slightly erythematous, raised borders; it was crusty and painless. CBC, ESR, CRP, and blood chemistries were within normal limits. A sample culture of the lesion grew Staphylococcus aureus. The lesion was treated sequentially with cephalexin, cloxacillin, amoxicillin–clavulanate, and steroids for 10 days, but these treatments failed to heal the lesion. Because cutaneous leishmaniasis occurs in the patient's area of residence and because of the lack of response to treatment, cutaneous leishmaniasis or basal cell carcinoma was proposed as the differential diagnosis.

Photographs obtained at presentation show an irregular, ulcerated/crusted lesion involving the lateral margin of the right pinna and an exophytic, ulcerated nodular lesion on the caudal aspect of the right tarsus.

A 68-year-old man from a mountainous area in Hebei Province, China, presented with fever, sweating, and fatigue. He first sought care on February 1 and was hospitalized at a local hospital with temperature 39.0°C, chills, and no respiratory, abdominal, diarrheal, or urinary symptoms. He had lost approximately 10 kg over the prior 6 months. Initial blood tests showed pancytopenia, a rapid erythrocyte sedimentation rate, elevated C-reactive protein and ferritin, hyponatremia, hypokalemia, hypoproteinemia, and elevated serum enzyme levels. Bone marrow aspiration smear at that time showed granulocytopenia with megakaryocyte maturation disorder. Abdominal ultrasound showed splenomegaly; brain CT showed bilateral basal ganglia lacunar infarction; chest CT showed bilateral fibrotic/bronchitic changes. After 11 days of antibiotic and supportive treatment his fever and fatigue persisted with temperatures >39°C, so he presented for further evaluation on February 16. On arrival his SARS-CoV-2 PCR was negative. On examination he was febrile to 38.2°C, poorly nourished, unable to walk (bilateral leg strength grade 3), and had pitting edema of the anterior tibias and dorsal feet. Repeat laboratory testing again showed pancytopenia, increased ESR, CRP and ferritin, and elevated liver enzymes. Empiric antibiotic therapy had not relieved his febrile illness.

A 42‑year‑old man presented with 1 year of progressive weakness and significant weight loss and intermittent low‑grade fevers. He had been treated for pulmonary tuberculosis 2 years earlier and was recently restarted on antitubercular therapy for the past month without improvement. On examination he was thin, pale, afebrile, and had abdominal distension. Left submandibular and left axillary lymph nodes were palpable, each about 1.5 cm. Mild hepatosplenomegaly was noted. Ultrasound of the abdomen showed multiple enlarged conglomerate mesenteric lymph nodes, the largest 22 × 18 mm. Clinical chemistry showed reversal of the albumin:globulin ratio with total protein 9.5 g/dL, albumin 2.0 g/dL, globulin 7.5 g/dL. Other liver and renal tests were within normal limits. Complete blood count showed pancytopenia: hemoglobin 6 g/dL, total leukocyte count 1,800/µL (polymorphs 47%, lymphocytes 51%), platelets 48,000/µL; ESR 50 mm/h. Peripheral smear demonstrated rouleaux formation. Fine needle aspiration cytology of left submandibular and axillary lymph nodes yielded thick aspirate; smears showed few epithelioid cell granulomas interspersed with discrete aggregates of histiocytes in a background of reactive lymphoid cells and many plasma cells.

He had intermittent fever, nausea and vomiting for 5 months; prior local evaluation found pancytopenia and splenomegaly. Bone marrow imaging earlier showed dysplasia of megakaryocytes with visible plasma cells and markedly reduced proliferation. Five days before admission he developed fever to 39.5°C with chills, chest tightness and shortness of breath but without cough or sputum production. Piperacillin‑tazobactam was given without symptom relief. Bone marrow aspiration detected Leishmania amastigotes. Bone marrow hyperplasia was extremely reduced without an increase in immature cells or lymphocytes. Blood mNGS performed at the referring hospital detected 40904 Leishmania infantum, 17878 Leishmania donovani, and 13978 Leishmania chagasi sequence readings, and "combined with clinical symptoms, the diagnosis of 'visceral leishmaniasis' was made." On transfer, renal lab values were abnormal (serum glucose 16.31 mmol/L, urea 39.74 mmol/L, creatinine 286.2 mmol/L, uric acid 591 mmol/L), and because of renal dysfunction and concern about amphotericin B toxicity, sodium antimony gluconate was started. Chest X‑ray demonstrated bilateral pulmonary edema. After ventilatory support and diuretics the pulmonary edema improved on chest X‑ray and respiratory symptoms were relieved. On July 6, 2022, blood smear and bone marrow cytology revealed no Leishmania bodies. Nevertheless, pancytopenia and respiratory failure did not fully resolve and cardiotoxic damage appeared.

A 55-year-old man with chronic severe hepatitis B (HBV‑DNA positive) was admitted for intermittent fever of 1 month (maximum 40°C). He had worked on a farm in Xinjiang Province one month earlier. On examination he had hepatosplenomegaly below the costal margin. Initial laboratory tests showed marked hepatic abnormalities (ALT 490 U/L, AST 558 U/L), low total protein and albumin (TP 51.54 g/L, ALB 26.83 g/L), TBIL 23.23 μmol/L, DBIL 14.37 μmol/L, and HBV‑DNA 3.19 × 10^4 IU/mL. Routine blood counts were abnormal (WBC 3.12 × 10^9/L, platelets 100 × 10^9/L). After 2 weeks the patient remained febrile with worsening labs (WBC 0.95 × 10^9/L, platelets 56 × 10^9/L, ALT 524 U/L, AST 640 U/L). Abdominal enhanced CT showed an enlarged spleen with multiple low‑density nodules that demonstrated sustained/delayed enhancement; angioma/hemangioma was suspected. 18F‑FDG PET/CT demonstrated a significant diffuse increase in FDG uptake in the enlarged spleen (SUVmax 6.6) and slightly diffuse bone‑marrow uptake. Bone‑marrow aspiration and biopsy were performed twice (2 months apart) and both showed phagocytosis of reticulum cells. Based on the clinical and imaging findings, splenic lymphoma was considered highly likely. The patient received chemotherapy for hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) and was discharged in remission, but was readmitted 2 months later with recurrent fever and pancytopenia; splenectomy was then undertaken to establish a diagnosis and reduce disease burden.

A 65-year-old man presented with diffuse abdominal pain for one year, 14 kg weight loss and fever for 4 months. The fever occurred once or twice daily with profuse sweating and shivers. He had no prior illnesses recorded and was a long‑time smoker. On examination he had swollen lymph nodes in several body regions; the largest measured 3 cm in the left inguinal region. Laboratory tests showed elevated C-reactive protein (99.9 mg/L), normocytic normochromic anemia (hemoglobin 11.1 g/dL; hematocrit 32.4%), sodium 130 mEq/L, leucocytes 5300/mm3 (neutrophils 3260/mm3; lymphocytes 910/mm3), gamma-glutamyl transferase 570 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 574 U/L, and beta-2 microglobulin 3.3 mcg/mL; all other routine blood tests, blood cultures, electrolytes, and kidney and liver functions were reported as normal. The following serologic tests were negative: HIV, syphilis, hepatitis C and B, toxoplasmosis, CMV, EBV, rk39 rapid test, enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay, and indirect immunofluorescence for L. (L.) major-like antigen. Positron emission tomography showed increased glycolytic metabolism in several lymph nodes (some forming conglomerates) above and below the diaphragm, with increased glycolytic metabolism in the spleen, liver and bones, findings described as suggestive of a lymphoproliferative disorder. Bone marrow aspiration identified the presence of Leishmania spp. on direct microscopy.

A 74-year-old woman from Tunis presented with several weeks of fever (oral temperature 38–39°C), sweats, chills, fatigue, diarrhea, intermittent vague abdominal pain, and occasional dry cough. Her only medical history was well-controlled hypertension. Examination showed a palpable spleen just below the left costal margin. On the right arm near the axilla there was "a single well-defined, ulcer surrounded by erythematous edging, with serous oozing" about 3 × 3 cm; the patient reported the lesion was painless, nonhealing, and present for 2–3 years. A Leishmania rk39 immunochromatography test was positive. Bone marrow aspiration parasitology revealed Leishmania amastigote forms, and serum immunofluorescence for Leishmania antibodies was positive (titer 1:400). Blood qPCR detected Leishmania DNA (400 parasites/mL). Direct microscopy of skin smears from the arm lesion showed no amastigotes, but Leishmania DNA amplification was obtained from dermal DNA extract by qPCR. ITS1 sequencing showed the Leishmania strains from the blood and the arm lesion corresponded to L. infantum and were 100% identical. Systemic response was rapid: fever resolved, general condition improved, splenomegaly regressed, blood counts normalized, and blood qPCR became negative after 28 days. However, "the skin lesion did not improve although Leishmania qPCR on dermal sample became negative." A skin biopsy was initially refused. One year later the lesion remained essentially unchanged.

A 47-year-old man presented to the emergency department with recurrent fever for 4 months and worsening symptoms including diarrhea for 1 month. About 4 months earlier he developed fever up to 39.9 °C that typically occurred in the afternoon and lasted several hours; associated symptoms included headache, myalgia, and nausea. After a temporary resolution he had a relapse with persistent high fever and frequent yellow watery diarrhea (>10 times/day). Past medical history included malaria diagnosed 6 years earlier in Africa treated with quinine. He reported hypersensitivity to quinolones (e.g., moxifloxacin). On admission, novel coronavirus nucleic acid test was negative. The schistosoma japonicum IgG antibody, echinococcus granulosus antibody, liver fluke antibody test, plasmodium antigen test, and blood smear test were all negative. Tests for hepatitis A and B, autoimmune liver disease markers, AFP, and CEA were negative. Abdominal ultrasound showed hepatomegaly and splenomegaly (intercostal spleen thickness ~7.0 cm). Chest and plain abdominal CT reported cirrhosis, splenomegaly, portal hypertension with collateral circulation, and peritoneal effusion. The admitting team considered sepsis and fever of undetermined origin (infection vs tumor) and noted Child-Pugh B decompensated cirrhosis. An emergency metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) blood test was sent to try to identify an occult pathogen.

A male born June 26, 1986, was seen at a tropical diseases referral center. Between 2009 and 2011 he was hospitalized seven times with a consistent diagnosis of kala-azar. He received multiple recommended treatments during these hospitalizations, including pentavalent antimony (glucantime, 20 mg of Sb + 5 kg/d for 30 d in the first hospitalization), liposomal amphotericin B (for 14 d at 3 mg/kg/d in three subsequent hospitalizations), and pentamidine in the last hospitalization before surgery (4 mg/kg/d every other day, total 15 doses), with only transient symptomatic improvement followed by recurrence. He had a negative HIV serological test. During two hospitalizations he presented with anemia and was transfused twice with packed red blood cells. After all possibilities of medical treatment were exhausted and the patient maintained a pancytopenia profile on blood counts attributed to hypersplenism, splenectomy was recommended. In January 2012 he was hospitalized for the planned surgical procedure. His clinical examination revealed mucocutaneous pallor (2+/4+), fever (38.5 C), dehydration (2+/4+), a distended abdomen with mild pain on deep palpation, and splenomegaly 8 cm below the left costal margin. Laboratory testing showed anemia, leukopenia, hypergammaglobulinemia, and elevated ESR and CRP.

A 47-year-old man presented to the emergency department on December 28, 2020 with recurrent fever for 4 months and worsening symptoms with diarrhea for 1 month. About 4 months earlier he developed fever without an evident cause, with a maximum temperature of 39.9 C; fevers usually occurred in the afternoon, lasted several hours, and were associated with headache, myalgia, and nausea. After a period of apparent improvement he redeveloped persistent high fever (≈39 C) accompanied by yellow watery diarrhea more than 10 times per day. Six years previously he had been diagnosed with malaria in Africa and treated with quinine. On admission: Novel Coronavirus nucleic acid test was negative. The cryptococcus antigen test, fungal G test, and GM test were negative. Serologic and parasitologic tests including schistosoma japonicum IgG antibody, echinococcus granulosus antibody, liver fluke antibody test, plasmodium antigen test, and blood smear were all negative. Chest and plain abdominal CT demonstrated cirrhosis, splenomegaly, portal hypertension with collateral circulation, and peritoneal effusion. The team considered sepsis and fever of undetermined origin (infection versus tumor) and assessed the patient as Child-Pugh B decompensated cirrhosis. An emergency blood metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) test was sent to help diagnose the fever of unknown cause.

contexts.text: A 30‑year‑old man presented with pain in his lower limbs and a non‑itchy erythematous rash over both lower limbs. He had low‑grade intermittent fever for three months. Initial testing showed: anti‑nuclear antibodies, complement levels (C3 = 94 mg/dL and C4 = 20 mg/dL), and rheumatoid factor were negative; urine examination was normal and serum cryoglobulins were not raised. Viral markers (HIV, hepatitis B surface antigen, and anti‑hepatitis C) were negative. Serology for rickettsia and scrub typhus were also negative.

A 65-year-old woman was admitted in March after collapsing in the street. She had been unwell for 14 months with night sweats and progressive loss of energy but denied fever. On examination she was afebrile and had hepatic enlargement and lymphadenopathy; liver function tests were within reference limits. Initial blood tests showed hemoglobin 8.1 g/dL, leukocyte count 4.62 × 10^9/L, and platelet count 143 × 10^9/L. Serologic tests for HIV, hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and Strongyloides spp. were negative. Her CD4 count was 790 cells/μL, rheumatoid factor was weakly positive, and immunoglobulin levels were within reference ranges. She was born in Guyana and had recent travel to Guyana in 2012 and 2013, to Grenada in 2012, to Ghana in 2005, and to France in 2003. Because a hematologic malignancy was suspected, a bone marrow aspiration was performed; Leishmania amastigotes were visible. Leishmania serology was negative by an rK39 rapid test and weakly positive by direct agglutination (1:3,200; cutoff 1:1,600).

He had intermittent fever, nausea and vomiting for 5 months; prior local evaluation found pancytopenia and splenomegaly. Bone marrow imaging earlier showed dysplasia of megakaryocytes with visible plasma cells and markedly reduced proliferation. Five days before admission he developed fever to 39.5°C with chills, chest tightness and shortness of breath but without cough or sputum production. Piperacillin‑tazobactam was given without symptom relief. Bone marrow aspiration detected Leishmania amastigotes. Bone marrow hyperplasia was extremely reduced without an increase in immature cells or lymphocytes. Blood mNGS performed at the referring hospital detected 40904 Leishmania infantum, 17878 Leishmania donovani, and 13978 Leishmania chagasi sequence readings, and "combined with clinical symptoms, the diagnosis of 'visceral leishmaniasis' was made." On transfer, renal lab values were abnormal (serum glucose 16.31 mmol/L, urea 39.74 mmol/L, creatinine 286.2 mmol/L, uric acid 591 mmol/L), and because of renal dysfunction and concern about amphotericin B toxicity, sodium antimony gluconate was started. Chest X‑ray demonstrated bilateral pulmonary edema. After ventilatory support and diuretics the pulmonary edema improved on chest X‑ray and respiratory symptoms were relieved. On July 6, 2022, blood smear and bone marrow cytology revealed no Leishmania bodies. Nevertheless, pancytopenia and respiratory failure did not fully resolve and cardiotoxic damage appeared.

A 22‑month‑old girl presented with 8 days of fever to 40°C and mild cough. Past history: failure to thrive; normal neurologic development. She was the first child of a non‑consanguineous couple; no family history of albinism; normal hair and skin. On exam she was stunted, pale, had non‑tender hepatomegaly 5–6 cm and splenomegaly palpable 4 cm below the left costal margin. Petechial rash developed on the chest and legs as she worsened. Initial laboratory results: WBC 5100/mm3 (ANC 1200/mm3), Hb 9.1 g/dl, platelets 47,000/mm3; mild transaminase elevation; hypoalbuminemia. Ferritin 1,134 ng/ml; soluble IL‑2 receptor (sCD25) 3,183 U/ml. Blood cultures were negative. Serum immunoglobulins and lymphocyte subsets were reported as normal. Infectious testing: EBV serology positive for IgM and IgG anti‑VCA with negative IgG anti‑EBNA; EBV viral load 637 copies/ml. Leishmania testing was discordant: immunochromatography and indirect immunofluorescence were negative, serum ELISA was slightly positive, and leishmanial antigen in urine was negative. Bone‑marrow aspiration revealed hemophagocytosis. Over the next day she clinically worsened with progressive splenomegaly and cytopenias (WBC 4,800/mm3 with ANC 800/mm3, Hb 6.8 g/dl, platelets 27,000/mm3), triglycerides 686 mg/dl, ferritin 3,849 ng/ml, and sCD25 3,596 U/ml. Clotting tests were normal and perforin expression by flow cytometry was reported as normal.

A 74-year-old woman from Tunis presented with several weeks of fever (oral temperature 38–39°C), sweats, chills, fatigue, diarrhea, intermittent vague abdominal pain, and occasional dry cough. Her only medical history was well-controlled hypertension. Examination showed a palpable spleen just below the left costal margin. On the right arm near the axilla there was "a single well-defined, ulcer surrounded by erythematous edging, with serous oozing" about 3 × 3 cm; the patient reported the lesion was painless, nonhealing, and present for 2–3 years. A Leishmania rk39 immunochromatography test was positive. Bone marrow aspiration parasitology revealed Leishmania amastigote forms, and serum immunofluorescence for Leishmania antibodies was positive (titer 1:400). Blood qPCR detected Leishmania DNA (400 parasites/mL). Direct microscopy of skin smears from the arm lesion showed no amastigotes, but Leishmania DNA amplification was obtained from dermal DNA extract by qPCR. ITS1 sequencing showed the Leishmania strains from the blood and the arm lesion corresponded to L. infantum and were 100% identical. Systemic response was rapid: fever resolved, general condition improved, splenomegaly regressed, blood counts normalized, and blood qPCR became negative after 28 days. However, "the skin lesion did not improve although Leishmania qPCR on dermal sample became negative." A skin biopsy was initially refused. One year later the lesion remained essentially unchanged.

A 60-year-old woman from Uttar Pradesh, India presented with a six‑week history of high‑grade continuous fever with chills and rigors, anorexia, malaise, joint pains, and severe lethargy. She reported "crops of round, raised lesions" that began on the left upper limb, progressed to the right upper limb and then involved the whole face, upper back, chest, and upper abdomen; the lesions were "closely associated with the febrile episodes." Some lesions enlarged, became nodular, developed sunken centers that drained pus‑like material, and were painful and red. One week before admission she developed jaundice with mild to moderate upper‑quadrant abdominal pain. She had no prior comorbidities, was a teetotaler, and denied taking over‑the‑counter or steroid/complementary medications or other potentially immunosuppressive drugs. Pallor and icterus were present; there was bilateral pitting, non‑tender symmetrical pedal edema. Skin exam showed "multiple crops of nodular, noduloulcerative, and papular lesions, dispersed throughout the body surface, mostly segregated to the face and upper back," some with pus drainage from central sunken areas. Laboratory studies: hemoglobin 10.5 g/dL, total leukocyte count 5600/mm3, platelet count 80,000/mm3, ESR 80 mm/hr with normocytic normochromic anemia. Liver tests: total bilirubin 3.2 mg/dL (direct 1.8), AST 50 IU/L, ALT 60 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 221 IU/L, GGT 150 IU/L, albumin 1.9 g/dL, INR 1.3. Serum IgG 22.6 g/L.

A 68-year-old man from a mountainous area in Hebei Province, China, presented with fever, sweating, and fatigue. He first sought care on February 1 and was hospitalized at a local hospital with temperature 39.0°C, chills, and no respiratory, abdominal, diarrheal, or urinary symptoms. He had lost approximately 10 kg over the prior 6 months. Initial blood tests showed pancytopenia, a rapid erythrocyte sedimentation rate, elevated C-reactive protein and ferritin, hyponatremia, hypokalemia, hypoproteinemia, and elevated serum enzyme levels. Bone marrow aspiration smear at that time showed granulocytopenia with megakaryocyte maturation disorder. Abdominal ultrasound showed splenomegaly; brain CT showed bilateral basal ganglia lacunar infarction; chest CT showed bilateral fibrotic/bronchitic changes. After 11 days of antibiotic and supportive treatment his fever and fatigue persisted with temperatures >39°C, so he presented for further evaluation on February 16. On arrival his SARS-CoV-2 PCR was negative. On examination he was febrile to 38.2°C, poorly nourished, unable to walk (bilateral leg strength grade 3), and had pitting edema of the anterior tibias and dorsal feet. Repeat laboratory testing again showed pancytopenia, increased ESR, CRP and ferritin, and elevated liver enzymes. Empiric antibiotic therapy had not relieved his febrile illness.

A 15-year-old female from the Macanao municipality on Margarita Island, Venezuela presented with a 6-month history of intermittent fever predominantly occurring at night, malaise, 6 kg weight loss, arthralgias, loss of appetite, dizziness, and amenorrhea. She lives in a rural area close to a landfill in a house built with cement ground, brick walls, and a metal roof without running water. She has one dog (unknown Leishmania infection status) and various turtles as pets. She has no history of traveling outside Venezuela. On examination she was pale, with increased respiratory and heart rate, and a fever of 39 C. Weight was 49 kg, height 1.57 m, and abdominal circumference 76 cm. She had cervical, axillary, and inguinal adenopathy. Cardiac and lung exams were normal. Abdominal exam revealed right upper-quadrant tenderness and hepatosplenomegaly (liver palpable 9.5 cm from the midclavicular line; spleen Hackett grade V). Laboratory values on admission demonstrated pancytopenia. Abdominal ultrasound and computed tomography confirmed hepatosplenomegaly. The initial clinical suspicion was a lymphoproliferative or myeloproliferative disorder. From an infectious disease perspective, the possibility of visceral leishmaniasis, a systemic mycosis, or tuberculosis were entertained. A bone marrow biopsy was performed to rule out a hematologic malignancy and to assess for infectious causes.

A 52-year-old woman from Jiuzhaigou, Sichuan province, China, presented with an unprovoked high fever beginning January 9, 2021. The body temperature reached 39.6 C and was accompanied by coughing, sputum expectoration, tiredness, anhelation, chilliness, and shivering. Initial evaluation included ultrasound of the urinary system, brain MRI, and chest CT, which showed no significant abnormality on those studies. She was treated empirically with ceftriaxone and clindamycin and received methylprednisolone; after a week the cough, sputum production, fatigue, and shortness of breath improved, but the fever persisted. On January 13, a bone marrow aspiration smear showed a low proliferation rate of nucleated cells, a decreased granulocyte/erythrocyte ratio, some erythroblasts with abnormal morphology, significantly reduced iron content in the marrow, and poor platelet production by megakaryocytes with scattered and clustered platelets observed. On January 14, routine blood tests demonstrated decreased white blood cells, red blood cells, hemoglobin, and platelets. She had a history of hypertension, diabetes, and anemia. Chest CT showed splenomegaly, and abdominal ultrasound revealed hepatosplenomegaly. Repeat bone-marrow testing on January 19 showed active bone-marrow hyperplasia with some dysplastic changes (>10%) in erythroid cells. Karyotype and gene-mutation analysis for myeloid blood diseases performed on January 20–21 showed no significant abnormalities.

A 56-year-old male farmer from Jinghe County in Xinjiang (northwestern China) with a 10-year history of coronary heart disease and 5 years of type 2 diabetes mellitus presented with sudden onset of fever and right upper abdominal pain beginning November 14, 2022. He had lived in Jinghe County for over 40 years and reported no travel history to areas endemic for visceral leishmaniasis. He initially sought care at two local hospitals and "was diagnosed with suspected pneumonia" and received a 15-day course of intravenous levofloxacin and ribavirin with supportive measures, but "the response to this treatment was inadequate." On admission to the tertiary fever clinic on November 29, 2022 his temperature was 38.5 C, pulse 80/min, respirations 20/min, and blood pressure 137/70 mmHg. Abdominal examination revealed tenderness in the right upper quadrant without rebound; the liver and spleen were not initially palpable below the rib cage, although during the course of the illness he developed abdominal pain, hepatomegaly, and jaundice. Laboratory testing showed leukopenia (3.10 x 10^9/L) and mild anemia (hemoglobin 99.0 g/L). Liver enzymes were elevated: ALT 168 U/L, AST 281 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 646 U/L, and gamma-GT 586 U/L. C-reactive protein was 52.3 mg/L and procalcitonin 0.21 ng/mL; renal function was within the normal range. Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated thickening of the gallbladder wall and hepatomegaly and splenomegaly.

A 74-year-old man from Yangquan City, Shanxi Province, presented with more than six months of generalized fatigue and pancytopenia. Prior intermittent evaluations included bone marrow aspirations that reportedly showed no special abnormalities. On admission he was afebrile; examination showed pallor and scattered hyperpigmented skin lesions from scratching. Liver was palpable 5 cm below the right costal margin; spleen was palpable 8 cm below the left costal margin. Abdominal ultrasound and CT reported hepatomegaly, cirrhotic-appearing liver, splenomegaly and ascites (spleen longitudinal diameter up to ~19–21 cm on serial imaging). Laboratory testing demonstrated persistent pancytopenia. Initial infectious-serology testing showed a positive HCV antibody; repeat hepatitis C antigen and antibody testing later returned negative. Tumor markers were negative. Hematology testing included a positive direct antiglobulin test; CD55 and CD59 testing were normal. Immunology testing showed elevated IgG and positive anti-cardiolipin antibody IgG and IgM. Multiple blood transfusions had little effect on the anemia. Repeat peripheral smear and bone marrow evaluation demonstrated some toxic granules in mature granulocytes but otherwise no diagnostic abnormalities and no parasites were seen.

A 44‑year‑old man from Shanxi Province with a 5‑year history of antisynthetase antibody syndrome on cyclosporine A was admitted in January 2020 with fever to 38.6°C. He reported exertional breathlessness (after walking ~100 m) and increasing weakness; broad‑spectrum antimicrobials produced no improvement. By March 2020 he had persistent fever. Laboratory results then showed WBC 1.3 × 10^9/L, hemoglobin 96 g/L, platelets 113 × 10^9/L, fibrinogen 1.36 g/L, serum ferritin >1500 μg/L, NK‑cell activity 14.96%, and soluble CD25 12,947 pg/mL; ALT, AST, CK and CK‑MB were normal. The clinical picture met criteria for hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH), and treatment was started with methylprednisolone (10 mg/kg per day) and etoposide (100 mg/m^2). After 2 weeks the patient became afebrile and WBC rose to 10.8 × 10^9/L, hemoglobin was 95 g/L and platelets 55 × 10^9/L. In June 2020, during prednisone taper, he redeveloped high fever to 39.5°C, was unable to stand independently, and subsequently had pancytopenia with recurrence of high ferritin, low NK‑cell activity, markedly elevated sCD25, splenomegaly, and hemophagocytosis on bone marrow examination.

A 55-year-old man with chronic severe hepatitis B (HBV‑DNA positive) was admitted for intermittent fever of 1 month (maximum 40°C). He had worked on a farm in Xinjiang Province one month earlier. On examination he had hepatosplenomegaly below the costal margin. Initial laboratory tests showed marked hepatic abnormalities (ALT 490 U/L, AST 558 U/L), low total protein and albumin (TP 51.54 g/L, ALB 26.83 g/L), TBIL 23.23 μmol/L, DBIL 14.37 μmol/L, and HBV‑DNA 3.19 × 10^4 IU/mL. Routine blood counts were abnormal (WBC 3.12 × 10^9/L, platelets 100 × 10^9/L). After 2 weeks the patient remained febrile with worsening labs (WBC 0.95 × 10^9/L, platelets 56 × 10^9/L, ALT 524 U/L, AST 640 U/L). Abdominal enhanced CT showed an enlarged spleen with multiple low‑density nodules that demonstrated sustained/delayed enhancement; angioma/hemangioma was suspected. 18F‑FDG PET/CT demonstrated a significant diffuse increase in FDG uptake in the enlarged spleen (SUVmax 6.6) and slightly diffuse bone‑marrow uptake. Bone‑marrow aspiration and biopsy were performed twice (2 months apart) and both showed phagocytosis of reticulum cells. Based on the clinical and imaging findings, splenic lymphoma was considered highly likely. The patient received chemotherapy for hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) and was discharged in remission, but was readmitted 2 months later with recurrent fever and pancytopenia; splenectomy was then undertaken to establish a diagnosis and reduce disease burden.

A 25-year-old man presented with a left-sided upper abdominal lump and multiple skin lesions present for the last 12 years. The abdominal lump had been very slowly increasing in size, was painless and produced a mild dragging sensation. The skin lesions were present primarily on his back and abdomen; they were described as depigmented, painless, and non-itchy. He denied current fever, loss of appetite, weight loss, cough, jaundice, hematemesis, melaena, and blood transfusion. He reported a history of kala-azar 15 years earlier treated with an injectable medication (he could not recall the drug name). He was a known chronic hepatitis B patient on entecavir 1 mg once daily. On examination there were multiple hypo- and hyperpigmented macular and maculopapular non-scaly skin lesions distributed over the trunk (mainly back, chest, and abdomen); lesion size ranged from a few millimeters (0.3–0.7 mm) for hypopigmented spots to 1–3 cm for hyperpigmented lesions, and sensation over the lesions was intact. Other vital signs were normal. Abdominal examination showed firm, non-tender hepatosplenomegaly with the liver 4 cm below the right costal margin and the spleen 6 cm along its long axis.

A 47-year-old man presented to the emergency department with recurrent fever for 4 months and worsening symptoms including diarrhea for 1 month. About 4 months earlier he developed fever up to 39.9 °C that typically occurred in the afternoon and lasted several hours; associated symptoms included headache, myalgia, and nausea. After a temporary resolution he had a relapse with persistent high fever and frequent yellow watery diarrhea (>10 times/day). Past medical history included malaria diagnosed 6 years earlier in Africa treated with quinine. He reported hypersensitivity to quinolones (e.g., moxifloxacin). The cryptococcus antigen test, fungal G test, and GM test were negative. The schistosoma japonicum IgG antibody, echinococcus granulosus antibody, liver fluke antibody test, plasmodium antigen test, and blood smear test were all negative. Tests for hepatitis A and B, autoimmune liver disease markers, AFP, and CEA were negative. Abdominal ultrasound showed hepatomegaly and splenomegaly (intercostal spleen thickness ~7.0 cm). Chest and plain abdominal CT reported cirrhosis, splenomegaly, portal hypertension with collateral circulation, and peritoneal effusion. The admitting team considered sepsis and fever of undetermined origin (infection vs tumor) and noted Child-Pugh B decompensated cirrhosis. An emergency metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) blood test was sent to try to identify an occult pathogen.

About 4 months earlier he developed fever without an evident cause, with a maximum temperature of 39.9 C; fevers usually occurred in the afternoon, lasted several hours, and were associated with headache, myalgia, and nausea. After a period of apparent improvement he redeveloped persistent high fever (≈39 C) accompanied by yellow watery diarrhea more than 10 times per day. Six years previously he had been diagnosed with malaria in Africa and treated with quinine. On admission: Novel Coronavirus nucleic acid test was negative. An emergency blood metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) test was sent to help diagnose the fever of unknown cause.

contexts.text: A 78-year-old man from a rural area in western Iran was referred for multiple ulcerative, exudative lesions involving the mid-face (upper lip and anterior nasal fossa), above the eyebrows, dorsal aspects of both hands, and posterior aspects of both heels. An initial skin biopsy showed a necrotizing and palisading granulomatous tissue pattern that suggested an infectious etiology, but initial smears of lesion material for fungal elements, mycobacteria and Leishmania were negative. A tuberculin skin test produced a 27 mm induration, and anti-tuberculosis therapy (isoniazid, rifampin, ethambutol, and pyrazinamide) was started.

A 52-year-old male farm worker from Ceara state, northeast Brazil, presented with a 4-month history of skin lesions. Lesions appeared first on the face and legs, than spread across much of his body, including the genitalia, soles of feet, and scalp. He reported daily fevers for the first 2 weeks of illness. On examination the patient had 178 lesions of different sizes and aspects; ulcerated, crusted, papular, nodular, and pustular. Many had apparent bacterial superinfections. The remainder of the physical examination was normal. A complete blood count and liver and kidney function tests were within normal limits. Serological tests for syphilis and human immunodeficiency virus were negative.

A 52-year-old woman presented with a single lesion on the tip of her nose that had existed for 14 months. It began as a papule and was slowly increasing in size, enlarging to a plaque. A smear of the lesion performed about 1 year earlier was positive, "showing leishmania bodies." All five members of her family had a history of proven leishmaniasis. Her past medical history was notable for renal failure diagnosed 11 years earlier; she "received a renal transplant 4 years after the diagnosis of renal failure." She also had hypertension and hyperlipidemia and was taking oral mycophenolate mofetil (2 g daily) and cyclosporine (100 mg daily). Skin examination showed skin type IV, "No actinic keratosis was present," and a 3x3 cm indurated ulcer with elevated borders was present on the tip of her nose. The therapeutic plan was intralesional glucantime injections (approximately 1 ml of 1.5 g vial per week). "After completing a therapeutic course of 20 sessions receiving intralesional glucantime injections, she was considered as glucantime therapy resistant."

A 55-year-old man from the Manaus region with no comorbidities had been treated for cutaneous leishmaniasis. He had completed treatment with a pentavalent antimonial drug 40 days earlier and had received a second outpatient 30-day cycle; ten days after the end of that treatment his leishmaniasis lesion was healed. He then developed grouped microvesicles on an erythematous-infiltrated base that began in the neck and ascended toward the right scalp margin. The vesicles involved the right pinna, external auditory canal, and right ear lobe and were associated with severe torticollis-like pain along the nerve distribution. HIV serology was negative.

A 38‑year‑old man from Yayu district, western Ethiopia, presented to the outpatient clinic with multiple skin lesions on his face and hands and mutilation of the nose; his upper lip was injured and swollen. Eight years earlier he had a small papule on the right cheek that progressed to an open ulcer, then to ulcers on the left cheek and forehead; those active lesions lasted about six months and healed spontaneously, leaving permanent hypopigmented scars. He had no fever, hepatosplenomegaly or lymphedema and reported no history of HIV, chronic disease, alcohol abuse, or immunomodulatory drug use. Parasitological testing of lesion smears at that time showed many macrophages filled with amastigote stages of Leishmania, graded as +6. A nonreactive rK39 rapid diagnostic test and absence of related systemic signs made visceral leishmaniasis unlikely. Based on the clinical manifestations and smear result he was diagnosed with mucocutaneous leishmaniasis and treated with intramuscular sodium stibogluconate (20 mg/kg/day for 30 days) with clinical cure. Two years later he returned with a different cutaneous eruption that had appeared over the previous three months and had been preceded by intense itching. On exam he had multiple, nonpitting, closed papules on his face, nose, hands and legs. A skin smear again showed intramacrophage amastigotes with a parasite load graded +6, and culture grew promastigotes.

A 27-year-old man from central Iran noted a small pimple on his right upper eyelid 4 months before presentation. The eyelid lesion enlarged slowly. On examination it was a well-defined, firm, nontender, subcutaneous, skin-colored nodule measuring about 1 cm × 1 cm, with slightly erythematous, raised borders; it was crusty and painless. CBC, ESR, CRP, and blood chemistries were within normal limits. A sample culture of the lesion grew Staphylococcus aureus. The lesion was treated sequentially with cephalexin, cloxacillin, amoxicillin–clavulanate, and steroids for 10 days, but these treatments failed to heal the lesion. Because cutaneous leishmaniasis occurs in the patient's area of residence and because of the lack of response to treatment, cutaneous leishmaniasis or basal cell carcinoma was proposed as the differential diagnosis.

Intrabuccal exam revealed a granulomatous lesion involving the entire palate and uvula, extending bilaterally to the pharynx with an erythematous appearance and areas of scratchable white plaques.

She initially noted a papule in the left malar region that later ulcerated and increased in size. Fifteen days after the facial lesion appeared, she developed another lesion on the right knee.

Her only medical history was well-controlled hypertension. Examination showed a palpable spleen just below the left costal margin. On the right arm near the axilla there was "a single well-defined, ulcer surrounded by erythematous edging, with serous oozing" about 3 × 3 cm; the patient reported the lesion was painless, nonhealing, and present for 2–3 years. The rest of the exam was essentially normal. A Leishmania rk39 immunochromatography test was positive. Bone marrow aspiration parasitology revealed Leishmania amastigote forms, and serum immunofluorescence for Leishmania antibodies was positive (titer 1:400). Blood qPCR detected Leishmania DNA (400 parasites/mL). Direct microscopy of skin smears from the arm lesion showed no amastigotes, but Leishmania DNA amplification was obtained from dermal DNA extract by qPCR. ITS1 sequencing showed the Leishmania strains from the blood and the arm lesion corresponded to L. infantum and were 100% identical. Systemic response was rapid: fever resolved, general condition improved, splenomegaly regressed, blood counts normalized, and blood qPCR became negative after 28 days. However, "the skin lesion did not improve although Leishmania qPCR on dermal sample became negative." A skin biopsy was initially refused. One year later the lesion remained essentially unchanged. A polarized dermoscopy examination showed "ulcerations and short, fine arborizing vessels," described as evocative of a basal cell carcinoma.

A 78-year-old man from a rural area in western Iran was referred for multiple ulcerative, exudative lesions involving the mid-face (upper lip and anterior nasal fossa), above the eyebrows, dorsal aspects of both hands, and posterior aspects of both heels. Lesions began three years earlier as papules on the dorsal hands and progressively enlarged to involve the face and heels and became ulcerative; involvement of the right hand progressed to destruction of tendons and soft tissue of the fifth finger, resulting in amputation of that finger. He had no history of comorbid conditions, no regular medications reported, and denied systemic symptoms — there was no weight loss, fever, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly or other signs of systemic involvement on examination or routine laboratory survey. Multiple prior empirical treatments for different presumed diagnoses, including pyoderma gangrenosum, sarcoidosis, and leishmaniasis, had been tried without improvement. An initial skin biopsy showed a necrotizing and palisading granulomatous tissue pattern that suggested an infectious etiology, but initial smears of lesion material for fungal elements, mycobacteria and Leishmania were negative. A tuberculin skin test produced a 27 mm induration, and anti-tuberculosis therapy (isoniazid, rifampin, ethambutol, and pyrazinamide) was started.

A 52-year-old male farm worker from Ceara state, northeast Brazil, presented with a 4-month history of skin lesions. Lesions appeared first on the face and legs, than spread across much of his body, including the genitalia, soles of feet, and scalp. He reported daily fevers for the first 2 weeks of illness. On examination the patient had 178 lesions of different sizes and aspects; ulcerated, crusted, papular, nodular, and pustular. Many had apparent bacterial superinfections. The remainder of the physical examination was normal. A complete blood count and liver and kidney function tests were within normal limits. Serological tests for syphilis and human immunodeficiency virus were negative.

A 55-year-old man from the Manaus region with no comorbidities had been treated for cutaneous leishmaniasis. He had completed treatment with a pentavalent antimonial drug 40 days earlier and had received a second outpatient 30-day cycle; ten days after the end of that treatment his leishmaniasis lesion was healed. He then developed grouped microvesicles on an erythematous-infiltrated base that began in the neck and ascended toward the right scalp margin. The vesicles involved the right pinna, external auditory canal, and right ear lobe and were associated with severe torticollis-like pain along the nerve distribution. HIV serology was negative.

A 22‑month‑old girl presented with 8 days of fever to 40°C and mild cough. Past history: failure to thrive; normal neurologic development. She was the first child of a non‑consanguineous couple; no family history of albinism; normal hair and skin. On exam she was stunted, pale, had non‑tender hepatomegaly 5–6 cm and splenomegaly palpable 4 cm below the left costal margin. Petechial rash developed on the chest and legs as she worsened. Initial laboratory results: WBC 5100/mm3 (ANC 1200/mm3), Hb 9.1 g/dl, platelets 47,000/mm3; mild transaminase elevation; hypoalbuminemia. Ferritin 1,134 ng/ml; soluble IL‑2 receptor (sCD25) 3,183 U/ml. Blood cultures were negative. Serum immunoglobulins and lymphocyte subsets were reported as normal. Infectious testing: EBV serology positive for IgM and IgG anti‑VCA with negative IgG anti‑EBNA; EBV viral load 637 copies/ml. Leishmania testing was discordant: immunochromatography and indirect immunofluorescence were negative, serum ELISA was slightly positive, and leishmanial antigen in urine was negative. Bone‑marrow aspiration revealed hemophagocytosis. Over the next day she clinically worsened with progressive splenomegaly and cytopenias (WBC 4,800/mm3 with ANC 800/mm3, Hb 6.8 g/dl, platelets 27,000/mm3), triglycerides 686 mg/dl, ferritin 3,849 ng/ml, and sCD25 3,596 U/ml. Clotting tests were normal and perforin expression by flow cytometry was reported as normal.

An atypical infection was considered.

contexts.text: A 60‑year‑old Austrian man presented in September 2016 with a three‑week history of fever of unknown origin, fatigue, and unintentional weight loss of 6 kg. Initial physical examination was inconspicuous. His medical history was notable for adequately treated diabetes mellitus type 2 and hypothyroidism. Travel history included a two‑week trip to the south of Crete in September 2015 and a two‑week trip the south of Spain in May 2016. Laboratory tests showed markedly elevated C‑reactive protein (CRP 94.2–188.9 mg/L), slight hypochromic normocytic anemia without signs of hemolysis (hemoglobin 12.5 g/dL), mild thrombocytopenia (127,000/µL), and a discreetly elevated gamma‑glutamyltransferase (GGT). The soluble interleukin‑2 receptor (IL‑2R) was elevated to 5156.1 pg/mL. Chest x‑ray, urine analysis, abdominal sonography, transthoracic and transesophageal echocardiography revealed no focus of infection but did show splenomegaly (7.2 × 16.4 cm). Empiric antibiotic therapy (initially ampicillin/sulbactam, later piperacillin/tazobactam plus vancomycin) did not lead to improvement. Over the next three weeks the patient’s discrete bicytopenia progressed to severe pancytopenia requiring blood transfusions. Lactate dehydrogenase rose to 1107 U/L, liver enzymes including GGT, alkaline phosphatase and AST increased, and fever persisted up to 40°C. Positron emission tomography–computed tomography showed tracer enhancement in the central and peripheral bone marrow.

A 21-year-old female presents with left-sided chest pain and low-grade fever for one month. Examination shows moderate pleural effusion. Fluid analysis reveals exudate with high lymphocyte count and ADA level. ESR is elevated. Mantoux test is positive.

A 62-year-old man from West Bengal presented with cough and chest pain for 6 months. He was a non-smoker, non-alcoholic, and reported no fever, hematemesis, melena, diarrhea, headache, or body aches. He had no history of tuberculosis, asthma, COPD, or GERD and was taking no medications. Initial examination at a local hospital showed moderate pallor and cachexia but no lymphadenopathy; chest auscultation revealed bilateral normal breath sounds. Chest radiograph showed a small left-sided pleural effusion. Routine hematology demonstrated pancytopenia with hemoglobin 7.7 g/dL and an ESR of 100 mm/h. Symptomatic treatment produced no improvement, and he was referred for further evaluation. At referral, chest radiograph again confirmed a small left pleural effusion. Known causes of pleural effusion such as heart failure, pneumonia, tuberculosis, or carcinoma of the lung were reported to be absent. He had no symptoms of arthritis. On further exam a mild splenomegaly was detected. Serum bilirubin, liver enzymes, and prothrombin time were within normal limits. HBsAg, anti-HCV, and anti-HIV antibodies were negative by ELISA. Widal test for enteric fever and test for malaria antigens were negative. Total serum protein was within the normal range; however, the albumin/globulin ratio was reversed at 0.2. Napier's aldehyde test was performed and produced opacification/solidification of serum after 10 minutes (positive result).

A 47-year-old man presented to the emergency department with recurrent fever for 4 months and worsening symptoms including diarrhea for 1 month. About 4 months earlier he developed fever up to 39.9 °C that typically occurred in the afternoon and lasted several hours; associated symptoms included headache, myalgia, and nausea. After a temporary resolution he had a relapse with persistent high fever and frequent yellow watery diarrhea (>10 times/day). Past medical history included malaria diagnosed 6 years earlier in Africa treated with quinine. He reported hypersensitivity to quinolones (e.g., moxifloxacin). The cryptococcus antigen test, fungal G test, and GM test were negative. The schistosoma japonicum IgG antibody, echinococcus granulosus antibody, liver fluke antibody test, plasmodium antigen test, and blood smear test were all negative. Tests for hepatitis A and B, autoimmune liver disease markers, AFP, and CEA were negative. Abdominal ultrasound showed hepatomegaly and splenomegaly (intercostal spleen thickness ~7.0 cm). Chest and plain abdominal CT reported cirrhosis, splenomegaly, portal hypertension with collateral circulation, and peritoneal effusion. The admitting team considered sepsis and fever of undetermined origin (infection vs tumor) and noted Child-Pugh B decompensated cirrhosis. An emergency metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) blood test was sent to try to identify an occult pathogen.

A 39‑year‑old man from Central America, living in Southeast Georgia, presents to the emergency department with abdominal pain and rectal bleeding. Past medical history: HIV/AIDS, alcohol abuse, tobacco dependency, and previously documented leishmaniasis diagnosed by bone marrow biopsy. He denied recent travel. Course and prior presentations: At initial presentation several years earlier he had diffuse moderate abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, chills and dysphagia; on exam he was tachycardic (heart rate 140/min) with mild abdominal tenderness. He was leukopenic and thrombocytopenic and was treated with amphotericin B and initiation of HAART; he was discharged on a 3‑month course of amphotericin B with ongoing HAART. Six months later he returned with acute abdominal pain and nausea; exam then showed a fine nodular skin rash across chest, abdomen and back described as consistent with cutaneous leishmaniasis, and thrombocytopenia persisted. At that time a bone marrow biopsy was performed to evaluate whether his new symptoms were due to HIV or a relapse of leishmaniasis, and he again received intravenous amphotericin B (inpatient 6 weeks) with plans for outpatient infusions. The patient subsequently was lost to follow‑up. Current presentation: Several years later he returned with a flare characterized by rectal bleeding and continued abdominal pain. Gastroenterology was consulted and an esophagogastroduodenoscopy was planned.

A 40-year-old man of Albanian descent who has lived in Athens for 20 years was admitted in February 2008 for progressive constitutional and respiratory symptoms. His symptoms began one year earlier with dry cough and gradual weight loss totaling 30 kg; night sweats and scant hemoptysis developed during the last month. Six months earlier a limited workup had revealed chronic active hepatitis B. He works in a restaurant, is a nonsmoker, and has no other remarkable medical history. On examination he was cachectic and had hepatosplenomegaly and small, discrete, nontender axillary and cervical lymph nodes. There were no clinical signs of liver failure or portal hypertension. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 100 mm/h. Serum albumin, bilirubin, and prothrombin time were within normal limits. Abdominal ultrasound showed enlarged liver and spleen and enlarged lymph nodes at the hepatic hilum; portal vein diameter and flow were normal and no ascites was present. Chest CT revealed limited adenopathy with a 2 × 1 cm mass at the right hilum and a 1.2 cm right lower paratracheal lymph node with a hypodense centre. Bronchoscopy disclosed epistaxis and pharyngeal inflammation consistent with candidiasis, mild diffuse redness throughout the tracheobronchial tree with more prominent inflammation on the medial aspect of the bronchus intermedius extending into the middle lobe bronchus, and a discreet mucosal polypoid lesion on the middle lobe carina.

A 25‑year‑old man with no prior medical history presented in November with sudden onset psychotic symptoms (paranoid delusions, auditory hallucinations, marked anxiety) accompanied by fever, cough and marked asthenia. He had travelled to Greece for one week and returned ten days before symptom onset, and reported unprotected sex with a man two months before and during travel. On admission he was febrile (38.5°C) and had pharyngitis, oral candidiasis and a skin rash. Initial labs showed C‑reactive protein 18 mg/L, hemoglobin 10.5 g/dL with low reticulocyte count, lymphopenia (500/mm3), neutropenia down to 600/mm3 and thrombocytopenia 90 G/L. HIV‑1 serology was positive and confirmed by immunoblot; initial viral load was 5.47 million copies/mL with CD4+ T‑cells 90/mm3. Two weeks after symptom onset HIV viral load was 6.85 million copies/mL with CD4+ T‑cells 30/mm3 and global lymphopenia (including CD8+ and NK cells). The immunoblot showed "an uncommon band pattern ... Combined antiretroviral therapy (tenofovir, emtricitabine, raltegravir) and cotrimoxazole prophylaxis were started. Neuroleptic drugs were given for psychosis; the patient developed neuroleptic malignant syndrome with extrapyramidal features that resolved after stopping neuroleptics, but fever, chills and night sweats persisted. Blood tests then showed worsening pancytopenia (hemoglobin 7.0 g/dL, platelets 50 G/L, neutrophils 600/mm3), hyperferritinemia, elevated liver enzymes and mildly elevated triglycerides.

A male born June 26, 1986, was seen at a tropical diseases referral center. Between 2009 and 2011 he was hospitalized seven times with a consistent diagnosis of kala-azar. He received multiple recommended treatments during these hospitalizations, including pentavalent antimony (glucantime, 20 mg of Sb + 5 kg/d for 30 d in the first hospitalization), liposomal amphotericin B (for 14 d at 3 mg/kg/d in three subsequent hospitalizations), and pentamidine in the last hospitalization before surgery (4 mg/kg/d every other day, total 15 doses), with only transient symptomatic improvement followed by recurrence. He had a negative HIV serological test. During two hospitalizations he presented with anemia and was transfused twice with packed red blood cells. After all possibilities of medical treatment were exhausted and the patient maintained a pancytopenia profile on blood counts attributed to hypersplenism, splenectomy was recommended. In January 2012 he was hospitalized for the planned surgical procedure. His clinical examination revealed mucocutaneous pallor (2+/4+), fever (38.5 C), dehydration (2+/4+), a distended abdomen with mild pain on deep palpation, and splenomegaly 8 cm below the left costal margin. Laboratory testing showed anemia, leukopenia, hypergammaglobulinemia, and elevated ESR and CRP.

A 68-year-old man from a mountainous area in Hebei Province, China, presented with fever, sweating, and fatigue. He first sought care on February 1 and was hospitalized at a local hospital with temperature 39.0°C, chills, and no respiratory, abdominal, diarrheal, or urinary symptoms. He had lost approximately 10 kg over the prior 6 months. Initial blood tests showed pancytopenia, a rapid erythrocyte sedimentation rate, elevated C-reactive protein and ferritin, hyponatremia, hypokalemia, hypoproteinemia, and elevated serum enzyme levels. Bone marrow aspiration smear at that time showed granulocytopenia with megakaryocyte maturation disorder. Abdominal ultrasound showed splenomegaly; brain CT showed bilateral basal ganglia lacunar infarction; chest CT showed bilateral fibrotic/bronchitic changes. After 11 days of antibiotic and supportive treatment his fever and fatigue persisted with temperatures >39°C, so he presented for further evaluation on February 16. On arrival his SARS-CoV-2 PCR was negative. On examination he was febrile to 38.2°C, poorly nourished, unable to walk (bilateral leg strength grade 3), and had pitting edema of the anterior tibias and dorsal feet. Repeat laboratory testing again showed pancytopenia, increased ESR, CRP and ferritin, and elevated liver enzymes. Empiric antibiotic therapy had not relieved his febrile illness.

A 56-year-old male farmer from Jinghe County in Xinjiang (northwestern China) with a 10-year history of coronary heart disease and 5 years of type 2 diabetes mellitus presented with sudden onset of fever and right upper abdominal pain beginning November 14, 2022. His maximum recorded temperature was 40.0 C with chills, weakness, dry throat, and dizziness. He had lived in Jinghe County for over 40 years and reported no travel history to areas endemic for visceral leishmaniasis. He initially sought care at two local hospitals and "was diagnosed with suspected pneumonia" and received a 15-day course of intravenous levofloxacin and ribavirin with supportive measures, but "the response to this treatment was inadequate." On admission to the tertiary fever clinic on November 29, 2022 his temperature was 38.5 C, pulse 80/min, respirations 20/min, and blood pressure 137/70 mmHg. Abdominal examination revealed tenderness in the right upper quadrant without rebound; the liver and spleen were not initially palpable below the rib cage, although during the course of the illness he developed abdominal pain, hepatomegaly, and jaundice. Laboratory testing showed leukopenia (3.10 x 10^9/L) and mild anemia (hemoglobin 99.0 g/L). Liver enzymes were elevated: ALT 168 U/L, AST 281 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 646 U/L, and gamma-GT 586 U/L. C-reactive protein was 52.3 mg/L and procalcitonin 0.21 ng/mL; renal function was within the normal range.
