A 35-year-old man from Russia presented to dermatology with two ulcerative skin lesions described as semi-dry with active borders: one in the lower left pre-atrial region and the other on the dorsal region of the left forearm. He reported travel to multiple countries between May and June 2019, including Middle Eastern countries (Israel, Turkey), the Balkan region (Armenia, Georgia), and Russia. In August 2019 he noted red, indurated papules and sought care in late August in San Cristobal de las Casas, Chiapas, Mexico. Cryotherapy with liquid nitrogen was applied initially with temporary reduction, followed by renewed flare-up of the lesion edges. At the Tropical Medicine Center he was clinically diagnosed as having localized cutaneous leishmaniasis (LCL). For confirmation, Giemsa-stained smears of the lesion and ELISA tests for L. braziliensis, L. infantum/chagasi, L. major and L. mexicana were performed. The Giemsa-stained smears showed abundant amastigotes within macrophages. The ELISA of the patient's serum revealed some degree of cross reactivity between four Leishmania species, with higher antibody levels recorded for L. major and L. mexicana antigens.

A 30-year-old woman from an area endemic for tegumentary leishmaniasis presented with a single skin complaint. She reported a small papular lesion on her right leg that had developed over 7–10 days. At age 10 she had had an ulcer on the left thigh that healed spontaneously and left a well-defined atrophic scar. On examination there was a depressed papular lesion on the right leg measuring 8 × 7 mm; there was a 30 × 20 mm atrophic scar on the left thigh and no lymphadenopathy. Because early lesions of the locally prevalent Leishmania species may be papular and nonulcerated, a Leishmania skin test (LST) was performed on the left forearm. After 48 hours the intradermal reaction was strongly positive, with an induration measuring 38 × 32 mm. Eight days after the skin test the original papular lesion on the right leg had resolved, and a new round cutaneous ulcer with raised borders measuring 26 × 24 mm was present at the site of the LST. A culture of aspirated material from the forearm lesion was negative for Leishmania.

A 52-year-old woman presented with a single lesion on the tip of her nose that had existed for 14 months. It began as a papule and was slowly increasing in size, enlarging to a plaque. A smear of the lesion performed about 1 year earlier was positive, "showing leishmania bodies." All five members of her family had a history of proven leishmaniasis. Her past medical history was notable for renal failure diagnosed 11 years earlier; she "received a renal transplant 4 years after the diagnosis of renal failure." She also had hypertension and hyperlipidemia and was taking oral mycophenolate mofetil (2 g daily) and cyclosporine (100 mg daily). Skin examination showed skin type IV, "No actinic keratosis was present," and a 3x3 cm indurated ulcer with elevated borders was present on the tip of her nose. The therapeutic plan was intralesional glucantime injections (approximately 1 ml of 1.5 g vial per week). "After completing a therapeutic course of 20 sessions receiving intralesional glucantime injections, she was considered as glucantime therapy resistant."

Her only medical history was well-controlled hypertension. Examination showed a palpable spleen just below the left costal margin. On the right arm near the axilla there was "a single well-defined, ulcer surrounded by erythematous edging, with serous oozing" about 3 × 3 cm; the patient reported the lesion was painless, nonhealing, and present for 2–3 years. A Leishmania rk39 immunochromatography test was positive. Bone marrow aspiration parasitology revealed Leishmania amastigote forms, and serum immunofluorescence for Leishmania antibodies was positive (titer 1:400). ITS1 sequencing showed the Leishmania strains from the blood and the arm lesion corresponded to L. infantum and were 100% identical. However, "the skin lesion did not improve although Leishmania qPCR on dermal sample became negative." A skin biopsy was initially refused. One year later the lesion remained essentially unchanged.

A 38‑year‑old man from Yayu district, western Ethiopia, presented to the outpatient clinic with multiple skin lesions on his face and hands and mutilation of the nose; his upper lip was injured and swollen. Eight years earlier he had a small papule on the right cheek that progressed to an open ulcer, then to ulcers on the left cheek and forehead; those active lesions lasted about six months and healed spontaneously, leaving permanent hypopigmented scars. He had no fever, hepatosplenomegaly or lymphedema and reported no history of HIV, chronic disease, alcohol abuse, or immunomodulatory drug use. Parasitological testing of lesion smears at that time showed many macrophages filled with amastigote stages of Leishmania, graded as +6. A nonreactive rK39 rapid diagnostic test and absence of related systemic signs made visceral leishmaniasis unlikely. Based on the clinical manifestations and smear result he was diagnosed with mucocutaneous leishmaniasis and treated with intramuscular sodium stibogluconate (20 mg/kg/day for 30 days) with clinical cure. Two years later he returned with a different cutaneous eruption that had appeared over the previous three months and had been preceded by intense itching. On exam he had multiple, nonpitting, closed papules on his face, nose, hands and legs. A skin smear again showed intramacrophage amastigotes with a parasite load graded +6, and culture grew promastigotes.

A 59-year-old Caucasian woman with a medical history of diabetes, hypertension, congestive heart failure, chronic renal disease, and paraparesis secondary to HTLV-1 infection presented in June 2012 with a skin lesion on her face. She initially noted a papule in the left malar region that later ulcerated and increased in size. Fifteen days after the facial lesion appeared, she developed another lesion on the right knee.

An 84‑year‑old woman presented with a large nodular lesion on the forehead of 2.5 months' duration. She had been seen at another hospital where a pre‑diagnosis of lymphoma was recorded; the prior punch biopsy report listed basal cell carcinoma, sarcoidosis, lupus vulgaris and pseudolymphoma among the clinical pre‑diagnoses and the material was sent for pathology consultation. Microscopic examination of the punch biopsy showed a dense nodular and diffuse lymphohistiocytic cell infiltration within the dermis. In the cytoplasm of histiocytes, small, round structures resembling organisms were noted. Immunohistochemical staining showed reactive T lymphocytes labelled with CD3 and CD5, reactive B lymphocytes labelled with CD20, and large clusters of histiocytes labelled with CD68; there was no staining with CD30. The pathology report recommended investigation of the aetiology of granulomatous dermatitis, especially cutaneous leishmaniasis.

A 45-year-old man from Apucarana, Paraná, presented with one atypical lesion on the right side of his back of approximately one month’s duration. He had applied topical antibiotics before seeking care without improvement. On examination the lesion was a rounded plaque with an erythematous-violaceous center, desquamative ulcerated edges, and an extensive surrounding area of lichenification, measuring 20 cm, located on the right scapular/back region. Based on the clinical appearance, the initial differential diagnosis included chronic simple lichen, psoriasis, squamous cell carcinoma, chromomycosis, cutaneous tuberculosis, syphilis, paracoccidioidomycosis, and sarcoidosis.

A 30‑year‑old man presented with pain in his lower limbs and a non‑itchy erythematous rash over both lower limbs. He had low‑grade intermittent fever for three months. On examination he was pale and malnourished (BMI 18.4 kg/m2) and had palpable purpura over both thighs and buttocks. Abdominal examination revealed palpable hepatomegaly with massive splenomegaly. Laboratory testing showed pancytopenia (hemoglobin 6.8 g/dL, total leukocyte count 2800/mm3, platelet count 45 000/muL) and polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia (4.9 g/dL); liver and renal function tests were within reference ranges. Contrast‑enhanced CT of chest and abdomen confirmed hepatosplenomegaly and was otherwise unremarkable. The treating team considered hematologic malignancy and a connective‑tissue disorder with vasculitis. Other infectious etiologies entertained included HIV, scrub typhus/rickettsial infection, and visceral leishmaniasis (given the patient lived in an endemic area). Initial testing showed: anti‑nuclear antibodies, complement levels (C3 = 94 mg/dL and C4 = 20 mg/dL), and rheumatoid factor were negative; urine examination was normal and serum cryoglobulins were not raised. Viral markers (HIV, hepatitis B surface antigen, and anti‑hepatitis C) were negative. Serology for rickettsia and scrub typhus were also negative.

contexts.text: A 38‑year‑old man from Yayu district, western Ethiopia, presented to the outpatient clinic with multiple skin lesions on his face and hands and mutilation of the nose; his upper lip was injured and swollen. Eight years earlier he had a small papule on the right cheek that progressed to an open ulcer, then to ulcers on the left cheek and forehead; those active lesions lasted about six months and healed spontaneously, leaving permanent hypopigmented scars. He had no fever, hepatosplenomegaly or lymphedema and reported no history of HIV, chronic disease, alcohol abuse, or immunomodulatory drug use. Parasitological testing of lesion smears at that time showed many macrophages filled with amastigote stages of Leishmania, graded as +6. A nonreactive rK39 rapid diagnostic test and absence of related systemic signs made visceral leishmaniasis unlikely. Based on the clinical manifestations and smear result he was diagnosed with mucocutaneous leishmaniasis and treated with intramuscular sodium stibogluconate (20 mg/kg/day for 30 days) with clinical cure. Two years later he returned with a different cutaneous eruption that had appeared over the previous three months and had been preceded by intense itching. On exam he had multiple, nonpitting, closed papules on his face, nose, hands and legs. A skin smear again showed intramacrophage amastigotes with a parasite load graded +6, and culture grew promastigotes.

A 43-year-old man from Cumanda (Chimborazo province, Ecuador), a subtropical mountainous community at ~500 m above sea level, presented with multiple chronic skin lesions. History of present illness: The lesion began as an insect-bite–like papular lesion on the forearm. Lesions then appeared on the right ear and the nose. About 2 years later, lesions developed on a wide range of the lower extremities and subsequently became multiple and confluent on the abdomen, thorax, body side, and thigh. A superficial involvement of mucosae of the nose and upper lip was observed. Treatment history: At the time of examination the patient had already received injections of nine ampoules of trivalent antimonials (Repodral, 20 mg/kg/day) at a rural health center; after finishing several courses he received pentavalent antimonials (Glucantime, 10 mg/kg/day) for about 5 months. Early investigations performed from active lesions included smear specimens, skin biopsies, syringe aspirates for culture, and material on FTA cards. Montenegro skin test showed a 17-mm induration, and an rK39 kit test revealed a strongly positive band. The smear specimen was positive for Leishmania amastigotes in scanty numbers. Promastigotes grown in vitro showed a tendency to decrease gradually and then disappear, an effect attributed by the investigators to prior antimonial treatment.

A 9-year-old boy presented with multiple papular lesions on the left cheek that had been present for three months and had gradually enlarged. His medical history was notable for an episode of cutaneous leishmaniasis located on the nose two years earlier, which had completely regressed after treatment with intralesional meglumine antimonate. Dermatologic examination showed multiple, coalescing, rough, slightly elevated, yellowish-brown papular lesions 3–6 mm in diameter on the left cheek. He also had a large atrophic scar on the nose. Nothing of interest was noted in his family history or his laboratory tests.

A 30-year-old Caucasian man, unemployed, HIV-negative and with no other concomitant infections, presented in 2014 with a papule on the inferior eyelid of the right eye. His past history included, in 2008, an isolated nodulation in the right leg that resolved after treatment. Over time new lesions progressively appeared on the chest, abdomen, back, feet, and in the oral cavity. Ulcerated oral lesions were present on the hard palate and on the left and right jugal mucosa. Disease progression was associated with fever, headache, and weight loss.

A 24-year-old man from a small rural village near the Pacific coast of Esmeraldas province, Ecuador, reports that at age 16 papules first appeared on his left knee and right cheek and gradually increased in size and number over years. For about 2 years he received various medications without a confirmed diagnosis; he was at one point treated clinically for leprosy with multidrug therapy (dapsone, rifampicin, clofazimine) for 1 month. On examination there are numerous cutaneous lesions: pea- to rice-grain–sized reddish papules on both ear lobes and auricles with palpable induration; miliary to pea-sized papules on the face; papules and nodules on the left shoulder; many miliary to hen-egg–sized papules, nodules, erythema, infiltrated erythema, and brownish freckles on the upper extremities, some with scaly or crusted surfaces; rice-grain to thumb-sized papules grouped on brownish freckle lesions of the lower back; satellite miliary papules around plaque-like lesions; thumb- to palm-sized erythema on the thigh; and various papules, nodules, infiltrated erythemas, and brownish freckles on the lower extremities. No loss of sensation was recognized anywhere on the body and there was no hypertrophy of peripheral nerves. The rK39 kit test gave a strong positive reaction. Stained slit-skin smears from lesions demonstrated numerous intracellular amastigotes identified as Leishmania on microscopy, and Ziehl–Neelsen stains showed no acid-fast bacilli.

A 36-year-old man presented with painless nodules on his left foot for a two-month duration. He had received a three-week course of systemic (ampicillin-cloxacillin) antibiotics without improvement. His medical and family history were unremarkable. Dermatologic examination showed a large ulcerative plaque on the dorsal aspect of the left foot surrounded by two satellite purple papules. There were also multiple grouped dusky erythematous nontender ulcerative nodules behind the lateral malleolus of the left leg. Histopathological examination of the margin of the ulcerative plaque showed ulceration of the epidermis and a diffuse dense mononuclear cellular infiltration of lymphocytes, histiocytes, and numerous plasma cells throughout the dermis with early granuloma formation. These changes involved the panniculus, causing septal and lobular panniculitis.

A 31-year-old woman from Salvador, State of Bahia, presented in 2013 with submandibular lymphadenopathy and multiple ulcerated lesions involving the lower lip frenulum, gingiva, nasal septum and a lesion on her back. She reported a prior cutaneous lesion on her back that had been recurrent over the prior year. On oral examination there was poor oral health and ulcerated lesions of the lower lip frenulum and adjacent gingiva. Excisional biopsies of the oral lesions were performed and reported as unspecific; microbiological analysis for fungi was negative.

A 24-year-old man from Tancredo Neves, State of Bahia, Brazil, was admitted in January 2012 with diffuse bullous lesions on the body, osteoarthritis of the distal interphalangeal joints and proteinuria of 399 mg/day. He was diagnosed with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and treated with mycophenolate mofetil (MMF), with the dose increased to 1 g per day intravenously. Two years after the SLE diagnosis (2014) he was hospitalized again, presenting with ulcerated, painless skin lesions on the face, upper lip, scalp, neck, and on the upper and lower limbs. Oral examination showed crusty upper lip lesions, poor oral health status, and amelogenesis imperfecta. He developed secondary infection with fever and was started on cephalexin (1 g/day) and maintained on prednisone 5 mg/day intravenously. On the third day of this hospitalization, biopsies were performed on the left nasal mucosa and on lesions of the right lower limb.

A 53-year-old man from Mundo Novo, State of Bahia, Brazil, presented in July with pain, nasal obstruction, odynophagia, and dysphagia. On examination there was a painful, hyperemic, friable lesion in the right nasal cavity and an infiltrative lesion involving the hard palate, soft palate, and uvula. Additional findings included an ulcerated lesion on the left eyebrow and right eye with seropurulent secretion, a small ulcer on the lower eyelid, a lesion on the lobe of the right ear, and a lesion in the malar region. The patient was admitted for diagnosis and management of disseminated skin lesions. A biopsy of the palate lesions showed a non-specific erosive chronic inflammatory process. HIV testing was negative.

A 32-year-old man from Djelfa, Algeria, with a history of contact eczema presented with a 6-week history of painless, non-healing skin lesions on the dorsal aspect of his right hand. He had applied topical corticosteroids and antiseptics without improvement and had received two courses of antibiotics (pristinamycin, amoxicillin + clavulanic acid) with no significant results. On examination there was a limited erythematous-papular plaque, approximately 8 cm in diameter, on the dorsal right hand formed by confluence of several papules with satellite lesions at the periphery. The initial plaque was associated with several firm, painless subcutaneous nodules 0.5–1.5 cm in diameter that tracked proximally along lymphatic drainage toward the elbow. The patient did not recall an insect bite, no other body sites were involved, and the remainder of the examination was unremarkable. Direct mycological examination and culture on Sabouraud medium at 25 °C and on BHI medium at 37 °C were negative for fungal presence.

contexts.text: A 57-year-old man underwent orthotopic liver transplantation in March 2019 for alcoholic-related liver disease and portal hypertension after 2 years of abstinence. He was born in Wales; his only travel outside the UK was a transient visit to Calais 15 years before transplantation. Postoperative care included a 2-day intensive-care admission. Immunosuppression was commenced with prednisolone, tacrolimus and mycophenolate (MMF); cotrimoxazole prophylaxis was given. Both donor and recipient were CMV IgG negative. One month after transplantation he had biopsy-proven moderate acute cellular rejection treated with 3 days of pulsed steroids. His graft function improved, with normalisation of alanine aminotransferase coinciding with the development of pancytopenia 4 months after transplantation. MMF dose was reduced from 1 g twice daily to 500 mg twice daily, but neutropenia worsened and pancytopenia persisted. He developed systemic symptoms of fever and rigours and was admitted to his local hospital with neutropenic sepsis and an acute kidney injury. He was transferred to the liver transplant centre for further investigation. He was treated empirically with meropenem, vancomycin and fluconazole. A bone marrow biopsy was performed in view of his pancytopenia.

A 38-year-old man presented with low-grade fever, weight loss, and anorexia for 6 weeks. On general examination he had mild pallor, splenomegaly, and mild hepatomegaly, with discrete enlarged lymph nodes at the right epitrochlear area and right cervical region. Routine biochemical tests were within normal limits except for mild elevation of liver enzymes (serum glutamic pyruvic transaminase 60 IU/L, serum glutamic oxaloacetic transaminase 53 IU/L) and lactic dehydrogenase 370 IU/L. Hemoglobin was 10.2 g/dL and erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 68 mm/h. Serologic screening was reactive for HIV‑1. Fine‑needle aspiration cytology of the lymph nodes was planned.

A 47-year-old man presented to the emergency department on December 28, 2020 with recurrent fever for 4 months and worsening symptoms with diarrhea for 1 month. About 4 months earlier he developed fever without an evident cause, with a maximum temperature of 39.9 C; fevers usually occurred in the afternoon, lasted several hours, and were associated with headache, myalgia, and nausea. After a period of apparent improvement he redeveloped persistent high fever (≈39 C) accompanied by yellow watery diarrhea more than 10 times per day. Six years previously he had been diagnosed with malaria in Africa and treated with quinine. On admission: Novel Coronavirus nucleic acid test was negative. Laboratory studies showed Hb 83 g/L, WBC 2.82 x 10^9/L, platelet count 16 x 10^9/L, neutrophil percentage 84.0%, lymphocyte percentage 8.0%, and procalcitonin 0.87 ng/ml. Hepatitis A and B testing were negative. Autoimmune liver markers, alpha fetoprotein (AFP), and carcinoembryonic antigen were negative. Abdominal ultrasound showed enlarged liver and spleen. Chest and plain abdominal CT demonstrated cirrhosis, splenomegaly, portal hypertension with collateral circulation, and peritoneal effusion. The team considered sepsis and fever of undetermined origin (infection versus tumor) and assessed the patient as Child-Pugh B decompensated cirrhosis. An emergency blood metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) test was sent to help diagnose the fever of unknown cause.

A 47-year-old man presented to the emergency department with recurrent fever for 4 months and worsening symptoms including diarrhea for 1 month. About 4 months earlier he developed fever up to 39.9 °C that typically occurred in the afternoon and lasted several hours; associated symptoms included headache, myalgia, and nausea. After a temporary resolution he had a relapse with persistent high fever and frequent yellow watery diarrhea (>10 times/day). Past medical history included malaria diagnosed 6 years earlier in Africa treated with quinine. He reported hypersensitivity to quinolones (e.g., moxifloxacin). On admission, novel coronavirus nucleic acid test was negative. Initial laboratory testing showed hemoglobin 83 g/L, platelet count 16 × 10^9/L, white-cell count 2.82 × 10^9/L, neutrophil percentage 84.0%, lymphocyte percentage 8.0%, and procalcitonin 0.87 ng/mL. Tests for hepatitis A and B, autoimmune liver disease markers, AFP, and CEA were negative. Abdominal ultrasound showed hepatomegaly and splenomegaly (intercostal spleen thickness ~7.0 cm). Chest and plain abdominal CT reported cirrhosis, splenomegaly, portal hypertension with collateral circulation, and peritoneal effusion. The admitting team considered sepsis and fever of undetermined origin (infection vs tumor) and noted Child-Pugh B decompensated cirrhosis. An emergency metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) blood test was sent to try to identify an occult pathogen.

A 58‑year‑old man with end‑stage renal failure and a history of three kidney transplantations (1979, 1981 and 2008) presented with recurrent febrile illness. His medical history included chronic hepatitis B, legionellosis, chronic Q fever and cytomegalovirus infection. The most recent transplant had required treatment for acute rejection with anti‑thymoglobulin, plasma exchanges, rituximab and maintenance immunosuppression consisting of mycophenolate mofetil 1 g/day, tacrolimus 4.5 mg/day and prednisone 10 mg/day. Leishmania PCR in blood had been positive in 2004; initial treatment with liposomal amphotericin B (L‑AmB) produced clinical cure. However, relapse occurred in August 2009 following plasma exchanges and corticosteroid boluses for graft rejection, with fever, anemia (Hb 9.1 g/dL), leukopenia (leukocytes 1,600/mm3) and quantitative PCR showing 431 Leishmania/ml of blood. L‑AmB (induction total dose 40 mg/kg) reduced parasitemia to 6.9 Leishmania/ml. L‑AmB was reintroduced and maintenance infusions were adjusted (including weekly and twice‑weekly dosing) with parasitemia fluctuating (from 88 to 0.6 Leishmania/ml). The patient later underwent transplant nephrectomy and returned to chronic dialysis. In February 2012 he had fever, splenomegaly, anemia (Hb 8.6 g/dL) and thrombocytopenia (platelets 50,000/mm3) with quantitative PCR showing 12,870 Leishmania/ml in blood and 60,440 Leishmania/ml in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid.

A 55-year-old man with chronic severe hepatitis B (HBV‑DNA positive) was admitted for intermittent fever of 1 month (maximum 40°C). He had worked on a farm in Xinjiang Province one month earlier. On examination he had hepatosplenomegaly below the costal margin. Initial laboratory tests showed marked hepatic abnormalities (ALT 490 U/L, AST 558 U/L), low total protein and albumin (TP 51.54 g/L, ALB 26.83 g/L), TBIL 23.23 μmol/L, DBIL 14.37 μmol/L, and HBV‑DNA 3.19 × 10^4 IU/mL. Routine blood counts were abnormal (WBC 3.12 × 10^9/L, platelets 100 × 10^9/L). After 2 weeks the patient remained febrile with worsening labs (WBC 0.95 × 10^9/L, platelets 56 × 10^9/L, ALT 524 U/L, AST 640 U/L). Abdominal enhanced CT showed an enlarged spleen with multiple low‑density nodules that demonstrated sustained/delayed enhancement; angioma/hemangioma was suspected. 18F‑FDG PET/CT demonstrated a significant diffuse increase in FDG uptake in the enlarged spleen (SUVmax 6.6) and slightly diffuse bone‑marrow uptake. Bone‑marrow aspiration and biopsy were performed twice (2 months apart) and both showed phagocytosis of reticulum cells. Based on the clinical and imaging findings, splenic lymphoma was considered highly likely. The patient received chemotherapy for hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) and was discharged in remission, but was readmitted 2 months later with recurrent fever and pancytopenia; splenectomy was then undertaken to establish a diagnosis and reduce disease burden.

A 37-year-old man from Georgia presented in France in October 2012. He had HIV infection since 2006 that had been treated inconsistently with HAART. Other medical history included adrenal insufficiency, cirrhosis due to chronic hepatitis C virus infection, and treatment-controlled tuberculosis. Visceral leishmaniasis had been diagnosed in 2010 and treated in Georgia with meglumine antimoniate and liposomal amphotericin B (doses and schedules unknown). In November 2012 he had hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathies, infiltrated cutaneous lesions, and anemia. Laboratory testing showed a CD4 lymphocyte count of 133/mm3, plasma HIV viral load <50 copies/mL, and parasitemia of 6 Leishmania/ml. He received a course of liposomal amphotericin B followed by maintenance therapy for 5 months. In May 2013 he developed weight loss with persistent hepatosplenomegaly and anemia. CD4 count was 177/mm3, viral load <40 copies/mL, and parasitemia was 12 Leishmania/ml. Liposomal amphotericin B treatment was intensified, but renal insufficiency and acute thrombocytopenia occurred. In June 2013 the splenomegaly and parasitemia remained unchanged.

A 44‑year‑old man from Shanxi Province with a 5‑year history of antisynthetase antibody syndrome on cyclosporine A was admitted in January 2020 with fever to 38.6°C. He reported exertional breathlessness (after walking ~100 m) and increasing weakness; broad‑spectrum antimicrobials produced no improvement. By March 2020 he had persistent fever. Laboratory results then showed WBC 1.3 × 10^9/L, hemoglobin 96 g/L, platelets 113 × 10^9/L, fibrinogen 1.36 g/L, serum ferritin >1500 μg/L, NK‑cell activity 14.96%, and soluble CD25 12,947 pg/mL; ALT, AST, CK and CK‑MB were normal. The clinical picture met criteria for hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH), and treatment was started with methylprednisolone (10 mg/kg per day) and etoposide (100 mg/m^2). After 2 weeks the patient became afebrile and WBC rose to 10.8 × 10^9/L, hemoglobin was 95 g/L and platelets 55 × 10^9/L. In June 2020, during prednisone taper, he redeveloped high fever to 39.5°C, was unable to stand independently, and subsequently had pancytopenia with recurrence of high ferritin, low NK‑cell activity, markedly elevated sCD25, splenomegaly, and hemophagocytosis on bone marrow examination.

A 15-year-old male student presented to the emergency fever clinic with "fever accompanied with cough for more than 10 days." He had developed fever after a cold >10 days before admission, with temperatures fluctuating between 37 and 38°C initially, later peaking to 41°C; associated symptoms included cough, fatigue, chills, and pharyngeal discomfort. A local hospital workup showed WBC 3.3 x 10^9/L, Hb 85 g/L, and PLT 87 x 10^9/L. Bone marrow puncture there showed "hematopoietic tissue hyperplasia was active and the proportion of three-line blood cells was roughly normal," with occasional atypical lymphocytes. Adenovirus IgM was weakly positive, ferritin was >2,000 ng/ml, and procalcitonin 4.14 ng/ml. After transfer, his vital signs were: T 37.1°C, pulse 110/min, respirations 19/min, BP 110/72 mmHg. Admission tests included WBC 4.68 x 10^9/L, Hb 100 g/L, RBC 3.65 x 10^12/L; ALT 204 IU/L, AST 176 IU/L, GGT 153 IU/L, LDH 889 IU/L; ferritin >2,000 ng/ml; PCT 2.11 ng/ml; CRP 53.5 mg/L; IL-6 31.58 pg/ml. TORCH/EBV: CMV, HSV, rubella virus, and EBV IgG were positive. Blood cultures showed no growth after 5 days. Abdominal ultrasound showed intercostal spleen thickness ~6.6 cm, compatible with splenomegaly. Empiric antibiotics (cefoperazone–sulbactam, then ceftriaxone) and dexamethasone were given without clear improvement. Lymphoma? Autoimmune disease?" Because the cause remained unclear, an mNGS test was performed on the second day after admission to the emergency department.

contexts.text: A 65-year-old woman was admitted in March after collapsing in the street. She had been unwell for 14 months with night sweats and progressive loss of energy but denied fever. On examination she was afebrile and had hepatic enlargement and lymphadenopathy; liver function tests were within reference limits. Initial blood tests showed hemoglobin 8.1 g/dL, leukocyte count 4.62 × 10^9/L, and platelet count 143 × 10^9/L. Serologic tests for HIV, hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and Strongyloides spp. were negative. Her CD4 count was 790 cells/μL, rheumatoid factor was weakly positive, and immunoglobulin levels were within reference ranges. She was born in Guyana and had recent travel to Guyana in 2012 and 2013, to Grenada in 2012, to Ghana in 2005, and to France in 2003. Because a hematologic malignancy was suspected, a bone marrow aspiration was performed; Leishmania amastigotes were visible. Leishmania serology was negative by an rK39 rapid test and weakly positive by direct agglutination (1:3,200; cutoff 1:1,600).

A 52-year-old man with known HIV infection from Rajasthan presented with a 3-month history of multiple papulonodular skin lesions located mainly on the dorsum of the hands, forearms, thighs, and back. Routine blood parameters were within normal limits. His CD4 count was 170/muL. On inspection there were multiple nodular lesions on the dorsum of both hands and on the listed sites of the upper and lower extremities and back. Early diagnostic considerations included Hansen's disease, sarcoidosis, and leishmaniasis.

A 68-year-old man from a mountainous area in Hebei Province, China, presented with fever, sweating, and fatigue. He first sought care on February 1 and was hospitalized at a local hospital with temperature 39.0°C, chills, and no respiratory, abdominal, diarrheal, or urinary symptoms. He had lost approximately 10 kg over the prior 6 months. Initial blood tests showed pancytopenia, a rapid erythrocyte sedimentation rate, elevated C-reactive protein and ferritin, hyponatremia, hypokalemia, hypoproteinemia, and elevated serum enzyme levels. Bone marrow aspiration smear at that time showed granulocytopenia with megakaryocyte maturation disorder. Abdominal ultrasound showed splenomegaly; brain CT showed bilateral basal ganglia lacunar infarction; chest CT showed bilateral fibrotic/bronchitic changes. After 11 days of antibiotic and supportive treatment his fever and fatigue persisted with temperatures >39°C, so he presented for further evaluation on February 16. On arrival his SARS-CoV-2 PCR was negative. On examination he was febrile to 38.2°C, poorly nourished, unable to walk (bilateral leg strength grade 3), and had pitting edema of the anterior tibias and dorsal feet. Repeat laboratory testing again showed pancytopenia, increased ESR, CRP and ferritin, and elevated liver enzymes. Empiric antibiotic therapy had not relieved his febrile illness.

A 30‑year‑old man presented with pain in his lower limbs and a non‑itchy erythematous rash over both lower limbs. He had low‑grade intermittent fever for three months. On examination he was pale and malnourished (BMI 18.4 kg/m2) and had palpable purpura over both thighs and buttocks. Abdominal examination revealed palpable hepatomegaly with massive splenomegaly. Laboratory testing showed pancytopenia (hemoglobin 6.8 g/dL, total leukocyte count 2800/mm3, platelet count 45 000/muL) and polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia (4.9 g/dL); liver and renal function tests were within reference ranges. Contrast‑enhanced CT of chest and abdomen confirmed hepatosplenomegaly and was otherwise unremarkable. The treating team considered hematologic malignancy and a connective‑tissue disorder with vasculitis. Other infectious etiologies entertained included HIV, scrub typhus/rickettsial infection, and visceral leishmaniasis (given the patient lived in an endemic area). Initial testing showed: anti‑nuclear antibodies, complement levels (C3 = 94 mg/dL and C4 = 20 mg/dL), and rheumatoid factor were negative; urine examination was normal and serum cryoglobulins were not raised. Viral markers (HIV, hepatitis B surface antigen, and anti‑hepatitis C) were negative. Serology for rickettsia and scrub typhus were also negative.

A 74-year-old man from Yangquan City, Shanxi Province, presented with more than six months of generalized fatigue and pancytopenia. He had a history of COVID-19 infection in January 2023 and reported persistent weakness thereafter. He lost approximately 10 kg over six months. Prior intermittent evaluations included bone marrow aspirations that reportedly showed no special abnormalities. On admission he was afebrile; examination showed pallor and scattered hyperpigmented skin lesions from scratching. Liver was palpable 5 cm below the right costal margin; spleen was palpable 8 cm below the left costal margin. Abdominal ultrasound and CT reported hepatomegaly, cirrhotic-appearing liver, splenomegaly and ascites (spleen longitudinal diameter up to ~19–21 cm on serial imaging). Laboratory testing demonstrated persistent pancytopenia. Initial infectious-serology testing showed a positive HCV antibody; repeat hepatitis C antigen and antibody testing later returned negative. Tumor markers were negative. Hematology testing included a positive direct antiglobulin test; CD55 and CD59 testing were normal. Immunology testing showed elevated IgG and positive anti-cardiolipin antibody IgG and IgM. Multiple blood transfusions had little effect on the anemia. Repeat peripheral smear and bone marrow evaluation demonstrated some toxic granules in mature granulocytes but otherwise no diagnostic abnormalities and no parasites were seen.

A 41-year-old Caucasian man was admitted during treatment with intravenous liposomal amphotericin B for laryngeal and facial mucocutaneous leishmaniasis because of marked elevation of creatine kinase (CK) (more than 10× upper limit of normal during admission; pretreatment CK up to ~2× ULN previously) and rising serum creatinine. Past medical history was notable for visceral leishmaniasis at age 13, recurrent otitis and an episode of bronchopneumonia in childhood, long-standing unexplained elevated CK attributed in the past to occupation and boxing, and chronic periorbital/facial swelling first noted in 2013. In January 2019 he developed hoarseness and dysphonia; laryngoscopy and biopsy were positive for Leishmania spp., and earlier periocular skin samples (2015) were retrospectively PCR-positive for Leishmania spp. He reported no travel outside Europe. There was a family history notable for a brother who died at age 20 from an unspecified lymphoproliferative disease and a sister with chronic myalgias. On examination he was in good general condition with bilateral orbital swelling. Peripheral blood count was unremarkable. T-lymphocyte subpopulations were within reference limits except for reduced circulating Tfh cells. There was no history of liver or biliary tract disease or neutropenia. The patient met criteria for common-variable immunodeficiency, but because of the opportunistic, persistent Leishmania infection further genetic studies were pursued.

A 47-year-old man presented to the emergency department on December 28, 2020 with recurrent fever for 4 months and worsening symptoms with diarrhea for 1 month. About 4 months earlier he developed fever without an evident cause, with a maximum temperature of 39.9 C; fevers usually occurred in the afternoon, lasted several hours, and were associated with headache, myalgia, and nausea. After a period of apparent improvement he redeveloped persistent high fever (≈39 C) accompanied by yellow watery diarrhea more than 10 times per day. Six years previously he had been diagnosed with malaria in Africa and treated with quinine. On admission: Novel Coronavirus nucleic acid test was negative. The cryptococcus antigen test, fungal G test, and GM test were negative. Serologic and parasitologic tests including schistosoma japonicum IgG antibody, echinococcus granulosus antibody, liver fluke antibody test, plasmodium antigen test, and blood smear were all negative. Hepatitis A and B testing were negative. Abdominal ultrasound showed enlarged liver and spleen. Chest and plain abdominal CT demonstrated cirrhosis, splenomegaly, portal hypertension with collateral circulation, and peritoneal effusion. The team considered sepsis and fever of undetermined origin (infection versus tumor) and assessed the patient as Child-Pugh B decompensated cirrhosis. An emergency blood metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) test was sent to help diagnose the fever of unknown cause.

A 60‑year‑old Austrian man presented in September 2016 with a three‑week history of fever of unknown origin, fatigue, and unintentional weight loss of 6 kg. Initial physical examination was inconspicuous. His medical history was notable for adequately treated diabetes mellitus type 2 and hypothyroidism. Travel history included a two‑week trip to the south of Crete in September 2015 and a two‑week trip the south of Spain in May 2016. Laboratory tests showed markedly elevated C‑reactive protein (CRP 94.2–188.9 mg/L), slight hypochromic normocytic anemia without signs of hemolysis (hemoglobin 12.5 g/dL), mild thrombocytopenia (127,000/µL), and a discreetly elevated gamma‑glutamyltransferase (GGT). The soluble interleukin‑2 receptor (IL‑2R) was elevated to 5156.1 pg/mL. Chest x‑ray, urine analysis, abdominal sonography, transthoracic and transesophageal echocardiography revealed no focus of infection but did show splenomegaly (7.2 × 16.4 cm). Empiric antibiotic therapy (initially ampicillin/sulbactam, later piperacillin/tazobactam plus vancomycin) did not lead to improvement. Over the next three weeks the patient’s discrete bicytopenia progressed to severe pancytopenia requiring blood transfusions. Lactate dehydrogenase rose to 1107 U/L, liver enzymes including GGT, alkaline phosphatase and AST increased, and fever persisted up to 40°C. Positron emission tomography–computed tomography showed tracer enhancement in the central and peripheral bone marrow.

A 65-year-old man presented with diffuse abdominal pain for one year, 14 kg weight loss and fever for 4 months. The fever occurred once or twice daily with profuse sweating and shivers. He had no prior illnesses recorded and was a long‑time smoker. He was born in Paraiba, lived in Sao Paulo since age 9, and reported no recent travel outside the city; he denied contact with unpasteurized milk, domestic animals, rodents or farm animals. On examination he had swollen lymph nodes in several body regions; the largest measured 3 cm in the left inguinal region. Laboratory tests showed elevated C-reactive protein (99.9 mg/L), normocytic normochromic anemia (hemoglobin 11.1 g/dL; hematocrit 32.4%), sodium 130 mEq/L, leucocytes 5300/mm3 (neutrophils 3260/mm3; lymphocytes 910/mm3), gamma-glutamyl transferase 570 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 574 U/L, and beta-2 microglobulin 3.3 mcg/mL; all other routine blood tests, blood cultures, electrolytes, and kidney and liver functions were reported as normal. (L.) major-like antigen. Positron emission tomography showed increased glycolytic metabolism in several lymph nodes (some forming conglomerates) above and below the diaphragm, with increased glycolytic metabolism in the spleen, liver and bones, findings described as suggestive of a lymphoproliferative disorder. Bone marrow aspiration identified the presence of Leishmania spp. on direct microscopy.

A 37-year-old man from Maranhão, Brazil, employed as a sugarcane cutter, and the son of a consanguineous marriage, presented with 5 months of daily fevers up to 39°C, progressive asthenia, about 10 kg weight loss, and increasing abdominal volume. He had a remote history: at age 21 he was diagnosed with rheumatoid arthritis and received NSAIDs and prednisone, with maintenance corticosteroid therapy (10 mg/day) for 7 years. He and his family reported no history of recurrent infections. On examination he had pallor of skin and mucous membranes, splenomegaly extending 21 cm below the left costal margin, and hepatomegaly 4 cm below the right costal margin. Laboratory testing demonstrated pancytopenia and hypoalbuminemia. Bone marrow aspirate showed relative hypocellularity of the granulocytes without visualization of amastigotes. Bone marrow biopsy showed a proportional increase in granulocytes. A liver biopsy was performed; immunohistochemistry was negative for Leishmania.

retrieval_query_text: A 70-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and no prior allergic reactions presented with a two-month history of asthenia, fever, and bilateral limb edema affecting both upper and lower extremities. He reported no recent initiation of new medications or vaccinations. On examination, there was skin thickening most notable over the forearms, thighs, abdomen, and back, with the forearms most affected. Initial laboratory testing revealed leukocytosis with marked eosinophilia (maximum 6920 cells/µL), thrombocytosis (531,000 cells/µL), and an elevated C-reactive protein (2.28 mg/dL); erythrocyte sedimentation rate was not measured. An etiologic workup showed negative parasite serologies (Strongyloides, Echinococcus, Fasciola, Toxocara, Leishmania) and negative stool parasitology. Immune testing returned negative for antinuclear antibodies and anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies; immunoglobulin levels were within normal limits and there was no complement depletion. Peripheral blood and myelogram immunophenotyping did not reveal signs of malignancy. Age-adjusted neoplasia screening including endoscopic studies, prostate-specific antigen testing, and a thoracoabdominal-pelvic CT scan did not reveal malignancy. Electromyography demonstrated sensorimotor polyneuropathy without myopathic involvement.

During the trip she stayed in a rain-forest hotel, took hikes, swam in the ocean and in chlorinated pools, saw many animals including rodents, and was splashed with fresh water. Five days after returning she developed a one-week history of fever up to 39.5°C, abdominal pain, nausea, and sore throat. Family members remained well. Laboratory evaluation at that time showed alanine aminotransferase 102 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 73 U/L, albumin 3.1 g/dL, total bilirubin 0.5 mg/dL, prothrombin time 12.9 s, partial thromboplastin time 38.1 s, and alkaline phosphatase 314 U/L. She was referred to infectious diseases; at her first clinic visit approximately 2 1/2 weeks after return she was afebrile and had complete symptomatic improvement. Serum creatinine and blood urea nitrogen remained within the normal range during this period.

contexts.text: She worked as a cleaner in the cemetery of Caju and denied any travel outside the city. Five months before admission she developed intermittent nocturnal fevers up to 39 °C that did not respond to antipyretics, with poor appetite, postprandial fullness, nausea and vomiting. Over the following months she noted progressive jaundice (yellow sclera and skin), dark urine, weight loss of ~10 kg, increasing abdominal girth and soft bilateral lower‑extremity edema to the knees. She had multiple prior emergency visits and received only symptomatic treatment. On admission her general state was poor with malnutrition; examination showed pallor 3–4/4, mild dehydration, jaundice 2/4, cyanosis, fever and tachycardia. Abdominal exam showed moderate ascites, hepatomegaly 7 cm below the right costal margin and splenomegaly palpable 2 cm below the umbilicus. Lower limbs had bilateral soft edema to the knees. The initial diagnostic hypotheses included disseminated tuberculosis and visceral leishmaniasis; other considered diagnoses were dengue, yellow fever, prolonged septicemic salmonellosis, brucellosis, malaria, Chagas disease and lymphoproliferative malignancies. Investigations ordered included thick and thin blood smears, blood cultures, stool tests, bone marrow biopsy and aspiration and serologies for dengue, yellow fever, brucellosis and Chagas disease. HIV testing was performed and was negative.

A 47-year-old man presented to the emergency department with recurrent fever for 4 months and worsening symptoms including diarrhea for 1 month. About 4 months earlier he developed fever up to 39.9 °C that typically occurred in the afternoon and lasted several hours; associated symptoms included headache, myalgia, and nausea. After a temporary resolution he had a relapse with persistent high fever and frequent yellow watery diarrhea (>10 times/day). Past medical history included malaria diagnosed 6 years earlier in Africa treated with quinine. He reported hypersensitivity to quinolones (e.g., moxifloxacin). On admission, novel coronavirus nucleic acid test was negative. Initial laboratory testing showed hemoglobin 83 g/L, platelet count 16 × 10^9/L, white-cell count 2.82 × 10^9/L, neutrophil percentage 84.0%, lymphocyte percentage 8.0%, and procalcitonin 0.87 ng/mL. Blood culture grew methicillin-resistant coagulase-negative Staphylococci. Abdominal ultrasound showed hepatomegaly and splenomegaly (intercostal spleen thickness ~7.0 cm). Chest and plain abdominal CT reported cirrhosis, splenomegaly, portal hypertension with collateral circulation, and peritoneal effusion. The admitting team considered sepsis and fever of undetermined origin (infection vs tumor) and noted Child-Pugh B decompensated cirrhosis. An emergency metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) blood test was sent to try to identify an occult pathogen.

A 22‑month‑old girl presented with 8 days of fever to 40°C and mild cough. Past history: failure to thrive; normal neurologic development. She was the first child of a non‑consanguineous couple; no family history of albinism; normal hair and skin. On exam she was stunted, pale, had non‑tender hepatomegaly 5–6 cm and splenomegaly palpable 4 cm below the left costal margin. Petechial rash developed on the chest and legs as she worsened. Initial laboratory results: WBC 5100/mm3 (ANC 1200/mm3), Hb 9.1 g/dl, platelets 47,000/mm3; mild transaminase elevation; hypoalbuminemia. Ferritin 1,134 ng/ml; soluble IL‑2 receptor (sCD25) 3,183 U/ml. Blood cultures were negative. Serum immunoglobulins and lymphocyte subsets were reported as normal. Infectious testing: EBV serology positive for IgM and IgG anti‑VCA with negative IgG anti‑EBNA; EBV viral load 637 copies/ml. Leishmania testing was discordant: immunochromatography and indirect immunofluorescence were negative, serum ELISA was slightly positive, and leishmanial antigen in urine was negative. Bone‑marrow aspiration revealed hemophagocytosis. Over the next day she clinically worsened with progressive splenomegaly and cytopenias (WBC 4,800/mm3 with ANC 800/mm3, Hb 6.8 g/dl, platelets 27,000/mm3), triglycerides 686 mg/dl, ferritin 3,849 ng/ml, and sCD25 3,596 U/ml. Clotting tests were normal and perforin expression by flow cytometry was reported as normal.

A 30-year-old male returned from a safari in Kenya and Tanzania with a 2-day history of an enlarging skin lesion, fever, rigor, and gastrointestinal symptoms. Initial lab tests showed elevated CRP, lymphopenia, thrombocytopenia, and mild hyponatremia.

A 17-month-old female from Berkane presented with a 3-month history of anarchic (intermittent) fever, pallor, and episodes of epistaxis. On examination her temperature was 39 °C. Findings included lower-limb edema, pallor of the skin and mucous membranes, gingival petechiae, bleached hair, and hepatosplenomegaly. Complete blood count showed pancytopenia with a deep aregenerative normochromic normocytic anemia (hemoglobin 3 g/dL), leukocytes 4860/mm3 with neutropenia 680/mm3, and platelets 12,000/mm3; the blood smear was reported as without abnormality. Additional laboratory results demonstrated hypoalbuminemia, hypertriglyceridemia, hyperferritinemia, lactate dehydrogenase 337 IU/L, prothrombin time 56%, fibrinogen 1 g/L, and a positive direct Coombs test.

A 15-year-old male student presented to the emergency fever clinic with "fever accompanied with cough for more than 10 days." He had developed fever after a cold >10 days before admission, with temperatures fluctuating between 37 and 38°C initially, later peaking to 41°C; associated symptoms included cough, fatigue, chills, and pharyngeal discomfort. A local hospital workup showed WBC 3.3 x 10^9/L, Hb 85 g/L, and PLT 87 x 10^9/L. Bone marrow puncture there showed "hematopoietic tissue hyperplasia was active and the proportion of three-line blood cells was roughly normal," with occasional atypical lymphocytes. Adenovirus IgM was weakly positive, ferritin was >2,000 ng/ml, and procalcitonin 4.14 ng/ml. Abdominal ultrasound and CT at the local hospital indicated hepatomegaly and splenomegaly. After transfer, his vital signs were: T 37.1°C, pulse 110/min, respirations 19/min, BP 110/72 mmHg. TORCH/EBV: CMV, HSV, rubella virus, and EBV IgG were positive. Blood cultures showed no growth after 5 days. Chest CT was unremarkable. Abdominal ultrasound showed intercostal spleen thickness ~6.6 cm, compatible with splenomegaly. Empiric antibiotics (cefoperazone–sulbactam, then ceftriaxone) and dexamethasone were given without clear improvement. Do not exclude the possibility of parasitic diseases? Hemophilic cell syndrome? Lymphoma? Autoimmune disease?" Because the cause remained unclear, an mNGS test was performed on the second day after admission to the emergency department.

A 15‑year‑old boy presented to the emergency fever clinic with fever and cough for more than 10 days. He developed fever after a cold, with temperatures initially 37–38°C, later peaking at 41°C. Symptoms included cough, fatigue, chills, and pharyngeal discomfort. Initial local-hospital testing showed WBC 3.3 × 10^9/L, Hb 85 g/L, and PLT 87 × 10^9/L. Bone marrow puncture at that time "indicated that hematopoietic tissue hyperplasia was active and the proportion of three-line blood cells was roughly normal. Lymphocytes accounted for 9.5%, and atypical lymphocytes were found occasionally." Adenovirus IgM was weakly positive; ferritin was >2,000 ng/mL; procalcitonin was 4.14 ng/mL. Abdominal ultrasound and CT indicated hepatomegaly and splenomegaly. He was referred for further care after lack of improvement with initial treatment. On arrival his vital signs were: T 37.1°C, pulse 110/min, RR 19/min, BP 110/72 mmHg. TORCH/EBV panel: CMV, HSV, rubella virus, and EBV IgG positive. Direct Coombs' test was positive (++). HIV and syphilis tests were negative. Blood cultures showed no bacterial growth at 5 days. Chest CT was unremarkable. Abdominal ultrasound showed intercostal spleen thickness ≈6.6 cm, consistent with splenomegaly. Do not exclude the possibility of parasitic diseases? Hemophilic cell syndrome? Lymphoma? Autoimmune disease?" An mNGS test on blood was performed on the second day after admission because the cause of fever remained unclear.

A 15-year-old female from the Macanao municipality on Margarita Island, Venezuela presented with a 6-month history of intermittent fever predominantly occurring at night, malaise, 6 kg weight loss, arthralgias, loss of appetite, dizziness, and amenorrhea. She lives in a rural area close to a landfill in a house built with cement ground, brick walls, and a metal roof without running water. She has one dog (unknown Leishmania infection status) and various turtles as pets. She has no history of traveling outside Venezuela. On examination she was pale, with increased respiratory and heart rate, and a fever of 39 C. Weight was 49 kg, height 1.57 m, and abdominal circumference 76 cm. She had cervical, axillary, and inguinal adenopathy. Cardiac and lung exams were normal. Abdominal exam revealed right upper-quadrant tenderness and hepatosplenomegaly (liver palpable 9.5 cm from the midclavicular line; spleen Hackett grade V). Laboratory values on admission demonstrated pancytopenia. Abdominal ultrasound and computed tomography confirmed hepatosplenomegaly. The initial clinical suspicion was a lymphoproliferative or myeloproliferative disorder. From an infectious disease perspective, the possibility of visceral leishmaniasis, a systemic mycosis, or tuberculosis were entertained. A bone marrow biopsy was performed to rule out a hematologic malignancy and to assess for infectious causes.

contexts.text: A health centre in Bangladesh was using a generic product labeled "Miltefos" to treat patients with visceral leishmaniasis (VL). Investigators collected a representative sample of "Miltefos" specimens directly in the field at that centre. Simultaneously, whole blood samples from five patients who were still under treatment with "Miltefos" and the exact blisters that had been used to treat these patients were collected. Both the blood and drug specimens were transported to a laboratory in sealed and signed envelopes to ensure the integrity of the parcel in transit. Case record forms and signed statements by the doctors of these patients indicating the origin and authenticity of the samples were included. All five patients had already been several days on "Miltefos" treatment; because miltefosine has extremely slow elimination, substantial miltefosine blood concentrations would be expected after several days of dosing.

A 67-year-old patient with visceral leishmaniasis was treated with liposomal amphotericin B (L-AmB). As part of longitudinal follow-up, blood was tested for Leishmania kinetoplast DNA (kDNA) by quantitative PCR (qPCR) at predefined time points up to 12 months after diagnosis. At 3 months after treatment, the patient's blood kDNA qPCR showed a 2-log increase in parasite load compared with earlier measurements.

A 75-year-old man from Algeria with long-standing HIV infection presented with progressive systemic symptoms and known prior visceral leishmaniasis. Medical history: HIV since 2001 treated previously with nevirapine and lamivudine/zidovudine and, from 2013, with darunavir, ritonavir, raltegravir and emtricitabine; prior opportunistic infections and comorbidities included cerebral toxoplasmosis, chronic hepatitis B, gastrointestinal CMV infection, and anal squamous cell carcinoma. Visceral leishmaniasis (VL) was first diagnosed in 2001 and treated with liposomal amphotericin B (L‑AmB) 5 mg/kg/day for 15 days with partial improvement; a maintenance regimen of L‑AmB 3 mg/kg weekly was planned but was irregularly administered. Recurrence was reported in March 2011 and the infecting species was identified as Leishmania infantum. At that time the CD4 lymphocyte count was 33/mm3 and HIV viral load was 75,000 copies/mL. The patient received additional courses of L‑AmB including a cumulative 40 mg/kg followed by 3 mg/kg every 15 days, later infusions at 3‑week intervals, and in 2013 a final course totaling 50 mg/kg. Despite this most recent complete course of L‑AmB, symptoms worsened with weight loss and fatigue; imaging showed clinical splenomegaly with a maximal diameter of 20 cm on CT. Quantitative parasitemia remained positive and essentially unchanged, from 126 Leishmania/ml before treatment to 118 Leishmania/ml three weeks after completion of the course.

A 38-year-old man with HIV on dolutegravir and emtricitabine–tenofovir presented without prior ocular problems. The report notes him as "well controlled (CD4 count of 213 cells/mm3 with an undetectable viral load)." He initially presented with a nonulcerative papulonodular hypopigmented rash on the extremities, trunk, and abdomen; "H and E staining of the cutaneous biopsy showed Leishmaniasis chassis and infantum." Thrombocytopenia and splenomegaly were also noted. He was treated with intravenous liposomal amphotericin B (received 7 of 9 doses) and was lost to follow-up; one year later he had recurrent cutaneous disease and was retreated with amphotericin (14-dose course) and received miltefosine for a 28-day course. Two days after stopping miltefosine, he developed progressive left-eye redness, pain, and photophobia. On day 7 of symptoms his visual acuity in the left eye had declined to count fingers.

A 39‑year‑old man from Central America, living in Southeast Georgia, presents to the emergency department with abdominal pain and rectal bleeding. Past medical history: HIV/AIDS, alcohol abuse, tobacco dependency, and previously documented leishmaniasis diagnosed by bone marrow biopsy. He denied recent travel. Course and prior presentations: At initial presentation several years earlier he had diffuse moderate abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, chills and dysphagia; on exam he was tachycardic (heart rate 140/min) with mild abdominal tenderness. He was leukopenic and thrombocytopenic and was treated with amphotericin B and initiation of HAART; he was discharged on a 3‑month course of amphotericin B with ongoing HAART. Six months later he returned with acute abdominal pain and nausea; exam then showed a fine nodular skin rash across chest, abdomen and back described as consistent with cutaneous leishmaniasis, and thrombocytopenia persisted. At that time a bone marrow biopsy was performed to evaluate whether his new symptoms were due to HIV or a relapse of leishmaniasis, and he again received intravenous amphotericin B (inpatient 6 weeks) with plans for outpatient infusions. The patient subsequently was lost to follow‑up. Current presentation: Several years later he returned with a flare characterized by rectal bleeding and continued abdominal pain. Gastroenterology was consulted and an esophagogastroduodenoscopy was planned.

A 13‑year‑old boy, born in São Paulo, who had traveled at age 12 to the state of Minas Gerais, presented with fever on alternate days, pallor, increased abdominal volume and unquantified weight loss. He had no prior history of recurrent infections. On admission he had anemia and thrombocytopenia. Bone marrow aspirate showed amastigotes of Leishmania. He was treated with liposomal amphotericin B (LAB) at a dose of 35 mg/kg and was discharged. Four months later he returned with fever and thrombocytopenia; a bone marrow aspirate again showed amastigotes of Leishmania and parasites were detected in bone marrow culture. He was treated with meglumine antimoniate and intravenous human immunoglobulin with clinical and laboratory improvement and was discharged in good health. Three weeks later he presented with seven days of fever, weakness, pallor and increased abdominal volume. On exam the spleen was palpable 23 cm below the left costal margin and the liver 5 cm from the right costal margin. Leishmania ELISA immunoassay and the rK‑39 antigen test were negative. Bone marrow biopsy showed a lymphocytic and histiocytic inflammatory reaction with a granulomatous pattern; no amastigotes were observed in the aspirate. He was re‑treated empirically for visceral leishmaniasis with liposomal amphotericin B. Notably, the patient had silvery hair and eyebrows, described as a phenotype suggestive of Griscelli Syndrome.

A 41-year-old Caucasian man was admitted during treatment with intravenous liposomal amphotericin B for laryngeal and facial mucocutaneous leishmaniasis because of marked elevation of creatine kinase (CK) (more than 10× upper limit of normal during admission; pretreatment CK up to ~2× ULN previously) and rising serum creatinine. Past medical history was notable for visceral leishmaniasis at age 13, recurrent otitis and an episode of bronchopneumonia in childhood, long-standing unexplained elevated CK attributed in the past to occupation and boxing, and chronic periorbital/facial swelling first noted in 2013. In January 2019 he developed hoarseness and dysphonia; laryngoscopy and biopsy were positive for Leishmania spp., and earlier periocular skin samples (2015) were retrospectively PCR-positive for Leishmania spp. He reported no travel outside Europe. There was a family history notable for a brother who died at age 20 from an unspecified lymphoproliferative disease and a sister with chronic myalgias. B-cell immunophenotyping disclosed a defect in the memory compartment with markedly low switched-memory B cells. T-lymphocyte subpopulations were within reference limits except for reduced circulating Tfh cells. There was no history of liver or biliary tract disease or neutropenia. The patient met criteria for common-variable immunodeficiency, but because of the opportunistic, persistent Leishmania infection further genetic studies were pursued.

In March 1997 a bone marrow specimen demonstrated intracellular organisms consistent with the causal agent, and infection was thought likely acquired during travel to Spain in 1992. Initial antimonial therapy produced clinical improvement and apparent clearance from bone marrow, but disease relapsed in July 1997 and remained a chronic relapsing problem over the next 15 years despite multiple courses and combinations of systemic therapies, including antimonials (sodium stibogluconate), paromomycin, liposomal amphotericin B (various dosing regimens), and, from 2005, intermittent courses of oral miltefosine. Organisms were visualized repeatedly in bone marrow (multiple dates between 2004–2011) and in biopsies from skin, lymph nodes and sigmoid colon. Treatment was complicated by drug-related toxicities (visual impairment attributed to antimonials; hearing loss attributed to aminoglycoside exposure) and recurrent bacteremia from an indwelling intravenous cannula. The patient developed progressive symptomatic splenomegaly with increasing transfusion requirements and pancytopenia. A Leishmania isolate cultured from a bone marrow aspirate in October 2007 was tested in January 2008 with reported in vitro resistance to antimonials but susceptibility to other agents. In view of the worsening clinical picture and increasing amastigote density in marrow despite available treatment, alternative therapeutic approaches were discussed with the patient and external experts.

He had lived in Jinghe County for over 40 years and reported no travel history to areas endemic for visceral leishmaniasis. He initially sought care at two local hospitals and "was diagnosed with suspected pneumonia" and received a 15-day course of intravenous levofloxacin and ribavirin with supportive measures, but "the response to this treatment was inadequate." On admission to the tertiary fever clinic on November 29, 2022 his temperature was 38.5 C, pulse 80/min, respirations 20/min, and blood pressure 137/70 mmHg. Abdominal examination revealed tenderness in the right upper quadrant without rebound; the liver and spleen were not initially palpable below the rib cage, although during the course of the illness he developed abdominal pain, hepatomegaly, and jaundice. Laboratory testing showed leukopenia (3.10 x 10^9/L) and mild anemia (hemoglobin 99.0 g/L). Liver enzymes were elevated: ALT 168 U/L, AST 281 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 646 U/L, and gamma-GT 586 U/L. Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated thickening of the gallbladder wall and hepatomegaly and splenomegaly. Microbiology and serology obtained during the initial evaluation were unrevealing: "Blood culture results were negative for bacteria and fungi as well as serological tests for coronavirus disease 2019, hepatitis B, hepatitis C, acquired immune deficiency syndrome, and syphilis." A blood sample was also tested by nested PCR for Leishmania and "the blood sample from the patient tested negative by nested PCR."

Eight years earlier he had a small papule on the right cheek that progressed to an open ulcer, then to ulcers on the left cheek and forehead; those active lesions lasted about six months and healed spontaneously, leaving permanent hypopigmented scars. On one presentation, physical examination showed multiple nodular lesions on his hands, face and nose, swelling of the upper lip, and crusted central ulcers with raised peripheral contours; multiple healed scars were present on both cheeks. He had no fever, hepatosplenomegaly or lymphedema and reported no history of HIV, chronic disease, alcohol abuse, or immunomodulatory drug use. Parasitological testing of lesion smears at that time showed many macrophages filled with amastigote stages of Leishmania, graded as +6. A nonreactive rK39 rapid diagnostic test and absence of related systemic signs made visceral leishmaniasis unlikely. Based on the clinical manifestations and smear result he was diagnosed with mucocutaneous leishmaniasis and treated with intramuscular sodium stibogluconate (20 mg/kg/day for 30 days) with clinical cure. Two years later he returned with a different cutaneous eruption that had appeared over the previous three months and had been preceded by intense itching. On exam he had multiple, nonpitting, closed papules on his face, nose, hands and legs. A skin smear again showed intramacrophage amastigotes with a parasite load graded +6, and culture grew promastigotes.

retrieval_query_text:
You are evaluating the diagnostic approach to suspected visceral leishmaniasis (VL) in HIV-infected adults. A systematic review identified 33 studies recruiting 1489 patients that evaluated diagnostic tests in this population. The evaluated index tests included direct agglutination test (DAT), indirect fluorescent antibody test (IFAT), enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), immunoblotting (Blot), rapid K39-based immunochromatographic test, and haemagglutination (HA), and several studies evaluated PCR on peripheral blood or bone marrow. The reference standard used across studies was a positive result on direct microscopic examination or culture of blood or bone marrow aspirate (in a few studies other tissue samples were used). Study designs were heterogeneous (prospective, retrospective, cross-sectional), most studies were small, and many did not report consecutive inclusion or blinding.

Pooled estimates from random-effects models (reported in the review) included approximate sensitivities and specificities: IFAT estimated sensitivity 51% (95% CI 43–58%); Blot sensitivity 84% (75–91%); DAT sensitivity 81% (61–95%); ELISA sensitivity 66% (40–88%); PCR in whole blood sensitivity 92% (83–98%); PCR in bone marrow sensitivity 98% (93–100%). Overall pooled specificities were generally high across tests. The review emphasized wide heterogeneity across studies and variable study quality.
