contexts.text: A 60-year-old woman from Uttar Pradesh, India presented with a six‑week history of high‑grade continuous fever with chills and rigors, anorexia, malaise, joint pains, and severe lethargy. She reported "crops of round, raised lesions" that began on the left upper limb, progressed to the right upper limb and then involved the whole face, upper back, chest, and upper abdomen; the lesions were "closely associated with the febrile episodes." Some lesions enlarged, became nodular, developed sunken centers that drained pus‑like material, and were painful and red. One week before admission she developed jaundice with mild to moderate upper‑quadrant abdominal pain. She also noted nonpainful bilateral leg swelling (pitting) and painful red eyes with nodular lesions on the eyelids and in the conjunctiva, associated with decreased vision. She had no prior comorbidities, was a teetotaler, and denied taking over‑the‑counter or steroid/complementary medications or other potentially immunosuppressive drugs. On examination her temperature was 100.8°F, blood pressure 128/88 mm Hg, heart rate 100/min. Pallor and icterus were present; there was bilateral pitting, non‑tender symmetrical pedal edema. Skin exam showed "multiple crops of nodular, noduloulcerative, and papular lesions, dispersed throughout the body surface, mostly segregated to the face and upper back," some with pus drainage from central sunken areas. Fundoscopy showed uveitis and small retinal hemorrhages. Serum IgG 22.6 g/L.

An 84‑year‑old woman presented with a large nodular lesion on the forehead of 2.5 months' duration. She had been seen at another hospital where a pre‑diagnosis of lymphoma was recorded; the prior punch biopsy report listed basal cell carcinoma, sarcoidosis, lupus vulgaris and pseudolymphoma among the clinical pre‑diagnoses and the material was sent for pathology consultation. Microscopic examination of the punch biopsy showed a dense nodular and diffuse lymphohistiocytic cell infiltration within the dermis. In the cytoplasm of histiocytes, small, round structures resembling organisms were noted. Immunohistochemical staining showed reactive T lymphocytes labelled with CD3 and CD5, reactive B lymphocytes labelled with CD20, and large clusters of histiocytes labelled with CD68; there was no staining with CD30. The pathology report recommended investigation of the aetiology of granulomatous dermatitis, especially cutaneous leishmaniasis.

A 52‑year‑old woman who works in sugarcane fields in a rural area was referred to Oral Medicine for evaluation of a granulomatous lesion on the palate and for hoarseness that she thought followed a flu 3 months earlier. According to the referring surgeon, she had an extensive oral lesion and had undergone laryngoscopy and biopsy; that biopsy produced a histopathological result of “pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia and an active chronic inflammatory process, suggesting a fungus investigation,” prompting the referral. She reported no chronic systemic disease or regular medications. She described a history of crusting and nasal bleeding that began about 4 years earlier. On examination she had nasal obstruction, a nasal (hyponasal) voice, and was a mouth breather. She had smoked for 6 months and used both upper and lower complete dental prostheses continuously. Extrabuccal exam showed a lowering of the right nasal wing and a nasal septum perforation. Intrabuccal exam revealed a granulomatous lesion involving the entire palate and uvula, extending bilaterally to the pharynx with an erythematous appearance and areas of scratchable white plaques.

A 30‑year‑old man presented with pain in his lower limbs and a non‑itchy erythematous rash over both lower limbs. He had low‑grade intermittent fever for three months. On examination he was pale and malnourished (BMI 18.4 kg/m2) and had palpable purpura over both thighs and buttocks. Abdominal examination revealed palpable hepatomegaly with massive splenomegaly. Laboratory testing showed pancytopenia (hemoglobin 6.8 g/dL, total leukocyte count 2800/mm3, platelet count 45 000/muL) and polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia (4.9 g/dL); liver and renal function tests were within reference ranges. Contrast‑enhanced CT of chest and abdomen confirmed hepatosplenomegaly and was otherwise unremarkable. The treating team considered hematologic malignancy and a connective‑tissue disorder with vasculitis. Other infectious etiologies entertained included HIV, scrub typhus/rickettsial infection, and visceral leishmaniasis (given the patient lived in an endemic area). Initial testing showed: anti‑nuclear antibodies, complement levels (C3 = 94 mg/dL and C4 = 20 mg/dL), and rheumatoid factor were negative; urine examination was normal and serum cryoglobulins were not raised. Viral markers (HIV, hepatitis B surface antigen, and anti‑hepatitis C) were negative. Serology for rickettsia and scrub typhus were also negative.

A 60‑year‑old Austrian man presented in September 2016 with a three‑week history of fever of unknown origin, fatigue, and unintentional weight loss of 6 kg. Initial physical examination was inconspicuous. His medical history was notable for adequately treated diabetes mellitus type 2 and hypothyroidism. Travel history included a two‑week trip to the south of Crete in September 2015 and a two‑week trip the south of Spain in May 2016. Laboratory tests showed markedly elevated C‑reactive protein (CRP 94.2–188.9 mg/L), slight hypochromic normocytic anemia without signs of hemolysis (hemoglobin 12.5 g/dL), mild thrombocytopenia (127,000/µL), and a discreetly elevated gamma‑glutamyltransferase (GGT). The soluble interleukin‑2 receptor (IL‑2R) was elevated to 5156.1 pg/mL. Chest x‑ray, urine analysis, abdominal sonography, transthoracic and transesophageal echocardiography revealed no focus of infection but did show splenomegaly (7.2 × 16.4 cm). Empiric antibiotic therapy (initially ampicillin/sulbactam, later piperacillin/tazobactam plus vancomycin) did not lead to improvement. Over the next three weeks the patient’s discrete bicytopenia progressed to severe pancytopenia requiring blood transfusions. Lactate dehydrogenase rose to 1107 U/L, liver enzymes including GGT, alkaline phosphatase and AST increased, and fever persisted up to 40°C. Positron emission tomography–computed tomography showed tracer enhancement in the central and peripheral bone marrow.

A 43-year-old male laborer with known HIV infection for 2 years (on antiretroviral therapy) and on anti-tubercular treatment for 9 months presented with a 7-month history of asymptomatic skin lesions all over his body. Lesions first appeared on the arm and progressively spread to involve the face, legs, and trunk. On examination there were multiple bilateral asymmetrical diffuse papulonodular, non‑itchy skin lesions measuring 2–25 mm on the face, trunk, and extremities. There were no signs of ulceration or scarring. There was no lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly. A photograph showed multiple papulonodular lesions of varying size over the elbow. Laboratory tests showed anemia (hemoglobin 9.1 g/dL); liver and renal function tests and lipid profile were within normal limits. Ultrasonography of the abdomen was normal. CD4 count was 50 cells/µL and HIV viral load was 1750 copies/mL. There was no history of travel to known endemic areas for leishmaniasis.

A 78-year-old man from a rural area in western Iran was referred for multiple ulcerative, exudative lesions involving the mid-face (upper lip and anterior nasal fossa), above the eyebrows, dorsal aspects of both hands, and posterior aspects of both heels. Lesions began three years earlier as papules on the dorsal hands and progressively enlarged to involve the face and heels and became ulcerative; involvement of the right hand progressed to destruction of tendons and soft tissue of the fifth finger, resulting in amputation of that finger. He had no history of comorbid conditions, no regular medications reported, and denied systemic symptoms — there was no weight loss, fever, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly or other signs of systemic involvement on examination or routine laboratory survey. Multiple prior empirical treatments for different presumed diagnoses, including pyoderma gangrenosum, sarcoidosis, and leishmaniasis, had been tried without improvement. An initial skin biopsy showed a necrotizing and palisading granulomatous tissue pattern that suggested an infectious etiology, but initial smears of lesion material for fungal elements, mycobacteria and Leishmania were negative. A tuberculin skin test produced a 27 mm induration, and anti-tuberculosis therapy (isoniazid, rifampin, ethambutol, and pyrazinamide) was started.

A 59‑year‑old man, mixed ethnicity, unemployed, previously healthy, reported that an erythematous‑crusty lesion appeared in the region of the mental protuberance and over two months evolved to involve other parts of the body, including the frontal and occipital regions, nasal septum, ears, hands, and lower limbs. Oral examination showed scattered ulcers on the face, lower labial mucosa, and on the left lip commissure, a pseudomembrane on the marginal gingiva, and an exophytic nodule in the left labial mucosa. The patient had a positive Montenegro intradermal test and was admitted to the University Hospital in December 2018. After admission, clinicians noted enlarged lymph nodes of hard consistency in the left inguinal region and an extensive irregular melanocytic lesion in the left plantar region presenting an area of hyperkeratosis with a grey‑bluish center; the plantar lesion was biopsied for further evaluation. A PCR analysis had been performed in an external laboratory.

A 42‑year‑old Italian man with a 20‑year history of plaque psoriasis and psoriasis arthropathica presented with lesions that had appeared 6 months earlier. He had been treated with subcutaneous methotrexate 25 mg weekly for 9 years and adalimumab 40 mg every other week for 7 years. Topical therapies had been used in the weeks before hospitalization. The patient was obese (BMI 39 kg/m2). On examination he had multiple erythemato‑squamous psoriatic plaques (PASI 16.6) and multiple erosive and partly ulcerating plaques and nodules—some with distinct brown crusts—on the right forearm, right knee, left flank, and abdomen. There was no lymphadenopathy and no other pathological findings on physical exam. An externally performed lesion biopsy reported dermal T‑cell infiltrates without evidence of malignancy. Two repeat biopsies from morphologically different lesions showed interface dermatitis with pseudolymphomatous infiltrates, thickening of the epidermis, follicular hyperparakeratosis, and perivascular and periadnexal superficially accentuated lymphocytic infiltrates with a preponderance of T cells. Tissue clonality analyses demonstrated polyclonal IgH and TCR gamma chain gene expression, thus excluding lymphoma. Direct immunofluorescence did not detect any IgG, IgM, IgA, or C3 depositions. Syphilis serology, carried out because numerous plasma cells were present in the tissue, yielded negative results.

A 32-year-old man from Djelfa, Algeria, with a history of contact eczema presented with a 6-week history of painless, non-healing skin lesions on the dorsal aspect of his right hand. He had applied topical corticosteroids and antiseptics without improvement and had received two courses of antibiotics (pristinamycin, amoxicillin + clavulanic acid) with no significant results. On examination there was a limited erythematous-papular plaque, approximately 8 cm in diameter, on the dorsal right hand formed by confluence of several papules with satellite lesions at the periphery. The initial plaque was associated with several firm, painless subcutaneous nodules 0.5–1.5 cm in diameter that tracked proximally along lymphatic drainage toward the elbow. The patient did not recall an insect bite, no other body sites were involved, and the remainder of the examination was unremarkable. Direct mycological examination and culture on Sabouraud medium at 25 °C and on BHI medium at 37 °C were negative for fungal presence.

contexts.text: A 54-year-old healthy woman presented to ophthalmology with a few months' history of a symptomatic lesion of the right eye. The lesion was located in the nasal bulbar conjunctiva within the interpalpebral zone. On examination there was an erythematous fibrovascular lesion approximately 5 mm in length. The lesion produced foreign-body sensation and discomfort. The lesion was clinically diagnosed as a pterygium, and surgical removal was performed.

A 29-year-old woman from Rio de Janeiro (resident of the Caju neighborhood) presented for diagnostic evaluation in January 2013. She worked as a cleaner in the cemetery of Caju and denied any travel outside the city. Five months before admission she developed intermittent nocturnal fevers up to 39 °C that did not respond to antipyretics, with poor appetite, postprandial fullness, nausea and vomiting. Over the following months she noted progressive jaundice (yellow sclera and skin), dark urine, weight loss of ~10 kg, increasing abdominal girth and soft bilateral lower‑extremity edema to the knees. She had multiple prior emergency visits and received only symptomatic treatment. On admission her general state was poor with malnutrition; examination showed pallor 3–4/4, mild dehydration, jaundice 2/4, cyanosis, fever and tachycardia. Abdominal exam showed moderate ascites, hepatomegaly 7 cm below the right costal margin and splenomegaly palpable 2 cm below the umbilicus. The initial diagnostic hypotheses included disseminated tuberculosis and visceral leishmaniasis; other considered diagnoses were dengue, yellow fever, prolonged septicemic salmonellosis, brucellosis, malaria, Chagas disease and lymphoproliferative malignancies. Investigations ordered included thick and thin blood smears, blood cultures, stool tests, bone marrow biopsy and aspiration and serologies for dengue, yellow fever, brucellosis and Chagas disease. HIV testing was performed and was negative.

A 52‑year‑old woman who works in sugarcane fields in a rural area was referred to Oral Medicine for evaluation of a granulomatous lesion on the palate and for hoarseness that she thought followed a flu 3 months earlier. According to the referring surgeon, she had an extensive oral lesion and had undergone laryngoscopy and biopsy; that biopsy produced a histopathological result of “pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia and an active chronic inflammatory process, suggesting a fungus investigation,” prompting the referral. She reported no chronic systemic disease or regular medications. She described a history of crusting and nasal bleeding that began about 4 years earlier. On examination she had nasal obstruction, a nasal (hyponasal) voice, and was a mouth breather. She had smoked for 6 months and used both upper and lower complete dental prostheses continuously. Extrabuccal exam showed a lowering of the right nasal wing and a nasal septum perforation. Intrabuccal exam revealed a granulomatous lesion involving the entire palate and uvula, extending bilaterally to the pharynx with an erythematous appearance and areas of scratchable white plaques.

A 53-year-old man from Mundo Novo, State of Bahia, Brazil, presented in July with pain, nasal obstruction, odynophagia, and dysphagia. On examination there was a painful, hyperemic, friable lesion in the right nasal cavity and an infiltrative lesion involving the hard palate, soft palate, and uvula. Additional findings included an ulcerated lesion on the left eyebrow and right eye with seropurulent secretion, a small ulcer on the lower eyelid, a lesion on the lobe of the right ear, and a lesion in the malar region. The patient was admitted for diagnosis and management of disseminated skin lesions. A biopsy of the palate lesions showed a non-specific erosive chronic inflammatory process. HIV testing was negative.

A 31-year-old woman from Salvador, State of Bahia, presented in 2013 with submandibular lymphadenopathy and multiple ulcerated lesions involving the lower lip frenulum, gingiva, nasal septum and a lesion on her back. She reported a prior cutaneous lesion on her back that had been recurrent over the prior year. On oral examination there was poor oral health and ulcerated lesions of the lower lip frenulum and adjacent gingiva. Excisional biopsies of the oral lesions were performed and reported as unspecific; microbiological analysis for fungi was negative.

A 55-year-old man from the Manaus region with no comorbidities had been treated for cutaneous leishmaniasis. He had completed treatment with a pentavalent antimonial drug 40 days earlier and had received a second outpatient 30-day cycle; ten days after the end of that treatment his leishmaniasis lesion was healed. He then developed grouped microvesicles on an erythematous-infiltrated base that began in the neck and ascended toward the right scalp margin. The vesicles involved the right pinna, external auditory canal, and right ear lobe and were associated with severe torticollis-like pain along the nerve distribution. HIV serology was negative.

A 40-year-old man of Albanian descent who has lived in Athens for 20 years was admitted in February 2008 for progressive constitutional and respiratory symptoms. A 59‑year‑old man, mixed ethnicity, unemployed, previously healthy, reported that an erythematous‑crusty lesion appeared in the region of the mental protuberance and over two months evolved to involve other parts of the body, including the frontal and occipital regions, nasal septum, ears, hands, and lower limbs. Oral examination showed scattered ulcers on the face, lower labial mucosa, and on the left lip commissure, a pseudomembrane on the marginal gingiva, and an exophytic nodule in the left labial mucosa. The patient had a positive Montenegro intradermal test and was admitted to the University Hospital in December 2018. After admission, clinicians noted enlarged lymph nodes of hard consistency in the left inguinal region and an extensive irregular melanocytic lesion in the left plantar region presenting an area of hyperkeratosis with a grey‑bluish center; the plantar lesion was biopsied for further evaluation. A PCR analysis had been performed in an external laboratory.

A 30-year-old woman with a history of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) diagnosed during pregnancy in 2010 presented with skin lesions. History of present illness and past medical history:
- She received antiretroviral therapy from 2013 to 2018 (zidovudine 300 mg orally twice daily, lamivudine 150 mg orally twice daily, efavirenz 600 mg orally once daily) but the antiretroviral regimen was discontinued several times. - In October 2020 she developed a single ulcerative lesion on a lower limb. - At that time a diagnosis of tegumentary leishmaniasis (TL) was confirmed by Giemsa‑stained slides from skin scraping. - She began treatment with meglumine antimoniate (20 mg Sb+5/kg IV daily for 20 days) but discontinued treatment soon after starting. - In late 2021 she returned with new lesions on the left lower limb and right upper limb; a biopsy sample was collected for parasite isolation. - She subsequently received liposomal amphotericin B (3 mg/kg) for 20 days, experienced a relapse, started another antimonial regimen which she abandoned after a few days, and in August 2022 had recurrence of the lower‑limb lesion followed by a 10‑day course of liposomal amphotericin B with complete healing. - Geographic context: patient resides in a municipality in the State of Maranhão, Brazil, within an ecotone region where leishmaniasis is endemic.

An 84‑year‑old woman presented with a large nodular lesion on the forehead of 2.5 months' duration. Postoperative recovery was uncomplicated with preserved phonation and swallowing and no residual palpable neck mass.

contexts.text: A 37-year-old man from Maranhão, Brazil, employed as a sugarcane cutter, and the son of a consanguineous marriage, presented with 5 months of daily fevers up to 39°C, progressive asthenia, about 10 kg weight loss, and increasing abdominal volume. He had a remote history: at age 21 he was diagnosed with rheumatoid arthritis and received NSAIDs and prednisone, with maintenance corticosteroid therapy (10 mg/day) for 7 years. He and his family reported no history of recurrent infections. On examination he had pallor of skin and mucous membranes, splenomegaly extending 21 cm below the left costal margin, and hepatomegaly 4 cm below the right costal margin. Laboratory testing demonstrated pancytopenia and hypoalbuminemia. Bone marrow aspirate showed relative hypocellularity of the granulocytes without visualization of amastigotes. Bone marrow biopsy showed a proportional increase in granulocytes. A liver biopsy was performed; immunohistochemistry was negative for Leishmania.

A 7‑month‑old male infant presented with fever for 10 days. On examination he had hepatosplenomegaly, pallor, and anasarca. Laboratory evaluation showed bicytopenia and increased ferritin. An immunochromatographic rapid test with rK39 antigen was positive for Leishmania spp., and amastigotes were detected on myelogram.

A 2-year-old domestic European neutered male cat was referred with a 1-year history of skin disease characterized by multiple nodular skin lesions, ulcerative dermatitis of all four limbs and fever. The owner reported prior empirical treatment for a presumptive pyodermatitis with prednisolone, amoxicillin/clavulanic acid and doxycycline without clinical improvement. At first admission the only abnormalities on physical examination were mild fever (39.5oC) and dermatological lesions on the head and limbs. Approximately 20–25 cutaneous nodules (2–10 mm diameter) were distributed on the outer pinnal surfaces and orbital regions, most notably on the pinnae with some coalescence. Single ulcerative dermatitis spots (20–50 mm diameter) with raised margins affected the antebrachial and hock regions. Differential diagnosis at presentation included pyodermatitis, allergic reaction, autoimmune disease, neoplastic disease or leishmaniosis. A complete blood count and biochemical profile were performed and values were within reference intervals; serum protein electrophoresis showed a slight hypergammaglobulinaemia. Fine-needle aspiration puncture from the ear skin nodules was performed for further analysis.

A 10-year-old neutered male domestic shorthair cat (5.2 kg, BCS 4/9) was evaluated for halitosis and several weeks of occasional discomfort and difficulty eating. The cat was a rescued animal with previous outdoor access and currently lives indoors alone. At adoption, immunologic tests for FIV and FeLV were negative. On clinical examination there was more severe periodontal disease on the right side and a right maxillary local stomatitis with a nodular, ulcerative appearance; on inspection the nodular lesion was slightly painful with spontaneous bleeding. Bilateral mandibular lymph node enlargement was present; no other abnormalities were noted. Under anesthesia a detailed oral exam and full-mouth radiographs demonstrated periodontal pocketing (7 mm) at the site of the nodular ulcero-hemorrhagic lesion (third right maxillary premolar), advanced periodontitis of multiple teeth on the right maxilla, tooth resorption in six teeth including the affected premolar, and radiographic vertical bone loss adjacent to the lesion. Treatment at that time included extraction of teeth with resorption and advanced attachment loss, routine closure of gingival flaps, and incisional biopsies of the maxillary lesion for histopathologic assessment. Two weeks after surgery the cat's appetite and weight had improved, but a nodular ulcero-hemorrhagic lesion with persistent swelling and inflammation of the right maxilla remained.

A 29-year-old woman from Rio de Janeiro (resident of the Caju neighborhood) presented for diagnostic evaluation in January 2013. She worked as a cleaner in the cemetery of Caju and denied any travel outside the city. Five months before admission she developed intermittent nocturnal fevers up to 39 °C that did not respond to antipyretics, with poor appetite, postprandial fullness, nausea and vomiting. Over the following months she noted progressive jaundice (yellow sclera and skin), dark urine, weight loss of ~10 kg, increasing abdominal girth and soft bilateral lower‑extremity edema to the knees. She had multiple prior emergency visits and received only symptomatic treatment. On admission her general state was poor with malnutrition; examination showed pallor 3–4/4, mild dehydration, jaundice 2/4, cyanosis, fever and tachycardia. Abdominal exam showed moderate ascites, hepatomegaly 7 cm below the right costal margin and splenomegaly palpable 2 cm below the umbilicus. The initial diagnostic hypotheses included disseminated tuberculosis and visceral leishmaniasis; other considered diagnoses were dengue, yellow fever, prolonged septicemic salmonellosis, brucellosis, malaria, Chagas disease and lymphoproliferative malignancies. Investigations ordered included thick and thin blood smears, blood cultures, stool tests, bone marrow biopsy and aspiration and serologies for dengue, yellow fever, brucellosis and Chagas disease. HIV testing was performed and was negative.

A 68-year-old man from a mountainous area in Hebei Province, China, presented with fever, sweating, and fatigue. He first sought care on February 1 and was hospitalized at a local hospital with temperature 39.0°C, chills, and no respiratory, abdominal, diarrheal, or urinary symptoms. He had lost approximately 10 kg over the prior 6 months. Initial blood tests showed pancytopenia, a rapid erythrocyte sedimentation rate, elevated C-reactive protein and ferritin, hyponatremia, hypokalemia, hypoproteinemia, and elevated serum enzyme levels. Bone marrow aspiration smear at that time showed granulocytopenia with megakaryocyte maturation disorder. Abdominal ultrasound showed splenomegaly; brain CT showed bilateral basal ganglia lacunar infarction; chest CT showed bilateral fibrotic/bronchitic changes. After 11 days of antibiotic and supportive treatment his fever and fatigue persisted with temperatures >39°C, so he presented for further evaluation on February 16. On arrival his SARS-CoV-2 PCR was negative. On examination he was febrile to 38.2°C, poorly nourished, unable to walk (bilateral leg strength grade 3), and had pitting edema of the anterior tibias and dorsal feet. Repeat laboratory testing again showed pancytopenia, increased ESR, CRP and ferritin, and elevated liver enzymes. Empiric antibiotic therapy had not relieved his febrile illness.

A 15-year-old female from the Macanao municipality on Margarita Island, Venezuela presented with a 6-month history of intermittent fever predominantly occurring at night, malaise, 6 kg weight loss, arthralgias, loss of appetite, dizziness, and amenorrhea. She lives in a rural area close to a landfill in a house built with cement ground, brick walls, and a metal roof without running water. She has one dog (unknown Leishmania infection status) and various turtles as pets. She has no history of traveling outside Venezuela. On examination she was pale, with increased respiratory and heart rate, and a fever of 39 C. Weight was 49 kg, height 1.57 m, and abdominal circumference 76 cm. She had cervical, axillary, and inguinal adenopathy. Cardiac and lung exams were normal. Abdominal exam revealed right upper-quadrant tenderness and hepatosplenomegaly (liver palpable 9.5 cm from the midclavicular line; spleen Hackett grade V). Laboratory values on admission demonstrated pancytopenia. Abdominal ultrasound and computed tomography confirmed hepatosplenomegaly. The initial clinical suspicion was a lymphoproliferative or myeloproliferative disorder. From an infectious disease perspective, the possibility of visceral leishmaniasis, a systemic mycosis, or tuberculosis were entertained. A bone marrow biopsy was performed to rule out a hematologic malignancy and to assess for infectious causes.

A 1-year-old boy was admitted with continuous fever for 3 months. On evaluation he had hepatosplenomegaly and anemia, and laboratory testing showed hypertriglyceridemia and increased ferritin; he experienced hemodynamic instability requiring blood transfusion. An immunochromatographic rapid test with rK39 antigen was positive for Leishmania, and the myelogram demonstrated Leishmania spp with hemophagocytosis. Treatment with meglumine antimoniate (glucantime) was started. As fever persisted, on day 8 nonresponse to glucantime was considered and therapy was changed to liposomal amphotericin. Due to fever and neutropenia, cefepime was also started.

A 7-year-old castrated male domestic short-haired cat, stray with unknown history, from the greater Athens area of Greece was presented for examination because of facial swelling and eye lesions. On examination there was a raised, nonalopecic, semifirm, poorly demarcated, painless swelling of the forehead. Periocular hypotrichosis, edema, and slight hyperpigmentation were present. Edema of the conjunctiva and third eyelid of the right eye was also observed. Clinical examination revealed no other abnormalities. A blood sample for complete blood count and biochemistry profile was obtained, and fine needle aspirates and a trucut biopsy were taken from the forehead swelling for cytological and histopathological examination. The patient had a nonregenerative anemia, hyperglobulinemia, and thrombocytopenia. Urinalysis showed no abnormalities. Further suggested serological tests for vector-borne diseases were not done because of financial restrictions. At presentation the clinicians listed the differential diagnosis as: subcutaneous abscess, atypical bacterial and mycobacterial infection, deep fungal infection, and neoplasia.

A 30‑year‑old man presented with pain in his lower limbs and a non‑itchy erythematous rash over both lower limbs. He had low‑grade intermittent fever for three months. On examination he was pale and malnourished (BMI 18.4 kg/m2) and had palpable purpura over both thighs and buttocks. Abdominal examination revealed palpable hepatomegaly with massive splenomegaly. Laboratory testing showed pancytopenia (hemoglobin 6.8 g/dL, total leukocyte count 2800/mm3, platelet count 45 000/muL) and polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia (4.9 g/dL); liver and renal function tests were within reference ranges. Contrast‑enhanced CT of chest and abdomen confirmed hepatosplenomegaly and was otherwise unremarkable. The treating team considered hematologic malignancy and a connective‑tissue disorder with vasculitis. Other infectious etiologies entertained included HIV, scrub typhus/rickettsial infection, and visceral leishmaniasis (given the patient lived in an endemic area). Initial testing showed: anti‑nuclear antibodies, complement levels (C3 = 94 mg/dL and C4 = 20 mg/dL), and rheumatoid factor were negative; urine examination was normal and serum cryoglobulins were not raised. Viral markers (HIV, hepatitis B surface antigen, and anti‑hepatitis C) were negative. Serology for rickettsia and scrub typhus were also negative.

contexts.text: A 42‑year‑old Italian man with a 20‑year history of plaque psoriasis and psoriasis arthropathica presented with lesions that had appeared 6 months earlier. He had been treated with subcutaneous methotrexate 25 mg weekly for 9 years and adalimumab 40 mg every other week for 7 years. Topical therapies had been used in the weeks before hospitalization. The patient was obese (BMI 39 kg/m2). On examination he had multiple erythemato‑squamous psoriatic plaques (PASI 16.6) and multiple erosive and partly ulcerating plaques and nodules—some with distinct brown crusts—on the right forearm, right knee, left flank, and abdomen. There was no lymphadenopathy and no other pathological findings on physical exam. An externally performed lesion biopsy reported dermal T‑cell infiltrates without evidence of malignancy. Two repeat biopsies from morphologically different lesions showed interface dermatitis with pseudolymphomatous infiltrates, thickening of the epidermis, follicular hyperparakeratosis, and perivascular and periadnexal superficially accentuated lymphocytic infiltrates with a preponderance of T cells. Tissue clonality analyses demonstrated polyclonal IgH and TCR gamma chain gene expression, thus excluding lymphoma. Direct immunofluorescence did not detect any IgG, IgM, IgA, or C3 depositions. A serum sample was negative for antibodies against extractable nuclear antigens and complement factors were within normal ranges.

A 30-year-old woman from an area endemic for tegumentary leishmaniasis presented with a single skin complaint. She reported a small papular lesion on her right leg that had developed over 7–10 days. At age 10 she had had an ulcer on the left thigh that healed spontaneously and left a well-defined atrophic scar. On examination there was a depressed papular lesion on the right leg measuring 8 × 7 mm; there was a 30 × 20 mm atrophic scar on the left thigh and no lymphadenopathy. Because early lesions of the locally prevalent Leishmania species may be papular and nonulcerated, a Leishmania skin test (LST) was performed on the left forearm. After 48 hours the intradermal reaction was strongly positive, with an induration measuring 38 × 32 mm. Eight days after the skin test the original papular lesion on the right leg had resolved, and a new round cutaneous ulcer with raised borders measuring 26 × 24 mm was present at the site of the LST. A culture of aspirated material from the forearm lesion was negative for Leishmania.

A 61-year-old man (weight 65 kg) was referred in January with a 2-month history of a 1 × 3 cm lesion on the left ear. He has diabetes and had not traveled outside Kashan during the previous year. He reported that the ear lesion felt uncomfortable and scabrous but was not painful and he had no systemic complaints. Direct microscopy of scales with 10% potassium hydroxide (KOH) preparation was negative for fungal elements. The lesion was cleaned and specimens were collected from the margin by scraping; two smears were fixed with methanol and stained with 10% Giemsa for 30 minutes. On microscopic examination of the stained smears, amastigote forms of Leishmania spp. were observed.

A 25-year-old man presented with a left-sided upper abdominal lump and multiple skin lesions present for the last 12 years. The abdominal lump had been very slowly increasing in size, was painless and produced a mild dragging sensation. The skin lesions were present primarily on his back and abdomen; they were described as depigmented, painless, and non-itchy. He denied current fever, loss of appetite, weight loss, cough, jaundice, hematemesis, melaena, and blood transfusion. He reported a history of kala-azar 15 years earlier treated with an injectable medication (he could not recall the drug name). He was a known chronic hepatitis B patient on entecavir 1 mg once daily. On examination there were multiple hypo- and hyperpigmented macular and maculopapular non-scaly skin lesions distributed over the trunk (mainly back, chest, and abdomen); lesion size ranged from a few millimeters (0.3–0.7 mm) for hypopigmented spots to 1–3 cm for hyperpigmented lesions, and sensation over the lesions was intact. Other vital signs were normal. Abdominal examination showed firm, non-tender hepatosplenomegaly with the liver 4 cm below the right costal margin and the spleen 6 cm along its long axis.

A 45-year-old Iranian man presented to dermatology in March 2008 with two large tumoral skin lesions. History of present illness and past history:
- Several years of chronic renal failure secondary to non–insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus (NIDDM). - In April 2006, after travel to an endemic area (Natanz in Isfahan province, Iran), he developed small papular lesions (reported as 2 x 5 millimeter) on the left wrist and the right shin. Those small lesions were left untreated. - Due to chronic renal failure, he underwent renal transplantation in August 2007. - After transplantation he was started on immunosuppression with prednisolone 50 mg/day and cyclosporine 7.5 mg/kg daily (reported as equivalent to 600 mg for an 80 kg patient). - Several weeks after transplantation and initiation of immunosuppressive therapy, the previously small papular lesions enlarged markedly into cauliflower-like, tumoral lesions. Physical examination:
- Two exophytic, cauliflower-like tumoral lesions: one on the left wrist measuring approximately 3 x 4 x 5 cm and one on the right shin measuring approximately 4 x 5 x 6 cm. No vital signs, routine laboratory values, or tissue diagnostic results are provided here.

A 54-year-old healthy woman presented to ophthalmology with a few months' history of a symptomatic lesion of the right eye. The lesion was located in the nasal bulbar conjunctiva within the interpalpebral zone. On examination there was an erythematous fibrovascular lesion approximately 5 mm in length. The lesion produced foreign-body sensation and discomfort. The lesion was clinically diagnosed as a pterygium, and surgical removal was performed.

A 32-year-old man from Djelfa, Algeria, with a history of contact eczema presented with a 6-week history of painless, non-healing skin lesions on the dorsal aspect of his right hand. He had applied topical corticosteroids and antiseptics without improvement and had received two courses of antibiotics (pristinamycin, amoxicillin + clavulanic acid) with no significant results. On examination there was a limited erythematous-papular plaque, approximately 8 cm in diameter, on the dorsal right hand formed by confluence of several papules with satellite lesions at the periphery. The initial plaque was associated with several firm, painless subcutaneous nodules 0.5–1.5 cm in diameter that tracked proximally along lymphatic drainage toward the elbow. The patient did not recall an insect bite, no other body sites were involved, and the remainder of the examination was unremarkable. Direct mycological examination and culture on Sabouraud medium at 25 °C and on BHI medium at 37 °C were negative for fungal presence.

A 45-year-old man with known HIV infection presented with nodules and plaques on the nasal area, dorsum of the left wrist, the right index finger, and the back; cervical lymphadenopathy was noted. He reported a history of fever 6 months earlier while working in the state of Bihar, and since then had mild intermittent fever and weight loss. Routine blood and urine examinations were reported as not revealing any abnormalities. Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay for HIV was positive, and the CD4 count was 210/muL. On inspection there were infiltrated plaques on the nose, left dorsum of the wrist, and on the index finger of the right hand.

contexts.text: A 17-month-old female from Berkane, born of a consanguineous marriage with a sister who died at age 6 (unknown etiology), presented with 3 months of "anarchic" fever, growth retardation, anemia and episodes of epistaxis. On exam the temperature was 39 °C. Findings included lower‑limb edema, pallor of skin and mucous membranes, gingival petechiae, bleached hair, and hepatosplenomegaly; other exams were unremarkable. Complete blood count: pancytopenia with a deep aregenerative normochromic normocytic anemia (hemoglobin 3 g/dL) with reticulocyte count 76,700/mm3, leukocytes 4,860/mm3 with neutropenia 680/mm3, and thrombocytopenia 12,000/mm3; peripheral blood smear without abnormality. Additional labs: hypoalbuminemia 13 g/L, hypertriglyceridemia 4.57 g/L, hyperferritinemia 626 µg/L, LDH 337 IU/L, prothrombin time 56%, fibrinogen 1 g/L. Direct Coombs test was positive. Hepatic and renal function were reported as without abnormality.

A 7-year-old castrated male domestic short-haired cat, stray with unknown history, from the greater Athens area of Greece was presented for examination because of facial swelling and eye lesions. On examination there was a raised, nonalopecic, semifirm, poorly demarcated, painless swelling of the forehead. Periocular hypotrichosis, edema, and slight hyperpigmentation were present. Edema of the conjunctiva and third eyelid of the right eye was also observed. Clinical examination revealed no other abnormalities. A blood sample for complete blood count and biochemistry profile was obtained, and fine needle aspirates and a trucut biopsy were taken from the forehead swelling for cytological and histopathological examination. The patient had a nonregenerative anemia, hyperglobulinemia, and thrombocytopenia. Urinalysis showed no abnormalities. Further suggested serological tests for vector-borne diseases were not done because of financial restrictions. At presentation the clinicians listed the differential diagnosis as: subcutaneous abscess, atypical bacterial and mycobacterial infection, deep fungal infection, and neoplasia.

A 37-year-old man from Maranhão, Brazil, employed as a sugarcane cutter, and the son of a consanguineous marriage, presented with 5 months of daily fevers up to 39°C, progressive asthenia, about 10 kg weight loss, and increasing abdominal volume. He had a remote history: at age 21 he was diagnosed with rheumatoid arthritis and received NSAIDs and prednisone, with maintenance corticosteroid therapy (10 mg/day) for 7 years. He and his family reported no history of recurrent infections. On examination he had pallor of skin and mucous membranes, splenomegaly extending 21 cm below the left costal margin, and hepatomegaly 4 cm below the right costal margin. Laboratory testing demonstrated pancytopenia and hypoalbuminemia. Bone marrow aspirate showed relative hypocellularity of the granulocytes without visualization of amastigotes. Bone marrow biopsy showed a proportional increase in granulocytes. A liver biopsy was performed; immunohistochemistry was negative for Leishmania.

A 59‑year‑old man, mixed ethnicity, unemployed, previously healthy, reported that an erythematous‑crusty lesion appeared in the region of the mental protuberance and over two months evolved to involve other parts of the body, including the frontal and occipital regions, nasal septum, ears, hands, and lower limbs. Oral examination showed scattered ulcers on the face, lower labial mucosa, and on the left lip commissure, a pseudomembrane on the marginal gingiva, and an exophytic nodule in the left labial mucosa. The patient had a positive Montenegro intradermal test and was admitted to the University Hospital in December 2018. After admission, clinicians noted enlarged lymph nodes of hard consistency in the left inguinal region and an extensive irregular melanocytic lesion in the left plantar region presenting an area of hyperkeratosis with a grey‑bluish center; the plantar lesion was biopsied for further evaluation. A PCR analysis had been performed in an external laboratory.

A 9-year-old boy presented with multiple papular lesions on the left cheek that had been present for three months and had gradually enlarged. His medical history was notable for an episode of cutaneous leishmaniasis located on the nose two years earlier, which had completely regressed after treatment with intralesional meglumine antimonate. Dermatologic examination showed multiple, coalescing, rough, slightly elevated, yellowish-brown papular lesions 3–6 mm in diameter on the left cheek. He also had a large atrophic scar on the nose. Nothing of interest was noted in his family history or his laboratory tests.

At adoption, immunologic tests for FIV and FeLV were negative. On clinical examination there was more severe periodontal disease on the right side and a right maxillary local stomatitis with a nodular, ulcerative appearance; on inspection the nodular lesion was slightly painful with spontaneous bleeding. Bilateral mandibular lymph node enlargement was present; no other abnormalities were noted. Preoperative laboratory testing showed leukopenia (4.93 x 10^3/μl; RR 5.5–19.5), elevated total protein (10.06 g/dl; RR 6.0–7.9) and globulins (7.76 g/dl; RR 2.6–5.1), hypoalbuminemia (2.3 g/dl; RR 2.8–3.9), and mild hyperbilirubinemia (0.12 mg/dl; RR 0.0–0.1). Under anesthesia a detailed oral exam and full-mouth radiographs demonstrated periodontal pocketing (7 mm) at the site of the nodular ulcero-hemorrhagic lesion (third right maxillary premolar), advanced periodontitis of multiple teeth on the right maxilla, tooth resorption in six teeth including the affected premolar, and radiographic vertical bone loss adjacent to the lesion. Treatment at that time included extraction of teeth with resorption and advanced attachment loss, routine closure of gingival flaps, and incisional biopsies of the maxillary lesion for histopathologic assessment. Two weeks after surgery the cat's appetite and weight had improved, but a nodular ulcero-hemorrhagic lesion with persistent swelling and inflammation of the right maxilla remained.

A 13‑year‑old boy, born in São Paulo, who had traveled at age 12 to the state of Minas Gerais, presented with fever on alternate days, pallor, increased abdominal volume and unquantified weight loss. He had no prior history of recurrent infections. On admission he had anemia and thrombocytopenia. Bone marrow aspirate showed amastigotes of Leishmania. He was treated with liposomal amphotericin B (LAB) at a dose of 35 mg/kg and was discharged. Four months later he returned with fever and thrombocytopenia; a bone marrow aspirate again showed amastigotes of Leishmania and parasites were detected in bone marrow culture. He was treated with meglumine antimoniate and intravenous human immunoglobulin with clinical and laboratory improvement and was discharged in good health. Three weeks later he presented with seven days of fever, weakness, pallor and increased abdominal volume. On exam the spleen was palpable 23 cm below the left costal margin and the liver 5 cm from the right costal margin. Leishmania ELISA immunoassay and the rK‑39 antigen test were negative. Bone marrow biopsy showed a lymphocytic and histiocytic inflammatory reaction with a granulomatous pattern; no amastigotes were observed in the aspirate. He was re‑treated empirically for visceral leishmaniasis with liposomal amphotericin B. Notably, the patient had silvery hair and eyebrows, described as a phenotype suggestive of Griscelli Syndrome.

A 24-year-old man from Tancredo Neves, State of Bahia, Brazil, was admitted in January 2012 with diffuse bullous lesions on the body, osteoarthritis of the distal interphalangeal joints and proteinuria of 399 mg/day. He was diagnosed with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and treated with mycophenolate mofetil (MMF), with the dose increased to 1 g per day intravenously. Two years after the SLE diagnosis (2014) he was hospitalized again, presenting with ulcerated, painless skin lesions on the face, upper lip, scalp, neck, and on the upper and lower limbs. Oral examination showed crusty upper lip lesions, poor oral health status, and amelogenesis imperfecta. He developed secondary infection with fever and was started on cephalexin (1 g/day) and maintained on prednisone 5 mg/day intravenously. On the third day of this hospitalization, biopsies were performed on the left nasal mucosa and on lesions of the right lower limb.

A 45-year-old woman presented with painless nodules on the anterior upper chest for a 10-week duration. She was treated with oral amoxicillin–clavulanic acid for two weeks without any response; otherwise she was completely healthy. On examination she had two nontender, nonulcerative, indurated dusky erythematous plaques on her upper anterior chest. Complete workup included chest radiograph, complete blood film, liver function tests, renal function tests, and abdominal sonography; all of these investigations were reported as normal. A 6 mm punch biopsy was taken from one of the nodules.

A 78-year-old man from a rural area in western Iran was referred for multiple ulcerative, exudative lesions involving the mid-face (upper lip and anterior nasal fossa), above the eyebrows, dorsal aspects of both hands, and posterior aspects of both heels. Lesions began three years earlier as papules on the dorsal hands and progressively enlarged to involve the face and heels and became ulcerative; involvement of the right hand progressed to destruction of tendons and soft tissue of the fifth finger, resulting in amputation of that finger. He had no history of comorbid conditions, no regular medications reported, and denied systemic symptoms — there was no weight loss, fever, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly or other signs of systemic involvement on examination or routine laboratory survey. Multiple prior empirical treatments for different presumed diagnoses, including pyoderma gangrenosum, sarcoidosis, and leishmaniasis, had been tried without improvement. An initial skin biopsy showed a necrotizing and palisading granulomatous tissue pattern that suggested an infectious etiology, but initial smears of lesion material for fungal elements, mycobacteria and Leishmania were negative. A tuberculin skin test produced a 27 mm induration, and anti-tuberculosis therapy (isoniazid, rifampin, ethambutol, and pyrazinamide) was started.

Their physical appearances were similar and were described as having short stature, short neck, protuberant chest, scoliosis, and a waddling gait. Their facial features included frontal bossing and a flat nasal bridge. History revealed pain in the hip region on walking that subsides at rest. The parents were not of different ethnicity, had a nonconsanguineous marriage, and there was no family history of any skeletal disorder.

On oral examination, exposed teeth with sharp cusps and rough enamel texture were noted. The orthopantomograph showed thin hypoplastic enamel of normal radiodensity. A multispecialty medical examination revealed no dysfunctional changes in major systems. Orthopedic and radiographic evaluation showed gross skeletal deformity: hand-wrist radiograph with proximally narrow metacarpals; anteroposterior spinal view with curvature of the thoracolumbar segment; lateral spinal view with anterior beaking of the vertebral body; and pelvic radiograph with an irregularly outlined square-shaped head of the femur and a coxa valga defect.

Her past medical history is notable for type 1 autoimmune hepatitis; current medications were prednisone 20 mg daily, azathioprine 100 mg daily, and clobetasol 0.05% cream.

A 30‑year‑old man presented with pain in his lower limbs and a non‑itchy erythematous rash over both lower limbs. He had low‑grade intermittent fever for three months. On examination he was pale and malnourished (BMI 18.4 kg/m2) and had palpable purpura over both thighs and buttocks. Abdominal examination revealed palpable hepatomegaly with massive splenomegaly. Laboratory testing showed pancytopenia (hemoglobin 6.8 g/dL, total leukocyte count 2800/mm3, platelet count 45 000/muL) and polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia (4.9 g/dL); liver and renal function tests were within reference ranges. Contrast‑enhanced CT of chest and abdomen confirmed hepatosplenomegaly and was otherwise unremarkable. The treating team considered hematologic malignancy and a connective‑tissue disorder with vasculitis. Other infectious etiologies entertained included HIV, scrub typhus/rickettsial infection, and visceral leishmaniasis (given the patient lived in an endemic area). Initial testing showed: anti‑nuclear antibodies, complement levels (C3 = 94 mg/dL and C4 = 20 mg/dL), and rheumatoid factor were negative; urine examination was normal and serum cryoglobulins were not raised. Viral markers (HIV, hepatitis B surface antigen, and anti‑hepatitis C) were negative. Serology for rickettsia and scrub typhus were also negative.

Eight years earlier he had a small papule on the right cheek that progressed to an open ulcer, then to ulcers on the left cheek and forehead; those active lesions lasted about six months and healed spontaneously, leaving permanent hypopigmented scars. On one presentation, physical examination showed multiple nodular lesions on his hands, face and nose, swelling of the upper lip, and crusted central ulcers with raised peripheral contours; multiple healed scars were present on both cheeks. He had no fever, hepatosplenomegaly or lymphedema and reported no history of HIV, chronic disease, alcohol abuse, or immunomodulatory drug use. Parasitological testing of lesion smears at that time showed many macrophages filled with amastigote stages of Leishmania, graded as +6. A nonreactive rK39 rapid diagnostic test and absence of related systemic signs made visceral leishmaniasis unlikely. Based on the clinical manifestations and smear result he was diagnosed with mucocutaneous leishmaniasis and treated with intramuscular sodium stibogluconate (20 mg/kg/day for 30 days) with clinical cure. Two years later he returned with a different cutaneous eruption that had appeared over the previous three months and had been preceded by intense itching. On exam he had multiple, nonpitting, closed papules on his face, nose, hands and legs. A skin smear again showed intramacrophage amastigotes with a parasite load graded +6, and culture grew promastigotes.

A 24-year-old Cuban immigrant presented with worsening nonhealing lower-extremity ulcers despite oral antibiotic therapy and wound care. The lesions gradually grew with subsequent ulceration over the course of 1 to 2 months. He recently arrived in the United States seeking asylum and first noticed the lesions while traveling in the jungle between Panama and Colombia (Darien Gap region). On examination, there was an ulcerative lesion measuring 4 cm on the dorsum of the right foot and a second 3.5 cm ulcer on the lower anterior shin. There was no evidence of mucosal or visceral involvement on initial physical exam. Photographs show ulcerative lesions on the right foot and left shin. As part of the clinical workup to rule out malaria, a rapid malaria antigen test for Plasmodium falciparum was obtained and reported positive.

A 36-year-old man presented with painless nodules on his left foot for a two-month duration. He had received a three-week course of systemic (ampicillin-cloxacillin) antibiotics without improvement. His medical and family history were unremarkable. Dermatologic examination showed a large ulcerative plaque on the dorsal aspect of the left foot surrounded by two satellite purple papules. There were also multiple grouped dusky erythematous nontender ulcerative nodules behind the lateral malleolus of the left leg. Histopathological examination of the margin of the ulcerative plaque showed ulceration of the epidermis and a diffuse dense mononuclear cellular infiltration of lymphocytes, histiocytes, and numerous plasma cells throughout the dermis with early granuloma formation. These changes involved the panniculus, causing septal and lobular panniculitis.

A 42‑year‑old Italian man with a 20‑year history of plaque psoriasis and psoriasis arthropathica presented with lesions that had appeared 6 months earlier. He had been treated with subcutaneous methotrexate 25 mg weekly for 9 years and adalimumab 40 mg every other week for 7 years. Topical therapies had been used in the weeks before hospitalization. The patient was obese (BMI 39 kg/m2). On examination he had multiple erythemato‑squamous psoriatic plaques (PASI 16.6) and multiple erosive and partly ulcerating plaques and nodules—some with distinct brown crusts—on the right forearm, right knee, left flank, and abdomen. There was no lymphadenopathy and no other pathological findings on physical exam. An externally performed lesion biopsy reported dermal T‑cell infiltrates without evidence of malignancy. Two repeat biopsies from morphologically different lesions showed interface dermatitis with pseudolymphomatous infiltrates, thickening of the epidermis, follicular hyperparakeratosis, and perivascular and periadnexal superficially accentuated lymphocytic infiltrates with a preponderance of T cells. Tissue clonality analyses demonstrated polyclonal IgH and TCR gamma chain gene expression, thus excluding lymphoma. Direct immunofluorescence did not detect any IgG, IgM, IgA, or C3 depositions. Syphilis serology, carried out because numerous plasma cells were present in the tissue, yielded negative results.

A 45-year-old Iranian man presented to dermatology in March 2008 with two large tumoral skin lesions. History of present illness and past history:
- Several years of chronic renal failure secondary to non–insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus (NIDDM). - In April 2006, after travel to an endemic area (Natanz in Isfahan province, Iran), he developed small papular lesions (reported as 2 x 5 millimeter) on the left wrist and the right shin. Those small lesions were left untreated. - Due to chronic renal failure, he underwent renal transplantation in August 2007. - After transplantation he was started on immunosuppression with prednisolone 50 mg/day and cyclosporine 7.5 mg/kg daily (reported as equivalent to 600 mg for an 80 kg patient). - Several weeks after transplantation and initiation of immunosuppressive therapy, the previously small papular lesions enlarged markedly into cauliflower-like, tumoral lesions. Physical examination:
- Two exophytic, cauliflower-like tumoral lesions: one on the left wrist measuring approximately 3 x 4 x 5 cm and one on the right shin measuring approximately 4 x 5 x 6 cm. No vital signs, routine laboratory values, or tissue diagnostic results are provided here.

A 35-year-old man from Russia presented to dermatology with two ulcerative skin lesions described as semi-dry with active borders: one in the lower left pre-atrial region and the other on the dorsal region of the left forearm. He reported travel to multiple countries between May and June 2019, including Middle Eastern countries (Israel, Turkey), the Balkan region (Armenia, Georgia), and Russia. In August 2019 he noted red, indurated papules and sought care in late August in San Cristobal de las Casas, Chiapas, Mexico. Cryotherapy with liquid nitrogen was applied initially with temporary reduction, followed by renewed flare-up of the lesion edges. At the Tropical Medicine Center he was clinically diagnosed as having localized cutaneous leishmaniasis (LCL). For confirmation, Giemsa-stained smears of the lesion and ELISA tests for L. braziliensis, L. infantum/chagasi, L. major and L. mexicana were performed. The Giemsa-stained smears showed abundant amastigotes within macrophages. The ELISA of the patient's serum revealed some degree of cross reactivity between four Leishmania species, with higher antibody levels recorded for L. major and L. mexicana antigens.

A 52-year-old male farm worker from Ceara state, northeast Brazil, presented with a 4-month history of skin lesions. Lesions appeared first on the face and legs, than spread across much of his body, including the genitalia, soles of feet, and scalp. He reported daily fevers for the first 2 weeks of illness. On examination the patient had 178 lesions of different sizes and aspects; ulcerated, crusted, papular, nodular, and pustular. Many had apparent bacterial superinfections. The remainder of the physical examination was normal. A complete blood count and liver and kidney function tests were within normal limits. Serological tests for syphilis and human immunodeficiency virus were negative.

A 64-year-old woman with a past medical history of type 1 diabetes mellitus was referred for 20 months of nonpruritic erythematous ulcerated lesions of both legs. On examination there was a large oval erythematoviolaceous plaque covering more than half of the right pretibial region; the border was slightly elevated, indurated, and infiltrative, and the center contained small necrotic crusted ulcers and small atrophic areas. Similar, smaller plaques were present on the left leg. No other systemic abnormalities were detected, including no regional lymphadenopathy. There was no history of trauma or insect bite, and she denied fever or other systemic symptoms. Blood count, routine biochemical tests, urine analysis and chest radiography were reported as normal except for hyperglycemia (11.8 mmol/L). Bacteriological tests were negative. Skin biopsy showed a dense lymphocytic infiltrate throughout the entire dermis admixed with multiple granuloma without necrosis; at higher magnification epithelioid cells, histiocytes and multinucleated giant cells were observed within the granulomatous zones, which were outlined by a dense infiltrate of lymphocytes.

contexts.text: A 60‑year‑old Austrian man presented in September 2016 with a three‑week history of fever of unknown origin, fatigue, and unintentional weight loss of 6 kg. Initial physical examination was inconspicuous. His medical history was notable for adequately treated diabetes mellitus type 2 and hypothyroidism. Travel history included a two‑week trip to the south of Crete in September 2015 and a two‑week trip the south of Spain in May 2016. Laboratory tests showed markedly elevated C‑reactive protein (CRP 94.2–188.9 mg/L), slight hypochromic normocytic anemia without signs of hemolysis (hemoglobin 12.5 g/dL), mild thrombocytopenia (127,000/µL), and a discreetly elevated gamma‑glutamyltransferase (GGT). The soluble interleukin‑2 receptor (IL‑2R) was elevated to 5156.1 pg/mL. Chest x‑ray, urine analysis, abdominal sonography, transthoracic and transesophageal echocardiography revealed no focus of infection but did show splenomegaly (7.2 × 16.4 cm). Empiric antibiotic therapy (initially ampicillin/sulbactam, later piperacillin/tazobactam plus vancomycin) did not lead to improvement. Over the next three weeks the patient’s discrete bicytopenia progressed to severe pancytopenia requiring blood transfusions. Lactate dehydrogenase rose to 1107 U/L, liver enzymes including GGT, alkaline phosphatase and AST increased, and fever persisted up to 40°C. Positron emission tomography–computed tomography showed tracer enhancement in the central and peripheral bone marrow.

A 68-year-old man from a mountainous area in Hebei Province, China, presented with fever, sweating, and fatigue. He first sought care on February 1 and was hospitalized at a local hospital with temperature 39.0°C, chills, and no respiratory, abdominal, diarrheal, or urinary symptoms. He had lost approximately 10 kg over the prior 6 months. Initial blood tests showed pancytopenia, a rapid erythrocyte sedimentation rate, elevated C-reactive protein and ferritin, hyponatremia, hypokalemia, hypoproteinemia, and elevated serum enzyme levels. Bone marrow aspiration smear at that time showed granulocytopenia with megakaryocyte maturation disorder. Abdominal ultrasound showed splenomegaly; brain CT showed bilateral basal ganglia lacunar infarction; chest CT showed bilateral fibrotic/bronchitic changes. After 11 days of antibiotic and supportive treatment his fever and fatigue persisted with temperatures >39°C, so he presented for further evaluation on February 16. On arrival his SARS-CoV-2 PCR was negative. On examination he was febrile to 38.2°C, poorly nourished, unable to walk (bilateral leg strength grade 3), and had pitting edema of the anterior tibias and dorsal feet. Repeat laboratory testing again showed pancytopenia, increased ESR, CRP and ferritin, and elevated liver enzymes. Empiric antibiotic therapy had not relieved his febrile illness.

A 47-year-old man presented to the emergency department on December 28, 2020 with recurrent fever for 4 months and worsening symptoms with diarrhea for 1 month. About 4 months earlier he developed fever without an evident cause, with a maximum temperature of 39.9 C; fevers usually occurred in the afternoon, lasted several hours, and were associated with headache, myalgia, and nausea. After a period of apparent improvement he redeveloped persistent high fever (≈39 C) accompanied by yellow watery diarrhea more than 10 times per day. Six years previously he had been diagnosed with malaria in Africa and treated with quinine. On admission: Novel Coronavirus nucleic acid test was negative. Laboratory studies showed Hb 83 g/L, WBC 2.82 x 10^9/L, platelet count 16 x 10^9/L, neutrophil percentage 84.0%, lymphocyte percentage 8.0%, and procalcitonin 0.87 ng/ml. Blood culture grew methicillin-resistant coagulase-negative Staphylococci. The cryptococcus antigen test, fungal G test, and GM test were negative. Abdominal ultrasound showed enlarged liver and spleen. Chest and plain abdominal CT demonstrated cirrhosis, splenomegaly, portal hypertension with collateral circulation, and peritoneal effusion. The team considered sepsis and fever of undetermined origin (infection versus tumor) and assessed the patient as Child-Pugh B decompensated cirrhosis. An emergency blood metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) test was sent to help diagnose the fever of unknown cause.

A 42‑year‑old man presented with 1 year of progressive weakness and significant weight loss and intermittent low‑grade fevers. He had been treated for pulmonary tuberculosis 2 years earlier and was recently restarted on antitubercular therapy for the past month without improvement. On examination he was thin, pale, afebrile, and had abdominal distension. Left submandibular and left axillary lymph nodes were palpable, each about 1.5 cm. Mild hepatosplenomegaly was noted. Ultrasound of the abdomen showed multiple enlarged conglomerate mesenteric lymph nodes, the largest 22 × 18 mm. Clinical chemistry showed reversal of the albumin:globulin ratio with total protein 9.5 g/dL, albumin 2.0 g/dL, globulin 7.5 g/dL. Other liver and renal tests were within normal limits. Complete blood count showed pancytopenia: hemoglobin 6 g/dL, total leukocyte count 1,800/µL (polymorphs 47%, lymphocytes 51%), platelets 48,000/µL; ESR 50 mm/h. Peripheral smear demonstrated rouleaux formation. Fine needle aspiration cytology of left submandibular and axillary lymph nodes yielded thick aspirate; smears showed few epithelioid cell granulomas interspersed with discrete aggregates of histiocytes in a background of reactive lymphoid cells and many plasma cells.

A 47-year-old man presented to the emergency department with recurrent fever for 4 months and worsening symptoms including diarrhea for 1 month. About 4 months earlier he developed fever up to 39.9 °C that typically occurred in the afternoon and lasted several hours; associated symptoms included headache, myalgia, and nausea. After a temporary resolution he had a relapse with persistent high fever and frequent yellow watery diarrhea (>10 times/day). Past medical history included malaria diagnosed 6 years earlier in Africa treated with quinine. He reported hypersensitivity to quinolones (e.g., moxifloxacin). On admission, novel coronavirus nucleic acid test was negative. Initial laboratory testing showed hemoglobin 83 g/L, platelet count 16 × 10^9/L, white-cell count 2.82 × 10^9/L, neutrophil percentage 84.0%, lymphocyte percentage 8.0%, and procalcitonin 0.87 ng/mL. Blood culture grew methicillin-resistant coagulase-negative Staphylococci. The schistosoma japonicum IgG antibody, echinococcus granulosus antibody, liver fluke antibody test, plasmodium antigen test, and blood smear test were all negative. Chest and plain abdominal CT reported cirrhosis, splenomegaly, portal hypertension with collateral circulation, and peritoneal effusion. An emergency metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) blood test was sent to try to identify an occult pathogen.

A 54-year-old man from southwest Iran presented with a 3-week history of continuous throbbing headache, fever, chills, weakness, anorexia, and weight loss. Past medical history included benign prostatic hyperplasia, gastroesophageal reflux disease, and hemorrhoids; current medications were tamsulosin, propranolol, rabeprazole, and cathartic syrup. On examination his temperature was 38.0 C and blood pressure 130/82 mm Hg. Abdominal examination revealed mild right upper-quadrant tenderness and moderate splenomegaly; all other examinations were normal. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 8.1 g/dL, white-cell count 1900/mm3, reticulocyte count 0.5%, and platelet count 20,000/mm3. ESR was 56 mm/h, alanine aminotransferase 84 IU/L, aspartate aminotransferase 67 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 401 IU/L, albumin 3.4 g/dL, conjugated bilirubin 0.6 mg/dL, ferritin 658.6 mcg/dL, serum iron 23 mcg/dL, and TIBC 116 mcg/dL. Creatinine, blood sugar, coagulation tests, urinalysis, stool and sputum exams, Wright test, 2ME, calcium, phosphorus, magnesium, and PSA were reported as normal. Serologic tests for HBV, HCV, and HIV were negative. Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated mild hepatomegaly and moderate splenomegaly. Doppler ultrasound showed dilation of the splenic vein and portal vein (15 mm each). Computed tomography of the brain revealed no abnormality. Axial FLAIR MRI of the brain showed increased signal intensity in the central part of the right side of the pons.

A 58‑year‑old man with end‑stage renal failure and a history of three kidney transplantations (1979, 1981 and 2008) presented with recurrent febrile illness. His medical history included chronic hepatitis B, legionellosis, chronic Q fever and cytomegalovirus infection. The most recent transplant had required treatment for acute rejection with anti‑thymoglobulin, plasma exchanges, rituximab and maintenance immunosuppression consisting of mycophenolate mofetil 1 g/day, tacrolimus 4.5 mg/day and prednisone 10 mg/day. Leishmania PCR in blood had been positive in 2004; initial treatment with liposomal amphotericin B (L‑AmB) produced clinical cure. However, relapse occurred in August 2009 following plasma exchanges and corticosteroid boluses for graft rejection, with fever, anemia (Hb 9.1 g/dL), leukopenia (leukocytes 1,600/mm3) and quantitative PCR showing 431 Leishmania/ml of blood. L‑AmB (induction total dose 40 mg/kg) reduced parasitemia to 6.9 Leishmania/ml. L‑AmB was reintroduced and maintenance infusions were adjusted (including weekly and twice‑weekly dosing) with parasitemia fluctuating (from 88 to 0.6 Leishmania/ml). A fourth recurrence in April–June 2011 again featured fever, leukopenia (leukocytes 1,200/mm3, CD4 186/mm3), anemia (Hb 9.1 g/dL) and parasitemia 40 Leishmania/ml. The patient later underwent transplant nephrectomy and returned to chronic dialysis.

A 30‑year‑old man presented with pain in his lower limbs and a non‑itchy erythematous rash over both lower limbs. He had low‑grade intermittent fever for three months. On examination he was pale and malnourished (BMI 18.4 kg/m2) and had palpable purpura over both thighs and buttocks. Abdominal examination revealed palpable hepatomegaly with massive splenomegaly. Laboratory testing showed pancytopenia (hemoglobin 6.8 g/dL, total leukocyte count 2800/mm3, platelet count 45 000/muL) and polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia (4.9 g/dL); liver and renal function tests were within reference ranges. Contrast‑enhanced CT of chest and abdomen confirmed hepatosplenomegaly and was otherwise unremarkable. The treating team considered hematologic malignancy and a connective‑tissue disorder with vasculitis. Other infectious etiologies entertained included HIV, scrub typhus/rickettsial infection, and visceral leishmaniasis (given the patient lived in an endemic area). Initial testing showed: anti‑nuclear antibodies, complement levels (C3 = 94 mg/dL and C4 = 20 mg/dL), and rheumatoid factor were negative; urine examination was normal and serum cryoglobulins were not raised. Viral markers (HIV, hepatitis B surface antigen, and anti‑hepatitis C) were negative. Serology for rickettsia and scrub typhus were also negative.

A 40-year-old man of Albanian descent who has lived in Athens for 20 years was admitted in February 2008 for progressive constitutional and respiratory symptoms. His symptoms began one year earlier with dry cough and gradual weight loss totaling 30 kg; night sweats and scant hemoptysis developed during the last month. Six months earlier a limited workup had revealed chronic active hepatitis B. He works in a restaurant, is a nonsmoker, and has no other remarkable medical history. On examination he was cachectic and had hepatosplenomegaly and small, discrete, nontender axillary and cervical lymph nodes. There were no clinical signs of liver failure or portal hypertension. Laboratory tests demonstrated pancytopenia, elevated hepatic aminotransferases (3–4 times the upper limit), and polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 100 mm/h. Serum albumin, bilirubin, and prothrombin time were within normal limits. HIV testing by ELISA was negative on two occasions three months apart; antibodies to hepatitis C virus were negative. Abdominal ultrasound showed enlarged liver and spleen and enlarged lymph nodes at the hepatic hilum; portal vein diameter and flow were normal and no ascites was present. Chest CT revealed limited adenopathy with a 2 × 1 cm mass at the right hilum and a 1.2 cm right lower paratracheal lymph node with a hypodense centre.

A 44‑year‑old man from Shanxi Province with a 5‑year history of antisynthetase antibody syndrome on cyclosporine A was admitted in January 2020 with fever to 38.6°C. He reported exertional breathlessness (after walking ~100 m) and increasing weakness; broad‑spectrum antimicrobials produced no improvement. By March 2020 he had persistent fever. The clinical picture met criteria for hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH), and treatment was started with methylprednisolone (10 mg/kg per day) and etoposide (100 mg/m^2). After 2 weeks the patient became afebrile and WBC rose to 10.8 × 10^9/L, hemoglobin was 95 g/L and platelets 55 × 10^9/L. In June 2020, during prednisone taper, he redeveloped high fever to 39.5°C, was unable to stand independently, and subsequently had pancytopenia with recurrence of high ferritin, low NK‑cell activity, markedly elevated sCD25, splenomegaly, and hemophagocytosis on bone marrow examination.
