contexts.text: A 60-year-old woman from Uttar Pradesh, India presented with a six‑week history of high‑grade continuous fever with chills and rigors, anorexia, malaise, joint pains, and severe lethargy. She reported "crops of round, raised lesions" that began on the left upper limb, progressed to the right upper limb and then involved the whole face, upper back, chest, and upper abdomen; the lesions were "closely associated with the febrile episodes." Some lesions enlarged, became nodular, developed sunken centers that drained pus‑like material, and were painful and red. One week before admission she developed jaundice with mild to moderate upper‑quadrant abdominal pain. She also noted nonpainful bilateral leg swelling (pitting) and painful red eyes with nodular lesions on the eyelids and in the conjunctiva, associated with decreased vision. She had no prior comorbidities, was a teetotaler, and denied taking over‑the‑counter or steroid/complementary medications or other potentially immunosuppressive drugs. Pallor and icterus were present; there was bilateral pitting, non‑tender symmetrical pedal edema. Skin exam showed "multiple crops of nodular, noduloulcerative, and papular lesions, dispersed throughout the body surface, mostly segregated to the face and upper back," some with pus drainage from central sunken areas. Eye exam demonstrated nodular lesions over the eyes and conjunctiva with conjunctival suffusion. Chest imaging was within normal limits. Serum IgG 22.6 g/L.

A 47-year-old man presented to the emergency department on December 28, 2020 with recurrent fever for 4 months and worsening symptoms with diarrhea for 1 month. About 4 months earlier he developed fever without an evident cause, with a maximum temperature of 39.9 C; fevers usually occurred in the afternoon, lasted several hours, and were associated with headache, myalgia, and nausea. After a period of apparent improvement he redeveloped persistent high fever (≈39 C) accompanied by yellow watery diarrhea more than 10 times per day. Six years previously he had been diagnosed with malaria in Africa and treated with quinine. On admission: Novel Coronavirus nucleic acid test was negative. Laboratory studies showed Hb 83 g/L, WBC 2.82 x 10^9/L, platelet count 16 x 10^9/L, neutrophil percentage 84.0%, lymphocyte percentage 8.0%, and procalcitonin 0.87 ng/ml. Blood culture grew methicillin-resistant coagulase-negative Staphylococci. The cryptococcus antigen test, fungal G test, and GM test were negative. Abdominal ultrasound showed enlarged liver and spleen. Chest and plain abdominal CT demonstrated cirrhosis, splenomegaly, portal hypertension with collateral circulation, and peritoneal effusion. The team considered sepsis and fever of undetermined origin (infection versus tumor) and assessed the patient as Child-Pugh B decompensated cirrhosis. An emergency blood metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) test was sent to help diagnose the fever of unknown cause.

Five months before admission she developed intermittent nocturnal fevers up to 39 °C that did not respond to antipyretics, with poor appetite, postprandial fullness, nausea and vomiting. Over the following months she noted progressive jaundice (yellow sclera and skin), dark urine, weight loss of ~10 kg, increasing abdominal girth and soft bilateral lower‑extremity edema to the knees. She had multiple prior emergency visits and received only symptomatic treatment. On admission her general state was poor with malnutrition; examination showed pallor 3–4/4, mild dehydration, jaundice 2/4, cyanosis, fever and tachycardia. Abdominal exam showed moderate ascites, hepatomegaly 7 cm below the right costal margin and splenomegaly palpable 2 cm below the umbilicus. Lower limbs had bilateral soft edema to the knees. Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated free peritoneal fluid, hepatomegaly ≈20 cm, splenomegaly ≈25 cm and gallstones. The initial diagnostic hypotheses included disseminated tuberculosis and visceral leishmaniasis; other considered diagnoses were dengue, yellow fever, prolonged septicemic salmonellosis, brucellosis, malaria, Chagas disease and lymphoproliferative malignancies. Investigations ordered included thick and thin blood smears, blood cultures, stool tests, bone marrow biopsy and aspiration and serologies for dengue, yellow fever, brucellosis and Chagas disease. HIV testing was performed and was negative.

A 27-year-old man from central Iran noted a small pimple on his right upper eyelid 4 months before presentation. The eyelid lesion enlarged slowly. On examination it was a well-defined, firm, nontender, subcutaneous, skin-colored nodule measuring about 1 cm × 1 cm, with slightly erythematous, raised borders; it was crusty and painless. CBC, ESR, CRP, and blood chemistries were within normal limits. A sample culture of the lesion grew Staphylococcus aureus. The lesion was treated sequentially with cephalexin, cloxacillin, amoxicillin–clavulanate, and steroids for 10 days, but these treatments failed to heal the lesion. Because cutaneous leishmaniasis occurs in the patient's area of residence and because of the lack of response to treatment, cutaneous leishmaniasis or basal cell carcinoma was proposed as the differential diagnosis.

A 50‑year‑old man born in Morocco was evaluated for PET‑positive visceral lymph nodes. He is HIV‑positive and has been on antiretroviral therapy for 5 years (receiving tenofovir, lamivudine, and efavirenz). He presented with a low‑grade fever of unknown origin. Routine laboratory abnormalities included a moderate leukopenia (white cells 2.45 x 10^9/L), hypergammaglobulinemia (38.7%), an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (85 mm/h), and a mildly increased β2‑microglobulin (5.5 mg/L). Computed tomography of the thorax and abdomen showed disseminated enlarged lymph nodes in the mediastinum and abdomen, an enlarged liver and spleen, and enlarged splenic and portal vein diameters. PET‑positive, accessible lymph nodes were mainly located in the mediastinum. Clinical reasoning focused on three elements: (1) the clinical profile of low‑grade fever in an HIV patient on therapy, (2) the laboratory pattern of cytopenia with hypergammaglobulinemia and raised inflammatory markers, and (3) imaging showing PET‑positive visceral lymphadenopathy. The leading differential diagnoses were lymphoproliferative disorders, infections (including fungal or parasitic), and metastatic epithelial tumors. Because the PET‑positive, reachable nodes were mainly mediastinal and lymphoproliferative disorders in HIV are often diagnosable with cytology, a transesophageal endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) with fine‑needle aspiration biopsy of a mediastinal node (station 4L) was scheduled.

A 75-year-old man was referred with lesions on the hands, legs, face, and the upper lid of the right eye. He is a farmer from Aran va Bidgol city, Isfahan province (central Iran). He reported that sandflies had bitten him when he went to the farm for irrigation on nights during the sandfly season. He described the appearance of 25 multiple nodular, ulcerative, and crusted lesions on his body. On examination the lesions varied in size from a few millimeters to several centimeters; there were eight lesions on the face, including one on the upper right eyelid. He had no particular medical history, no fever, the lesions were painless, and his general condition was good.

A 39‑year‑old man from Central America, living in Southeast Georgia, presents to the emergency department with abdominal pain and rectal bleeding. Past medical history: HIV/AIDS, alcohol abuse, tobacco dependency, and previously documented leishmaniasis diagnosed by bone marrow biopsy. He denied recent travel. Course and prior presentations: At initial presentation several years earlier he had diffuse moderate abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, chills and dysphagia; on exam he was tachycardic (heart rate 140/min) with mild abdominal tenderness. He was leukopenic and thrombocytopenic and was treated with amphotericin B and initiation of HAART; he was discharged on a 3‑month course of amphotericin B with ongoing HAART. Six months later he returned with acute abdominal pain and nausea; exam then showed a fine nodular skin rash across chest, abdomen and back described as consistent with cutaneous leishmaniasis, and thrombocytopenia persisted. At that time a bone marrow biopsy was performed to evaluate whether his new symptoms were due to HIV or a relapse of leishmaniasis, and he again received intravenous amphotericin B (inpatient 6 weeks) with plans for outpatient infusions. The patient subsequently was lost to follow‑up. Current presentation: Several years later he returned with a flare characterized by rectal bleeding and continued abdominal pain. Gastroenterology was consulted and an esophagogastroduodenoscopy was planned.

contexts.text: A 52‑year‑old woman who works in sugarcane fields in a rural area was referred to Oral Medicine for evaluation of a granulomatous lesion on the palate and for hoarseness that she thought followed a flu 3 months earlier. According to the referring surgeon, she had an extensive oral lesion and had undergone laryngoscopy and biopsy; that biopsy produced a histopathological result of “pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia and an active chronic inflammatory process, suggesting a fungus investigation,” prompting the referral. She reported no chronic systemic disease or regular medications. She described a history of crusting and nasal bleeding that began about 4 years earlier. On examination she had nasal obstruction, a nasal (hyponasal) voice, and was a mouth breather. She had smoked for 6 months and used both upper and lower complete dental prostheses continuously. Extrabuccal exam showed a lowering of the right nasal wing and a nasal septum perforation. Intrabuccal exam revealed a granulomatous lesion involving the entire palate and uvula, extending bilaterally to the pharynx with an erythematous appearance and areas of scratchable white plaques.

A 9-year-old boy presented with multiple papular lesions on the left cheek that had been present for three months and had gradually enlarged. His medical history was notable for an episode of cutaneous leishmaniasis located on the nose two years earlier, which had completely regressed after treatment with intralesional meglumine antimonate. Dermatologic examination showed multiple, coalescing, rough, slightly elevated, yellowish-brown papular lesions 3–6 mm in diameter on the left cheek. He also had a large atrophic scar on the nose. Nothing of interest was noted in his family history or his laboratory tests.

A 30-year-old Caucasian man, unemployed, HIV-negative and with no other concomitant infections, presented in 2014 with a papule on the inferior eyelid of the right eye. His past history included, in 2008, an isolated nodulation in the right leg that resolved after treatment. Over time new lesions progressively appeared on the chest, abdomen, back, feet, and in the oral cavity. Ulcerated oral lesions were present on the hard palate and on the left and right jugal mucosa. Disease progression was associated with fever, headache, and weight loss.

A 38‑year‑old man from Yayu district, western Ethiopia, presented to the outpatient clinic with multiple skin lesions on his face and hands and mutilation of the nose; his upper lip was injured and swollen. On one presentation, physical examination showed multiple nodular lesions on his hands, face and nose, swelling of the upper lip, and crusted central ulcers with raised peripheral contours; multiple healed scars were present on both cheeks. He had no fever, hepatosplenomegaly or lymphedema and reported no history of HIV, chronic disease, alcohol abuse, or immunomodulatory drug use. Parasitological testing of lesion smears at that time showed many macrophages filled with amastigote stages of Leishmania, graded as +6. A nonreactive rK39 rapid diagnostic test and absence of related systemic signs made visceral leishmaniasis unlikely. Based on the clinical manifestations and smear result he was diagnosed with mucocutaneous leishmaniasis and treated with intramuscular sodium stibogluconate (20 mg/kg/day for 30 days) with clinical cure. Two years later he returned with a different cutaneous eruption that had appeared over the previous three months and had been preceded by intense itching. On exam he had multiple, nonpitting, closed papules on his face, nose, hands and legs. A skin smear again showed intramacrophage amastigotes with a parasite load graded +6, and culture grew promastigotes.

A 30-year-old woman from an area endemic for tegumentary leishmaniasis presented with a single skin complaint. She reported a small papular lesion on her right leg that had developed over 7–10 days. At age 10 she had had an ulcer on the left thigh that healed spontaneously and left a well-defined atrophic scar. On examination there was a depressed papular lesion on the right leg measuring 8 × 7 mm; there was a 30 × 20 mm atrophic scar on the left thigh and no lymphadenopathy. Because early lesions of the locally prevalent Leishmania species may be papular and nonulcerated, a Leishmania skin test (LST) was performed on the left forearm. After 48 hours the intradermal reaction was strongly positive, with an induration measuring 38 × 32 mm. Eight days after the skin test the original papular lesion on the right leg had resolved, and a new round cutaneous ulcer with raised borders measuring 26 × 24 mm was present at the site of the LST. A culture of aspirated material from the forearm lesion was negative for Leishmania.

A 78-year-old man from a rural area in western Iran was referred for multiple ulcerative, exudative lesions involving the mid-face (upper lip and anterior nasal fossa), above the eyebrows, dorsal aspects of both hands, and posterior aspects of both heels. Lesions began three years earlier as papules on the dorsal hands and progressively enlarged to involve the face and heels and became ulcerative; involvement of the right hand progressed to destruction of tendons and soft tissue of the fifth finger, resulting in amputation of that finger. He had no history of comorbid conditions, no regular medications reported, and denied systemic symptoms — there was no weight loss, fever, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly or other signs of systemic involvement on examination or routine laboratory survey. Multiple prior empirical treatments for different presumed diagnoses, including pyoderma gangrenosum, sarcoidosis, and leishmaniasis, had been tried without improvement. An initial skin biopsy showed a necrotizing and palisading granulomatous tissue pattern that suggested an infectious etiology, but initial smears of lesion material for fungal elements, mycobacteria and Leishmania were negative. A tuberculin skin test produced a 27 mm induration, and anti-tuberculosis therapy (isoniazid, rifampin, ethambutol, and pyrazinamide) was started.

A 59‑year‑old man, mixed ethnicity, unemployed, previously healthy, reported that an erythematous‑crusty lesion appeared in the region of the mental protuberance and over two months evolved to involve other parts of the body, including the frontal and occipital regions, nasal septum, ears, hands, and lower limbs. Oral examination showed scattered ulcers on the face, lower labial mucosa, and on the left lip commissure, a pseudomembrane on the marginal gingiva, and an exophytic nodule in the left labial mucosa. The patient had a positive Montenegro intradermal test and was admitted to the University Hospital in December 2018. After admission, clinicians noted enlarged lymph nodes of hard consistency in the left inguinal region and an extensive irregular melanocytic lesion in the left plantar region presenting an area of hyperkeratosis with a grey‑bluish center; the plantar lesion was biopsied for further evaluation. A PCR analysis had been performed in an external laboratory.

An 8‑year‑old Caucasian boy from Salvador, Bahia, Brazil, presented with a hyperemic, pruritic lesion of the upper lip that had persisted for six months. Initial outpatient therapy consisted of topical acyclovir 5% applied five times daily and oral cefadroxil (50 mg/kg/day) for seven days, without clinical improvement. The lesion subsequently worsened, and a Montenegro intradermal examination was performed.

A 42‑year‑old Italian man with a 20‑year history of plaque psoriasis and psoriasis arthropathica presented with lesions that had appeared 6 months earlier. He had been treated with subcutaneous methotrexate 25 mg weekly for 9 years and adalimumab 40 mg every other week for 7 years. Topical therapies had been used in the weeks before hospitalization. The patient was obese (BMI 39 kg/m2). On examination he had multiple erythemato‑squamous psoriatic plaques (PASI 16.6) and multiple erosive and partly ulcerating plaques and nodules—some with distinct brown crusts—on the right forearm, right knee, left flank, and abdomen. There was no lymphadenopathy and no other pathological findings on physical exam. An externally performed lesion biopsy reported dermal T‑cell infiltrates without evidence of malignancy. Two repeat biopsies from morphologically different lesions showed interface dermatitis with pseudolymphomatous infiltrates, thickening of the epidermis, follicular hyperparakeratosis, and perivascular and periadnexal superficially accentuated lymphocytic infiltrates with a preponderance of T cells. Tissue clonality analyses demonstrated polyclonal IgH and TCR gamma chain gene expression, thus excluding lymphoma. Direct immunofluorescence did not detect any IgG, IgM, IgA, or C3 depositions. A serum sample was negative for antibodies against extractable nuclear antigens and complement factors were within normal ranges.

An 84‑year‑old woman presented with a large nodular lesion on the forehead of 2.5 months' duration. She had been seen at another hospital where a pre‑diagnosis of lymphoma was recorded; the prior punch biopsy report listed basal cell carcinoma, sarcoidosis, lupus vulgaris and pseudolymphoma among the clinical pre‑diagnoses and the material was sent for pathology consultation. Microscopic examination of the punch biopsy showed a dense nodular and diffuse lymphohistiocytic cell infiltration within the dermis. In the cytoplasm of histiocytes, small, round structures resembling organisms were noted. Immunohistochemical staining showed reactive T lymphocytes labelled with CD3 and CD5, reactive B lymphocytes labelled with CD20, and large clusters of histiocytes labelled with CD68; there was no staining with CD30. The pathology report recommended investigation of the aetiology of granulomatous dermatitis, especially cutaneous leishmaniasis.

retrieval_query_text: A 34‑year‑old Caucasian woman presented with a 2‑year history of recurrent oral ulceration. Her medical history was notable only for hypothyroidism treated with levothyroxine 125 mcg daily. Blood chemistry showed elevations of PCR (about 4–5 times the threshold parameter) and abnormalities of serum proteins. On clinical examination the oral cavity revealed several large, symptomatic ulcers. One aphthous lesion on the buccal mucosa had been present for more than 40 days despite topical cortisone applications and was associated with significant pain and interference with nutrition. The patient reported prior treatment without benefit with topical locorten gel and with systemic deltacortene 25 mg/day. Intraoral photographs show large ulcers with a yellow–white fibrinous membrane and surrounding erythematous halos on the buccal mucosa and inner lip.

contexts.text: A 54-year-old healthy woman presented to ophthalmology with a few months' history of a symptomatic lesion of the right eye. The lesion was located in the nasal bulbar conjunctiva within the interpalpebral zone. On examination there was an erythematous fibrovascular lesion approximately 5 mm in length. The lesion produced foreign-body sensation and discomfort. The lesion was clinically diagnosed as a pterygium, and surgical removal was performed.

A 32-year-old man from Djelfa, Algeria, with a history of contact eczema presented with a 6-week history of painless, non-healing skin lesions on the dorsal aspect of his right hand. He had applied topical corticosteroids and antiseptics without improvement and had received two courses of antibiotics (pristinamycin, amoxicillin + clavulanic acid) with no significant results. On examination there was a limited erythematous-papular plaque, approximately 8 cm in diameter, on the dorsal right hand formed by confluence of several papules with satellite lesions at the periphery. The initial plaque was associated with several firm, painless subcutaneous nodules 0.5–1.5 cm in diameter that tracked proximally along lymphatic drainage toward the elbow. The patient did not recall an insect bite, no other body sites were involved, and the remainder of the examination was unremarkable. Direct mycological examination and culture on Sabouraud medium at 25 °C and on BHI medium at 37 °C were negative for fungal presence.

A 38-year-old man with HIV on dolutegravir and emtricitabine–tenofovir presented without prior ocular problems. The report notes him as "well controlled (CD4 count of 213 cells/mm3 with an undetectable viral load)." He initially presented with a nonulcerative papulonodular hypopigmented rash on the extremities, trunk, and abdomen; "H and E staining of the cutaneous biopsy showed Leishmaniasis chassis and infantum." Thrombocytopenia and splenomegaly were also noted. He was treated with intravenous liposomal amphotericin B (received 7 of 9 doses) and was lost to follow-up; one year later he had recurrent cutaneous disease and was retreated with amphotericin (14-dose course) and received miltefosine for a 28-day course. Two days after stopping miltefosine, he developed progressive left-eye redness, pain, and photophobia. On day 7 of symptoms his visual acuity in the left eye had declined to count fingers.

A 7-year-old castrated male domestic short-haired cat, stray with unknown history, from the greater Athens area of Greece was presented for examination because of facial swelling and eye lesions. On examination there was a raised, nonalopecic, semifirm, poorly demarcated, painless swelling of the forehead. Periocular hypotrichosis, edema, and slight hyperpigmentation were present. Edema of the conjunctiva and third eyelid of the right eye was also observed. Clinical examination revealed no other abnormalities. A blood sample for complete blood count and biochemistry profile was obtained, and fine needle aspirates and a trucut biopsy were taken from the forehead swelling for cytological and histopathological examination. The patient had a nonregenerative anemia, hyperglobulinemia, and thrombocytopenia. Urinalysis showed no abnormalities. Further suggested serological tests for vector-borne diseases were not done because of financial restrictions. At presentation the clinicians listed the differential diagnosis as: subcutaneous abscess, atypical bacterial and mycobacterial infection, deep fungal infection, and neoplasia.

A 54-year-old man from southwest Iran presented with a 3-week history of continuous throbbing headache, fever, chills, weakness, anorexia, and weight loss. Past medical history included benign prostatic hyperplasia, gastroesophageal reflux disease, and hemorrhoids; current medications were tamsulosin, propranolol, rabeprazole, and cathartic syrup. On examination his temperature was 38.0 C and blood pressure 130/82 mm Hg. Abdominal examination revealed mild right upper-quadrant tenderness and moderate splenomegaly; all other examinations were normal. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 8.1 g/dL, white-cell count 1900/mm3, reticulocyte count 0.5%, and platelet count 20,000/mm3. ESR was 56 mm/h, alanine aminotransferase 84 IU/L, aspartate aminotransferase 67 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 401 IU/L, albumin 3.4 g/dL, conjugated bilirubin 0.6 mg/dL, ferritin 658.6 mcg/dL, serum iron 23 mcg/dL, and TIBC 116 mcg/dL. Creatinine, blood sugar, coagulation tests, urinalysis, stool and sputum exams, Wright test, 2ME, calcium, phosphorus, magnesium, and PSA were reported as normal. Serologic tests for HBV, HCV, and HIV were negative. Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated mild hepatomegaly and moderate splenomegaly. Doppler ultrasound showed dilation of the splenic vein and portal vein (15 mm each). Computed tomography of the brain revealed no abnormality. Axial FLAIR MRI of the brain showed increased signal intensity in the central part of the right side of the pons.

A 25-year-old man presented with a left-sided upper abdominal lump and multiple skin lesions present for the last 12 years. The abdominal lump had been very slowly increasing in size, was painless and produced a mild dragging sensation. The skin lesions were present primarily on his back and abdomen; they were described as depigmented, painless, and non-itchy. He denied current fever, loss of appetite, weight loss, cough, jaundice, hematemesis, melaena, and blood transfusion. He reported a history of kala-azar 15 years earlier treated with an injectable medication (he could not recall the drug name). He was a known chronic hepatitis B patient on entecavir 1 mg once daily. On examination there were multiple hypo- and hyperpigmented macular and maculopapular non-scaly skin lesions distributed over the trunk (mainly back, chest, and abdomen); lesion size ranged from a few millimeters (0.3–0.7 mm) for hypopigmented spots to 1–3 cm for hyperpigmented lesions, and sensation over the lesions was intact. Other vital signs were normal. Abdominal examination showed firm, non-tender hepatosplenomegaly with the liver 4 cm below the right costal margin and the spleen 6 cm along its long axis.

On July 2019, a 29-year-old female with no history of immunodeficiency or underlying diseases presented to an ENT clinic in northern Iran. She had a 3-month history of an itching intranasal lesion on the right side of her nasal canal and recurrent nasal congestion each year. An ENT specialist diagnosed her with an intranasal polyp and recommended polypectomy and rhinoplasty. Three months after surgery, she returned to the specialist with swelling and inflammation in the nasal cavity, suggesting recurrence. To rule out bacterial infections as possible complications of polypectomy, the specialist performed a fine needle aspiration (FNA) from the intranasal lesion. The FNA fluid specimen was stored at ambient temperature for 3 hours before being delivered to the laboratory, where a direct smear was prepared, fixed, and stained using the Gram technique. Microscopic examination revealed spindle-shaped Leishmania promastigote-like structures without any amastigotes of the parasite. In reviewing the history, the patient reported traveling to an endemic area of cutaneous leishmaniasis in Mashhad (eastern Iran) suburb area 3 months prior and noticing a bite in her nasal cavity. A direct smear of the FNA sample stained with Gram stain showed numerous developed and undeveloped promastigote forms of Leishmania parasite on microscopy.

A 42‑year‑old Italian man with a 20‑year history of plaque psoriasis and psoriasis arthropathica presented with lesions that had appeared 6 months earlier. He had been treated with subcutaneous methotrexate 25 mg weekly for 9 years and adalimumab 40 mg every other week for 7 years. Topical therapies had been used in the weeks before hospitalization. The patient was obese (BMI 39 kg/m2). On examination he had multiple erythemato‑squamous psoriatic plaques (PASI 16.6) and multiple erosive and partly ulcerating plaques and nodules—some with distinct brown crusts—on the right forearm, right knee, left flank, and abdomen. Two repeat biopsies from morphologically different lesions showed interface dermatitis with pseudolymphomatous infiltrates, thickening of the epidermis, follicular hyperparakeratosis, and perivascular and periadnexal superficially accentuated lymphocytic infiltrates with a preponderance of T cells. Tissue clonality analyses demonstrated polyclonal IgH and TCR gamma chain gene expression, thus excluding lymphoma. Direct immunofluorescence did not detect any IgG, IgM, IgA, or C3 depositions. Syphilis serology, carried out because numerous plasma cells were present in the tissue, yielded negative results.

A 61-year-old man (weight 65 kg) was referred in January with a 2-month history of a 1 × 3 cm lesion on the left ear. He has diabetes and had not traveled outside Kashan during the previous year. He reported that the ear lesion felt uncomfortable and scabrous but was not painful and he had no systemic complaints. Direct microscopy of scales with 10% potassium hydroxide (KOH) preparation was negative for fungal elements. The lesion was cleaned and specimens were collected from the margin by scraping; two smears were fixed with methanol and stained with 10% Giemsa for 30 minutes. On microscopic examination of the stained smears, amastigote forms of Leishmania spp. were observed.

A 24-year-old man from a small rural village near the Pacific coast of Esmeraldas province, Ecuador, reports that at age 16 papules first appeared on his left knee and right cheek and gradually increased in size and number over years. For about 2 years he received various medications without a confirmed diagnosis; he was at one point treated clinically for leprosy with multidrug therapy (dapsone, rifampicin, clofazimine) for 1 month. On examination there are numerous cutaneous lesions: pea- to rice-grain–sized reddish papules on both ear lobes and auricles with palpable induration; miliary to pea-sized papules on the face; papules and nodules on the left shoulder; many miliary to hen-egg–sized papules, nodules, erythema, infiltrated erythema, and brownish freckles on the upper extremities, some with scaly or crusted surfaces; rice-grain to thumb-sized papules grouped on brownish freckle lesions of the lower back; satellite miliary papules around plaque-like lesions; thumb- to palm-sized erythema on the thigh; and various papules, nodules, infiltrated erythemas, and brownish freckles on the lower extremities. No loss of sensation was recognized anywhere on the body and there was no hypertrophy of peripheral nerves. The rK39 kit test gave a strong positive reaction. Stained slit-skin smears from lesions demonstrated numerous intracellular amastigotes identified as Leishmania on microscopy, and Ziehl–Neelsen stains showed no acid-fast bacilli.

The episodes recurred after a symptom-free interval: at age 18 attacks returned at a frequency of two to three per day for 15 days, and thereafter typically recurred approximately every year to year-and-a-half as two attacks per day over a two-week period. A 27-year-old man from central Iran noted a small pimple on his right upper eyelid 4 months before presentation. The eyelid lesion enlarged slowly. On examination it was a well-defined, firm, nontender, subcutaneous, skin-colored nodule measuring about 1 cm × 1 cm, with slightly erythematous, raised borders; it was crusty and painless. CBC, ESR, CRP, and blood chemistries were within normal limits. A sample culture of the lesion grew Staphylococcus aureus. The lesion was treated sequentially with cephalexin, cloxacillin, amoxicillin–clavulanate, and steroids for 10 days, but these treatments failed to heal the lesion. Because cutaneous leishmaniasis occurs in the patient's area of residence and because of the lack of response to treatment, cutaneous leishmaniasis or basal cell carcinoma was proposed as the differential diagnosis.

A 47-year-old man presented to the emergency department with recurrent fever for 4 months and worsening symptoms including diarrhea for 1 month. About 4 months earlier he developed fever up to 39.9 °C that typically occurred in the afternoon and lasted several hours; associated symptoms included headache, myalgia, and nausea. After a temporary resolution he had a relapse with persistent high fever and frequent yellow watery diarrhea (>10 times/day). Past medical history included malaria diagnosed 6 years earlier in Africa treated with quinine. He reported hypersensitivity to quinolones (e.g., moxifloxacin). On admission, novel coronavirus nucleic acid test was negative. The schistosoma japonicum IgG antibody, echinococcus granulosus antibody, liver fluke antibody test, plasmodium antigen test, and blood smear test were all negative. Tests for hepatitis A and B, autoimmune liver disease markers, AFP, and CEA were negative. Abdominal ultrasound showed hepatomegaly and splenomegaly (intercostal spleen thickness ~7.0 cm). Chest and plain abdominal CT reported cirrhosis, splenomegaly, portal hypertension with collateral circulation, and peritoneal effusion. The admitting team considered sepsis and fever of undetermined origin (infection vs tumor) and noted Child-Pugh B decompensated cirrhosis. An emergency metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) blood test was sent to try to identify an occult pathogen.

A 52-year-old woman presented with a single lesion on the tip of her nose that had existed for 14 months. It began as a papule and was slowly increasing in size, enlarging to a plaque. A smear of the lesion performed about 1 year earlier was positive, "showing leishmania bodies." All five members of her family had a history of proven leishmaniasis. Her past medical history was notable for renal failure diagnosed 11 years earlier; she "received a renal transplant 4 years after the diagnosis of renal failure." She also had hypertension and hyperlipidemia and was taking oral mycophenolate mofetil (2 g daily) and cyclosporine (100 mg daily). Skin examination showed skin type IV, "No actinic keratosis was present," and a 3x3 cm indurated ulcer with elevated borders was present on the tip of her nose. The therapeutic plan was intralesional glucantime injections (approximately 1 ml of 1.5 g vial per week). "After completing a therapeutic course of 20 sessions receiving intralesional glucantime injections, she was considered as glucantime therapy resistant."

A 75-year-old man was referred with lesions on the hands, legs, face, and the upper lid of the right eye. He is a farmer from Aran va Bidgol city, Isfahan province (central Iran). He reported that sandflies had bitten him when he went to the farm for irrigation on nights during the sandfly season. He described the appearance of 25 multiple nodular, ulcerative, and crusted lesions on his body. On examination the lesions varied in size from a few millimeters to several centimeters; there were eight lesions on the face, including one on the upper right eyelid. He had no particular medical history, no fever, the lesions were painless, and his general condition was good.

A 43-year-old man from Cumanda (Chimborazo province, Ecuador), a subtropical mountainous community at ~500 m above sea level, presented with multiple chronic skin lesions. History of present illness: The lesion began as an insect-bite–like papular lesion on the forearm. Lesions then appeared on the right ear and the nose. About 2 years later, lesions developed on a wide range of the lower extremities and subsequently became multiple and confluent on the abdomen, thorax, body side, and thigh. A superficial involvement of mucosae of the nose and upper lip was observed. Treatment history: At the time of examination the patient had already received injections of nine ampoules of trivalent antimonials (Repodral, 20 mg/kg/day) at a rural health center; after finishing several courses he received pentavalent antimonials (Glucantime, 10 mg/kg/day) for about 5 months. Early investigations performed from active lesions included smear specimens, skin biopsies, syringe aspirates for culture, and material on FTA cards. Montenegro skin test showed a 17-mm induration, and an rK39 kit test revealed a strongly positive band. The smear specimen was positive for Leishmania amastigotes in scanty numbers. Promastigotes grown in vitro showed a tendency to decrease gradually and then disappear, an effect attributed by the investigators to prior antimonial treatment.

A 65-year-old man from Brasilia presented with an erythematous plaque on his nose that began one month after fishing in the state of Amazonas, Brazil. HIV serology was negative. The Leishmania skin test (LST) and indirect immunofluorescence results were negative. The patient was treated with NMG (meglumine antimoniate) 20 mg SbV/kg/day for 20 days without improvement; treatment was continued with additional dosing that again did not result in improvement. After a month off therapy he resumed NMG combined with allopurinol (1,200 mg/day); NMG was stopped at one point because of intense myalgia, then resumed to a cumulative dose reported in the chart, yet clinical improvement was not achieved during these courses of therapy.

At adoption, immunologic tests for FIV and FeLV were negative. On clinical examination there was more severe periodontal disease on the right side and a right maxillary local stomatitis with a nodular, ulcerative appearance; on inspection the nodular lesion was slightly painful with spontaneous bleeding. Bilateral mandibular lymph node enlargement was present; no other abnormalities were noted. Preoperative laboratory testing showed leukopenia (4.93 x 10^3/μl; RR 5.5–19.5), elevated total protein (10.06 g/dl; RR 6.0–7.9) and globulins (7.76 g/dl; RR 2.6–5.1), hypoalbuminemia (2.3 g/dl; RR 2.8–3.9), and mild hyperbilirubinemia (0.12 mg/dl; RR 0.0–0.1). Under anesthesia a detailed oral exam and full-mouth radiographs demonstrated periodontal pocketing (7 mm) at the site of the nodular ulcero-hemorrhagic lesion (third right maxillary premolar), advanced periodontitis of multiple teeth on the right maxilla, tooth resorption in six teeth including the affected premolar, and radiographic vertical bone loss adjacent to the lesion. Treatment at that time included extraction of teeth with resorption and advanced attachment loss, routine closure of gingival flaps, and incisional biopsies of the maxillary lesion for histopathologic assessment. Two weeks after surgery the cat's appetite and weight had improved, but a nodular ulcero-hemorrhagic lesion with persistent swelling and inflammation of the right maxilla remained.

retrieval_query_text: A patient began having attacks of severe unilateral periorbital pain that initially lasted about one hour and recurred daily at varying times for about one week; these episodes were always associated with agitation and ipsilateral autonomic signs including lacrimation, nasal congestion, ptosis, lid edema, and redness of the eye. The episodes recurred after a symptom-free interval: at age 18 attacks returned at a frequency of two to three per day for 15 days, and thereafter typically recurred approximately every year to year-and-a-half as two attacks per day over a two-week period. Multiple prophylactic therapies (verapamil, lithium carbonate, topiramate, valproic acid, gabapentin, and baclofen) produced no benefit, and acute treatments including oxygen, octreotide, local anesthetics, dihydroergotamine, and indomethacin were ineffective. From age 20, subcutaneous sumatriptan 6 mg was the only therapy that could abort an individual attack, typically stopping pain within 10 to 20 minutes. Over time the attack frequency increased, with three to four daily attacks by age 32. Rarely, pain occurred on the left. Following a dental extraction in 2013 the attacks remitted for three years but then reappeared in January 2016 as daily clusters (4–5 attacks) without headache-free periods through December 2016. During September–December 2016 the patient also took oral prednisone 75 mg daily without benefit. The patient consumes no alcohol.

contexts.text: A 50‑year‑old man born in Morocco was evaluated for PET‑positive visceral lymph nodes. He is HIV‑positive and has been on antiretroviral therapy for 5 years (receiving tenofovir, lamivudine, and efavirenz). He is a former smoker (31 pack‑years) and recently underwent surgery and radiotherapy for rectal cancer. He presented with a low‑grade fever of unknown origin. Physical examination documented hepatosplenomegaly and enlarged inguinal lymph nodes. Routine laboratory abnormalities included a moderate leukopenia (white cells 2.45 x 10^9/L), hypergammaglobulinemia (38.7%), an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (85 mm/h), and a mildly increased β2‑microglobulin (5.5 mg/L). PET‑positive, accessible lymph nodes were mainly located in the mediastinum. Clinical reasoning focused on three elements: (1) the clinical profile of low‑grade fever in an HIV patient on therapy, (2) the laboratory pattern of cytopenia with hypergammaglobulinemia and raised inflammatory markers, and (3) imaging showing PET‑positive visceral lymphadenopathy. The leading differential diagnoses were lymphoproliferative disorders, infections (including fungal or parasitic), and metastatic epithelial tumors. Because the PET‑positive, reachable nodes were mainly mediastinal and lymphoproliferative disorders in HIV are often diagnosable with cytology, a transesophageal endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) with fine‑needle aspiration biopsy of a mediastinal node (station 4L) was scheduled.

A 55-year-old man with chronic severe hepatitis B (HBV‑DNA positive) was admitted for intermittent fever of 1 month (maximum 40°C). He had worked on a farm in Xinjiang Province one month earlier. On examination he had hepatosplenomegaly below the costal margin. Initial laboratory tests showed marked hepatic abnormalities (ALT 490 U/L, AST 558 U/L), low total protein and albumin (TP 51.54 g/L, ALB 26.83 g/L), TBIL 23.23 μmol/L, DBIL 14.37 μmol/L, and HBV‑DNA 3.19 × 10^4 IU/mL. Routine blood counts were abnormal (WBC 3.12 × 10^9/L, platelets 100 × 10^9/L). After 2 weeks the patient remained febrile with worsening labs (WBC 0.95 × 10^9/L, platelets 56 × 10^9/L, ALT 524 U/L, AST 640 U/L). Abdominal enhanced CT showed an enlarged spleen with multiple low‑density nodules that demonstrated sustained/delayed enhancement; angioma/hemangioma was suspected. 18F‑FDG PET/CT demonstrated a significant diffuse increase in FDG uptake in the enlarged spleen (SUVmax 6.6) and slightly diffuse bone‑marrow uptake. Bone‑marrow aspiration and biopsy were performed twice (2 months apart) and both showed phagocytosis of reticulum cells. Based on the clinical and imaging findings, splenic lymphoma was considered highly likely. The patient received chemotherapy for hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) and was discharged in remission, but was readmitted 2 months later with recurrent fever and pancytopenia; splenectomy was then undertaken to establish a diagnosis and reduce disease burden.

A 60-year-old woman from Uttar Pradesh, India presented with a six‑week history of high‑grade continuous fever with chills and rigors, anorexia, malaise, joint pains, and severe lethargy. She reported "crops of round, raised lesions" that began on the left upper limb, progressed to the right upper limb and then involved the whole face, upper back, chest, and upper abdomen; the lesions were "closely associated with the febrile episodes." Some lesions enlarged, became nodular, developed sunken centers that drained pus‑like material, and were painful and red. She also noted nonpainful bilateral leg swelling (pitting) and painful red eyes with nodular lesions on the eyelids and in the conjunctiva, associated with decreased vision. She had no prior comorbidities, was a teetotaler, and denied taking over‑the‑counter or steroid/complementary medications or other potentially immunosuppressive drugs. Eye exam demonstrated nodular lesions over the eyes and conjunctiva with conjunctival suffusion. Abdominal exam and imaging showed hepatosplenomegaly without ascites or intrahepatic biliary dilatation and no abdominal lymphadenopathy. Laboratory studies: hemoglobin 10.5 g/dL, total leukocyte count 5600/mm3, platelet count 80,000/mm3, ESR 80 mm/hr with normocytic normochromic anemia. Liver tests: total bilirubin 3.2 mg/dL (direct 1.8), AST 50 IU/L, ALT 60 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 221 IU/L, GGT 150 IU/L, albumin 1.9 g/dL, INR 1.3. Serum IgG 22.6 g/L.

A 47-year-old man presented to the emergency department on December 28, 2020 with recurrent fever for 4 months and worsening symptoms with diarrhea for 1 month. About 4 months earlier he developed fever without an evident cause, with a maximum temperature of 39.9 C; fevers usually occurred in the afternoon, lasted several hours, and were associated with headache, myalgia, and nausea. After a period of apparent improvement he redeveloped persistent high fever (≈39 C) accompanied by yellow watery diarrhea more than 10 times per day. Six years previously he had been diagnosed with malaria in Africa and treated with quinine. On admission: Novel Coronavirus nucleic acid test was negative. Laboratory studies showed Hb 83 g/L, WBC 2.82 x 10^9/L, platelet count 16 x 10^9/L, neutrophil percentage 84.0%, lymphocyte percentage 8.0%, and procalcitonin 0.87 ng/ml. Blood culture grew methicillin-resistant coagulase-negative Staphylococci. The cryptococcus antigen test, fungal G test, and GM test were negative. Abdominal ultrasound showed enlarged liver and spleen. Chest and plain abdominal CT demonstrated cirrhosis, splenomegaly, portal hypertension with collateral circulation, and peritoneal effusion. The team considered sepsis and fever of undetermined origin (infection versus tumor) and assessed the patient as Child-Pugh B decompensated cirrhosis. An emergency blood metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) test was sent to help diagnose the fever of unknown cause.

A 30‑year‑old man presented with pain in his lower limbs and a non‑itchy erythematous rash over both lower limbs. He had low‑grade intermittent fever for three months. On examination he was pale and malnourished (BMI 18.4 kg/m2) and had palpable purpura over both thighs and buttocks. Abdominal examination revealed palpable hepatomegaly with massive splenomegaly. Laboratory testing showed pancytopenia (hemoglobin 6.8 g/dL, total leukocyte count 2800/mm3, platelet count 45 000/muL) and polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia (4.9 g/dL); liver and renal function tests were within reference ranges. Contrast‑enhanced CT of chest and abdomen confirmed hepatosplenomegaly and was otherwise unremarkable. The treating team considered hematologic malignancy and a connective‑tissue disorder with vasculitis. Other infectious etiologies entertained included HIV, scrub typhus/rickettsial infection, and visceral leishmaniasis (given the patient lived in an endemic area). Initial testing showed: anti‑nuclear antibodies, complement levels (C3 = 94 mg/dL and C4 = 20 mg/dL), and rheumatoid factor were negative; urine examination was normal and serum cryoglobulins were not raised. Viral markers (HIV, hepatitis B surface antigen, and anti‑hepatitis C) were negative. Serology for rickettsia and scrub typhus were also negative.

A 47-year-old man presented to the emergency department with recurrent fever for 4 months and worsening symptoms including diarrhea for 1 month. About 4 months earlier he developed fever up to 39.9 °C that typically occurred in the afternoon and lasted several hours; associated symptoms included headache, myalgia, and nausea. After a temporary resolution he had a relapse with persistent high fever and frequent yellow watery diarrhea (>10 times/day). Past medical history included malaria diagnosed 6 years earlier in Africa treated with quinine. He reported hypersensitivity to quinolones (e.g., moxifloxacin). On admission, novel coronavirus nucleic acid test was negative. The schistosoma japonicum IgG antibody, echinococcus granulosus antibody, liver fluke antibody test, plasmodium antigen test, and blood smear test were all negative. Tests for hepatitis A and B, autoimmune liver disease markers, AFP, and CEA were negative. Abdominal ultrasound showed hepatomegaly and splenomegaly (intercostal spleen thickness ~7.0 cm). Chest and plain abdominal CT reported cirrhosis, splenomegaly, portal hypertension with collateral circulation, and peritoneal effusion. The admitting team considered sepsis and fever of undetermined origin (infection vs tumor) and noted Child-Pugh B decompensated cirrhosis. An emergency metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) blood test was sent to try to identify an occult pathogen.

A 15‑year‑old boy presented to the emergency fever clinic with fever and cough for more than 10 days. He developed fever after a cold, with temperatures initially 37–38°C, later peaking at 41°C. Initial local-hospital testing showed WBC 3.3 × 10^9/L, Hb 85 g/L, and PLT 87 × 10^9/L. Bone marrow puncture at that time "indicated that hematopoietic tissue hyperplasia was active and the proportion of three-line blood cells was roughly normal. Lymphocytes accounted for 9.5%, and atypical lymphocytes were found occasionally." Adenovirus IgM was weakly positive; ferritin was >2,000 ng/mL; procalcitonin was 4.14 ng/mL. Abdominal ultrasound and CT indicated hepatomegaly and splenomegaly. He was referred for further care after lack of improvement with initial treatment. On arrival his vital signs were: T 37.1°C, pulse 110/min, RR 19/min, BP 110/72 mmHg. Admission labs showed WBC 4.68 × 10^9/L, Hb 100 g/L, RBC 3.65 × 10^12/L; ALT 204 IU/L; AST 176 IU/L; GGT 153 IU/L; LDH 889 IU/L; ferritin >2,000 ng/mL; PCT 2.11 ng/mL; CRP 53.5 mg/L; IL‑6 31.58 pg/mL. TORCH/EBV panel: CMV, HSV, rubella virus, and EBV IgG positive. Chest CT was unremarkable. Abdominal ultrasound showed intercostal spleen thickness ≈6.6 cm, consistent with splenomegaly. Do not exclude the possibility of parasitic diseases? Hemophilic cell syndrome? Lymphoma? Autoimmune disease?" An mNGS test on blood was performed on the second day after admission because the cause of fever remained unclear.

A 65-year-old man presented with diffuse abdominal pain for one year, 14 kg weight loss and fever for 4 months. The fever occurred once or twice daily with profuse sweating and shivers. He had no prior illnesses recorded and was a long‑time smoker. He was born in Paraiba, lived in Sao Paulo since age 9, and reported no recent travel outside the city; he denied contact with unpasteurized milk, domestic animals, rodents or farm animals. On examination he had swollen lymph nodes in several body regions; the largest measured 3 cm in the left inguinal region. Laboratory tests showed elevated C-reactive protein (99.9 mg/L), normocytic normochromic anemia (hemoglobin 11.1 g/dL; hematocrit 32.4%), sodium 130 mEq/L, leucocytes 5300/mm3 (neutrophils 3260/mm3; lymphocytes 910/mm3), gamma-glutamyl transferase 570 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 574 U/L, and beta-2 microglobulin 3.3 mcg/mL; all other routine blood tests, blood cultures, electrolytes, and kidney and liver functions were reported as normal. (L.) major-like antigen. Positron emission tomography showed increased glycolytic metabolism in several lymph nodes (some forming conglomerates) above and below the diaphragm, with increased glycolytic metabolism in the spleen, liver and bones, findings described as suggestive of a lymphoproliferative disorder. Bone marrow aspiration identified the presence of Leishmania spp. on direct microscopy.

A 42‑year‑old man presented with 1 year of progressive weakness and significant weight loss and intermittent low‑grade fevers. He had been treated for pulmonary tuberculosis 2 years earlier and was recently restarted on antitubercular therapy for the past month without improvement. On examination he was thin, pale, afebrile, and had abdominal distension. Left submandibular and left axillary lymph nodes were palpable, each about 1.5 cm. Mild hepatosplenomegaly was noted. Ultrasound of the abdomen showed multiple enlarged conglomerate mesenteric lymph nodes, the largest 22 × 18 mm. Clinical chemistry showed reversal of the albumin:globulin ratio with total protein 9.5 g/dL, albumin 2.0 g/dL, globulin 7.5 g/dL. Other liver and renal tests were within normal limits. Complete blood count showed pancytopenia: hemoglobin 6 g/dL, total leukocyte count 1,800/µL (polymorphs 47%, lymphocytes 51%), platelets 48,000/µL; ESR 50 mm/h. Peripheral smear demonstrated rouleaux formation. Fine needle aspiration cytology of left submandibular and axillary lymph nodes yielded thick aspirate; smears showed few epithelioid cell granulomas interspersed with discrete aggregates of histiocytes in a background of reactive lymphoid cells and many plasma cells.

A 29-year-old woman from Rio de Janeiro (resident of the Caju neighborhood) presented for diagnostic evaluation in January 2013. She worked as a cleaner in the cemetery of Caju and denied any travel outside the city. Over the following months she noted progressive jaundice (yellow sclera and skin), dark urine, weight loss of ~10 kg, increasing abdominal girth and soft bilateral lower‑extremity edema to the knees. She had multiple prior emergency visits and received only symptomatic treatment. On admission her general state was poor with malnutrition; examination showed pallor 3–4/4, mild dehydration, jaundice 2/4, cyanosis, fever and tachycardia. Laboratory testing revealed severe pancytopenia, prolonged prothrombin time, marked elevation of aminotransferases, hypoalbuminemia and hypergammaglobulinemia with severe cholestatic jaundice. Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated free peritoneal fluid, hepatomegaly ≈20 cm, splenomegaly ≈25 cm and gallstones. The initial diagnostic hypotheses included disseminated tuberculosis and visceral leishmaniasis; other considered diagnoses were dengue, yellow fever, prolonged septicemic salmonellosis, brucellosis, malaria, Chagas disease and lymphoproliferative malignancies. Investigations ordered included thick and thin blood smears, blood cultures, stool tests, bone marrow biopsy and aspiration and serologies for dengue, yellow fever, brucellosis and Chagas disease. HIV testing was performed and was negative.

contexts.text: A 43-year-old man from Cumanda (Chimborazo province, Ecuador), a subtropical mountainous community at ~500 m above sea level, presented with multiple chronic skin lesions. History of present illness: The lesion began as an insect-bite–like papular lesion on the forearm. Lesions then appeared on the right ear and the nose. About 2 years later, lesions developed on a wide range of the lower extremities and subsequently became multiple and confluent on the abdomen, thorax, body side, and thigh. A superficial involvement of mucosae of the nose and upper lip was observed. Treatment history: At the time of examination the patient had already received injections of nine ampoules of trivalent antimonials (Repodral, 20 mg/kg/day) at a rural health center; after finishing several courses he received pentavalent antimonials (Glucantime, 10 mg/kg/day) for about 5 months. Early investigations performed from active lesions included smear specimens, skin biopsies, syringe aspirates for culture, and material on FTA cards. Montenegro skin test showed a 17-mm induration, and an rK39 kit test revealed a strongly positive band. The smear specimen was positive for Leishmania amastigotes in scanty numbers. Promastigotes grown in vitro showed a tendency to decrease gradually and then disappear, an effect attributed by the investigators to prior antimonial treatment.

A 32-year-old man from Djelfa, Algeria, with a history of contact eczema presented with a 6-week history of painless, non-healing skin lesions on the dorsal aspect of his right hand. He had applied topical corticosteroids and antiseptics without improvement and had received two courses of antibiotics (pristinamycin, amoxicillin + clavulanic acid) with no significant results. On examination there was a limited erythematous-papular plaque, approximately 8 cm in diameter, on the dorsal right hand formed by confluence of several papules with satellite lesions at the periphery. The initial plaque was associated with several firm, painless subcutaneous nodules 0.5–1.5 cm in diameter that tracked proximally along lymphatic drainage toward the elbow. The patient did not recall an insect bite, no other body sites were involved, and the remainder of the examination was unremarkable. Direct mycological examination and culture on Sabouraud medium at 25 °C and on BHI medium at 37 °C were negative for fungal presence.

A 42‑year‑old Italian man with a 20‑year history of plaque psoriasis and psoriasis arthropathica presented with lesions that had appeared 6 months earlier. He had been treated with subcutaneous methotrexate 25 mg weekly for 9 years and adalimumab 40 mg every other week for 7 years. Topical therapies had been used in the weeks before hospitalization. The patient was obese (BMI 39 kg/m2). On examination he had multiple erythemato‑squamous psoriatic plaques (PASI 16.6) and multiple erosive and partly ulcerating plaques and nodules—some with distinct brown crusts—on the right forearm, right knee, left flank, and abdomen. There was no lymphadenopathy and no other pathological findings on physical exam. An externally performed lesion biopsy reported dermal T‑cell infiltrates without evidence of malignancy. Two repeat biopsies from morphologically different lesions showed interface dermatitis with pseudolymphomatous infiltrates, thickening of the epidermis, follicular hyperparakeratosis, and perivascular and periadnexal superficially accentuated lymphocytic infiltrates with a preponderance of T cells. Tissue clonality analyses demonstrated polyclonal IgH and TCR gamma chain gene expression, thus excluding lymphoma. Direct immunofluorescence did not detect any IgG, IgM, IgA, or C3 depositions. Syphilis serology, carried out because numerous plasma cells were present in the tissue, yielded negative results.

A 24-year-old man from a small rural village near the Pacific coast of Esmeraldas province, Ecuador, reports that at age 16 papules first appeared on his left knee and right cheek and gradually increased in size and number over years. For about 2 years he received various medications without a confirmed diagnosis; he was at one point treated clinically for leprosy with multidrug therapy (dapsone, rifampicin, clofazimine) for 1 month. On examination there are numerous cutaneous lesions: pea- to rice-grain–sized reddish papules on both ear lobes and auricles with palpable induration; miliary to pea-sized papules on the face; papules and nodules on the left shoulder; many miliary to hen-egg–sized papules, nodules, erythema, infiltrated erythema, and brownish freckles on the upper extremities, some with scaly or crusted surfaces; rice-grain to thumb-sized papules grouped on brownish freckle lesions of the lower back; satellite miliary papules around plaque-like lesions; thumb- to palm-sized erythema on the thigh; and various papules, nodules, infiltrated erythemas, and brownish freckles on the lower extremities. No loss of sensation was recognized anywhere on the body and there was no hypertrophy of peripheral nerves. The rK39 kit test gave a strong positive reaction. Stained slit-skin smears from lesions demonstrated numerous intracellular amastigotes identified as Leishmania on microscopy, and Ziehl–Neelsen stains showed no acid-fast bacilli.

A 9-year-old boy presented with multiple papular lesions on the left cheek that had been present for three months and had gradually enlarged. His medical history was notable for an episode of cutaneous leishmaniasis located on the nose two years earlier, which had completely regressed after treatment with intralesional meglumine antimonate. Dermatologic examination showed multiple, coalescing, rough, slightly elevated, yellowish-brown papular lesions 3–6 mm in diameter on the left cheek. He also had a large atrophic scar on the nose. Nothing of interest was noted in his family history or his laboratory tests.

A 40‑year‑old woman from Balao Chico (Guayas province, Ecuador) presented in August 1979 with a progressive widespread skin eruption. The illness began with a lesion on the lumbar region; papular lesions developed and became pustulous vesicles at the right lumbar region and then disseminated over the body, with 308 generalized lesions counted. She reported marked right lumbar pain; some body‑surface lesions were thought clinically to resemble herpes zoster. The presumptive clinical diagnoses listed were paracoccidioidomycosis, cutaneous leishmaniasis, or staphylococcal infections. Examination of the ulcers showed most lesions to be crusty; when crusts were lifted they were excavated with purulent fluid from severe secondary infections. Ulcer sizes ranged from 0.5 to 20 mm in diameter; some lesions had thick, adherent crusts that bled when separated, others were small crusty ulcers with excavations, and confluent erythematous papular plaques were present on the lumbar–dorsal region. Laboratory tests on ulcer material did not demonstrate Paracoccidioides braziliensis or Staphylococcus aureus. Routine laboratory examinations revealed positivity for beta‑hemolytic streptococcus (antibiotic‑sensitive), and stool examination was positive for Trichuris trichiura, Ascaris lumbricoides, and Ancylostoma duodenale. Several smear samples from diverse regions of the body surface were taken at random.

Her only medical history was well-controlled hypertension. Examination showed a palpable spleen just below the left costal margin. On the right arm near the axilla there was "a single well-defined, ulcer surrounded by erythematous edging, with serous oozing" about 3 × 3 cm; the patient reported the lesion was painless, nonhealing, and present for 2–3 years. The rest of the exam was essentially normal. A Leishmania rk39 immunochromatography test was positive. Bone marrow aspiration parasitology revealed Leishmania amastigote forms, and serum immunofluorescence for Leishmania antibodies was positive (titer 1:400). Blood qPCR detected Leishmania DNA (400 parasites/mL). Direct microscopy of skin smears from the arm lesion showed no amastigotes, but Leishmania DNA amplification was obtained from dermal DNA extract by qPCR. ITS1 sequencing showed the Leishmania strains from the blood and the arm lesion corresponded to L. infantum and were 100% identical. Systemic response was rapid: fever resolved, general condition improved, splenomegaly regressed, blood counts normalized, and blood qPCR became negative after 28 days. However, "the skin lesion did not improve although Leishmania qPCR on dermal sample became negative." A skin biopsy was initially refused. One year later the lesion remained essentially unchanged. A polarized dermoscopy examination showed "ulcerations and short, fine arborizing vessels," described as evocative of a basal cell carcinoma.

A 43-year-old male laborer with known HIV infection for 2 years (on antiretroviral therapy) and on anti-tubercular treatment for 9 months presented with a 7-month history of asymptomatic skin lesions all over his body. Lesions first appeared on the arm and progressively spread to involve the face, legs, and trunk. On examination there were multiple bilateral asymmetrical diffuse papulonodular, non‑itchy skin lesions measuring 2–25 mm on the face, trunk, and extremities. There were no signs of ulceration or scarring. There was no lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly. A photograph showed multiple papulonodular lesions of varying size over the elbow. Laboratory tests showed anemia (hemoglobin 9.1 g/dL); liver and renal function tests and lipid profile were within normal limits. Ultrasonography of the abdomen was normal. CD4 count was 50 cells/µL and HIV viral load was 1750 copies/mL. There was no history of travel to known endemic areas for leishmaniasis.

An 84‑year‑old woman presented with a large nodular lesion on the forehead of 2.5 months' duration. She had been seen at another hospital where a pre‑diagnosis of lymphoma was recorded; the prior punch biopsy report listed basal cell carcinoma, sarcoidosis, lupus vulgaris and pseudolymphoma among the clinical pre‑diagnoses and the material was sent for pathology consultation. Microscopic examination of the punch biopsy showed a dense nodular and diffuse lymphohistiocytic cell infiltration within the dermis. In the cytoplasm of histiocytes, small, round structures resembling organisms were noted. Immunohistochemical staining showed reactive T lymphocytes labelled with CD3 and CD5, reactive B lymphocytes labelled with CD20, and large clusters of histiocytes labelled with CD68; there was no staining with CD30. The pathology report recommended investigation of the aetiology of granulomatous dermatitis, especially cutaneous leishmaniasis.

A 38‑year‑old man from Yayu district, western Ethiopia, presented to the outpatient clinic with multiple skin lesions on his face and hands and mutilation of the nose; his upper lip was injured and swollen. Eight years earlier he had a small papule on the right cheek that progressed to an open ulcer, then to ulcers on the left cheek and forehead; those active lesions lasted about six months and healed spontaneously, leaving permanent hypopigmented scars. He had no fever, hepatosplenomegaly or lymphedema and reported no history of HIV, chronic disease, alcohol abuse, or immunomodulatory drug use. Parasitological testing of lesion smears at that time showed many macrophages filled with amastigote stages of Leishmania, graded as +6. A nonreactive rK39 rapid diagnostic test and absence of related systemic signs made visceral leishmaniasis unlikely. Based on the clinical manifestations and smear result he was diagnosed with mucocutaneous leishmaniasis and treated with intramuscular sodium stibogluconate (20 mg/kg/day for 30 days) with clinical cure. Two years later he returned with a different cutaneous eruption that had appeared over the previous three months and had been preceded by intense itching. On exam he had multiple, nonpitting, closed papules on his face, nose, hands and legs. A skin smear again showed intramacrophage amastigotes with a parasite load graded +6, and culture grew promastigotes.
