contexts.text: A 65-year-old woman was admitted in March after collapsing in the street. She had been unwell for 14 months with night sweats and progressive loss of energy but denied fever. On examination she was afebrile and had hepatic enlargement and lymphadenopathy; liver function tests were within reference limits. Initial blood tests showed hemoglobin 8.1 g/dL, leukocyte count 4.62 × 10^9/L, and platelet count 143 × 10^9/L. Serologic tests for HIV, hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and Strongyloides spp. were negative. Her CD4 count was 790 cells/μL, rheumatoid factor was weakly positive, and immunoglobulin levels were within reference ranges. She was born in Guyana and had recent travel to Guyana in 2012 and 2013, to Grenada in 2012, to Ghana in 2005, and to France in 2003. Because a hematologic malignancy was suspected, a bone marrow aspiration was performed; Leishmania amastigotes were visible. Leishmania serology was negative by an rK39 rapid test and weakly positive by direct agglutination (1:3,200; cutoff 1:1,600).

A 60-year-old woman from Uttar Pradesh, India presented with a six‑week history of high‑grade continuous fever with chills and rigors, anorexia, malaise, joint pains, and severe lethargy. She reported "crops of round, raised lesions" that began on the left upper limb, progressed to the right upper limb and then involved the whole face, upper back, chest, and upper abdomen; the lesions were "closely associated with the febrile episodes." Some lesions enlarged, became nodular, developed sunken centers that drained pus‑like material, and were painful and red. One week before admission she developed jaundice with mild to moderate upper‑quadrant abdominal pain. She had no prior comorbidities, was a teetotaler, and denied taking over‑the‑counter or steroid/complementary medications or other potentially immunosuppressive drugs. On examination her temperature was 100.8°F, blood pressure 128/88 mm Hg, heart rate 100/min. Pallor and icterus were present; there was bilateral pitting, non‑tender symmetrical pedal edema. Eye exam demonstrated nodular lesions over the eyes and conjunctiva with conjunctival suffusion. Chest imaging was within normal limits. Laboratory studies: hemoglobin 10.5 g/dL, total leukocyte count 5600/mm3, platelet count 80,000/mm3, ESR 80 mm/hr with normocytic normochromic anemia. Liver tests: total bilirubin 3.2 mg/dL (direct 1.8), AST 50 IU/L, ALT 60 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 221 IU/L, GGT 150 IU/L, albumin 1.9 g/dL, INR 1.3. Serum IgG 22.6 g/L.

A 55‑year‑old man presented with recurrent high fevers and acute febrile symptoms. On admission he had a body temperature of 39.6 C. One month before admission he had developed a fever of unknown origin, with a highest temperature of 41 C accompanied by shivering. Before transfer he received piperacillin/tazobactam without improvement. He reported a past history of pancreatitis and prior septicemia and denied relevant family history. On admission (January 25, 2021) laboratory testing showed reduced WBC, RBC, hemoglobin, and platelets. Abdominal color ultrasound demonstrated hepatosplenomegaly. Serum amylase and lipase were elevated. A positive result was noted for Epstein‑Barr virus (EBV); no other blood or respiratory pathogens were detected. Over the next 14 days the cytopenias persisted. On February 7, 2021, bone marrow aspiration showed active marrow hyperplasia and hemophagocytosis, but no pathogenic microorganism was identified on the smear.

A 74-year-old woman from Tunis presented with several weeks of fever (oral temperature 38–39°C), sweats, chills, fatigue, diarrhea, intermittent vague abdominal pain, and occasional dry cough. Her only medical history was well-controlled hypertension. She had no reported HIV risk factors, transfusion, chronic immunosuppression, or other chronic disease. Initial labs showed pancytopenia with normocytic normochromic anemia (Hb 8.7 g/dL), leukopenia (2,900/mm3), thrombocytopenia (113,000/mm3); ESR 115 mm, CRP 215 mg/L, procalcitonin <0.5 ng/mL. A Leishmania rk39 immunochromatography test was positive. Bone marrow aspiration parasitology revealed Leishmania amastigote forms, and serum immunofluorescence for Leishmania antibodies was positive (titer 1:400). Blood qPCR detected Leishmania DNA (400 parasites/mL). Direct microscopy of skin smears from the arm lesion showed no amastigotes, but Leishmania DNA amplification was obtained from dermal DNA extract by qPCR. ITS1 sequencing showed the Leishmania strains from the blood and the arm lesion corresponded to L. infantum and were 100% identical. Systemic response was rapid: fever resolved, general condition improved, splenomegaly regressed, blood counts normalized, and blood qPCR became negative after 28 days. However, "the skin lesion did not improve although Leishmania qPCR on dermal sample became negative." A skin biopsy was initially refused. One year later the lesion remained essentially unchanged.

A 15-year-old female from the Macanao municipality on Margarita Island, Venezuela presented with a 6-month history of intermittent fever predominantly occurring at night, malaise, 6 kg weight loss, arthralgias, loss of appetite, dizziness, and amenorrhea. She lives in a rural area close to a landfill in a house built with cement ground, brick walls, and a metal roof without running water. She has one dog (unknown Leishmania infection status) and various turtles as pets. She has no history of traveling outside Venezuela. On examination she was pale, with increased respiratory and heart rate, and a fever of 39 C. Weight was 49 kg, height 1.57 m, and abdominal circumference 76 cm. She had cervical, axillary, and inguinal adenopathy. Cardiac and lung exams were normal. Abdominal exam revealed right upper-quadrant tenderness and hepatosplenomegaly (liver palpable 9.5 cm from the midclavicular line; spleen Hackett grade V). Laboratory values on admission demonstrated pancytopenia. Abdominal ultrasound and computed tomography confirmed hepatosplenomegaly. The initial clinical suspicion was a lymphoproliferative or myeloproliferative disorder. From an infectious disease perspective, the possibility of visceral leishmaniasis, a systemic mycosis, or tuberculosis were entertained. A bone marrow biopsy was performed to rule out a hematologic malignancy and to assess for infectious causes.

A 15‑year‑old boy presented to the emergency fever clinic with fever and cough for more than 10 days. He developed fever after a cold, with temperatures initially 37–38°C, later peaking at 41°C. Initial local-hospital testing showed WBC 3.3 × 10^9/L, Hb 85 g/L, and PLT 87 × 10^9/L. Bone marrow puncture at that time "indicated that hematopoietic tissue hyperplasia was active and the proportion of three-line blood cells was roughly normal. Lymphocytes accounted for 9.5%, and atypical lymphocytes were found occasionally." Adenovirus IgM was weakly positive; ferritin was >2,000 ng/mL; procalcitonin was 4.14 ng/mL. Abdominal ultrasound and CT indicated hepatomegaly and splenomegaly. He was referred for further care after lack of improvement with initial treatment. On arrival his vital signs were: T 37.1°C, pulse 110/min, RR 19/min, BP 110/72 mmHg. Admission labs showed WBC 4.68 × 10^9/L, Hb 100 g/L, RBC 3.65 × 10^12/L; ALT 204 IU/L; AST 176 IU/L; GGT 153 IU/L; LDH 889 IU/L; ferritin >2,000 ng/mL; PCT 2.11 ng/mL; CRP 53.5 mg/L; IL‑6 31.58 pg/mL. TORCH/EBV panel: CMV, HSV, rubella virus, and EBV IgG positive. Blood cultures showed no bacterial growth at 5 days. Chest CT was unremarkable. Abdominal ultrasound showed intercostal spleen thickness ≈6.6 cm, consistent with splenomegaly. Do not exclude the possibility of parasitic diseases? Lymphoma? Autoimmune disease?" An mNGS test on blood was performed on the second day after admission because the cause of fever remained unclear.

A 29-year-old woman from Rio de Janeiro (resident of the Caju neighborhood) presented for diagnostic evaluation in January 2013. She worked as a cleaner in the cemetery of Caju and denied any travel outside the city. Five months before admission she developed intermittent nocturnal fevers up to 39 °C that did not respond to antipyretics, with poor appetite, postprandial fullness, nausea and vomiting. Over the following months she noted progressive jaundice (yellow sclera and skin), dark urine, weight loss of ~10 kg, increasing abdominal girth and soft bilateral lower‑extremity edema to the knees. She had multiple prior emergency visits and received only symptomatic treatment. On admission her general state was poor with malnutrition; examination showed pallor 3–4/4, mild dehydration, jaundice 2/4, cyanosis, fever and tachycardia. Abdominal exam showed moderate ascites, hepatomegaly 7 cm below the right costal margin and splenomegaly palpable 2 cm below the umbilicus. The initial diagnostic hypotheses included disseminated tuberculosis and visceral leishmaniasis; other considered diagnoses were dengue, yellow fever, prolonged septicemic salmonellosis, brucellosis, malaria, Chagas disease and lymphoproliferative malignancies. Investigations ordered included thick and thin blood smears, blood cultures, stool tests, bone marrow biopsy and aspiration and serologies for dengue, yellow fever, brucellosis and Chagas disease. HIV testing was performed and was negative.

A 22‑month‑old girl presented with 8 days of fever to 40°C and mild cough. Past history: failure to thrive; normal neurologic development. She was the first child of a non‑consanguineous couple; no family history of albinism; normal hair and skin. On exam she was stunted, pale, had non‑tender hepatomegaly 5–6 cm and splenomegaly palpable 4 cm below the left costal margin. Petechial rash developed on the chest and legs as she worsened. Initial laboratory results: WBC 5100/mm3 (ANC 1200/mm3), Hb 9.1 g/dl, platelets 47,000/mm3; mild transaminase elevation; hypoalbuminemia. Ferritin 1,134 ng/ml; soluble IL‑2 receptor (sCD25) 3,183 U/ml. Blood cultures were negative. Serum immunoglobulins and lymphocyte subsets were reported as normal. Infectious testing: EBV serology positive for IgM and IgG anti‑VCA with negative IgG anti‑EBNA; EBV viral load 637 copies/ml. Leishmania testing was discordant: immunochromatography and indirect immunofluorescence were negative, serum ELISA was slightly positive, and leishmanial antigen in urine was negative. Bone‑marrow aspiration revealed hemophagocytosis. Over the next day she clinically worsened with progressive splenomegaly and cytopenias (WBC 4,800/mm3 with ANC 800/mm3, Hb 6.8 g/dl, platelets 27,000/mm3), triglycerides 686 mg/dl, ferritin 3,849 ng/ml, and sCD25 3,596 U/ml. Clotting tests were normal and perforin expression by flow cytometry was reported as normal.

A 52-year-old woman from Jiuzhaigou, Sichuan province, China, presented with an unprovoked high fever beginning January 9, 2021. The body temperature reached 39.6 C and was accompanied by coughing, sputum expectoration, tiredness, anhelation, chilliness, and shivering. Initial evaluation included ultrasound of the urinary system, brain MRI, and chest CT, which showed no significant abnormality on those studies. She was treated empirically with ceftriaxone and clindamycin and received methylprednisolone; after a week the cough, sputum production, fatigue, and shortness of breath improved, but the fever persisted. On January 13, a bone marrow aspiration smear showed a low proliferation rate of nucleated cells, a decreased granulocyte/erythrocyte ratio, some erythroblasts with abnormal morphology, significantly reduced iron content in the marrow, and poor platelet production by megakaryocytes with scattered and clustered platelets observed. On January 14, routine blood tests demonstrated decreased white blood cells, red blood cells, hemoglobin, and platelets. She had a history of hypertension, diabetes, and anemia. Chest CT showed splenomegaly, and abdominal ultrasound revealed hepatosplenomegaly. Repeat bone-marrow testing on January 19 showed active bone-marrow hyperplasia with some dysplastic changes (>10%) in erythroid cells. Karyotype and gene-mutation analysis for myeloid blood diseases performed on January 20–21 showed no significant abnormalities.

He had intermittent fever, nausea and vomiting for 5 months; prior local evaluation found pancytopenia and splenomegaly. Bone marrow imaging earlier showed dysplasia of megakaryocytes with visible plasma cells and markedly reduced proliferation. Five days before admission he developed fever to 39.5°C with chills, chest tightness and shortness of breath but without cough or sputum production. Piperacillin‑tazobactam was given without symptom relief. Bone marrow aspiration detected Leishmania amastigotes. Bone marrow hyperplasia was extremely reduced without an increase in immature cells or lymphocytes. Blood mNGS performed at the referring hospital detected 40904 Leishmania infantum, 17878 Leishmania donovani, and 13978 Leishmania chagasi sequence readings, and "combined with clinical symptoms, the diagnosis of 'visceral leishmaniasis' was made." On transfer, renal lab values were abnormal (serum glucose 16.31 mmol/L, urea 39.74 mmol/L, creatinine 286.2 mmol/L, uric acid 591 mmol/L), and because of renal dysfunction and concern about amphotericin B toxicity, sodium antimony gluconate was started. Chest X‑ray demonstrated bilateral pulmonary edema. After ventilatory support and diuretics the pulmonary edema improved on chest X‑ray and respiratory symptoms were relieved. On July 6, 2022, blood smear and bone marrow cytology revealed no Leishmania bodies. Nevertheless, pancytopenia and respiratory failure did not fully resolve and cardiotoxic damage appeared.

Clinical Context: A 34-year-old man with stage IV cirrhosis secondary to autoimmune hepatitis (AH) and concomitant alcoholism presented to a regional emergency department with fever, vomiting, and altered mentation in the setting of presumed alcohol withdrawal. His prior diagnosis of AH was made two years earlier by transhepatic biopsy; treatment had been started with azathioprine and prednisone but the patient was nonadherent. He immigrated from Pakistan in 2009.

At initial assessment he was hyperthermic to 41.5 C, tachycardic to 132 beats per minute, and tachypneic at 24 breaths per minute with normal oxygen saturation. Bedside examination showed livedo reticularis of the lower extremities and palmar erythema with spider nevi. His abdomen was slightly firm with tenderness in the right upper quadrant; no organomegaly or peritoneal signs were identified.

Because of suspected sepsis and severe alcohol withdrawal, he was transferred to the intensive care unit for intubation and agitation management. Broad‑spectrum antimicrobial therapy was started to cover spontaneous bacterial peritonitis and presumed community‑acquired meningitis, with meropenem, vancomycin, and acyclovir.

contexts.text: A 39‑year‑old man from Central America, living in Southeast Georgia, presents to the emergency department with abdominal pain and rectal bleeding. Past medical history: HIV/AIDS, alcohol abuse, tobacco dependency, and previously documented leishmaniasis diagnosed by bone marrow biopsy. He denied recent travel. Course and prior presentations: At initial presentation several years earlier he had diffuse moderate abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, chills and dysphagia; on exam he was tachycardic (heart rate 140/min) with mild abdominal tenderness. He was leukopenic and thrombocytopenic and was treated with amphotericin B and initiation of HAART; he was discharged on a 3‑month course of amphotericin B with ongoing HAART. Six months later he returned with acute abdominal pain and nausea; exam then showed a fine nodular skin rash across chest, abdomen and back described as consistent with cutaneous leishmaniasis, and thrombocytopenia persisted. At that time a bone marrow biopsy was performed to evaluate whether his new symptoms were due to HIV or a relapse of leishmaniasis, and he again received intravenous amphotericin B (inpatient 6 weeks) with plans for outpatient infusions. The patient subsequently was lost to follow‑up. Current presentation: Several years later he returned with a flare characterized by rectal bleeding and continued abdominal pain. Gastroenterology was consulted and an esophagogastroduodenoscopy was planned.

A 44‑year‑old man from Shanxi Province with a 5‑year history of antisynthetase antibody syndrome on cyclosporine A was admitted in January 2020 with fever to 38.6°C. He reported exertional breathlessness (after walking ~100 m) and increasing weakness; broad‑spectrum antimicrobials produced no improvement. By March 2020 he had persistent fever. Laboratory results then showed WBC 1.3 × 10^9/L, hemoglobin 96 g/L, platelets 113 × 10^9/L, fibrinogen 1.36 g/L, serum ferritin >1500 μg/L, NK‑cell activity 14.96%, and soluble CD25 12,947 pg/mL; ALT, AST, CK and CK‑MB were normal. The clinical picture met criteria for hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH), and treatment was started with methylprednisolone (10 mg/kg per day) and etoposide (100 mg/m^2). After 2 weeks the patient became afebrile and WBC rose to 10.8 × 10^9/L, hemoglobin was 95 g/L and platelets 55 × 10^9/L. In June 2020, during prednisone taper, he redeveloped high fever to 39.5°C, was unable to stand independently, and subsequently had pancytopenia with recurrence of high ferritin, low NK‑cell activity, markedly elevated sCD25, splenomegaly, and hemophagocytosis on bone marrow examination.

A 47-year-old man presented to the emergency department on December 28, 2020 with recurrent fever for 4 months and worsening symptoms with diarrhea for 1 month. About 4 months earlier he developed fever without an evident cause, with a maximum temperature of 39.9 C; fevers usually occurred in the afternoon, lasted several hours, and were associated with headache, myalgia, and nausea. After a period of apparent improvement he redeveloped persistent high fever (≈39 C) accompanied by yellow watery diarrhea more than 10 times per day. Six years previously he had been diagnosed with malaria in Africa and treated with quinine. On admission: Novel Coronavirus nucleic acid test was negative. Laboratory studies showed Hb 83 g/L, WBC 2.82 x 10^9/L, platelet count 16 x 10^9/L, neutrophil percentage 84.0%, lymphocyte percentage 8.0%, and procalcitonin 0.87 ng/ml. Hepatitis A and B testing were negative. Autoimmune liver markers, alpha fetoprotein (AFP), and carcinoembryonic antigen were negative. Abdominal ultrasound showed enlarged liver and spleen. Chest and plain abdominal CT demonstrated cirrhosis, splenomegaly, portal hypertension with collateral circulation, and peritoneal effusion. The team considered sepsis and fever of undetermined origin (infection versus tumor) and assessed the patient as Child-Pugh B decompensated cirrhosis. An emergency blood metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) test was sent to help diagnose the fever of unknown cause.

A 57-year-old man underwent orthotopic liver transplantation in March 2019 for alcoholic-related liver disease and portal hypertension after 2 years of abstinence. He was born in Wales; his only travel outside the UK was a transient visit to Calais 15 years before transplantation. Postoperative care included a 2-day intensive-care admission. Immunosuppression was commenced with prednisolone, tacrolimus and mycophenolate (MMF); cotrimoxazole prophylaxis was given. Both donor and recipient were CMV IgG negative. One month after transplantation he had biopsy-proven moderate acute cellular rejection treated with 3 days of pulsed steroids. His graft function improved, with normalisation of alanine aminotransferase coinciding with the development of pancytopenia 4 months after transplantation. MMF dose was reduced from 1 g twice daily to 500 mg twice daily, but neutropenia worsened and pancytopenia persisted. He developed systemic symptoms of fever and rigours and was admitted to his local hospital with neutropenic sepsis and an acute kidney injury. He was transferred to the liver transplant centre for further investigation. He was treated empirically with meropenem, vancomycin and fluconazole. A bone marrow biopsy was performed in view of his pancytopenia.

A 55-year-old man with chronic severe hepatitis B (HBV‑DNA positive) was admitted for intermittent fever of 1 month (maximum 40°C). He had worked on a farm in Xinjiang Province one month earlier. On examination he had hepatosplenomegaly below the costal margin. Initial laboratory tests showed marked hepatic abnormalities (ALT 490 U/L, AST 558 U/L), low total protein and albumin (TP 51.54 g/L, ALB 26.83 g/L), TBIL 23.23 μmol/L, DBIL 14.37 μmol/L, and HBV‑DNA 3.19 × 10^4 IU/mL. Routine blood counts were abnormal (WBC 3.12 × 10^9/L, platelets 100 × 10^9/L). After 2 weeks the patient remained febrile with worsening labs (WBC 0.95 × 10^9/L, platelets 56 × 10^9/L, ALT 524 U/L, AST 640 U/L). Abdominal enhanced CT showed an enlarged spleen with multiple low‑density nodules that demonstrated sustained/delayed enhancement; angioma/hemangioma was suspected. 18F‑FDG PET/CT demonstrated a significant diffuse increase in FDG uptake in the enlarged spleen (SUVmax 6.6) and slightly diffuse bone‑marrow uptake. Bone‑marrow aspiration and biopsy were performed twice (2 months apart) and both showed phagocytosis of reticulum cells. Based on the clinical and imaging findings, splenic lymphoma was considered highly likely. The patient received chemotherapy for hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) and was discharged in remission, but was readmitted 2 months later with recurrent fever and pancytopenia; splenectomy was then undertaken to establish a diagnosis and reduce disease burden.

A 25-year-old man presented with a left-sided upper abdominal lump and multiple skin lesions present for the last 12 years. The abdominal lump had been very slowly increasing in size, was painless and produced a mild dragging sensation. The skin lesions were present primarily on his back and abdomen; they were described as depigmented, painless, and non-itchy. He denied current fever, loss of appetite, weight loss, cough, jaundice, hematemesis, melaena, and blood transfusion. He reported a history of kala-azar 15 years earlier treated with an injectable medication (he could not recall the drug name). He was a known chronic hepatitis B patient on entecavir 1 mg once daily. On examination there were multiple hypo- and hyperpigmented macular and maculopapular non-scaly skin lesions distributed over the trunk (mainly back, chest, and abdomen); lesion size ranged from a few millimeters (0.3–0.7 mm) for hypopigmented spots to 1–3 cm for hyperpigmented lesions, and sensation over the lesions was intact. Other vital signs were normal. Abdominal examination showed firm, non-tender hepatosplenomegaly with the liver 4 cm below the right costal margin and the spleen 6 cm along its long axis.

A 47-year-old man presented to the emergency department with recurrent fever for 4 months and worsening symptoms including diarrhea for 1 month. About 4 months earlier he developed fever up to 39.9 °C that typically occurred in the afternoon and lasted several hours; associated symptoms included headache, myalgia, and nausea. After a temporary resolution he had a relapse with persistent high fever and frequent yellow watery diarrhea (>10 times/day). Past medical history included malaria diagnosed 6 years earlier in Africa treated with quinine. He reported hypersensitivity to quinolones (e.g., moxifloxacin). On admission, novel coronavirus nucleic acid test was negative. The schistosoma japonicum IgG antibody, echinococcus granulosus antibody, liver fluke antibody test, plasmodium antigen test, and blood smear test were all negative. Tests for hepatitis A and B, autoimmune liver disease markers, AFP, and CEA were negative. Abdominal ultrasound showed hepatomegaly and splenomegaly (intercostal spleen thickness ~7.0 cm). Chest and plain abdominal CT reported cirrhosis, splenomegaly, portal hypertension with collateral circulation, and peritoneal effusion. The admitting team considered sepsis and fever of undetermined origin (infection vs tumor) and noted Child-Pugh B decompensated cirrhosis. An emergency metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) blood test was sent to try to identify an occult pathogen.

A 68-year-old man from a mountainous area in Hebei Province, China, presented with fever, sweating, and fatigue. He first sought care on February 1 and was hospitalized at a local hospital with temperature 39.0°C, chills, and no respiratory, abdominal, diarrheal, or urinary symptoms. He had lost approximately 10 kg over the prior 6 months. Initial blood tests showed pancytopenia, a rapid erythrocyte sedimentation rate, elevated C-reactive protein and ferritin, hyponatremia, hypokalemia, hypoproteinemia, and elevated serum enzyme levels. Bone marrow aspiration smear at that time showed granulocytopenia with megakaryocyte maturation disorder. Abdominal ultrasound showed splenomegaly; brain CT showed bilateral basal ganglia lacunar infarction; chest CT showed bilateral fibrotic/bronchitic changes. After 11 days of antibiotic and supportive treatment his fever and fatigue persisted with temperatures >39°C, so he presented for further evaluation on February 16. On arrival his SARS-CoV-2 PCR was negative. On examination he was febrile to 38.2°C, poorly nourished, unable to walk (bilateral leg strength grade 3), and had pitting edema of the anterior tibias and dorsal feet. Repeat laboratory testing again showed pancytopenia, increased ESR, CRP and ferritin, and elevated liver enzymes. Empiric antibiotic therapy had not relieved his febrile illness.

A 34-year-old man with stage IV cirrhosis secondary to autoimmune hepatitis (AH) and concomitant alcoholism presented to a regional emergency department with fever, vomiting, and altered mentation in the setting of presumed alcohol withdrawal. His prior diagnosis of AH was made two years earlier by transhepatic biopsy; treatment had been started with azathioprine and prednisone but the patient was nonadherent. He immigrated from Pakistan in 2009.

At initial assessment he was hyperthermic to 41.5 C, tachycardic to 132 beats per minute, and tachypneic at 24 breaths per minute with normal oxygen saturation. Bedside examination showed livedo reticularis of the lower extremities and palmar erythema with spider nevi. His abdomen was slightly firm with tenderness in the right upper quadrant; no organomegaly or peritoneal signs were identified.

Because of suspected sepsis and severe alcohol withdrawal, he was transferred to the intensive care unit for intubation and agitation management. Broad‑spectrum antimicrobial therapy was started to cover spontaneous bacterial peritonitis and presumed community‑acquired meningitis, with meropenem, vancomycin, and acyclovir.

contexts.text: A 60-year-old woman from Uttar Pradesh, India presented with a six‑week history of high‑grade continuous fever with chills and rigors, anorexia, malaise, joint pains, and severe lethargy. She reported "crops of round, raised lesions" that began on the left upper limb, progressed to the right upper limb and then involved the whole face, upper back, chest, and upper abdomen; the lesions were "closely associated with the febrile episodes." Some lesions enlarged, became nodular, developed sunken centers that drained pus‑like material, and were painful and red. One week before admission she developed jaundice with mild to moderate upper‑quadrant abdominal pain. She had no prior comorbidities, was a teetotaler, and denied taking over‑the‑counter or steroid/complementary medications or other potentially immunosuppressive drugs. On examination her temperature was 100.8°F, blood pressure 128/88 mm Hg, heart rate 100/min. Pallor and icterus were present; there was bilateral pitting, non‑tender symmetrical pedal edema. Eye exam demonstrated nodular lesions over the eyes and conjunctiva with conjunctival suffusion. Chest imaging was within normal limits. Laboratory studies: hemoglobin 10.5 g/dL, total leukocyte count 5600/mm3, platelet count 80,000/mm3, ESR 80 mm/hr with normocytic normochromic anemia. Liver tests: total bilirubin 3.2 mg/dL (direct 1.8), AST 50 IU/L, ALT 60 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 221 IU/L, GGT 150 IU/L, albumin 1.9 g/dL, INR 1.3. Serum IgG 22.6 g/L.

A 22‑month‑old girl presented with 8 days of fever to 40°C and mild cough. Past history: failure to thrive; normal neurologic development. She was the first child of a non‑consanguineous couple; no family history of albinism; normal hair and skin. On exam she was stunted, pale, had non‑tender hepatomegaly 5–6 cm and splenomegaly palpable 4 cm below the left costal margin. Petechial rash developed on the chest and legs as she worsened. Initial laboratory results: WBC 5100/mm3 (ANC 1200/mm3), Hb 9.1 g/dl, platelets 47,000/mm3; mild transaminase elevation; hypoalbuminemia. Ferritin 1,134 ng/ml; soluble IL‑2 receptor (sCD25) 3,183 U/ml. Blood cultures were negative. Serum immunoglobulins and lymphocyte subsets were reported as normal. Infectious testing: EBV serology positive for IgM and IgG anti‑VCA with negative IgG anti‑EBNA; EBV viral load 637 copies/ml. Leishmania testing was discordant: immunochromatography and indirect immunofluorescence were negative, serum ELISA was slightly positive, and leishmanial antigen in urine was negative. Bone‑marrow aspiration revealed hemophagocytosis. Over the next day she clinically worsened with progressive splenomegaly and cytopenias (WBC 4,800/mm3 with ANC 800/mm3, Hb 6.8 g/dl, platelets 27,000/mm3), triglycerides 686 mg/dl, ferritin 3,849 ng/ml, and sCD25 3,596 U/ml. Clotting tests were normal and perforin expression by flow cytometry was reported as normal.

A 65-year-old woman was admitted in March after collapsing in the street. She had been unwell for 14 months with night sweats and progressive loss of energy but denied fever. On examination she was afebrile and had hepatic enlargement and lymphadenopathy; liver function tests were within reference limits. Initial blood tests showed hemoglobin 8.1 g/dL, leukocyte count 4.62 × 10^9/L, and platelet count 143 × 10^9/L. Serologic tests for HIV, hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and Strongyloides spp. were negative. Her CD4 count was 790 cells/μL, rheumatoid factor was weakly positive, and immunoglobulin levels were within reference ranges. She was born in Guyana and had recent travel to Guyana in 2012 and 2013, to Grenada in 2012, to Ghana in 2005, and to France in 2003. Because a hematologic malignancy was suspected, a bone marrow aspiration was performed; Leishmania amastigotes were visible. Leishmania serology was negative by an rK39 rapid test and weakly positive by direct agglutination (1:3,200; cutoff 1:1,600).

A 17-month-old female from Berkane, born of a consanguineous marriage with a sister who died at age 6 (unknown etiology), presented with 3 months of "anarchic" fever, growth retardation, anemia and episodes of epistaxis. On exam the temperature was 39 °C. Findings included lower‑limb edema, pallor of skin and mucous membranes, gingival petechiae, bleached hair, and hepatosplenomegaly; other exams were unremarkable. Complete blood count: pancytopenia with a deep aregenerative normochromic normocytic anemia (hemoglobin 3 g/dL) with reticulocyte count 76,700/mm3, leukocytes 4,860/mm3 with neutropenia 680/mm3, and thrombocytopenia 12,000/mm3; peripheral blood smear without abnormality. Additional labs: hypoalbuminemia 13 g/L, hypertriglyceridemia 4.57 g/L, hyperferritinemia 626 µg/L, LDH 337 IU/L, prothrombin time 56%, fibrinogen 1 g/L. Direct Coombs test was positive. Hepatic and renal function were reported as without abnormality.

A 30‑year‑old man presented with pain in his lower limbs and a non‑itchy erythematous rash over both lower limbs. He had low‑grade intermittent fever for three months. On examination he was pale and malnourished (BMI 18.4 kg/m2) and had palpable purpura over both thighs and buttocks. Abdominal examination revealed palpable hepatomegaly with massive splenomegaly. Laboratory testing showed pancytopenia (hemoglobin 6.8 g/dL, total leukocyte count 2800/mm3, platelet count 45 000/muL) and polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia (4.9 g/dL); liver and renal function tests were within reference ranges. Contrast‑enhanced CT of chest and abdomen confirmed hepatosplenomegaly and was otherwise unremarkable. The treating team considered hematologic malignancy and a connective‑tissue disorder with vasculitis. Other infectious etiologies entertained included HIV, scrub typhus/rickettsial infection, and visceral leishmaniasis (given the patient lived in an endemic area). Initial testing showed: anti‑nuclear antibodies, complement levels (C3 = 94 mg/dL and C4 = 20 mg/dL), and rheumatoid factor were negative; urine examination was normal and serum cryoglobulins were not raised. Viral markers (HIV, hepatitis B surface antigen, and anti‑hepatitis C) were negative. Serology for rickettsia and scrub typhus were also negative.

A 15‑year‑old boy presented to the emergency fever clinic with fever and cough for more than 10 days. He developed fever after a cold, with temperatures initially 37–38°C, later peaking at 41°C. Symptoms included cough, fatigue, chills, and pharyngeal discomfort. Initial local-hospital testing showed WBC 3.3 × 10^9/L, Hb 85 g/L, and PLT 87 × 10^9/L. Bone marrow puncture at that time "indicated that hematopoietic tissue hyperplasia was active and the proportion of three-line blood cells was roughly normal. Lymphocytes accounted for 9.5%, and atypical lymphocytes were found occasionally." Adenovirus IgM was weakly positive; ferritin was >2,000 ng/mL; procalcitonin was 4.14 ng/mL. Abdominal ultrasound and CT indicated hepatomegaly and splenomegaly. He was referred for further care after lack of improvement with initial treatment. On arrival his vital signs were: T 37.1°C, pulse 110/min, RR 19/min, BP 110/72 mmHg. Admission labs showed WBC 4.68 × 10^9/L, Hb 100 g/L, RBC 3.65 × 10^12/L; ALT 204 IU/L; AST 176 IU/L; GGT 153 IU/L; LDH 889 IU/L; ferritin >2,000 ng/mL; PCT 2.11 ng/mL; CRP 53.5 mg/L; IL‑6 31.58 pg/mL. TORCH/EBV panel: CMV, HSV, rubella virus, and EBV IgG positive. Direct Coombs' test was positive (++). Chest CT was unremarkable. Abdominal ultrasound showed intercostal spleen thickness ≈6.6 cm, consistent with splenomegaly. Lymphoma? Autoimmune disease?" An mNGS test on blood was performed on the second day after admission because the cause of fever remained unclear.

A 55-year-old man with chronic severe hepatitis B (HBV‑DNA positive) was admitted for intermittent fever of 1 month (maximum 40°C). He had worked on a farm in Xinjiang Province one month earlier. On examination he had hepatosplenomegaly below the costal margin. Initial laboratory tests showed marked hepatic abnormalities (ALT 490 U/L, AST 558 U/L), low total protein and albumin (TP 51.54 g/L, ALB 26.83 g/L), TBIL 23.23 μmol/L, DBIL 14.37 μmol/L, and HBV‑DNA 3.19 × 10^4 IU/mL. Routine blood counts were abnormal (WBC 3.12 × 10^9/L, platelets 100 × 10^9/L). After 2 weeks the patient remained febrile with worsening labs (WBC 0.95 × 10^9/L, platelets 56 × 10^9/L, ALT 524 U/L, AST 640 U/L). Abdominal enhanced CT showed an enlarged spleen with multiple low‑density nodules that demonstrated sustained/delayed enhancement; angioma/hemangioma was suspected. 18F‑FDG PET/CT demonstrated a significant diffuse increase in FDG uptake in the enlarged spleen (SUVmax 6.6) and slightly diffuse bone‑marrow uptake. Bone‑marrow aspiration and biopsy were performed twice (2 months apart) and both showed phagocytosis of reticulum cells. Based on the clinical and imaging findings, splenic lymphoma was considered highly likely. The patient received chemotherapy for hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) and was discharged in remission, but was readmitted 2 months later with recurrent fever and pancytopenia; splenectomy was then undertaken to establish a diagnosis and reduce disease burden.

He had intermittent fever, nausea and vomiting for 5 months; prior local evaluation found pancytopenia and splenomegaly. Bone marrow imaging earlier showed dysplasia of megakaryocytes with visible plasma cells and markedly reduced proliferation. Five days before admission he developed fever to 39.5°C with chills, chest tightness and shortness of breath but without cough or sputum production. Piperacillin‑tazobactam was given without symptom relief. Bone marrow aspiration detected Leishmania amastigotes. Bone marrow hyperplasia was extremely reduced without an increase in immature cells or lymphocytes. Blood mNGS performed at the referring hospital detected 40904 Leishmania infantum, 17878 Leishmania donovani, and 13978 Leishmania chagasi sequence readings, and "combined with clinical symptoms, the diagnosis of 'visceral leishmaniasis' was made." On transfer, renal lab values were abnormal (serum glucose 16.31 mmol/L, urea 39.74 mmol/L, creatinine 286.2 mmol/L, uric acid 591 mmol/L), and because of renal dysfunction and concern about amphotericin B toxicity, sodium antimony gluconate was started. Chest X‑ray demonstrated bilateral pulmonary edema. After ventilatory support and diuretics the pulmonary edema improved on chest X‑ray and respiratory symptoms were relieved. On July 6, 2022, blood smear and bone marrow cytology revealed no Leishmania bodies. Nevertheless, pancytopenia and respiratory failure did not fully resolve and cardiotoxic damage appeared.

A 74-year-old woman from Tunis presented with several weeks of fever (oral temperature 38–39°C), sweats, chills, fatigue, diarrhea, intermittent vague abdominal pain, and occasional dry cough. Her only medical history was well-controlled hypertension. Examination showed a palpable spleen just below the left costal margin. On the right arm near the axilla there was "a single well-defined, ulcer surrounded by erythematous edging, with serous oozing" about 3 × 3 cm; the patient reported the lesion was painless, nonhealing, and present for 2–3 years. A Leishmania rk39 immunochromatography test was positive. Bone marrow aspiration parasitology revealed Leishmania amastigote forms, and serum immunofluorescence for Leishmania antibodies was positive (titer 1:400). Blood qPCR detected Leishmania DNA (400 parasites/mL). Direct microscopy of skin smears from the arm lesion showed no amastigotes, but Leishmania DNA amplification was obtained from dermal DNA extract by qPCR. ITS1 sequencing showed the Leishmania strains from the blood and the arm lesion corresponded to L. infantum and were 100% identical. Systemic response was rapid: fever resolved, general condition improved, splenomegaly regressed, blood counts normalized, and blood qPCR became negative after 28 days. However, "the skin lesion did not improve although Leishmania qPCR on dermal sample became negative." A skin biopsy was initially refused. One year later the lesion remained essentially unchanged.

A 42‑year‑old man presented with 1 year of progressive weakness and significant weight loss and intermittent low‑grade fevers. He had been treated for pulmonary tuberculosis 2 years earlier and was recently restarted on antitubercular therapy for the past month without improvement. On examination he was thin, pale, afebrile, and had abdominal distension. Left submandibular and left axillary lymph nodes were palpable, each about 1.5 cm. Mild hepatosplenomegaly was noted. Ultrasound of the abdomen showed multiple enlarged conglomerate mesenteric lymph nodes, the largest 22 × 18 mm. Clinical chemistry showed reversal of the albumin:globulin ratio with total protein 9.5 g/dL, albumin 2.0 g/dL, globulin 7.5 g/dL. Other liver and renal tests were within normal limits. Complete blood count showed pancytopenia: hemoglobin 6 g/dL, total leukocyte count 1,800/µL (polymorphs 47%, lymphocytes 51%), platelets 48,000/µL; ESR 50 mm/h. Peripheral smear demonstrated rouleaux formation. Fine needle aspiration cytology of left submandibular and axillary lymph nodes yielded thick aspirate; smears showed few epithelioid cell granulomas interspersed with discrete aggregates of histiocytes in a background of reactive lymphoid cells and many plasma cells.

contexts.text: A 52‑year‑old woman who works in sugarcane fields in a rural area was referred to Oral Medicine for evaluation of a granulomatous lesion on the palate and for hoarseness that she thought followed a flu 3 months earlier. According to the referring surgeon, she had an extensive oral lesion and had undergone laryngoscopy and biopsy; that biopsy produced a histopathological result of “pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia and an active chronic inflammatory process, suggesting a fungus investigation,” prompting the referral. She reported no chronic systemic disease or regular medications. She described a history of crusting and nasal bleeding that began about 4 years earlier. On examination she had nasal obstruction, a nasal (hyponasal) voice, and was a mouth breather. She had smoked for 6 months and used both upper and lower complete dental prostheses continuously. Extrabuccal exam showed a lowering of the right nasal wing and a nasal septum perforation. Intrabuccal exam revealed a granulomatous lesion involving the entire palate and uvula, extending bilaterally to the pharynx with an erythematous appearance and areas of scratchable white plaques.

A 38‑year‑old man from Yayu district, western Ethiopia, presented to the outpatient clinic with multiple skin lesions on his face and hands and mutilation of the nose; his upper lip was injured and swollen. Eight years earlier he had a small papule on the right cheek that progressed to an open ulcer, then to ulcers on the left cheek and forehead; those active lesions lasted about six months and healed spontaneously, leaving permanent hypopigmented scars. He had no fever, hepatosplenomegaly or lymphedema and reported no history of HIV, chronic disease, alcohol abuse, or immunomodulatory drug use. Parasitological testing of lesion smears at that time showed many macrophages filled with amastigote stages of Leishmania, graded as +6. A nonreactive rK39 rapid diagnostic test and absence of related systemic signs made visceral leishmaniasis unlikely. Based on the clinical manifestations and smear result he was diagnosed with mucocutaneous leishmaniasis and treated with intramuscular sodium stibogluconate (20 mg/kg/day for 30 days) with clinical cure. Two years later he returned with a different cutaneous eruption that had appeared over the previous three months and had been preceded by intense itching. On exam he had multiple, nonpitting, closed papules on his face, nose, hands and legs. A skin smear again showed intramacrophage amastigotes with a parasite load graded +6, and culture grew promastigotes.

A 30-year-old Caucasian man, unemployed, HIV-negative and with no other concomitant infections, presented in 2014 with a papule on the inferior eyelid of the right eye. His past history included, in 2008, an isolated nodulation in the right leg that resolved after treatment. Over time new lesions progressively appeared on the chest, abdomen, back, feet, and in the oral cavity. Ulcerated oral lesions were present on the hard palate and on the left and right jugal mucosa. Disease progression was associated with fever, headache, and weight loss.

A 35-year-old man from Rio de Janeiro with a history of alcohol and cocaine abuse presented in 2014 with progressively enlarging mucocutaneous lesions that began in 2013 as erythematous, painful papules. On admission he had ulcerated lesions involving the nasal septum and nasal cavity, the palate, and the balanopreputial sulcus. He reported headache, nasal obstruction, asthenia, and weight loss. The initial differential diagnoses listed by the treating team were mucocutaneous infectious and inflammatory conditions, neoplasia, and tuberculosis. Early laboratory and imaging testing reported that viral and fungal serological tests, direct mycological examination, acid-fast bacilli testing (BAAR), chest tomography, and respiratory function tests were all negative.

A 53-year-old man from Mundo Novo, State of Bahia, Brazil, presented in July with pain, nasal obstruction, odynophagia, and dysphagia. On examination there was a painful, hyperemic, friable lesion in the right nasal cavity and an infiltrative lesion involving the hard palate, soft palate, and uvula. Additional findings included an ulcerated lesion on the left eyebrow and right eye with seropurulent secretion, a small ulcer on the lower eyelid, a lesion on the lobe of the right ear, and a lesion in the malar region. The patient was admitted for diagnosis and management of disseminated skin lesions. A biopsy of the palate lesions showed a non-specific erosive chronic inflammatory process. HIV testing was negative.

A 24-year-old man from Tancredo Neves, State of Bahia, Brazil, was admitted in January 2012 with diffuse bullous lesions on the body, osteoarthritis of the distal interphalangeal joints and proteinuria of 399 mg/day. He was diagnosed with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and treated with mycophenolate mofetil (MMF), with the dose increased to 1 g per day intravenously. Two years after the SLE diagnosis (2014) he was hospitalized again, presenting with ulcerated, painless skin lesions on the face, upper lip, scalp, neck, and on the upper and lower limbs. Oral examination showed crusty upper lip lesions, poor oral health status, and amelogenesis imperfecta. He developed secondary infection with fever and was started on cephalexin (1 g/day) and maintained on prednisone 5 mg/day intravenously. On the third day of this hospitalization, biopsies were performed on the left nasal mucosa and on lesions of the right lower limb.

A 52-year-old male farm worker from Ceara state, northeast Brazil, presented with a 4-month history of skin lesions. Lesions appeared first on the face and legs, than spread across much of his body, including the genitalia, soles of feet, and scalp. He reported daily fevers for the first 2 weeks of illness. On examination the patient had 178 lesions of different sizes and aspects; ulcerated, crusted, papular, nodular, and pustular. Many had apparent bacterial superinfections. The remainder of the physical examination was normal. A complete blood count and liver and kidney function tests were within normal limits. Serological tests for syphilis and human immunodeficiency virus were negative.

A 45-year-old man with known HIV infection presented with nodules and plaques on the nasal area, dorsum of the left wrist, the right index finger, and the back; cervical lymphadenopathy was noted. He reported a history of fever 6 months earlier while working in the state of Bihar, and since then had mild intermittent fever and weight loss. Routine blood and urine examinations were reported as not revealing any abnormalities. Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay for HIV was positive, and the CD4 count was 210/muL. On inspection there were infiltrated plaques on the nose, left dorsum of the wrist, and on the index finger of the right hand.

A 43-year-old male laborer with known HIV infection for 2 years (on antiretroviral therapy) and on anti-tubercular treatment for 9 months presented with a 7-month history of asymptomatic skin lesions all over his body. Lesions first appeared on the arm and progressively spread to involve the face, legs, and trunk. On examination there were multiple bilateral asymmetrical diffuse papulonodular, non‑itchy skin lesions measuring 2–25 mm on the face, trunk, and extremities. There were no signs of ulceration or scarring. There was no lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly. A photograph showed multiple papulonodular lesions of varying size over the elbow. Laboratory tests showed anemia (hemoglobin 9.1 g/dL); liver and renal function tests and lipid profile were within normal limits. Ultrasonography of the abdomen was normal. CD4 count was 50 cells/µL and HIV viral load was 1750 copies/mL. There was no history of travel to known endemic areas for leishmaniasis.

A 40-year-old man of Albanian descent who has lived in Athens for 20 years was admitted in February 2008 for progressive constitutional and respiratory symptoms. His symptoms began one year earlier with dry cough and gradual weight loss totaling 30 kg; night sweats and scant hemoptysis developed during the last month. Six months earlier a limited workup had revealed chronic active hepatitis B. He works in a restaurant, is a nonsmoker, and has no other remarkable medical history. On examination he was cachectic and had hepatosplenomegaly and small, discrete, nontender axillary and cervical lymph nodes. Serum albumin, bilirubin, and prothrombin time were within normal limits. HIV testing by ELISA was negative on two occasions three months apart; antibodies to hepatitis C virus were negative. Abdominal ultrasound showed enlarged liver and spleen and enlarged lymph nodes at the hepatic hilum; portal vein diameter and flow were normal and no ascites was present. Chest CT revealed limited adenopathy with a 2 × 1 cm mass at the right hilum and a 1.2 cm right lower paratracheal lymph node with a hypodense centre. Bronchoscopy disclosed epistaxis and pharyngeal inflammation consistent with candidiasis, mild diffuse redness throughout the tracheobronchial tree with more prominent inflammation on the medial aspect of the bronchus intermedius extending into the middle lobe bronchus, and a discreet mucosal polypoid lesion on the middle lobe carina.

contexts.text: A 38-year-old man with HIV on dolutegravir and emtricitabine–tenofovir presented without prior ocular problems. The report notes him as "well controlled (CD4 count of 213 cells/mm3 with an undetectable viral load)." He initially presented with a nonulcerative papulonodular hypopigmented rash on the extremities, trunk, and abdomen; "H and E staining of the cutaneous biopsy showed Leishmaniasis chassis and infantum." Thrombocytopenia and splenomegaly were also noted. He was treated with intravenous liposomal amphotericin B (received 7 of 9 doses) and was lost to follow-up; one year later he had recurrent cutaneous disease and was retreated with amphotericin (14-dose course) and received miltefosine for a 28-day course. Two days after stopping miltefosine, he developed progressive left-eye redness, pain, and photophobia. On day 7 of symptoms his visual acuity in the left eye had declined to count fingers.

A 7-year-old castrated male domestic short-haired cat, stray with unknown history, from the greater Athens area of Greece was presented for examination because of facial swelling and eye lesions. On examination there was a raised, nonalopecic, semifirm, poorly demarcated, painless swelling of the forehead. Periocular hypotrichosis, edema, and slight hyperpigmentation were present. Edema of the conjunctiva and third eyelid of the right eye was also observed. Clinical examination revealed no other abnormalities. A blood sample for complete blood count and biochemistry profile was obtained, and fine needle aspirates and a trucut biopsy were taken from the forehead swelling for cytological and histopathological examination. The patient had a nonregenerative anemia, hyperglobulinemia, and thrombocytopenia. Urinalysis showed no abnormalities. Further suggested serological tests for vector-borne diseases were not done because of financial restrictions. At presentation the clinicians listed the differential diagnosis as: subcutaneous abscess, atypical bacterial and mycobacterial infection, deep fungal infection, and neoplasia.

A 54-year-old healthy woman presented to ophthalmology with a few months' history of a symptomatic lesion of the right eye. The lesion was located in the nasal bulbar conjunctiva within the interpalpebral zone. On examination there was an erythematous fibrovascular lesion approximately 5 mm in length. The lesion produced foreign-body sensation and discomfort. The lesion was clinically diagnosed as a pterygium, and surgical removal was performed.

A 32-year-old man from Djelfa, Algeria, with a history of contact eczema presented with a 6-week history of painless, non-healing skin lesions on the dorsal aspect of his right hand. He had applied topical corticosteroids and antiseptics without improvement and had received two courses of antibiotics (pristinamycin, amoxicillin + clavulanic acid) with no significant results. On examination there was a limited erythematous-papular plaque, approximately 8 cm in diameter, on the dorsal right hand formed by confluence of several papules with satellite lesions at the periphery. The initial plaque was associated with several firm, painless subcutaneous nodules 0.5–1.5 cm in diameter that tracked proximally along lymphatic drainage toward the elbow. The patient did not recall an insect bite, no other body sites were involved, and the remainder of the examination was unremarkable. Direct mycological examination and culture on Sabouraud medium at 25 °C and on BHI medium at 37 °C were negative for fungal presence.

A 61-year-old man (weight 65 kg) was referred in January with a 2-month history of a 1 × 3 cm lesion on the left ear. He has diabetes and had not traveled outside Kashan during the previous year. He reported that the ear lesion felt uncomfortable and scabrous but was not painful and he had no systemic complaints. Direct microscopy of scales with 10% potassium hydroxide (KOH) preparation was negative for fungal elements. The lesion was cleaned and specimens were collected from the margin by scraping; two smears were fixed with methanol and stained with 10% Giemsa for 30 minutes. On microscopic examination of the stained smears, amastigote forms of Leishmania spp. were observed.

A 74-year-old woman from Tunis presented with several weeks of fever (oral temperature 38–39°C), sweats, chills, fatigue, diarrhea, intermittent vague abdominal pain, and occasional dry cough. Her only medical history was well-controlled hypertension. Examination showed a palpable spleen just below the left costal margin. On the right arm near the axilla there was "a single well-defined, ulcer surrounded by erythematous edging, with serous oozing" about 3 × 3 cm; the patient reported the lesion was painless, nonhealing, and present for 2–3 years. A Leishmania rk39 immunochromatography test was positive. Bone marrow aspiration parasitology revealed Leishmania amastigote forms, and serum immunofluorescence for Leishmania antibodies was positive (titer 1:400). Blood qPCR detected Leishmania DNA (400 parasites/mL). Direct microscopy of skin smears from the arm lesion showed no amastigotes, but Leishmania DNA amplification was obtained from dermal DNA extract by qPCR. ITS1 sequencing showed the Leishmania strains from the blood and the arm lesion corresponded to L. infantum and were 100% identical. Systemic response was rapid: fever resolved, general condition improved, splenomegaly regressed, blood counts normalized, and blood qPCR became negative after 28 days. However, "the skin lesion did not improve although Leishmania qPCR on dermal sample became negative." A skin biopsy was initially refused. One year later the lesion remained essentially unchanged.

A 25-year-old man presented with a left-sided upper abdominal lump and multiple skin lesions present for the last 12 years. The abdominal lump had been very slowly increasing in size, was painless and produced a mild dragging sensation. The skin lesions were present primarily on his back and abdomen; they were described as depigmented, painless, and non-itchy. He denied current fever, loss of appetite, weight loss, cough, jaundice, hematemesis, melaena, and blood transfusion. He reported a history of kala-azar 15 years earlier treated with an injectable medication (he could not recall the drug name). He was a known chronic hepatitis B patient on entecavir 1 mg once daily. On examination there were multiple hypo- and hyperpigmented macular and maculopapular non-scaly skin lesions distributed over the trunk (mainly back, chest, and abdomen); lesion size ranged from a few millimeters (0.3–0.7 mm) for hypopigmented spots to 1–3 cm for hyperpigmented lesions, and sensation over the lesions was intact. Other vital signs were normal. Abdominal examination showed firm, non-tender hepatosplenomegaly with the liver 4 cm below the right costal margin and the spleen 6 cm along its long axis.

An 84‑year‑old woman presented with a large nodular lesion on the forehead of 2.5 months' duration. She had been seen at another hospital where a pre‑diagnosis of lymphoma was recorded; the prior punch biopsy report listed basal cell carcinoma, sarcoidosis, lupus vulgaris and pseudolymphoma among the clinical pre‑diagnoses and the material was sent for pathology consultation. Microscopic examination of the punch biopsy showed a dense nodular and diffuse lymphohistiocytic cell infiltration within the dermis. In the cytoplasm of histiocytes, small, round structures resembling organisms were noted. Immunohistochemical staining showed reactive T lymphocytes labelled with CD3 and CD5, reactive B lymphocytes labelled with CD20, and large clusters of histiocytes labelled with CD68; there was no staining with CD30. The pathology report recommended investigation of the aetiology of granulomatous dermatitis, especially cutaneous leishmaniasis.

A 13‑year‑old boy, born in São Paulo, who had traveled at age 12 to the state of Minas Gerais, presented with fever on alternate days, pallor, increased abdominal volume and unquantified weight loss. He had no prior history of recurrent infections. On admission he had anemia and thrombocytopenia. Bone marrow aspirate showed amastigotes of Leishmania. He was treated with liposomal amphotericin B (LAB) at a dose of 35 mg/kg and was discharged. Four months later he returned with fever and thrombocytopenia; a bone marrow aspirate again showed amastigotes of Leishmania and parasites were detected in bone marrow culture. He was treated with meglumine antimoniate and intravenous human immunoglobulin with clinical and laboratory improvement and was discharged in good health. Three weeks later he presented with seven days of fever, weakness, pallor and increased abdominal volume. On exam the spleen was palpable 23 cm below the left costal margin and the liver 5 cm from the right costal margin. Leishmania ELISA immunoassay and the rK‑39 antigen test were negative. Bone marrow biopsy showed a lymphocytic and histiocytic inflammatory reaction with a granulomatous pattern; no amastigotes were observed in the aspirate. He was re‑treated empirically for visceral leishmaniasis with liposomal amphotericin B. Notably, the patient had silvery hair and eyebrows, described as a phenotype suggestive of Griscelli Syndrome.

A 9-year-old boy presented with multiple papular lesions on the left cheek that had been present for three months and had gradually enlarged. His medical history was notable for an episode of cutaneous leishmaniasis located on the nose two years earlier, which had completely regressed after treatment with intralesional meglumine antimonate. Dermatologic examination showed multiple, coalescing, rough, slightly elevated, yellowish-brown papular lesions 3–6 mm in diameter on the left cheek. He also had a large atrophic scar on the nose. Nothing of interest was noted in his family history or his laboratory tests.

contexts.text: A 50‑year‑old male agriculturist with known HIV infection (diagnosed 1½ years earlier) on antiretroviral therapy presented with a 6‑month history of asymptomatic skin lesions over his limbs. Physical examination showed multiple, diffuse, non‑ulcerating, papulonodular and non‑itchy skin lesions measuring 2–18 mm; history indicated the lesions first appeared on the feet and then involved the hands. There was no history of travel to endemic areas of leishmaniasis. There was no hepatosplenomegaly and lymphadenopathy. Laboratory investigations showed anemia with hemoglobin 8.3 g/dL; platelet count reported as "2 lacs/muL" and total leukocyte count 5,100/muL. Liver and renal function tests, lipid profile and blood sugar were within normal limits. Chest X‑ray and ultrasound of the abdomen were normal. His CD4 count was 126 cells/muL and HIV viral load was <47 copies/mL.

A 43-year-old male laborer with known HIV infection for 2 years (on antiretroviral therapy) and on anti-tubercular treatment for 9 months presented with a 7-month history of asymptomatic skin lesions all over his body. Lesions first appeared on the arm and progressively spread to involve the face, legs, and trunk. On examination there were multiple bilateral asymmetrical diffuse papulonodular, non‑itchy skin lesions measuring 2–25 mm on the face, trunk, and extremities. There were no signs of ulceration or scarring. There was no lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly. A photograph showed multiple papulonodular lesions of varying size over the elbow. Laboratory tests showed anemia (hemoglobin 9.1 g/dL); liver and renal function tests and lipid profile were within normal limits. Ultrasonography of the abdomen was normal. CD4 count was 50 cells/µL and HIV viral load was 1750 copies/mL. There was no history of travel to known endemic areas for leishmaniasis.

A 30‑year‑old man presented with pain in his lower limbs and a non‑itchy erythematous rash over both lower limbs. He had low‑grade intermittent fever for three months. On examination he was pale and malnourished (BMI 18.4 kg/m2) and had palpable purpura over both thighs and buttocks. Abdominal examination revealed palpable hepatomegaly with massive splenomegaly. Laboratory testing showed pancytopenia (hemoglobin 6.8 g/dL, total leukocyte count 2800/mm3, platelet count 45 000/muL) and polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia (4.9 g/dL); liver and renal function tests were within reference ranges. Contrast‑enhanced CT of chest and abdomen confirmed hepatosplenomegaly and was otherwise unremarkable. The treating team considered hematologic malignancy and a connective‑tissue disorder with vasculitis. Other infectious etiologies entertained included HIV, scrub typhus/rickettsial infection, and visceral leishmaniasis (given the patient lived in an endemic area). Initial testing showed: anti‑nuclear antibodies, complement levels (C3 = 94 mg/dL and C4 = 20 mg/dL), and rheumatoid factor were negative; urine examination was normal and serum cryoglobulins were not raised. Viral markers (HIV, hepatitis B surface antigen, and anti‑hepatitis C) were negative. Serology for rickettsia and scrub typhus were also negative.

A 33‑year‑old Italian man with HIV infection and a history of visceral leishmaniasis (VL) presented initially in May 2002 with fever, weight loss, diarrhea, mucocutaneous lesions suggestive of Kaposi's sarcoma, hepatosplenomegaly, pancytopenia, and polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia. Bone marrow smear at that time showed Leishmania spp. amastigotes and he was treated with meglumine antimoniate for 30 days and started on HAART. He had multiple clinical relapses of VL over the ensuing years, each treated with intravenous liposomal amphotericin B (L‑AMB) given as 4 mg/kg/day for 5 days then weekly for 4 weeks. In February 2008 maintenance secondary prophylaxis with L‑AMB 4 mg/kg once monthly was started. At that time his HIV RNA was stably below 50 copies/mL and CD4+ T‑cell count was 125 cells/µL; his HAART regimen was Abacavir‑Lamivudine‑Lopinavir/ritonavir. Some weeks after starting secondary prophylaxis with L‑AMB, he developed a maculopapular and nodular rash on his trunk and upper limbs that gradually worsened. The rash was described as diffuse maculopapular and nodular on the upper limbs and trunk. Four months later, L‑AMB was stopped and a cutaneous biopsy was performed.

A 45-year-old man with known HIV infection presented with nodules and plaques on the nasal area, dorsum of the left wrist, the right index finger, and the back; cervical lymphadenopathy was noted. He reported a history of fever 6 months earlier while working in the state of Bihar, and since then had mild intermittent fever and weight loss. Routine blood and urine examinations were reported as not revealing any abnormalities. Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay for HIV was positive, and the CD4 count was 210/muL. On inspection there were infiltrated plaques on the nose, left dorsum of the wrist, and on the index finger of the right hand.

A 52-year-old man with known HIV infection from Rajasthan presented with a 3-month history of multiple papulonodular skin lesions located mainly on the dorsum of the hands, forearms, thighs, and back. Routine blood parameters were within normal limits. His CD4 count was 170/muL. On inspection there were multiple nodular lesions on the dorsum of both hands and on the listed sites of the upper and lower extremities and back. Early diagnostic considerations included Hansen's disease, sarcoidosis, and leishmaniasis.

A 60-year-old woman from Uttar Pradesh, India presented with a six‑week history of high‑grade continuous fever with chills and rigors, anorexia, malaise, joint pains, and severe lethargy. She reported "crops of round, raised lesions" that began on the left upper limb, progressed to the right upper limb and then involved the whole face, upper back, chest, and upper abdomen; the lesions were "closely associated with the febrile episodes." Some lesions enlarged, became nodular, developed sunken centers that drained pus‑like material, and were painful and red. One week before admission she developed jaundice with mild to moderate upper‑quadrant abdominal pain. She also noted nonpainful bilateral leg swelling (pitting) and painful red eyes with nodular lesions on the eyelids and in the conjunctiva, associated with decreased vision. She had no prior comorbidities, was a teetotaler, and denied taking over‑the‑counter or steroid/complementary medications or other potentially immunosuppressive drugs. Pallor and icterus were present; there was bilateral pitting, non‑tender symmetrical pedal edema. Skin exam showed "multiple crops of nodular, noduloulcerative, and papular lesions, dispersed throughout the body surface, mostly segregated to the face and upper back," some with pus drainage from central sunken areas. Eye exam demonstrated nodular lesions over the eyes and conjunctiva with conjunctival suffusion. Fundoscopy showed uveitis and small retinal hemorrhages. Serum IgG 22.6 g/L.

The abdominal lump had been very slowly increasing in size, was painless and produced a mild dragging sensation. The skin lesions were present primarily on his back and abdomen; they were described as depigmented, painless, and non-itchy. He reported a history of kala-azar 15 years earlier treated with an injectable medication (he could not recall the drug name). He was a known chronic hepatitis B patient on entecavir 1 mg once daily. On examination there were multiple hypo- and hyperpigmented macular and maculopapular non-scaly skin lesions distributed over the trunk (mainly back, chest, and abdomen); lesion size ranged from a few millimeters (0.3–0.7 mm) for hypopigmented spots to 1–3 cm for hyperpigmented lesions, and sensation over the lesions was intact. Other vital signs were normal. Abdominal examination showed firm, non-tender hepatosplenomegaly with the liver 4 cm below the right costal margin and the spleen 6 cm along its long axis.

A 38‑year‑old man from Yayu district, western Ethiopia, presented to the outpatient clinic with multiple skin lesions on his face and hands and mutilation of the nose; his upper lip was injured and swollen. Eight years earlier he had a small papule on the right cheek that progressed to an open ulcer, then to ulcers on the left cheek and forehead; those active lesions lasted about six months and healed spontaneously, leaving permanent hypopigmented scars. He had no fever, hepatosplenomegaly or lymphedema and reported no history of HIV, chronic disease, alcohol abuse, or immunomodulatory drug use. Parasitological testing of lesion smears at that time showed many macrophages filled with amastigote stages of Leishmania, graded as +6. A nonreactive rK39 rapid diagnostic test and absence of related systemic signs made visceral leishmaniasis unlikely. Based on the clinical manifestations and smear result he was diagnosed with mucocutaneous leishmaniasis and treated with intramuscular sodium stibogluconate (20 mg/kg/day for 30 days) with clinical cure. Two years later he returned with a different cutaneous eruption that had appeared over the previous three months and had been preceded by intense itching. On exam he had multiple, nonpitting, closed papules on his face, nose, hands and legs. A skin smear again showed intramacrophage amastigotes with a parasite load graded +6, and culture grew promastigotes.

A 39‑year‑old man from Central America, living in Southeast Georgia, presents to the emergency department with abdominal pain and rectal bleeding. Past medical history: HIV/AIDS, alcohol abuse, tobacco dependency, and previously documented leishmaniasis diagnosed by bone marrow biopsy. He denied recent travel. Course and prior presentations: At initial presentation several years earlier he had diffuse moderate abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, chills and dysphagia; on exam he was tachycardic (heart rate 140/min) with mild abdominal tenderness. He was leukopenic and thrombocytopenic and was treated with amphotericin B and initiation of HAART; he was discharged on a 3‑month course of amphotericin B with ongoing HAART. Six months later he returned with acute abdominal pain and nausea; exam then showed a fine nodular skin rash across chest, abdomen and back described as consistent with cutaneous leishmaniasis, and thrombocytopenia persisted. At that time a bone marrow biopsy was performed to evaluate whether his new symptoms were due to HIV or a relapse of leishmaniasis, and he again received intravenous amphotericin B (inpatient 6 weeks) with plans for outpatient infusions. The patient subsequently was lost to follow‑up. Current presentation: Several years later he returned with a flare characterized by rectal bleeding and continued abdominal pain. Gastroenterology was consulted and an esophagogastroduodenoscopy was planned.
