contexts.text: A 60‑year‑old Austrian man presented in September 2016 with a three‑week history of fever of unknown origin, fatigue, and unintentional weight loss of 6 kg. Initial physical examination was inconspicuous. His medical history was notable for adequately treated diabetes mellitus type 2 and hypothyroidism. Travel history included a two‑week trip to the south of Crete in September 2015 and a two‑week trip the south of Spain in May 2016. Laboratory tests showed markedly elevated C‑reactive protein (CRP 94.2–188.9 mg/L), slight hypochromic normocytic anemia without signs of hemolysis (hemoglobin 12.5 g/dL), mild thrombocytopenia (127,000/µL), and a discreetly elevated gamma‑glutamyltransferase (GGT). The soluble interleukin‑2 receptor (IL‑2R) was elevated to 5156.1 pg/mL. Chest x‑ray, urine analysis, abdominal sonography, transthoracic and transesophageal echocardiography revealed no focus of infection but did show splenomegaly (7.2 × 16.4 cm). Empiric antibiotic therapy (initially ampicillin/sulbactam, later piperacillin/tazobactam plus vancomycin) did not lead to improvement. Over the next three weeks the patient’s discrete bicytopenia progressed to severe pancytopenia requiring blood transfusions. Lactate dehydrogenase rose to 1107 U/L, liver enzymes including GGT, alkaline phosphatase and AST increased, and fever persisted up to 40°C. Positron emission tomography–computed tomography showed tracer enhancement in the central and peripheral bone marrow.

A 60-year-old woman from Uttar Pradesh, India presented with a six‑week history of high‑grade continuous fever with chills and rigors, anorexia, malaise, joint pains, and severe lethargy. She reported "crops of round, raised lesions" that began on the left upper limb, progressed to the right upper limb and then involved the whole face, upper back, chest, and upper abdomen; the lesions were "closely associated with the febrile episodes." Some lesions enlarged, became nodular, developed sunken centers that drained pus‑like material, and were painful and red. One week before admission she developed jaundice with mild to moderate upper‑quadrant abdominal pain. She also noted nonpainful bilateral leg swelling (pitting) and painful red eyes with nodular lesions on the eyelids and in the conjunctiva, associated with decreased vision. She had no prior comorbidities, was a teetotaler, and denied taking over‑the‑counter or steroid/complementary medications or other potentially immunosuppressive drugs. On examination her temperature was 100.8°F, blood pressure 128/88 mm Hg, heart rate 100/min. Pallor and icterus were present; there was bilateral pitting, non‑tender symmetrical pedal edema. Skin exam showed "multiple crops of nodular, noduloulcerative, and papular lesions, dispersed throughout the body surface, mostly segregated to the face and upper back," some with pus drainage from central sunken areas. Fundoscopy showed uveitis and small retinal hemorrhages. Serum IgG 22.6 g/L.

A 40‑year‑old woman from Balao Chico (Guayas province, Ecuador) presented in August 1979 with a progressive widespread skin eruption. The illness began with a lesion on the lumbar region; papular lesions developed and became pustulous vesicles at the right lumbar region and then disseminated over the body, with 308 generalized lesions counted. She reported marked right lumbar pain; some body‑surface lesions were thought clinically to resemble herpes zoster. The presumptive clinical diagnoses listed were paracoccidioidomycosis, cutaneous leishmaniasis, or staphylococcal infections. Examination of the ulcers showed most lesions to be crusty; when crusts were lifted they were excavated with purulent fluid from severe secondary infections. Ulcer sizes ranged from 0.5 to 20 mm in diameter; some lesions had thick, adherent crusts that bled when separated, others were small crusty ulcers with excavations, and confluent erythematous papular plaques were present on the lumbar–dorsal region. Laboratory tests on ulcer material did not demonstrate Paracoccidioides braziliensis or Staphylococcus aureus. Routine laboratory examinations revealed positivity for beta‑hemolytic streptococcus (antibiotic‑sensitive), and stool examination was positive for Trichuris trichiura, Ascaris lumbricoides, and Ancylostoma duodenale. Several smear samples from diverse regions of the body surface were taken at random.

A 30-year-old woman with a history of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) diagnosed during pregnancy in 2010 presented with skin lesions. History of present illness and past medical history:
- She received antiretroviral therapy from 2013 to 2018 (zidovudine 300 mg orally twice daily, lamivudine 150 mg orally twice daily, efavirenz 600 mg orally once daily) but the antiretroviral regimen was discontinued several times. - In October 2020 she developed a single ulcerative lesion on a lower limb. - At that time a diagnosis of tegumentary leishmaniasis (TL) was confirmed by Giemsa‑stained slides from skin scraping. - She began treatment with meglumine antimoniate (20 mg Sb+5/kg IV daily for 20 days) but discontinued treatment soon after starting. - In late 2021 she returned with new lesions on the left lower limb and right upper limb; a biopsy sample was collected for parasite isolation. - She subsequently received liposomal amphotericin B (3 mg/kg) for 20 days, experienced a relapse, started another antimonial regimen which she abandoned after a few days, and in August 2022 had recurrence of the lower‑limb lesion followed by a 10‑day course of liposomal amphotericin B with complete healing. - Geographic context: patient resides in a municipality in the State of Maranhão, Brazil, within an ecotone region where leishmaniasis is endemic.

A 52‑year‑old woman who works in sugarcane fields in a rural area was referred to Oral Medicine for evaluation of a granulomatous lesion on the palate and for hoarseness that she thought followed a flu 3 months earlier. According to the referring surgeon, she had an extensive oral lesion and had undergone laryngoscopy and biopsy; that biopsy produced a histopathological result of “pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia and an active chronic inflammatory process, suggesting a fungus investigation,” prompting the referral. She reported no chronic systemic disease or regular medications. She described a history of crusting and nasal bleeding that began about 4 years earlier. On examination she had nasal obstruction, a nasal (hyponasal) voice, and was a mouth breather. She had smoked for 6 months and used both upper and lower complete dental prostheses continuously. Extrabuccal exam showed a lowering of the right nasal wing and a nasal septum perforation. Intrabuccal exam revealed a granulomatous lesion involving the entire palate and uvula, extending bilaterally to the pharynx with an erythematous appearance and areas of scratchable white plaques.

A 52-year-old woman from Jiuzhaigou, Sichuan province, China, presented with an unprovoked high fever beginning January 9, 2021. A mass of rash was seen on the face, chest, and groin. Initial evaluation included ultrasound of the urinary system, brain MRI, and chest CT, which showed no significant abnormality on those studies. She was treated empirically with ceftriaxone and clindamycin and received methylprednisolone; after a week the cough, sputum production, fatigue, and shortness of breath improved, but the fever persisted. On January 13, a bone marrow aspiration smear showed a low proliferation rate of nucleated cells, a decreased granulocyte/erythrocyte ratio, some erythroblasts with abnormal morphology, significantly reduced iron content in the marrow, and poor platelet production by megakaryocytes with scattered and clustered platelets observed. On January 14, routine blood tests demonstrated decreased white blood cells, red blood cells, hemoglobin, and platelets. She had a history of hypertension, diabetes, and anemia. Chest CT showed splenomegaly, and abdominal ultrasound revealed hepatosplenomegaly. Repeat bone-marrow testing on January 19 showed active bone-marrow hyperplasia with some dysplastic changes (>10%) in erythroid cells. Karyotype and gene-mutation analysis for myeloid blood diseases performed on January 20–21 showed no significant abnormalities. Peripheral blood metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) was performed on January 24.

A 15-year-old female from the Macanao municipality on Margarita Island, Venezuela presented with a 6-month history of intermittent fever predominantly occurring at night, malaise, 6 kg weight loss, arthralgias, loss of appetite, dizziness, and amenorrhea. She lives in a rural area close to a landfill in a house built with cement ground, brick walls, and a metal roof without running water. She has one dog (unknown Leishmania infection status) and various turtles as pets. She has no history of traveling outside Venezuela. On examination she was pale, with increased respiratory and heart rate, and a fever of 39 C. Weight was 49 kg, height 1.57 m, and abdominal circumference 76 cm. She had cervical, axillary, and inguinal adenopathy. Cardiac and lung exams were normal. Abdominal exam revealed right upper-quadrant tenderness and hepatosplenomegaly (liver palpable 9.5 cm from the midclavicular line; spleen Hackett grade V). Laboratory values on admission demonstrated pancytopenia. Abdominal ultrasound and computed tomography confirmed hepatosplenomegaly. The initial clinical suspicion was a lymphoproliferative or myeloproliferative disorder. From an infectious disease perspective, the possibility of visceral leishmaniasis, a systemic mycosis, or tuberculosis were entertained. A bone marrow biopsy was performed to rule out a hematologic malignancy and to assess for infectious causes.

A 62-year-old woman presents with ulcerated lesions on her left upper limb, followed by new lesions on lower limbs, right upper limb, and cervical region. She has a history of RYGB surgery and contact with a cat with sporotrichosis.

A 40-year-old man of Albanian descent who has lived in Athens for 20 years was admitted in February 2008 for progressive constitutional and respiratory symptoms. His symptoms began one year earlier with dry cough and gradual weight loss totaling 30 kg; night sweats and scant hemoptysis developed during the last month. Six months earlier a limited workup had revealed chronic active hepatitis B. On examination he was cachectic and had hepatosplenomegaly and small, discrete, nontender axillary and cervical lymph nodes. There were no clinical signs of liver failure or portal hypertension. Laboratory tests demonstrated pancytopenia, elevated hepatic aminotransferases (3–4 times the upper limit), and polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 100 mm/h. Abdominal ultrasound showed enlarged liver and spleen and enlarged lymph nodes at the hepatic hilum; portal vein diameter and flow were normal and no ascites was present. Chest CT revealed limited adenopathy with a 2 × 1 cm mass at the right hilum and a 1.2 cm right lower paratracheal lymph node with a hypodense centre. Bronchoscopy disclosed epistaxis and pharyngeal inflammation consistent with candidiasis, mild diffuse redness throughout the tracheobronchial tree with more prominent inflammation on the medial aspect of the bronchus intermedius extending into the middle lobe bronchus, and a discreet mucosal polypoid lesion on the middle lobe carina.

A 43-year-old man from Cumanda (Chimborazo province, Ecuador), a subtropical mountainous community at ~500 m above sea level, presented with multiple chronic skin lesions. History of present illness: The lesion began as an insect-bite–like papular lesion on the forearm. Lesions then appeared on the right ear and the nose. About 2 years later, lesions developed on a wide range of the lower extremities and subsequently became multiple and confluent on the abdomen, thorax, body side, and thigh. A superficial involvement of mucosae of the nose and upper lip was observed. Treatment history: At the time of examination the patient had already received injections of nine ampoules of trivalent antimonials (Repodral, 20 mg/kg/day) at a rural health center; after finishing several courses he received pentavalent antimonials (Glucantime, 10 mg/kg/day) for about 5 months. Early investigations performed from active lesions included smear specimens, skin biopsies, syringe aspirates for culture, and material on FTA cards. Montenegro skin test showed a 17-mm induration, and an rK39 kit test revealed a strongly positive band. The smear specimen was positive for Leishmania amastigotes in scanty numbers. Promastigotes grown in vitro showed a tendency to decrease gradually and then disappear, an effect attributed by the investigators to prior antimonial treatment.

A 47-year-old man presented to the emergency department with recurrent fever for 4 months and worsening symptoms including diarrhea for 1 month. About 4 months earlier he developed fever up to 39.9 °C that typically occurred in the afternoon and lasted several hours; associated symptoms included headache, myalgia, and nausea. After a temporary resolution he had a relapse with persistent high fever and frequent yellow watery diarrhea (>10 times/day). Past medical history included malaria diagnosed 6 years earlier in Africa treated with quinine. He reported hypersensitivity to quinolones (e.g., moxifloxacin). On admission, novel coronavirus nucleic acid test was negative. Initial laboratory testing showed hemoglobin 83 g/L, platelet count 16 × 10^9/L, white-cell count 2.82 × 10^9/L, neutrophil percentage 84.0%, lymphocyte percentage 8.0%, and procalcitonin 0.87 ng/mL. The cryptococcus antigen test, fungal G test, and GM test were negative. Abdominal ultrasound showed hepatomegaly and splenomegaly (intercostal spleen thickness ~7.0 cm). Chest and plain abdominal CT reported cirrhosis, splenomegaly, portal hypertension with collateral circulation, and peritoneal effusion. The admitting team considered sepsis and fever of undetermined origin (infection vs tumor) and noted Child-Pugh B decompensated cirrhosis. An emergency metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) blood test was sent to try to identify an occult pathogen.

A 47-year-old man presented to the emergency department on December 28, 2020 with recurrent fever for 4 months and worsening symptoms with diarrhea for 1 month. About 4 months earlier he developed fever without an evident cause, with a maximum temperature of 39.9 C; fevers usually occurred in the afternoon, lasted several hours, and were associated with headache, myalgia, and nausea. After a period of apparent improvement he redeveloped persistent high fever (≈39 C) accompanied by yellow watery diarrhea more than 10 times per day. Six years previously he had been diagnosed with malaria in Africa and treated with quinine. On admission: Novel Coronavirus nucleic acid test was negative. Laboratory studies showed Hb 83 g/L, WBC 2.82 x 10^9/L, platelet count 16 x 10^9/L, neutrophil percentage 84.0%, lymphocyte percentage 8.0%, and procalcitonin 0.87 ng/ml. Blood culture grew methicillin-resistant coagulase-negative Staphylococci. The cryptococcus antigen test, fungal G test, and GM test were negative. Abdominal ultrasound showed enlarged liver and spleen. Chest and plain abdominal CT demonstrated cirrhosis, splenomegaly, portal hypertension with collateral circulation, and peritoneal effusion. The team considered sepsis and fever of undetermined origin (infection versus tumor) and assessed the patient as Child-Pugh B decompensated cirrhosis. An emergency blood metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) test was sent to help diagnose the fever of unknown cause.

A 68-year-old man from a mountainous area in Hebei Province, China, presented with fever, sweating, and fatigue. He first sought care on February 1 and was hospitalized at a local hospital with temperature 39.0°C, chills, and no respiratory, abdominal, diarrheal, or urinary symptoms. He had lost approximately 10 kg over the prior 6 months. Initial blood tests showed pancytopenia, a rapid erythrocyte sedimentation rate, elevated C-reactive protein and ferritin, hyponatremia, hypokalemia, hypoproteinemia, and elevated serum enzyme levels. Bone marrow aspiration smear at that time showed granulocytopenia with megakaryocyte maturation disorder. Abdominal ultrasound showed splenomegaly; brain CT showed bilateral basal ganglia lacunar infarction; chest CT showed bilateral fibrotic/bronchitic changes. After 11 days of antibiotic and supportive treatment his fever and fatigue persisted with temperatures >39°C, so he presented for further evaluation on February 16. On arrival his SARS-CoV-2 PCR was negative. On examination he was febrile to 38.2°C, poorly nourished, unable to walk (bilateral leg strength grade 3), and had pitting edema of the anterior tibias and dorsal feet. Repeat laboratory testing again showed pancytopenia, increased ESR, CRP and ferritin, and elevated liver enzymes. Empiric antibiotic therapy had not relieved his febrile illness.

A 39‑year‑old man from Central America, living in Southeast Georgia, presents to the emergency department with abdominal pain and rectal bleeding. Past medical history: HIV/AIDS, alcohol abuse, tobacco dependency, and previously documented leishmaniasis diagnosed by bone marrow biopsy. He denied recent travel. Course and prior presentations: At initial presentation several years earlier he had diffuse moderate abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, chills and dysphagia; on exam he was tachycardic (heart rate 140/min) with mild abdominal tenderness. He was leukopenic and thrombocytopenic and was treated with amphotericin B and initiation of HAART; he was discharged on a 3‑month course of amphotericin B with ongoing HAART. Six months later he returned with acute abdominal pain and nausea; exam then showed a fine nodular skin rash across chest, abdomen and back described as consistent with cutaneous leishmaniasis, and thrombocytopenia persisted. At that time a bone marrow biopsy was performed to evaluate whether his new symptoms were due to HIV or a relapse of leishmaniasis, and he again received intravenous amphotericin B (inpatient 6 weeks) with plans for outpatient infusions. The patient subsequently was lost to follow‑up. Current presentation: Several years later he returned with a flare characterized by rectal bleeding and continued abdominal pain. Gastroenterology was consulted and an esophagogastroduodenoscopy was planned.

A 42‑year‑old man presented with 1 year of progressive weakness and significant weight loss and intermittent low‑grade fevers. He had been treated for pulmonary tuberculosis 2 years earlier and was recently restarted on antitubercular therapy for the past month without improvement. On examination he was thin, pale, afebrile, and had abdominal distension. Left submandibular and left axillary lymph nodes were palpable, each about 1.5 cm. Mild hepatosplenomegaly was noted. Ultrasound of the abdomen showed multiple enlarged conglomerate mesenteric lymph nodes, the largest 22 × 18 mm. Clinical chemistry showed reversal of the albumin:globulin ratio with total protein 9.5 g/dL, albumin 2.0 g/dL, globulin 7.5 g/dL. Other liver and renal tests were within normal limits. Complete blood count showed pancytopenia: hemoglobin 6 g/dL, total leukocyte count 1,800/µL (polymorphs 47%, lymphocytes 51%), platelets 48,000/µL; ESR 50 mm/h. Peripheral smear demonstrated rouleaux formation. Fine needle aspiration cytology of left submandibular and axillary lymph nodes yielded thick aspirate; smears showed few epithelioid cell granulomas interspersed with discrete aggregates of histiocytes in a background of reactive lymphoid cells and many plasma cells.

A 22‑month‑old girl presented with 8 days of fever to 40°C and mild cough. Past history: failure to thrive; normal neurologic development. She was the first child of a non‑consanguineous couple; no family history of albinism; normal hair and skin. On exam she was stunted, pale, had non‑tender hepatomegaly 5–6 cm and splenomegaly palpable 4 cm below the left costal margin. Petechial rash developed on the chest and legs as she worsened. Initial laboratory results: WBC 5100/mm3 (ANC 1200/mm3), Hb 9.1 g/dl, platelets 47,000/mm3; mild transaminase elevation; hypoalbuminemia. Ferritin 1,134 ng/ml; soluble IL‑2 receptor (sCD25) 3,183 U/ml. Blood cultures were negative. Serum immunoglobulins and lymphocyte subsets were reported as normal. Infectious testing: EBV serology positive for IgM and IgG anti‑VCA with negative IgG anti‑EBNA; EBV viral load 637 copies/ml. Leishmania testing was discordant: immunochromatography and indirect immunofluorescence were negative, serum ELISA was slightly positive, and leishmanial antigen in urine was negative. Bone‑marrow aspiration revealed hemophagocytosis. Over the next day she clinically worsened with progressive splenomegaly and cytopenias (WBC 4,800/mm3 with ANC 800/mm3, Hb 6.8 g/dl, platelets 27,000/mm3), triglycerides 686 mg/dl, ferritin 3,849 ng/ml, and sCD25 3,596 U/ml. Clotting tests were normal and perforin expression by flow cytometry was reported as normal.

A 65-year-old woman was admitted in March after collapsing in the street. She had been unwell for 14 months with night sweats and progressive loss of energy but denied fever. On examination she was afebrile and had hepatic enlargement and lymphadenopathy; liver function tests were within reference limits. Initial blood tests showed hemoglobin 8.1 g/dL, leukocyte count 4.62 × 10^9/L, and platelet count 143 × 10^9/L. Serologic tests for HIV, hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and Strongyloides spp. were negative. Her CD4 count was 790 cells/μL, rheumatoid factor was weakly positive, and immunoglobulin levels were within reference ranges. She was born in Guyana and had recent travel to Guyana in 2012 and 2013, to Grenada in 2012, to Ghana in 2005, and to France in 2003. Because a hematologic malignancy was suspected, a bone marrow aspiration was performed; Leishmania amastigotes were visible. Leishmania serology was negative by an rK39 rapid test and weakly positive by direct agglutination (1:3,200; cutoff 1:1,600).

contexts.text: A 2-year-old domestic European neutered male cat was referred with a 1-year history of skin disease characterized by multiple nodular skin lesions, ulcerative dermatitis of all four limbs and fever. The owner reported prior empirical treatment for a presumptive pyodermatitis with prednisolone, amoxicillin/clavulanic acid and doxycycline without clinical improvement. At first admission the only abnormalities on physical examination were mild fever (39.5oC) and dermatological lesions on the head and limbs. Approximately 20–25 cutaneous nodules (2–10 mm diameter) were distributed on the outer pinnal surfaces and orbital regions, most notably on the pinnae with some coalescence. Single ulcerative dermatitis spots (20–50 mm diameter) with raised margins affected the antebrachial and hock regions. Differential diagnosis at presentation included pyodermatitis, allergic reaction, autoimmune disease, neoplastic disease or leishmaniosis. A complete blood count and biochemical profile were performed and values were within reference intervals; serum protein electrophoresis showed a slight hypergammaglobulinaemia. Fine-needle aspiration puncture from the ear skin nodules was performed for further analysis.

A 38‑year‑old man from Yayu district, western Ethiopia, presented to the outpatient clinic with multiple skin lesions on his face and hands and mutilation of the nose; his upper lip was injured and swollen. Eight years earlier he had a small papule on the right cheek that progressed to an open ulcer, then to ulcers on the left cheek and forehead; those active lesions lasted about six months and healed spontaneously, leaving permanent hypopigmented scars. He had no fever, hepatosplenomegaly or lymphedema and reported no history of HIV, chronic disease, alcohol abuse, or immunomodulatory drug use. Based on the clinical manifestations and smear result he was diagnosed with mucocutaneous leishmaniasis and treated with intramuscular sodium stibogluconate (20 mg/kg/day for 30 days) with clinical cure. Two years later he returned with a different cutaneous eruption that had appeared over the previous three months and had been preceded by intense itching. On exam he had multiple, nonpitting, closed papules on his face, nose, hands and legs. A skin smear again showed intramacrophage amastigotes with a parasite load graded +6, and culture grew promastigotes.

A 24-year-old Cuban immigrant presented with worsening nonhealing lower-extremity ulcers despite oral antibiotic therapy and wound care. The lesions gradually grew with subsequent ulceration over the course of 1 to 2 months. He recently arrived in the United States seeking asylum and first noticed the lesions while traveling in the jungle between Panama and Colombia (Darien Gap region). On examination, there was an ulcerative lesion measuring 4 cm on the dorsum of the right foot and a second 3.5 cm ulcer on the lower anterior shin. There was no evidence of mucosal or visceral involvement on initial physical exam. Photographs show ulcerative lesions on the right foot and left shin. As part of the clinical workup to rule out malaria, a rapid malaria antigen test for Plasmodium falciparum was obtained and reported positive.

A 78-year-old man from a rural area in western Iran was referred for multiple ulcerative, exudative lesions involving the mid-face (upper lip and anterior nasal fossa), above the eyebrows, dorsal aspects of both hands, and posterior aspects of both heels. Lesions began three years earlier as papules on the dorsal hands and progressively enlarged to involve the face and heels and became ulcerative; involvement of the right hand progressed to destruction of tendons and soft tissue of the fifth finger, resulting in amputation of that finger. He had no history of comorbid conditions, no regular medications reported, and denied systemic symptoms — there was no weight loss, fever, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly or other signs of systemic involvement on examination or routine laboratory survey. Multiple prior empirical treatments for different presumed diagnoses, including pyoderma gangrenosum, sarcoidosis, and leishmaniasis, had been tried without improvement. An initial skin biopsy showed a necrotizing and palisading granulomatous tissue pattern that suggested an infectious etiology, but initial smears of lesion material for fungal elements, mycobacteria and Leishmania were negative. A tuberculin skin test produced a 27 mm induration, and anti-tuberculosis therapy (isoniazid, rifampin, ethambutol, and pyrazinamide) was started.

A 74-year-old woman from Tunis presented with several weeks of fever (oral temperature 38–39°C), sweats, chills, fatigue, diarrhea, intermittent vague abdominal pain, and occasional dry cough. Her only medical history was well-controlled hypertension. Examination showed a palpable spleen just below the left costal margin. On the right arm near the axilla there was "a single well-defined, ulcer surrounded by erythematous edging, with serous oozing" about 3 × 3 cm; the patient reported the lesion was painless, nonhealing, and present for 2–3 years. A Leishmania rk39 immunochromatography test was positive. Bone marrow aspiration parasitology revealed Leishmania amastigote forms, and serum immunofluorescence for Leishmania antibodies was positive (titer 1:400). Blood qPCR detected Leishmania DNA (400 parasites/mL). Direct microscopy of skin smears from the arm lesion showed no amastigotes, but Leishmania DNA amplification was obtained from dermal DNA extract by qPCR. ITS1 sequencing showed the Leishmania strains from the blood and the arm lesion corresponded to L. infantum and were 100% identical. However, "the skin lesion did not improve although Leishmania qPCR on dermal sample became negative." A skin biopsy was initially refused. One year later the lesion remained essentially unchanged.

A 15‑year‑old boy presented to the emergency fever clinic with fever and cough for more than 10 days. He developed fever after a cold, with temperatures initially 37–38°C, later peaking at 41°C. Symptoms included cough, fatigue, chills, and pharyngeal discomfort. Initial local-hospital testing showed WBC 3.3 × 10^9/L, Hb 85 g/L, and PLT 87 × 10^9/L. Bone marrow puncture at that time "indicated that hematopoietic tissue hyperplasia was active and the proportion of three-line blood cells was roughly normal. Lymphocytes accounted for 9.5%, and atypical lymphocytes were found occasionally." Adenovirus IgM was weakly positive; ferritin was >2,000 ng/mL; procalcitonin was 4.14 ng/mL. Abdominal ultrasound and CT indicated hepatomegaly and splenomegaly. He was referred for further care after lack of improvement with initial treatment. On arrival his vital signs were: T 37.1°C, pulse 110/min, RR 19/min, BP 110/72 mmHg. Admission labs showed WBC 4.68 × 10^9/L, Hb 100 g/L, RBC 3.65 × 10^12/L; ALT 204 IU/L; AST 176 IU/L; GGT 153 IU/L; LDH 889 IU/L; ferritin >2,000 ng/mL; PCT 2.11 ng/mL; CRP 53.5 mg/L; IL‑6 31.58 pg/mL. TORCH/EBV panel: CMV, HSV, rubella virus, and EBV IgG positive. Blood cultures showed no bacterial growth at 5 days. Chest CT was unremarkable. Do not exclude the possibility of parasitic diseases? Hemophilic cell syndrome? Lymphoma? Autoimmune disease?" An mNGS test on blood was performed on the second day after admission because the cause of fever remained unclear.

A 55‑year‑old man presented with recurrent high fevers and acute febrile symptoms. On admission he had a body temperature of 39.6 C. One month before admission he had developed a fever of unknown origin, with a highest temperature of 41 C accompanied by shivering. Before transfer he received piperacillin/tazobactam without improvement. He reported a past history of pancreatitis and prior septicemia and denied relevant family history. On admission (January 25, 2021) laboratory testing showed reduced WBC, RBC, hemoglobin, and platelets. Abdominal color ultrasound demonstrated hepatosplenomegaly. Serum amylase and lipase were elevated. A positive result was noted for Epstein‑Barr virus (EBV); no other blood or respiratory pathogens were detected. Over the next 14 days the cytopenias persisted. On February 7, 2021, bone marrow aspiration showed active marrow hyperplasia and hemophagocytosis, but no pathogenic microorganism was identified on the smear.

A 60-year-old woman from Uttar Pradesh, India presented with a six‑week history of high‑grade continuous fever with chills and rigors, anorexia, malaise, joint pains, and severe lethargy. She reported "crops of round, raised lesions" that began on the left upper limb, progressed to the right upper limb and then involved the whole face, upper back, chest, and upper abdomen; the lesions were "closely associated with the febrile episodes." Some lesions enlarged, became nodular, developed sunken centers that drained pus‑like material, and were painful and red. One week before admission she developed jaundice with mild to moderate upper‑quadrant abdominal pain. She also noted nonpainful bilateral leg swelling (pitting) and painful red eyes with nodular lesions on the eyelids and in the conjunctiva, associated with decreased vision. She had no prior comorbidities, was a teetotaler, and denied taking over‑the‑counter or steroid/complementary medications or other potentially immunosuppressive drugs. On examination her temperature was 100.8°F, blood pressure 128/88 mm Hg, heart rate 100/min. Pallor and icterus were present; there was bilateral pitting, non‑tender symmetrical pedal edema. Skin exam showed "multiple crops of nodular, noduloulcerative, and papular lesions, dispersed throughout the body surface, mostly segregated to the face and upper back," some with pus drainage from central sunken areas. Fundoscopy showed uveitis and small retinal hemorrhages. Serum IgG 22.6 g/L.

A male born June 26, 1986, was seen at a tropical diseases referral center. Between 2009 and 2011 he was hospitalized seven times with a consistent diagnosis of kala-azar. He received multiple recommended treatments during these hospitalizations, including pentavalent antimony (glucantime, 20 mg of Sb + 5 kg/d for 30 d in the first hospitalization), liposomal amphotericin B (for 14 d at 3 mg/kg/d in three subsequent hospitalizations), and pentamidine in the last hospitalization before surgery (4 mg/kg/d every other day, total 15 doses), with only transient symptomatic improvement followed by recurrence. He had a negative HIV serological test. During two hospitalizations he presented with anemia and was transfused twice with packed red blood cells. After all possibilities of medical treatment were exhausted and the patient maintained a pancytopenia profile on blood counts attributed to hypersplenism, splenectomy was recommended. In January 2012 he was hospitalized for the planned surgical procedure. His clinical examination revealed mucocutaneous pallor (2+/4+), fever (38.5 C), dehydration (2+/4+), a distended abdomen with mild pain on deep palpation, and splenomegaly 8 cm below the left costal margin. Laboratory testing showed anemia, leukopenia, hypergammaglobulinemia, and elevated ESR and CRP.

A 37-year-old man from Maranhão, Brazil, employed as a sugarcane cutter, and the son of a consanguineous marriage, presented with 5 months of daily fevers up to 39°C, progressive asthenia, about 10 kg weight loss, and increasing abdominal volume. He had a remote history: at age 21 he was diagnosed with rheumatoid arthritis and received NSAIDs and prednisone, with maintenance corticosteroid therapy (10 mg/day) for 7 years. He and his family reported no history of recurrent infections. On examination he had pallor of skin and mucous membranes, splenomegaly extending 21 cm below the left costal margin, and hepatomegaly 4 cm below the right costal margin. Laboratory testing demonstrated pancytopenia and hypoalbuminemia. Bone marrow aspirate showed relative hypocellularity of the granulocytes without visualization of amastigotes. Bone marrow biopsy showed a proportional increase in granulocytes. A liver biopsy was performed; immunohistochemistry was negative for Leishmania.

"However, based on the patient's history of recent trauma and physical examination, we were highly suspicious of pseudoaneurysm."

A 7-year-old castrated male domestic short-haired cat, stray with unknown history, from the greater Athens area of Greece was presented for examination because of facial swelling and eye lesions. On examination there was a raised, nonalopecic, semifirm, poorly demarcated, painless swelling of the forehead. Periocular hypotrichosis, edema, and slight hyperpigmentation were present. Edema of the conjunctiva and third eyelid of the right eye was also observed. Clinical examination revealed no other abnormalities. A blood sample for complete blood count and biochemistry profile was obtained, and fine needle aspirates and a trucut biopsy were taken from the forehead swelling for cytological and histopathological examination. The patient had a nonregenerative anemia, hyperglobulinemia, and thrombocytopenia. Urinalysis showed no abnormalities. Further suggested serological tests for vector-borne diseases were not done because of financial restrictions. At presentation the clinicians listed the differential diagnosis as: subcutaneous abscess, atypical bacterial and mycobacterial infection, deep fungal infection, and neoplasia.

A 47-year-old man presented to the emergency department on December 28, 2020 with recurrent fever for 4 months and worsening symptoms with diarrhea for 1 month. About 4 months earlier he developed fever without an evident cause, with a maximum temperature of 39.9 C; fevers usually occurred in the afternoon, lasted several hours, and were associated with headache, myalgia, and nausea. After a period of apparent improvement he redeveloped persistent high fever (≈39 C) accompanied by yellow watery diarrhea more than 10 times per day. Six years previously he had been diagnosed with malaria in Africa and treated with quinine. On admission: Novel Coronavirus nucleic acid test was negative. Laboratory studies showed Hb 83 g/L, WBC 2.82 x 10^9/L, platelet count 16 x 10^9/L, neutrophil percentage 84.0%, lymphocyte percentage 8.0%, and procalcitonin 0.87 ng/ml. Blood culture grew methicillin-resistant coagulase-negative Staphylococci. The cryptococcus antigen test, fungal G test, and GM test were negative. Abdominal ultrasound showed enlarged liver and spleen. Chest and plain abdominal CT demonstrated cirrhosis, splenomegaly, portal hypertension with collateral circulation, and peritoneal effusion. The team considered sepsis and fever of undetermined origin (infection versus tumor) and assessed the patient as Child-Pugh B decompensated cirrhosis. An emergency blood metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) test was sent to help diagnose the fever of unknown cause.

A 30-year-old woman from an area endemic for tegumentary leishmaniasis presented with a single skin complaint. She reported a small papular lesion on her right leg that had developed over 7–10 days. At age 10 she had had an ulcer on the left thigh that healed spontaneously and left a well-defined atrophic scar. On examination there was a depressed papular lesion on the right leg measuring 8 × 7 mm; there was a 30 × 20 mm atrophic scar on the left thigh and no lymphadenopathy. Because early lesions of the locally prevalent Leishmania species may be papular and nonulcerated, a Leishmania skin test (LST) was performed on the left forearm. After 48 hours the intradermal reaction was strongly positive, with an induration measuring 38 × 32 mm. Eight days after the skin test the original papular lesion on the right leg had resolved, and a new round cutaneous ulcer with raised borders measuring 26 × 24 mm was present at the site of the LST. A culture of aspirated material from the forearm lesion was negative for Leishmania.

A 32-year-old man from Djelfa, Algeria, with a history of contact eczema presented with a 6-week history of painless, non-healing skin lesions on the dorsal aspect of his right hand. He had applied topical corticosteroids and antiseptics without improvement and had received two courses of antibiotics (pristinamycin, amoxicillin + clavulanic acid) with no significant results. On examination there was a limited erythematous-papular plaque, approximately 8 cm in diameter, on the dorsal right hand formed by confluence of several papules with satellite lesions at the periphery. The initial plaque was associated with several firm, painless subcutaneous nodules 0.5–1.5 cm in diameter that tracked proximally along lymphatic drainage toward the elbow. The patient did not recall an insect bite, no other body sites were involved, and the remainder of the examination was unremarkable. Direct mycological examination and culture on Sabouraud medium at 25 °C and on BHI medium at 37 °C were negative for fungal presence.

A 30‑year‑old man presented with pain in his lower limbs and a non‑itchy erythematous rash over both lower limbs. He had low‑grade intermittent fever for three months. On examination he was pale and malnourished (BMI 18.4 kg/m2) and had palpable purpura over both thighs and buttocks. Abdominal examination revealed palpable hepatomegaly with massive splenomegaly. Laboratory testing showed pancytopenia (hemoglobin 6.8 g/dL, total leukocyte count 2800/mm3, platelet count 45 000/muL) and polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia (4.9 g/dL); liver and renal function tests were within reference ranges. Contrast‑enhanced CT of chest and abdomen confirmed hepatosplenomegaly and was otherwise unremarkable. The treating team considered hematologic malignancy and a connective‑tissue disorder with vasculitis. Other infectious etiologies entertained included HIV, scrub typhus/rickettsial infection, and visceral leishmaniasis (given the patient lived in an endemic area). Initial testing showed: anti‑nuclear antibodies, complement levels (C3 = 94 mg/dL and C4 = 20 mg/dL), and rheumatoid factor were negative; urine examination was normal and serum cryoglobulins were not raised. Viral markers (HIV, hepatitis B surface antigen, and anti‑hepatitis C) were negative. Serology for rickettsia and scrub typhus were also negative.

A 17-month-old boy was initially admitted in March 2022 for insidious onset of fever, ecchymosis of skin, anhelation, and pancytopenia. On admission, blood routine examination results were: white blood cell (WBC) 2.5 x 109/L, hemoglobin (Hb) 60 g/L, platelet (PLT) 45 x 109/L, and immature granulocytes found in peripheral blood smears. Bone marrow studies established a diagnosis of B‑cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (B‑ALL), and the patient received induction chemotherapy with achievement of complete remission. During consolidation therapy, the child was hospitalized again in October 2022 for a repeated fever of 13 days and coagulopathy after the second cycle of consolidation chemotherapy. Color Doppler ultrasonic examination showed swollen liver and spleen. The treating team considered chemotherapy-related bone marrow suppression, infection, and coagulation dysfunction, and started empiric antimicrobial therapy with vancomycin, imipenem, and voriconazole; fresh frozen plasma, fibrinogen, and prothrombin complex were given to improve coagulation. Seven days after therapy the patient remained febrile (38.4–39.4 C) and continued to have hepatosplenomegaly; CRP and PCT levels were 125.5 mg/L and 3.99 mg/L, respectively. No microorganisms were detected by blood culture. Metagenomic next‑generation sequencing (mNGS) was then performed on peripheral blood.

A 22‑month‑old girl presented with 8 days of fever to 40°C and mild cough. Past history: failure to thrive; normal neurologic development. She was the first child of a non‑consanguineous couple; no family history of albinism; normal hair and skin. On exam she was stunted, pale, had non‑tender hepatomegaly 5–6 cm and splenomegaly palpable 4 cm below the left costal margin. Petechial rash developed on the chest and legs as she worsened. Initial laboratory results: WBC 5100/mm3 (ANC 1200/mm3), Hb 9.1 g/dl, platelets 47,000/mm3; mild transaminase elevation; hypoalbuminemia. Ferritin 1,134 ng/ml; soluble IL‑2 receptor (sCD25) 3,183 U/ml. Blood cultures were negative. Serum immunoglobulins and lymphocyte subsets were reported as normal. Infectious testing: EBV serology positive for IgM and IgG anti‑VCA with negative IgG anti‑EBNA; EBV viral load 637 copies/ml. Leishmania testing was discordant: immunochromatography and indirect immunofluorescence were negative, serum ELISA was slightly positive, and leishmanial antigen in urine was negative. Bone‑marrow aspiration revealed hemophagocytosis. Over the next day she clinically worsened with progressive splenomegaly and cytopenias (WBC 4,800/mm3 with ANC 800/mm3, Hb 6.8 g/dl, platelets 27,000/mm3), triglycerides 686 mg/dl, ferritin 3,849 ng/ml, and sCD25 3,596 U/ml. Clotting tests were normal and perforin expression by flow cytometry was reported as normal.

Two years later he returned with a different cutaneous eruption that had appeared over the previous three months and had been preceded by intense itching. On exam he had multiple, nonpitting, closed papules on his face, nose, hands and legs. A skin smear again showed intramacrophage amastigotes with a parasite load graded +6, and culture grew promastigotes.

A 30-year-old woman from an area endemic for tegumentary leishmaniasis presented with a single skin complaint. She reported a small papular lesion on her right leg that had developed over 7–10 days. At age 10 she had had an ulcer on the left thigh that healed spontaneously and left a well-defined atrophic scar. On examination there was a depressed papular lesion on the right leg measuring 8 × 7 mm; there was a 30 × 20 mm atrophic scar on the left thigh and no lymphadenopathy. Because early lesions of the locally prevalent Leishmania species may be papular and nonulcerated, a Leishmania skin test (LST) was performed on the left forearm. After 48 hours the intradermal reaction was strongly positive, with an induration measuring 38 × 32 mm. Eight days after the skin test the original papular lesion on the right leg had resolved, and a new round cutaneous ulcer with raised borders measuring 26 × 24 mm was present at the site of the LST. A culture of aspirated material from the forearm lesion was negative for Leishmania.

A 35-year-old man from Russia presented to dermatology with two ulcerative skin lesions described as semi-dry with active borders: one in the lower left pre-atrial region and the other on the dorsal region of the left forearm. He reported travel to multiple countries between May and June 2019, including Middle Eastern countries (Israel, Turkey), the Balkan region (Armenia, Georgia), and Russia. In August 2019 he noted red, indurated papules and sought care in late August in San Cristobal de las Casas, Chiapas, Mexico. Cryotherapy with liquid nitrogen was applied initially with temporary reduction, followed by renewed flare-up of the lesion edges. At the Tropical Medicine Center he was clinically diagnosed as having localized cutaneous leishmaniasis (LCL). For confirmation, Giemsa-stained smears of the lesion and ELISA tests for L. braziliensis, L. infantum/chagasi, L. major and L. mexicana were performed. The Giemsa-stained smears showed abundant amastigotes within macrophages. The ELISA of the patient's serum revealed some degree of cross reactivity between four Leishmania species, with higher antibody levels recorded for L. major and L. mexicana antigens.

A 61-year-old immunocompetent Italian man, born and residing in Abruzzo, presented because of the persistence of multiple ulcerative nodules on the skin of his right cheek; the largest nodule measured 2 cm in maximum diameter and was partially covered by scaly scabs. A complete blood picture was normal. The patient reported no travel history and had received several topical treatments (antibiotics, antimycotics, steroids), which had failed. After cleaning off the excess blood, cytology smears were performed by sampling cells from the ulcer with a sterile lancet and by smearing the sample directly onto glass slides.

A 29-year-old man from Cutris de San Carlos (Alajuela province), in northern Costa Rica, presented with a single skin lesion on the right side of the neck. The lesion was a 5-cm, 3-month–old, deep ulcer with pruritic and sanguine-purulent tissue. A visibly swollen lymph node was present below the right ear, just above the ulcer. No other symptoms were reported. At the Area de Salud de Santa Rosa de Pocosol the diagnosis was confirmed locally through light microscopy of a direct smear, and the stained slide, along with culture media seeded with lesion aspirate, were sent to the national reference laboratory (Inciensa) for confirmation and species characterization.

A 43-year-old male laborer with known HIV infection for 2 years (on antiretroviral therapy) and on anti-tubercular treatment for 9 months presented with a 7-month history of asymptomatic skin lesions all over his body. Lesions first appeared on the arm and progressively spread to involve the face, legs, and trunk. On examination there were multiple bilateral asymmetrical diffuse papulonodular, non‑itchy skin lesions measuring 2–25 mm on the face, trunk, and extremities. There were no signs of ulceration or scarring. There was no lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly. A photograph showed multiple papulonodular lesions of varying size over the elbow. Laboratory tests showed anemia (hemoglobin 9.1 g/dL); liver and renal function tests and lipid profile were within normal limits. Ultrasonography of the abdomen was normal. CD4 count was 50 cells/µL and HIV viral load was 1750 copies/mL. There was no history of travel to known endemic areas for leishmaniasis.

A 52-year-old woman presented with a single lesion on the tip of her nose that had existed for 14 months. It began as a papule and was slowly increasing in size, enlarging to a plaque. A smear of the lesion performed about 1 year earlier was positive, "showing leishmania bodies." All five members of her family had a history of proven leishmaniasis. Her past medical history was notable for renal failure diagnosed 11 years earlier; she "received a renal transplant 4 years after the diagnosis of renal failure." She also had hypertension and hyperlipidemia and was taking oral mycophenolate mofetil (2 g daily) and cyclosporine (100 mg daily). Skin examination showed skin type IV, "No actinic keratosis was present," and a 3x3 cm indurated ulcer with elevated borders was present on the tip of her nose. The therapeutic plan was intralesional glucantime injections (approximately 1 ml of 1.5 g vial per week). "After completing a therapeutic course of 20 sessions receiving intralesional glucantime injections, she was considered as glucantime therapy resistant."

A 9-year-old boy presented with multiple papular lesions on the left cheek that had been present for three months and had gradually enlarged. His medical history was notable for an episode of cutaneous leishmaniasis located on the nose two years earlier, which had completely regressed after treatment with intralesional meglumine antimonate. Dermatologic examination showed multiple, coalescing, rough, slightly elevated, yellowish-brown papular lesions 3–6 mm in diameter on the left cheek. He also had a large atrophic scar on the nose. Nothing of interest was noted in his family history or his laboratory tests.

A 37-year-old man from Georgia presented in France in October 2012. He had HIV infection since 2006 that had been treated inconsistently with HAART. Other medical history included adrenal insufficiency, cirrhosis due to chronic hepatitis C virus infection, and treatment-controlled tuberculosis. Visceral leishmaniasis had been diagnosed in 2010 and treated in Georgia with meglumine antimoniate and liposomal amphotericin B (doses and schedules unknown). In November 2012 he had hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathies, infiltrated cutaneous lesions, and anemia. Laboratory testing showed a CD4 lymphocyte count of 133/mm3, plasma HIV viral load <50 copies/mL, and parasitemia of 6 Leishmania/ml. He received a course of liposomal amphotericin B followed by maintenance therapy for 5 months. In May 2013 he developed weight loss with persistent hepatosplenomegaly and anemia. CD4 count was 177/mm3, viral load <40 copies/mL, and parasitemia was 12 Leishmania/ml. Liposomal amphotericin B treatment was intensified, but renal insufficiency and acute thrombocytopenia occurred. In June 2013 the splenomegaly and parasitemia remained unchanged.

A 59‑year‑old man, mixed ethnicity, unemployed, previously healthy, reported that an erythematous‑crusty lesion appeared in the region of the mental protuberance and over two months evolved to involve other parts of the body, including the frontal and occipital regions, nasal septum, ears, hands, and lower limbs. Oral examination showed scattered ulcers on the face, lower labial mucosa, and on the left lip commissure, a pseudomembrane on the marginal gingiva, and an exophytic nodule in the left labial mucosa. The patient had a positive Montenegro intradermal test and was admitted to the University Hospital in December 2018. After admission, clinicians noted enlarged lymph nodes of hard consistency in the left inguinal region and an extensive irregular melanocytic lesion in the left plantar region presenting an area of hyperkeratosis with a grey‑bluish center; the plantar lesion was biopsied for further evaluation. A PCR analysis had been performed in an external laboratory.

retrieval_query_text: An 81-year-old man had intentional inoculation with live Leishmania (leishmanization) at age 29 before travel to an endemic region. A typical lesion appeared at the inoculation site and healed to a scar approximately 2.5 cm in diameter after seven months. There were no local activities in the scar for about 15 years. Later, small recurrent ulcerations appeared in the leishmanial scar; these lesions were painless, self-curing with spontaneous epithelialization, and recurred multiple times, with ulceration periods progressively lengthening and erosion-free intervals shortening. He underwent surgery for a peptic ulcer and for a papillary thyroid carcinoma (the latter followed by X‑ray therapy), and received prostate brachytherapy in 2012. For the last four years he has had a permanently persistent indurated skin ulcer with elevated borders, varying in size from 2 to 3 cm; there were no surrounding inflammations, regional lymphadenopathies, or general symptoms. The use of antibiotics and antiseptics was ineffective. BCC was suspected and a standard wide surgical full-thickness excision within healthy tissue limits was performed in 2019; the patient recovered completely.

He is able to ambulate independently in the community and perform self-care and activities of daily living. A 24-year-old male presents with a 12-week non-healing ulcer on his left leg. He recently returned from a year-long trip to Senegal, where he worked on construction near stagnant water. The ulcer is necrotizing with central crusting and an erythematous border.

A male born June 6, 1960, from Acaua municipality, Piaui State, married, was diagnosed with kala-azar in January 2014 and had a negative serology to HIV. Since then he had recurrent pancytopenia, persistent splenomegaly and a history of five previous hospitalizations at the IDTNP for kala-azar treatment. Prior anti-leishmanial therapies included pentavalent antimony (glucantime, 20 mg of Sb + 5 kg/d for 30 d at the first hospitalization) and liposomal amphotericin B (for 14 d at a dose of 3 mg/kg/d, given during three hospitalizations), without durable clinical resolution. On admission in July 2015 he had a palpable spleen 12 cm below the left costal margin. Abdominal ultrasound showed an enlarged spleen extending to the left iliac fossa. Preoperative complete blood count: hemoglobin 8.7 g/dL, hematocrit 27.9%, leukocytes 1,090/microL, and platelets 155,000/microL.

Other medical history included adrenal insufficiency, cirrhosis due to chronic hepatitis C virus infection, and treatment-controlled tuberculosis. Visceral leishmaniasis had been diagnosed in 2010 and treated in Georgia with meglumine antimoniate and liposomal amphotericin B (doses and schedules unknown). In June 2013 the splenomegaly and parasitemia remained unchanged.

A 24-year-old man from Tancredo Neves, State of Bahia, Brazil, was admitted in January 2012 with diffuse bullous lesions on the body, osteoarthritis of the distal interphalangeal joints and proteinuria of 399 mg/day. He was diagnosed with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and treated with mycophenolate mofetil (MMF), with the dose increased to 1 g per day intravenously. Two years after the SLE diagnosis (2014) he was hospitalized again, presenting with ulcerated, painless skin lesions on the face, upper lip, scalp, neck, and on the upper and lower limbs. Oral examination showed crusty upper lip lesions, poor oral health status, and amelogenesis imperfecta. He developed secondary infection with fever and was started on cephalexin (1 g/day) and maintained on prednisone 5 mg/day intravenously. On the third day of this hospitalization, biopsies were performed on the left nasal mucosa and on lesions of the right lower limb.

A 41-year-old Caucasian man was admitted during treatment with intravenous liposomal amphotericin B for laryngeal and facial mucocutaneous leishmaniasis because of marked elevation of creatine kinase (CK) (more than 10× upper limit of normal during admission; pretreatment CK up to ~2× ULN previously) and rising serum creatinine. Past medical history was notable for visceral leishmaniasis at age 13, recurrent otitis and an episode of bronchopneumonia in childhood, long-standing unexplained elevated CK attributed in the past to occupation and boxing, and chronic periorbital/facial swelling first noted in 2013. In January 2019 he developed hoarseness and dysphonia; laryngoscopy and biopsy were positive for Leishmania spp., and earlier periocular skin samples (2015) were retrospectively PCR-positive for Leishmania spp. He reported no travel outside Europe. There was a family history notable for a brother who died at age 20 from an unspecified lymphoproliferative disease and a sister with chronic myalgias. On examination he was in good general condition with bilateral orbital swelling. Peripheral blood count was unremarkable. B-cell immunophenotyping disclosed a defect in the memory compartment with markedly low switched-memory B cells. There was no history of liver or biliary tract disease or neutropenia. The patient met criteria for common-variable immunodeficiency, but because of the opportunistic, persistent Leishmania infection further genetic studies were pursued.

A 24-year-old Cuban immigrant presented with worsening nonhealing lower-extremity ulcers despite oral antibiotic therapy and wound care. The lesions gradually grew with subsequent ulceration over the course of 1 to 2 months. He recently arrived in the United States seeking asylum and first noticed the lesions while traveling in the jungle between Panama and Colombia (Darien Gap region). On examination, there was an ulcerative lesion measuring 4 cm on the dorsum of the right foot and a second 3.5 cm ulcer on the lower anterior shin. There was no evidence of mucosal or visceral involvement on initial physical exam. Photographs show ulcerative lesions on the right foot and left shin. As part of the clinical workup to rule out malaria, a rapid malaria antigen test for Plasmodium falciparum was obtained and reported positive.

A 60‑year‑old Austrian man presented in September 2016 with a three‑week history of fever of unknown origin, fatigue, and unintentional weight loss of 6 kg. Initial physical examination was inconspicuous. His medical history was notable for adequately treated diabetes mellitus type 2 and hypothyroidism. Travel history included a two‑week trip to the south of Crete in September 2015 and a two‑week trip the south of Spain in May 2016. Laboratory tests showed markedly elevated C‑reactive protein (CRP 94.2–188.9 mg/L), slight hypochromic normocytic anemia without signs of hemolysis (hemoglobin 12.5 g/dL), mild thrombocytopenia (127,000/µL), and a discreetly elevated gamma‑glutamyltransferase (GGT). The soluble interleukin‑2 receptor (IL‑2R) was elevated to 5156.1 pg/mL. Chest x‑ray, urine analysis, abdominal sonography, transthoracic and transesophageal echocardiography revealed no focus of infection but did show splenomegaly (7.2 × 16.4 cm). Empiric antibiotic therapy (initially ampicillin/sulbactam, later piperacillin/tazobactam plus vancomycin) did not lead to improvement. Over the next three weeks the patient’s discrete bicytopenia progressed to severe pancytopenia requiring blood transfusions. Lactate dehydrogenase rose to 1107 U/L, liver enzymes including GGT, alkaline phosphatase and AST increased, and fever persisted up to 40°C. Positron emission tomography–computed tomography showed tracer enhancement in the central and peripheral bone marrow.

A male born June 26, 1986, was seen at a tropical diseases referral center. Between 2009 and 2011 he was hospitalized seven times with a consistent diagnosis of kala-azar. He received multiple recommended treatments during these hospitalizations, including pentavalent antimony (glucantime, 20 mg of Sb + 5 kg/d for 30 d in the first hospitalization), liposomal amphotericin B (for 14 d at 3 mg/kg/d in three subsequent hospitalizations), and pentamidine in the last hospitalization before surgery (4 mg/kg/d every other day, total 15 doses), with only transient symptomatic improvement followed by recurrence. He had a negative HIV serological test. During two hospitalizations he presented with anemia and was transfused twice with packed red blood cells. After all possibilities of medical treatment were exhausted and the patient maintained a pancytopenia profile on blood counts attributed to hypersplenism, splenectomy was recommended. In January 2012 he was hospitalized for the planned surgical procedure. His clinical examination revealed mucocutaneous pallor (2+/4+), fever (38.5 C), dehydration (2+/4+), a distended abdomen with mild pain on deep palpation, and splenomegaly 8 cm below the left costal margin. Laboratory testing showed anemia, leukopenia, hypergammaglobulinemia, and elevated ESR and CRP.

A 75-year-old man from Algeria with long-standing HIV infection presented with progressive systemic symptoms and known prior visceral leishmaniasis. Medical history: HIV since 2001 treated previously with nevirapine and lamivudine/zidovudine and, from 2013, with darunavir, ritonavir, raltegravir and emtricitabine; prior opportunistic infections and comorbidities included cerebral toxoplasmosis, chronic hepatitis B, gastrointestinal CMV infection, and anal squamous cell carcinoma. Visceral leishmaniasis (VL) was first diagnosed in 2001 and treated with liposomal amphotericin B (L‑AmB) 5 mg/kg/day for 15 days with partial improvement; a maintenance regimen of L‑AmB 3 mg/kg weekly was planned but was irregularly administered. Recurrence was reported in March 2011 and the infecting species was identified as Leishmania infantum. At that time the CD4 lymphocyte count was 33/mm3 and HIV viral load was 75,000 copies/mL. The patient received additional courses of L‑AmB including a cumulative 40 mg/kg followed by 3 mg/kg every 15 days, later infusions at 3‑week intervals, and in 2013 a final course totaling 50 mg/kg. Despite this most recent complete course of L‑AmB, symptoms worsened with weight loss and fatigue; imaging showed clinical splenomegaly with a maximal diameter of 20 cm on CT. Quantitative parasitemia remained positive and essentially unchanged, from 126 Leishmania/ml before treatment to 118 Leishmania/ml three weeks after completion of the course.
